title: ‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’ | David Bowie | The Guardian
description: Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says
Content: ‘The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027’ … David Bowie performing on the 1978 Isolar II tour.Photograph: Masayoshi Sukita/David Bowie ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027’ … David Bowie performing on the 1978 Isolar II tour.Photograph: Masayoshi Sukita/David Bowie ArchiveDavid BowieInterview‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’Dave SimpsonMoonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett MorgenTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2017, when Brett Morgen began work on his acclaimed 2022 David Bowie documentary,Moonage Daydream, he was given complete access to the late star’s entire, cavernous archive. “My eyes were immediately drawn to a stack of gleaming 35mm cans with the word ‘Stage’ written on them,” he remembers.At first, the director – whose work also includesKurt Cobain: Montage of Heckand the Rolling Stones documentary Crossfire Hurricane – assumed the cans might contain some sort of footage shot around Bowie’s 1978 live album, Stage, recorded in mostly in Philadelphia. However, he soon realised they actually contained the holy grail of Bowie artefacts: footage of the legendary Earl’s Court shows later that year, which had remained unseen for almost 50 years. “Making Moonage Daydream, I had access to every filmed performance in existence of David Bowie,” he says, “but when I saw this one I knew this was without question the greatest filmed performance of his career.”In 1978, Bowie had commissioned Just a Gigolo director David Hemmings to film two of the three sold-out summer shows at the venue – where the star was touring Low and “Heroes” – with a view to showing the film in theatres in lieu of a physical tour (he wouldn’t take the road again until 1983). However, the singer subsequently started making the Lodger album, moved to Switzerland, was reportedly unhappy with the film’s editing and the entire project was subsequently left behind. “He was moving on to other things at the speed of light,” Morgen explains. “So at that point I think the idea of looking backwards was distasteful to him.”The trailer for David Bowie: Stage – videoBefore his death in 2016, though, Bowie had floated the idea of finally putting it out. In the new year it will debut in arenas – not cinemas – almost half a century after it was made. Morgen and team spent nearly 10 years readying it for 2027 as a multimedia experience. “It became something of an obsession,” he admits. “We spent over 1,000 hours colour-grading the footage, which I believe is some sort of record, but we really wanted it to look and feel like something you would experience today.”It helped that the footage had been beautifully shot and perfectly preserved in Bowie’s storage unit, with excellent sound recorded by Bowie’s producer, Tony Visconti. Missing from Morgen’s film will be the extraneous stuff Hemmings added to the concerts. “I found a lot of footage of a young boy playing David that I was a bit confused by,” the director grins. “That’s not in the film.” Instead, it focuses on Bowie – in wonderfully billowing trousers and makeup – at the peak of his performance powers. “He looks amazing,” Morgen smiles. “I’ve looked at close-ups and I think: how on earth is this man not sweating?”By the time the Isolar II tour reached Earl’s Court, Bowie and band were at the pinnacle of their game, signposting the future. “To have an electric violin, a piano and a synth player in a rock show in 1978 was extraordinary,” says Morgen, whose film combines songs from both nights because “It was very improvisational. Different arrangements two nights running. You can feel the danger and excitement that it could have gone off the rails at any moment and David was very charged by that.“The audacity of starting the show with Warszawa, perhaps the lowest-energy first song of any rock concert ever – but that’s Bowie. By the end of the first set he’s reeled them in and by the end of the second set the place is just insane. The performance of Station to Station is incredible.”View image in fullscreenBowie in a still from Brett Morgen’s remastered Stage.Photograph: PRDuring the second show, on 1 July, Bowie quips, “OK, this will be interesting”, and performs Sound and Vision for the first time ever. “And he’s cracking up throughout the song because I think the electric violin was trying to do the horn section, which David thought was kind of amusing. It’s a great moment. Then the camera stays with David when he goes off to the sides, having a glass of beer or smoking a cigarette, and he’s so engaged, dancing and smiling. It’s very joyous. I think this was the first time he’d performed without a mask, or ‘character’, so to speak.”Morgen isn’t giving everything away but promises “surprises” as well as “a new medium of entertainment”.“It’s not a movie that’s being shown in arenas,” he insists. “There’s multiple screens, a fully integrated lighting package, a 7.1 [surround sound] sound mix. The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027. The audience is invited to gaze where they want to gaze: choose your own adventure. Eleven years after his passing, it makes perfect sense that Bowie will be trailblazing again.”Stage premieres at theBerlin film festival, Germany, in February 2027, before touring.Explore more on these topicsDavid BowieDocumentary filmsPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why won’t MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope | Faiza Shaheen | The Guardian
description: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue, says Faiza Shaheen, executive director of Tax Justice UK
Author: Faiza Shaheen
Headline: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue, says Faiza Shaheen, executive director of Tax Justice UK
Content: March in central London on 7 June 2025.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarch in central London on 7 June 2025.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionBudget 2026Why won’t MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hopeFaiza ShaheenEven most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issueTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTShareIn John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax?Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m?Off the table. Eventhe briefed increasein the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it wasuntil the Conservativescut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.Pollafterpollshows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – includingthree in five Reform-leaningvoters. We know that wealth inequality – with therichest 50 families in the UKpossessing more wealth than half of the UK population – isweakening our economy,eroding our social fabricandundermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source.We interviewed30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully trickingordinary homeownersinto thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actuallyleft a decade ago– and quote “millionaire flight” figures froma seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUltimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UKExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionBudgetTax and spendingThe super-richAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyTaxcommentShareReuse this content

title: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween | Games | The Guardian
description: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Content: Night moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionView image in fullscreenNight moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionGamesEight great new indie horror games for HalloweenWhether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching seasonKeith StuartTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTis almost All Hallows’ Eve and naturally, the thoughts of all good video game players are turning to horror. 2026 has already been a bloody good year for the genre withResident Evil RequiemandSilent Hill: Townfallleading the rabble. But this autumn sees a festering surge of indie horror releases, featuring everything from cursed card games to Nazi-hunting penguins. Here are eight terrifying titles we think you should sample while jack-o-lanterns burn and spirits walk the moonlit streets.Allogloom (PC)View image in fullscreenShady story … Allogloom.Photograph: Galactic GhostlyMixing dark fairytales with classic point-and-click adventure gameplay, Allogloom follows a young girl who must leave her isolated village alone to hunt for her lost mother. The game’s eerie picture book aesthetic and doll-like characters have the feel of a 1970s Czech animation, making for a surreal and disquieting experience.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival (PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox)View image in fullscreenComing for more … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThis latest extension of Barker’s seminal horror novella The Hellbound Heart received mixed reviews, but then so did the Hellraiser films, and they were largely awesome. You play as Aidan, looking to rescue his girlfriend from the nightmarish realm of the Cenobites and their S&M obsessed followers. Gory, kinky and ridiculous it is quite literally a hell of a ride.Grease Trap 99 (PC)View image in fullscreenFrying to fright … Grease Trap 99.Photograph: James MuirheadYou’re working in a quiet Scottish takeaway, frying and serving fish, chips and pizza, when your boss asks you to start serving a “special” dish. But what is it, and what’s that strange gurgling noise coming from the cellar? Created by lone developer James Muirhead with dialogue in Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig), this is more of a short interactive horror movie than a game, but its glitch-ridden, low-poly visuals and dark humour keep you serving until the gruesome finale.Hunter’s Moon (PS5)View image in fullscreenDark tale … Hunter’s Moon.Photograph: Twin SwansBased on the real-life witch-hunts of the 17th century, this atmospheric immersive adventure has you playing as a young woman accused of devilry and now running for her life through woods, rivers and abandoned mines as her hunters pursue. Poetic and strangely beguiling, fans of the classic folk horror movie Witchfinder General, will feel oddly at home.The Killing Stone (PC, PS5, Xbox)View image in fullscreenFeast of occult delights … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionFans of deck-building card battlers are spoiled for choice these days, but The Killing Stone is the perfect choice forHalloween. Set in a remote 17th-century mansion, you must play an ancient card game against the devil to win back the soul of your beloved mistress. The set-up is familiar but there are lovely occult touches, and you get to explore the gloomy house in first-person between bouts, leaning its dark lore. An engrossing fireside treat.Penguin Colony (PC)View image in fullscreenShivers … Penguin Colony.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerA Nazi base in the desolate Antarctic is beset by Lovecraftian entities, driving its inhabitants to madness. But in a neat twist, you play as a penguin observing the chaos and exploring the wilderness, discovering weird obelisks and winding labyrinths as the cosmic horrors threaten your colony.Read our review.Silver Pines (PC, PS5, Xbox, Switch 2)View image in fullscreenCurious case … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17On the trail of a missing singer, troubled private investigator Red Walker finds himself in an abandoned town, but quickly discovers he is far from alone. Influenced by Twin Peaks, Silent Hill and Alan Wake, this haunting 2D adventure is rich in atmosphere and crammed with intriguing puzzles.Read our review.Tenebris Somnia(Switch,PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox)View image in fullscreenUnrest room … Tenebris Somnia.Photograph: New Blood InteractiveWhen a young actor visits her estranged boyfriend, she discovers that his apartment has been trashed and he’s nowhere to be seen. Where is he and what are those weird symbols daubed on the wall? Heavily inspired by early 90s point-and-click adventures as well as interactive movie games such as Night Trap, Tenebris Somnia mixes beautiful pixelated visuals and FMV sequences to eerie effect.Explore more on these topicsGamesXboxPCPlayStationPlayStation 5Nintendo Switch 2HalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’ | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferred
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferred
Content: John Healey prepares for the budget in the kitchen of his Downing Street flat.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryView image in fullscreenJohn Healey prepares for the budget in the kitchen of his Downing Street flat.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryBudget 2026Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferredPippa CrerarandHeather StewartTue 27 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.The budget, which will be interpreted as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, is nevertheless expected to be a relatively modest affair as Healey grapples with stark fiscal realities, putting off important decisions on tax and spending until next year.“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellorRead moreHealey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.The chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran conflict, but changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily.In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families before a steep rise in typical energy bills in January; while pledging energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was keen to see the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – abolished. The move would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, and the cost would be picked up by those who use more.Industry experts fear further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture is likely to bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, in a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected toend the carers’ allowance cliff edge, which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence a week. Healey is also expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.But while he is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – Healey is expected to wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.Consumer confidencehas fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distresshas hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for younger people under the age of 21 after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs but prompting accusations that Labour had broken a manifesto pledge.He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for their retirement by shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost to middle-earners.You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the booksRead moreTo help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised toraise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyUK cost of living crisisEnergy billsBudgetTax and spendingHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Emissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaigners
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Emissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaigners
Content: Protesters against the Rosebank oilfield in Edinburgh this month.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenProtesters against the Rosebank oilfield in Edinburgh this month.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianGreenhouse gas emissionsRosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insidersEmissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaignersKiran StaceyandPippa CrerarTue 27 Oct 2026 15.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, wasleaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues,including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.Map of North Sea oil and gasfieldsA decision to approve the oilfield would be met withdismay from climate campaignersand some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earthwrote to the prime ministerurging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”Rosebank row: will Labour block the oilfield? – podcastRead moreGreg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong toapprove the Jackdaw gasfield last weekand would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.Ajudge ruled in 2024that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approvalRead moreFahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated inScotlandwith the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.View image in fullscreenFahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and Healey, the chancellor, are understood to be in disagreement over the North Sea oilfield.Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing StreetFahnbullehtold the Guardianlast week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment.In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.A spokesperson for the Department forEnergySecurity and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsMiatta FahnbullehScotlandOil and gas companiesOil (Business)Oil (Environment)CommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban | Vaping | The Guardian
description: Three-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research finds
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Three-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research finds
Content: It is thought to have been the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.Photograph: Tim Parker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is thought to have been the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.Photograph: Tim Parker/Getty ImagesVapingAI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes banThree-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research findsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorTue 27 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.The Department ofHealthand Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”More than 6m vapes and pods discarded weekly in UK despite single-use ban, study findsRead moreAzzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”Explore more on these topicsVapingHealth policyAI (artificial intelligence)HealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rape | UK news | The Guardian
description: Mark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assault
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Mark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assault
Content: Mark Tyrell, pictured in 2024, was based in the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, where the convicted rapists Wayne Couzens and David Carrick both worked.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenMark Tyrell, pictured in 2024, was based in the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, where the convicted rapists Wayne Couzens and David Carrick both worked.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.UK newsFormer Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rapeMark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assaultNadeem BadshahTue 27 Oct 2026 16.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday.Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday.Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBrazilFlávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports sayFar-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to LulaTiago Rogeroin Brasília andTom Phillipsin São PauloTue 27 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right senatorFlávio Bolsonarohas reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”.A report by the news websiteMetrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like.Brazilis their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fledBrazilafter losing on Sunday.A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in BrazilRead moreBolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60 million votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fantastic Fleetwood seal shootout success in Carabao Cup shock against Arsenal | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty in Fleetwood’s 5-3 shootout win against 10-man Arsenal, after the Carabao Cup fourth round tie finished 1-1
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty in Fleetwood’s 5-3 shootout win against 10-man Arsenal, after the Carabao Cup fourth round tie finished 1-1
Content: Rhys Bennett leads the celebrations after Fleetwood’s dramatic shootout win.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersView image in fullscreenRhys Bennett leads the celebrations after Fleetwood’s dramatic shootout win.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersCarabao CupFantastic Fleetwood seal shootout success in Carabao Cup shock against ArsenalWill Unwinat Highbury StadiumTue 27 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is more than 20 years since Arsenal played at Highbury but their trip to League Two Fleetwood – and a stadium of the same name – did not bring back fond memories as they were dumped out of theCarabao Cupon penalties. It was the team with red shirts and white sleeves that triumphed, but on this occasion it caused one of the greatest upsets in English football history.Aaron Loupalo-Bi and Viktor Gyökeres exchanged goals in normal time butArsenalwere unable to find a winner, despite being the dominant force, as Fleetwood battled to the end. The home manager, Matt Lawlor, was almost in tears, unable to cope after the tension was released when Conor Haughey smashed the ball into the top corner to settle the shootout.Fleetwood Town stun Arsenal on penalties: Carabao Cup fourth round – liveRead moreThat came after Jay Lynch had saved from Bruno Guimarães, a former warehouse worker stopping the Brazilian international. It is the storylines everyone wants but so rarely gets in the sanitised modern football world.Fleetwood were aiming to earn £400,000 from the night but got something priceless in the end. Everyone in attendance will never forget they saw the fourth-tier side knock out thePremier League champions. Of course they had to ride their luck and were helped by Max Dowman’s debatable sending off but football is rarely about logic, it is one of emotion. This is once in a lifetime for the Cod Army, for anyone at their level, and they enjoyed it.A year ago Lawlor was not even a football manager, he never played professionally and started his coaching career with the Manchester United Foundation. Lynch had spent much of his early career in non-league, only dreaming of playing a team who narrowlylost the Champions League finalin the spring.Everyone was expecting a routine victory, even with Mikel Arteta giving youngsters the chance to impress. If Arteta wanted to test his youngsters then Marli Salmon’s naivety was shown up by Loupalo-Bi, on loan from Fulham.He has been learning his trade in the fourth tier this season and put into practice the skill of using his body against a defender, spinning and holding off the 17-year-old before slotting under Illan Meslier to bring lift-off for the second time of the night.View image in fullscreenAaron Loupalo-Bi fires Fleetwood into a first-half lead.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersBy that point the game had already had a six-minute delay due to a drone being flown above the pitch. The referee Michael Salisbury had to take the players to the sidelines while the police searched for the culprit outside the ground. It was an unordinary start to what became an extraordinary night on the Fylde Coast. It had started with a plethora of pyrotechnics that created a red haze across the pitch and, frankly, it never dissipated, literally or metaphorically.The first half was one of toil for Arsenal, unable to create anything meaningful, constantly being thwarted by the disciplined defence, well organised by Lawlor and his staff. The Gunners were pedestrian against a team happy to watch them go through the motions. Kai Havertz missed the best chance to equalise before the break but his header was wayward, summing up a difficult match for him.View image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães’ penalty is saved by the Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAAfter the break it was different as Martin Ødegaard came on to become the quarterback for Arsenal, creating the rhythm they had sorely lacked. He brought cohesion and intensity, getting them back into the game.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was Gyökeres who bundled home the equaliser and few would have doubted Arsenal going on to win the match but Fleetwood held firm.The home side had been direct from the start, accepting their limitations and knowing the conditions would help them. Swirling wind helped hold the ball up in the sky and confused defenders not used to the gales by the sea.Fleetwood’s robust play irritated Arsenal and Dowman was wound up, getting himself sent off for reacting to enforcer-in-chief Harrison Neal. He was the second Gunners teenager to learn a valuable lesson of life outside the top flight after Salmon was exposed for the goal.It may have been harsh but it was needlessly petulant from Dowman on an already challenging night for his side. Mikel Arteta had a word with him on the way off. What did Arteta say? “Something that we discussed already before the match.”Arsenal had two late chances through Ben White and Gyökeres to settle it before the need for spot-kicks, but Lynch produced two fantastic saves as the clock went past 90 minutes to ensure it went to a fittingly dramatic finale, where he could be the hero again on a great night for football and the town of Fleetwood.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupFleetwood TownArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor  | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: From tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for him
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: From tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for him
Content: The chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to fiscal rules.Composite: PA/EPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to fiscal rules.Composite: PA/EPA/ShutterstockBudget 2026Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellorFrom tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for himYou be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the booksRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East.Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules.Healey will also flesh out Andy Burnham’s pledge to deliver “good growth in every postcode”, with measures to hand local leaders more money and power.Here are six charts that will underpin the chancellor’s decisions.Sticking to the fiscal rulesFscal headroom chartAt the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament.However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East causes a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.The Resolution Foundation estimates headroom has been halved to about £12bn. Much will depend on the judgment of theOffice for Budget Responsibility(OBR), the independent Treasury watchdog, which will take into account the hit from rising debt costs, but also other positive and negative developments for the public finances – including inflation, pay growth, employment and productivity.Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors will be looking for him to retain some headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.‘Breathing space’ measuresEnergy price cap chartThe chancellor has pledged “breathing space” measures for households and businesses grappling with the cost of living crisis, as the energy price shock fuelled by the Iran conflict hits consumers.Petrol and diesel priceshave surged close to record highs and energy bills are forecast to increase to£2,000 a year from Januaryfor the typical household. Since 2021, consumers have paid almost£14,000 on average in additional costsfor mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.Healey is thought to have earmarked more than£1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which will go on increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. He has also vowed to help businesses, and has been urged to extend a cut infuel duty.Alongside energy support, Andy Burnham has already promisedLabourwill cut living costs through other measures – including a new mortgage scheme for first-time buyers, and a pledge to build more social homes.Rewiring the stateTax revenue chartBurnham has made “growth in every postcode” his top political slogan since becoming prime minister. With devolution likely to be a central theme of the budget, a raft of measures are expected to add some substance to the rhetoric.Central to the devolution package will be plans to allow local leaders in England to retain a share of income tax, alongside a new£1.5bn borrowing facility for directly elected mayors.Britain is the most centralised G7 country for tax and spending policy, and is among the most economically unequal, according to the Centre for Cities thinktank. The aim of redrawing the political map – including establishinga new hub for No 10 in the north, based in Manchester – is to increase regional economic growth, and with it the performance of the UK economy at large.Burnham has also signalled that a strengthened industrial strategy will be key to his agenda, as well as measures to support high streets and towns.Tackling the youth jobs crisisNeet interactiveThe prime minister has said Britain is facing an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” after a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million.Tackling the youth jobs crisis will be a key budget theme. Business leaders havepressed Healey for tax cutsand help with labour costs to encourage youth recruitment, while ministers have explored options for overhauling the benefits system and making changes to apprenticeships.Healey has indicated that welfare reform will be critical. There could though be costs attached – as any savings from changes to the system could be offset by higher spending on employment support. The government is handling the process carefully to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion faced by Keir Starmer, and is still awaiting recommendations from two key reviews – by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn and the Department for Work and Pensions minister Stephen Timms.The government is understood to favour handing local leaders more power and money to support young people as part of the solution. Analysis from the Youth Futures Foundation, a charity, shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is geographically uneven: rates are significantly higher in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford than in Bath, Harrogate or Guildford.Increasing defence spendingUK defence spending interactiveHaving resigned as Starmer’s defence secretary over funding, Healey is widely tipped to use his budget to find more cash for the military. Burnham has also spoken of the importance of the defence sector for his reindustrialisation plans.First, the chancellor will need to find an additional £1bn a year to fund Labour’sdefence investment plan. Announced by Starmer in his final weeks in office, that put defence spending on track to reach 2.7% of gross domestic product by 2029.However, Healey has expressed an ambition to spend 3% by 2030. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates an extra £11bn would be needed in that year. Longer term, the government is targeting spending of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. This is equivalent to a £25bn increase in today’s terms.Repairing the economic damage of BrexitNet migration chartBurnham reopened the debate over Brexit in his speech to Labour conference in Liverpool, arguing that leaving the EU had damaged the UK economy and failed to bring the benefits promised.This week’s budget is expected to underscore the economic hit, including from a drop in net migration.Net migration to the UK hasfallen sharply from a record peak of almost a millionin 2023. Earlier this year, the Office for National Statistics downgraded its estimate for the long-run figure to settle at about 230,000 annually, down from a previous assumption of 340,000.On average, immigrants are net contributors to the exchequer, and so how the OBR accounts for this drop in its forecasts will be critical. Should it adopt a similar approach to the ONS, the Resolution Foundation thinktank estimates this could lead to a drop in tax receipts of £4.7bn by 2029-30 relative to previous forecasts.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026Economic growth (GDP)Tax and spendingGovernment borrowingEconomicsInflationUK cost of living crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content
