title: ‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assault | Cynthia Erivo | The Guardian
description: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success
Content: Cynthia Erivo at the Toronto international film festival in September 2026.Photograph: Josh Telles/Deadline/Contour RAView image in fullscreenCynthia Erivo at the Toronto international film festival in September 2026.Photograph: Josh Telles/Deadline/Contour RACynthia ErivoInterview‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assaultLanre BakareIn Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric successTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCynthia Erivo is contemplating her favourite crisps, the ridged American brand Ruffles, as we sit talking in a quiet corner of a west London restaurant. Dressed all in black and sporting her signature elongated nails, she is known for her healthy lifestyle, but everyone, it seems, has their vices. “Ruffles are just perfect,” she says. “When you get a good batch, and the salt-to-potato ratio is perfect … it’s amazing.”Erivo has just touched down after singing in Phoenix, Arizona, the night before, and has been running me through the health routine that helps her maintain her frantic schedule. Before her concert, there was the Dior front row at Paris fashion week, and she has just been announced as a guest host on SNL UK. Erivo doesn’t drink alcohol (today she orders some peppermint tea); she’s vegan; she doesn’t eat airline food, only her own prepacked meals. She even has an infra-red sauna “to help me heal from the inside”. Earlier this year she ran the London Marathon before jumping on stage to perform Dracula, where she played all 23 parts; she had rehearsed her lines while going on gruelling marathon training runs. All that requires discipline – and snacks – to keep the show on the road.View image in fullscreenErivo in Prima Facie (2026).Photograph: Nicola DoveShe has flown in this morning to promote her new film, the legal drama Prima Facie, an adaptation of the one-woman Suzie Miller play about sexual assault, in which Jodie Comerwowed audiences in 2022. Erivo bristles when I ask if she was hesitant about picking up a role so associated with someone else. “I get asked that question a lot,” she says. The pair actually met at a fashion dinner and spoke about the role – “Not asking any tips or anything” – and Erivo insists she was always going to make Tessa her own. “I’m never worried about what someone else has done,” she says. “I try to be respectful.”Erivo plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual assault. Tessa knows how to dance around the courtroom – and the victim – raising inconsistencies that mean convicting a man “beyond reasonable doubt” becomes almost impossible. When Tessa is raped by a colleague, her world implodes and it’s made clear just how brutal the British justice system can be for women, who,according toRape Crisis, have a one in four chance of being sexually assaulted, while only 2.7% of reported rapes result in charges being brought.double quotation markI think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t beMiller, a former barrister herself,said the inspiration for the storycame from her realisation that: “It’s almost impossible to actually run a sexual assault case and win it.” Tessa, says Erivo, doesn’t see how hard it is for anyone to recall traumatic events in detail, or how lopsided the system is, until it’s swallowing her whole. “I don’t think she realises that until she’s on the other side. I think it’s only then she realises what she’s been asking other people to do – when it comes to recall – is actually impossible.”Is Erivo hopeful the film can have a lasting impact? “We have had judges see it, we’ve had lawyers see it, [but] one of the major issues is the way we view consent,” says Erivo. “I hope that as this film filters out, we start to have a conversation not just among us as people, but within law.”View image in fullscreenWith Daniel Ings in Prima Facie.Photograph: Nicola DoveThe film’s central struggle is twofold: the legal system victims have to navigate, and the bigger question of consent, which is something Erivo thinks is often far simpler than it seems. “I think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t be,” she says, leaning forward. “It’s very clear what consent is: if a person isn’t conscious, or conscious enough to say yes, they’re not saying yes. If a person doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes. If the body language doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes.”Tessa’s rise through the legal ranks as a working-class Black woman mirrors Erivo’s ascent through the West End, Broadway and Hollywood. After arriving at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada), Erivo had to traverse a strange world, deeply rooted in tradition and privilege that she wasn’t exposed to growing up in south London.When I ask Erivo what it was like navigating that space she gives a one-word answer: “Hard.” She held down three jobs, including working every imaginable role at the Stratford East theatre, while classmates with means simply had to turn up. “I was exhausted all the time,” she says. “We’re in the classes, and it’s a Monday; I’ve worked all day on a Sunday, and probably done a gig at night, and I’ve come in. I’m falling asleep in class, so people were like: ‘She doesn’t care.’”View image in fullscreenOn stage as Celie in The Color Purple at Menier Chocolate Factory, London, in 2013.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianErivo tells me the story about how she had to turn down a backing singer gig with Westlife that would have lasted two weeks and paid her £10,000 – enough for a couple of years’ tuition. “When I went to the registrar to say, ‘Hey, can I take these two weeks to go and do this? It will pay for my fees,’ they said, ‘No, you can’t. If you go, you leave. If you stay, you stay.’” Erivo says the incident showed how at Rada there could often be “a deep misunderstanding of what it is like to need money”, which is something she is trying to address in the role she has held since 2024 as vice-president of the institution.“I want it to be different,” she says. “Rada is not an easy place to go to school. It asks a lot of you. If you’re a kid who is just really talented, but you’ve not picked up a Shakespeare before, you now have to learn a new language. If you’ve never read a Greek before, now you have to understand what anything means with the Greeks. That’s a big shift from doing plays at school.”James Norton was in Erivo’s year at Rada and recently recalled how she would occasionally burst into song, something she had been doing since her school days in Clapham, where she’d perform Brandy and Monica’s The Boy Is Mine in the playground. “The room would go completely silent,” said Norton, which is no surprise because despite Erivo being little over 5ft tall, she possesses a gigantic voice. It’s a tool capable of the grandstanding volume needed for musical theatre, but also the subtler demands of R&B. In her forthcoming memoir, Erivo recalls being asked at Rada to sing the parts of a white student who was ill, but rather than being replaced was allowed to mime along. “The powers that be took my voice away and gave it to someone else,” is how she described it. In 2020Rada apologisedfor institutional racism, later publishing an anti-racism action plan andappointing David Harewood presidentalongside Erivo.View image in fullscreenIn Steve McQueen’s film adaptation of Widows (2018).Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyErivo set about reclaiming that voice in her post-Rada career, at first mostly on the stage, including a star-making Broadway turn in 2015 as Celie in The Color Purple. The New Yorker’s Hilton Als went to see the production not expecting much (he’d been disappointed by the film adaptation) but remembers Erivo’s Celie as being a revelation. “It was like listening to Judy Garland when she first started out,” he told me. “She keeps you marvelling at what is surely a God-given talent.” Erivo says that show was pivotal for her. “The Color Purple was one of those moments where I went from a jobbing actress and just pleased to be there to someone who was known for this particular piece. My life looked different after that.”Before Broadway she’d had fleeting TV roles in Michaela Coel’s Chewing Gum and in Mr Selfridge, but things shifted again in 2018 when Erivo starred in Steve McQueen’s take on the Lynda La Plante, all-female heist story Widows. Hollywood took notice and she was cast as two African-American icons: the soul star Aretha Franklin and the abolitionist activistHarriet Tubman. But playing Tubman triggered a backlash. Some argued that because she is British-Nigerian, the casting was “disrespectful to African Americans” and part of a wider trend of Black British actors – including Daniel Kaluuya (who played Fred Hampton in Judas and the Black Messiah) and David Oyelowo (who played Dr Martin Luther King in Selma) – bagging roles that some felt should be reserved for Black Americans.View image in fullscreenWith Ariana Grande at the Screen Actors Guild awards in LA, in 2025.Photograph: Jay L Clendenin/Rex/Shutterstock for SAGThe criticism stung Erivo, and at the time shetold the Guardian: “Before I’m British, I’m a Black woman. The first things people see are the colour of my skin and my sex.” I’m interested in her thoughts now, almost a decade on. “I still think it’s happening,” she says, answering almost before I’m able to get the question out. “And I think it’s a waste of everyone’s time.“I think we could all just sit in a room and be like: ‘OK, so what’s the problem? What’s going on? How do we fix this? How do we stop doing this?’ Because nobody else does this. Nobody else is having this conversation. The Australians and the Americans and the English white folk are not having this conversation. They don’t care.” Does she have sympathy with the argument that African Americans do face – on average – more inbuilt disadvantages than some other Black immigrant groups who move to the US? “I have empathy,” she says. “But I also think that it’s hard for a Black English kid from London to also make it.”In person, Erivo can be measured and precise, her arms and adorned fingernails spreading out wide when she wants to make a point. As we talk, she really comes alive when we discuss her experiences after the release ofWicked: For Goodin 2025, the sequel to the 2024 adaptation of the long-running Wizard of Oz musical Wicked.The film, a heartwarming story of friendship between Ariana Grande’s good witch, Glinda, and Erivo’s bad witch, Elphaba, swiftly became the highest-grossing movie adaptation of a stage musical. For Erivo, it was another new high-water mark, one which shot her into the upper echelons of fame.double quotation markThere was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friendsThe Wicked: For Good press tour became a must-follow, not just for fans of the film but for a meme-hungry internet, which feasted on any interview where Erivo and Grande were paired together. Erivo and Grande sat cheek by jowl; they hugged, cried, and – famously – “held space” for each other while holding each other’s index fingers in micro embrace. Erivo says she has seen most of the gifs and loves many. But there was a point at which it seemed to tip into something else, something darker.Commentators started to ask why the pair were apparently so close. Was it all faked as part of a Hollywood psyop? What was really going on here between Erivo – a queer star – and Grande? “It was interesting that there were many people who had become psychologists from their couches,” says Erivo. “There was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friends. Like, why are they friends? Why are they connected? There must be something wrong with them.”She leans forward and takes off her glasses, before beginning to sound like Tessa, the barrister. “Why are they showing emotion? How dare they cry? And how dare they laugh? And how dare they be emotive and alive?” she asks, sounding both hurt and confused. “It’s a double-edged sword,” she adds. “Because if we were dead behind the eyes and showing no emotion, there would have been something else to say about it. I wish there was someone who could have been like, ‘Right, this is the proper balance of emotion that you should show. Don’t show this. Don’t show that. Just this amount,’” she says, pinching her fingers together.The speculation and online hysteria became even more heightened after an Australian prankster, Johnson Wen, jumped on to the red carpet in Singapore,grabbing Grandein an attempt to get a selfie with her. Erivo, who was by her side, immediately confronted him and put her arm around Grande. The moment was terrifying, says Erivo. “No one else was moving. We were on a carpet. We were exposed. My immediate response was: ‘Get this man away from us now.’”The internet’s response was to give thinly veiled praise to Erivo, who was recast as Grande’s “bodyguard” – something she took exception to,arguing thather “humanity had been bastardised” after the incident. Today, Erivo says the reaction was one cloaked in a mix of misogyny and misogynoir – with people seemingly taking great joy in mocking a queer, muscular, bald, Black woman looking out for her friend. Erivo was asked by a journalist on another red carpet whether she was a “protector”, a question that still rankles. “I was like: ‘Oh, you think because I look like this that you could talk to me this way about something that was a human thing that I would have done for any friend, and hopefully a friend would have done for me,’” she says. “But I must be a bodyguard.‘I felt my humanity was bastardised’: Cynthia Erivo says reaction to Ariana Grande red carpet incident rooted in racismRead more“I think the idea that it’s OK to rip a person to shreds in that way when they’re doing something that’s a naturally human thing to do just felt crazy,” she says. People in the public eye are supposed to just take abuse, she continues. “I think that this particular moment went just too far.”I wonder if that experience made Erivo reconsider her career. She has often talked about wanting to push the limits of what’s possible – does she still feel that way? She reverts to her Tessa barrister mode, firing rhetorical questions like darts. “What else have I not discovered about myself as a person, as an artist, as a friend? Like what can I do? If I’m working towards what could be a possible limit, then it means I’m never doing the same thing over and over again. In order to push a limit, it’s gonna hurt a little bit. It’s gonna feel uncomfortable, which means I’m never staying the same. I’m always having to build.” To this very average human, that sounds exhausting, but for Erivo, perhaps it’s nothing a few Ruffles can’t fix.Prima Facie is in UK cinemas from 13 November and Australian cinemas on 14 January.Explore more on these topicsCynthia ErivoWicked: For GoodWickedMusicalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Babydoll phenomenon: how Jamie Miller’s song got the world dancing – and put Wales back on top | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: It has been 40 years since a Welsh man topped the UK charts. Now a little-known singer has done it again, with the help of the year’s biggest earworm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It has been 40 years since a Welsh man topped the UK charts. Now a little-known singer has done it again, with the help of the year’s biggest earworm
Content: Just getting started … Jamie Miller.Photograph: Ryan Emberley/amfAR/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJust getting started … Jamie Miller.Photograph: Ryan Emberley/amfAR/Getty ImagesPass notesPop and rockThe Babydoll phenomenon: how Jamie Miller’s song got the world dancing – and put Wales back on topIt has been 40 years since a Welsh man topped the UK charts. Now a little-known singer has done it again, with the help of the year’s biggest earwormTue 27 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The Babydoll trend.Age:Older than you think.Meaning?Let’s come back to that.OK. Appearance?Everywhere. TikTok, Insta, all your socials. Also on the radio, if you still do that.I call it the wireless. A song, right?More than a song, but we’ll come to that too. But yes, a song, currently No 1 in the UK singles charts, by Jamie Miller.That name rings a bell.He was on The Voice in 2017.From Wales, no?From Wales, yes! He grew up in Pontprennau in the north of Cardiff. Now he’s the first Welsh solo male artist to top the singles chart since …Tom Jones?Not quite that far back. No, since Shakin’ Stevens’festive hit Merry Christmas Everyonein 1985.So after The Voice, Jamie’s career took off?Not really. He only came third, for a start. And even the aforementioned Sir Tom didn’t “spin his chair” for his fellow Welshman. Since then he’s played venues such as The Globe in Cardiff, and brought out a few records, but he has hardly taken the world by storm. He wasconsidering quitting musicaltogether.Until now, and Babydoll?Sort of. It was originally released in early August.A slow burn, asthey say.Correct, though now smoking hot. It really got going afterJennifer Love Hewittposted videos of herself singing along and doing the dance routine.There’s a dance?Oh yes.How do I do it?Start with a chug, stepping on your right foot, raising your left knee and heel, then switching sides. Do eight of them, while rolling your shoulders.[Chugging, kindof.] Got it!Next you’re going to go out with your right foot, and back, then out with the left, and back, and so on. Times eight again, while popping your arms.This is getting complicated.Maybe it would be easier if you found a tutorial video.[Having found a tutorial video] OK, now I’mpulling my arm up, with a little finger-click, five, six, seven, eight … Maybe I’m too old for Babydoll.Nonsense. Look around, everyone’s doing it: the very young, very old, dogs, more slebs …Who?Antonio Cipriano (offOff Campus), who recorded aversion with Miller. And Alison Hammond did it, with Miller – very well,until she fell over a boulder and injured her wrist.I knew it was dangerous. Anyway, are we declaring it a viral dance craze?To the extent that Miller and Cipriano were on Strictly at the weekend,doing it with the entire cast.I’d call that viral.It’s really catching on. “If you’re gonna leave me broken-hearted / Then maybe, baby, we should just get started …”Do say:“Who’s laughing now, Sir Tom?”Don’t say:“And now shall we do … the Macarena?”Explore more on these topicsPop and rockPass notesDancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the Telephone | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?
Content: ‘It was like being in boot camp’ … from left, Peter Case, Jack Lee and Paul Collins in 1975.View image in fullscreen‘It was like being in boot camp’ … from left, Peter Case, Jack Lee and Paul Collins in 1975.Pop and rockInterview‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the TelephoneAlex DellerThey gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nerves should have had it all. Formed in 1974 and gifted with earworm melodies, good looks and a painstaking work ethic, the trio of Jack Lee (guitar, vocals), Peter Case (bass, vocals) and Paul Collins (drums, vocals) wrote, rehearsed and gigged as if their lives depended on it. Not quite punk and dismissive of the description “power pop”, they aimed to cram epic brilliance into effervescent, two-minute songs.When the music industry ignored them, the Nerves opted to make their own luck, pressing their own EP and booking a gruelling nationwide tour that saw them share stages with Devo and the Ramones. After they split in 1978, a bittersweet coda to their brief career swiftly followed: Parallel Lines, Blondie’s smash-hit third album, opened with a cover version of their song Hanging on the Telephone. Previously a Nerves calling card, theBlondietake seemed to scrub them from history.“I figured it would be two weeks, or a month tops, before we were famous,” smiles Paul Collins from his New York home today. A Juilliard student with a bohemian upbringing and an overriding love of rock’n’roll, Collins dropped out and headed for the west coast. “I was barely 18, I had 80 bucks in my pocket and I was scared to death,” he recalls. Within three days of arriving in San Francisco, he found an ad tacked to the wall of a record store which led him to the enigmatic Jack Lee, a transplant from Sitka, Alaska.double quotation markMy snare drum would be covered with blood because we were playing so fastPeter Case proved harder to woo. Baling on school at 15 and ditching Buffalo for San Francisco, he played blues and country standards on the street to pay for food. “I slept in a beat-up van parked down by the water,” says Case. “It wasn’t even my van.” Lee and Case struck up a friendship when the latter was busking. When Collins came on board, the Nerves were transformed from idea to actuality. “You just couldn’t find people that wanted to do something that was that out of joint,” Case recalls. “There was nobody else like Jack around – someone who had a vision, wanted to go with it and couldwrite.”The band set up shop in a three-storey flophouse, immersing themselves in practice sessions that could last up to 16 hours. “It was like being in boot camp,” says Collins. “My snare drum would be covered with blood because we were playing so fast. It was three people acting as one person, and it was a 24-hour endeavour. There was no on and off.”For all their commitment, it soon became apparent that the Nerves were going nowhere. With no peers beyondthe Flamin’ Grooviesand the aloof, leather-clad Crime, the trio saw no future playing to barflies and fist-swinging off-duty servicemen. After Lee recovered from a near-fatal stabbing, the band left for LA. There they rubbed shoulders with scenesters such asKim FowleyandRodney Bingenheimer, and organised early shows for punk bands the Germs and the Weirdos. “It turned out to be a bitter pill to swallow, because they instantly became much more popular than we did!” says Collins.View image in fullscreenPerennially under the radar … the Nerves in Los Angeles in 1977.Photograph: No creditUnperturbed, the band concocted a national tour in 1977 that spanned 71 days, 39 gigs and 16 cities, during which they connected with the Dead Boys and Cheap Trick, and played a series of dates with the Ramones. “The Ramones’ work ethic was even more stringent than ours,” recalls Collins. “They’d be practising before the show, and afterwards they’d go back to the hotel and work on songs. I remember sitting at this big wooden table with them after a show, and Dee Dee goes, ‘May I be excused? I have to go to the bathroom.’ It was like he was at the dinner table with his parents!”If the Ramones were a picture of politeness, other soon to be stars were less welcoming. “We played Boston, and when we were loading in, there were these four guys completely dressed in leather,” says Collins. “One of them goes, ‘What the fuck do you think you’re doing? You’re touring all over the country. You don’t have a manager. You don’t have an agent. It’s bullshit. We know what we’re fucking doing. We’re going to be huge.’ So we look at them and say, ‘Yeah, well what’s the name of your band? The Cars? What a stupid name…’”Inevitably, travelling thousands of miles in a station wagon and booking gigs on the fly took its toll. “It’s like a plant,” says Collins. “You don’t give it water, you don’t give it sunlight, it’s gonna die. We couldn’t get any industry acceptance, and I think we’d taken all we could.”After a stint in the Breakaways, Collins and Case respectively formed the Beat and the Plimsouls, with both bands enjoying the success that eluded the Nerves. Lee, meanwhile, worked on a solo career, self-funding two albums and encountering more proxy success whenCome Back and Staybecame a hit for Paul Young. While Hanging on the Telephone would be covered by everyone from L7 and Def Leppard to Girls Aloud, the Nerves remained perennially under the radar, never achieving the same cut-through as the bands they’d served with in the trenches.View image in fullscreen‘There’s about three albums’ worth of releasable material’ … Collins, Case and Lee in Denver.Photograph: Patty HeffleyFifty years on, a new anthology may redress the balance. “My dad tasked me with this on his deathbed,” says Lee’s daughter, Cynthia Cook. “His dream was to be on Jack White’s label Third Man Records.” While Cook may have grown up writing songs with her father – their first was titled Rock’n’Roll Rabbit, penned when she was five – the music industry wasn’t her home turf. “My dad was all about the long shot,” she smiles. “You know, I’m a mom who works in real estate … but I should go get a deal with Third Man.”The long shot eventually paid off, however, and Cook seems both overwhelmed and overjoyed by the challenge of sifting through a lifetime’s worth of songs. “I have cassettes from the 70s, 80s, 90s and 2000s,” she says. “There’s about three albums’ worth of releasable material.” Her finds to date include a swiftly junked MySpace cut preserved by a fan, and a live tape recorded by an off-duty Whiskey a Go Go waitress and unearthed in a closet 50 years later.As for the Nerves’ legacy, the surviving members are philosophical. “It makes me realise that we did everything wrong in certain ways, and everything right in others,” says Case. “It didn’t work out well at the time, but the music is here now, 50 years later. Who would have ever thought that?”The Nerves: Best Collection is out now on Third Man RecordsExplore more on these topicsPop and rockPunkBlondiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rule of thumb: why don’t we use weight measures for fresh ginger? | Herbs and spices | The Guardian
description: When it comes to ginger, personal taste often trumps strict precision, say our experts as they get to the root of the issue
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: When it comes to ginger, personal taste often trumps strict precision, say our experts as they get to the root of the issue
Content: ‘If you give a precise weight, people will perhaps think it’s very important and worry if they’re a few grams out.’Photograph: Maksim Lashcheuski/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If you give a precise weight, people will perhaps think it’s very important and worry if they’re a few grams out.’Photograph: Maksim Lashcheuski/AlamyKitchen aideHerbs and spicesRule of thumb: why don’t we use weight measures for fresh ginger?When it comes to ginger, personal taste often trumps strict precision, say our experts as they get to the root of the issueAnna BerrillTue 27 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy do so many recipesstate the amount of fresh ginger in “thumbs” or centimetres. Withit being so variable in shape, why don’t you use weight?Nick,by emailLet’s gather some of the Guardian food troops and ask them to explain themselves. First up in front of the class is our own perfectionist,Felicity Cloake: “That’s a very good question, and I don’t think there is a very good answer,” she says. “Maybe it’s just convention, because sometimes it feels a bit fussy to give a precise weight for the likes of ginger, onions and other staples if you’re not, say, Heston Blumenthal.” Often, it doesn’t really matter that much, either: “If you give a precise weight, people will perhaps think it’s very important and worry if they’re a few grams out,” she adds. In other words, if Nick were to use a smidge more (or less) ginger than Cloake in, say,her dal, it’s unlikely to make or break it.Cloake’s fellow columnistGeorgina Haydenagrees: “Unlike measuring a ratio of risotto rice to stock, or making a cake, the typical recipes I use ginger in, such as curries, don’t have to be precise,” she says. “After all, cooking should be as instinctive as possible, rather than relying on digital scales.” However, Nick is right in that ginger does vary hugely in shape, Cloake says: “If it was a very thick piece, or it wasn’t thumb-shaped, I’d cut it so the cumulative flesh of the ginger was roughly the same as the cumulative flesh of a thumb. You’re just trying to give a rough amount, without being too prescriptive. But he’s right, we should probably move to grams.”In that same spirit, another columnist,Ravinder Bhogal, nails down the thumb measurement even further, taking it to mean a piece that’s about 5cm long, the length of an average adult thumb, and weighing about 15g. “I get that ‘a thumb’ as a measurement is not exactly scientific, but how much ginger you put in a dish is also up to you – more if you like it stronger and less if you don’t,” Bhogal says. If, for example, a recipe were to call for garlic as well as ginger, she would be inclined to use the same weight of each, although, she adds: “Remember the flavour of ginger softens as it cooks. But a centimetre here or there is not going to make a huge difference, so go with your own personal taste.”After all, that’s a big part of cooking, right? When Hayden writes a recipe, she says, its purpose is also to empower home cooks to take a bit of creative licence: “A knob of butter, a pinch of salt, a bunch of herbs … sometimes, vague measurements are a good thing. Also, it’s mad to get out the scales for something as small as ginger.”Cloake, however, imagines Nick “to be a more scientifically minded cook” than she is, so here are some final words: “Essentially, there’s no good reason for it, except to say that it gives an idea that you don’t have to worry too much. It’s just a guideline.” And there’s plenty enough to worry about in this world already right now.Got a culinary dilemma? title: I struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to her | Swimming | The Guardian
description: My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away
Content: Angela Giuffrida, centre, holding her nose, on a swimming trip in the Ionian Sea off Greece last year.Photograph: Courtesy of Lauren ElderView image in fullscreenAngela Giuffrida, centre, holding her nose, on a swimming trip in the Ionian Sea off Greece last year.Photograph: Courtesy of Lauren ElderSeascape: the state of our oceansSwimmingI struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to herMy mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed awaySupported byAbout this contentAngela GiuffridaTue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey. Watching the slightly choppy sea from a boat, the last thing I felt like doing was embarking on another 5km (3-mile) swim. Mind fog had sapped my energy, and my mood was decidedly Eeyore-like. But as I pulled on my cap and flippers, adjusted my goggles and took the plunge, something shifted.Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen. Breathing came properly. There was respite.My swimming is far from sophisticated – my strokes are messy and I am mostly kicking from the knees. Still, I manage to move forward, albeit slowly, hugging the coastline ofTurkey’s Lycian Way, turning a corner and entering an area of calm. The water is blue-green. Fish glide purposefully beneath, and I’m uplifted when I see a turtle navigating around a rock on the seabed.I came to Turkey with SwimTrek,a Brighton-based company offering guided open-water swim tours. The plan is to complete 25km over five days. On the one hand, it is a holiday; but for me, the combination of swimming and the sea has become something more than that.It began in Croatia in June 2024, eight months after my mother died unexpectedly, when a friend persuaded me to sign up to swim 3km a day for a week.I had been feeling lost as I tried to come to terms with my mum not being here any more, and generally anxious, made worse by sleepless nights. Even on calm days, at times it felt difficult to breathe, the tightness in the throat unrelenting.The only thing that seemed to help was swimming, especially with the focus on the Croatia challenge. My preparation was mostly in the pool, pretty much all of it breaststroke.I had a rude awakening on the first day of the trip when I tried to swim either breast or backstroke – the latter steering me wildly off course. On day two I was kitted out with flippers and one of the SwimTrek guides taught me the basic front crawl technique. From that point, my confidence in the sea grew.View image in fullscreenA secluded cove near Kaş, which can only be reached on foot or by water.Photograph: N Duzen/GettyThe sensation of being immersed in the open water is difficult to describe, but it brings me instant relief. I feel weightless yet anchored by the buoyancy. The rhythmic movement while watching the sea life helps to clear my mind of clutter.This is a far cry from my early experience of swimming. Growing up in the south London town of Croydon, the closest I got to the water was a municipal pool. I was taken there by my mum. I would bob around in the freezing water of the children’s pool while she would swim laps in the adult one.Going swimming in those days – the 1980s – was synonymous with verrucas and posters featuring cartoon images warning against “bombing” and “heavy petting”. The latter made me and other children giggle although none of us really knew what it meant.The changing rooms were grim and you would travel home with wet hair, laden down by a damp towel and stink of chlorine for days. The highlight was a post-pool Curly Wurly from the snack machine.On a hot summer’s day, my mum would take us on the train to Brighton. I would go reluctantly, more enthused by amusement arcades than the sea.But I was lucky. There were glimmers of the sea winning me over. With an Italian father, every two years we would go on holiday toItaly, travelling by train from the UK to see relatives in Turin and then along the Mediterranean coast to see those in Sicily, where my dad was born.View image in fullscreenMy mum and I, taken on a beach in Catania, Sicily, in the 1980s, when most of my swimming was confined to a municipal pool in south London.Photograph: Courtesy of Angela GiuffridaWhen we were at the beach, my mum would swim up and down, seemingly for hours. I would look out for her now and then from the shore.It is only now, since I have started swimming myself, that I wonder what those swims meant to her.My mum lived with depression and anxiety, and I believe the sea might have given her the same kind of respite it has given me.I don’t know because we never spoke about it. The only time we really talked about her swimming was when she called needing help to buy a cap, which had to be of a particular variety, or goggles, online.My mum, who was 73 when she died, did other things to keep active, too – going to the gym every morning, at least until Covid, and she loved playing tennis and walking.The search for the perfect wetsuit: is there one that doesn’t harm the planet?Read moreAfter years of talking about it, my parents moved to Bexhill-on-Sea in East Sussex a few years before she died. So now, whenever I return to the UK from Italy, Bexhill is where I go. I appreciate the UK coastline much more and find that walking by the sea when there, or even just listening to it for a few minutes, helps to centre me. Now and then, I brave a cold-water dip.But it is the swim tours that have become a powerful source of all-round wellbeing, helped also by a welcoming swimming community and new friendships made. A year after Croatia, I did a 4km-a-day trip in Greece, where I celebrated my 50th birthday.I managed to complete the Turkey one, too, feeling a huge sense of achievement and absolutely no shame about being the slowest in the group.I’m already planning next year’s swim. And even though I’m sad that I can’t tell my mum about it, the sea makes me feel connected to her.Explore more on these topicsSwimmingSeascape: the state of our oceansFitnessMental healthHealthBereavementHealth & wellbeingItalyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Want to know what you’re really like? Just ask the people who see you twice a year | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Apparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Apparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘I was so wet the labrador backed away from me.’Photograph: Posed by model; Bohdan Bevz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I was so wet the labrador backed away from me.’Photograph: Posed by model; Bohdan Bevz/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleWant to know what you’re really like? Just ask the people who see you twice a yearZoe WilliamsApparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is?Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTShareThe worst kind of professional relationship is with the person you see twice a year, in a variety of different locations, because whatever they notice about you from that tiny observational sample, that’s what you’re like. So on the first rainy day in folk memory, the opening bars of Storm Austen, I turned up to a job with a photographer, soaked. I’d been on my bike and had tucked my trousers into my socks, so the accumulated water in the ankle area had seeped upwards, giving me a confusing wet leg-warmer effect, then a couple of dry inches, then an unbelievably wet rest of body. I was so wet that when I went to hug the studio’s labrador, he backed away from me like I was trying to give him a bath.“You were really wet last time!” the photographer exclaimed, remembering our previous meeting back in March. “Well, it’s a wet country,” I replied, before the person we were there to shoot chipped in: “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” Then the photographer asked, “Have you thought about getting some wet-weather clothes, if you’re going to cycle?” and I said, “Obviously this is the first time that’s occurred to me, otherwise it would have happened at some point between March and now,” except she didn’t hear me because I had my mouth full of Haribo chewy sours.“You ate all the Haribos last time,” my colleague observed, and I’ll skip the denials because even though I can’t remember that, it sounds true. Something about getting soaked on a bike makes me powerfully hungry – I think the sense of grievance messes with my blood sugar. “Have you ever thought of having breakfast?” came the next bolt of blue-sky thinking. It’s a great ice-breaker, making such a fist of your life choices that you become a human suggestions box, everyone mucking in with some basic improvements. But this, I insist, was two freak days of 2026; all the others have panned out fine.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: A year after the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, this is what our lives look like: no privacy, no peace | Akram Al-Sourani | The Guardian
description: I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves, says Akram Al-Sourani, a writer and poet from Gaza City
Author: Akram Al-Sourani
Headline: I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves, says Akram Al-Sourani, a writer and poet from Gaza City
Content: Two girls walk past collapsed buildings in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip on 25 August 2026.Photograph: Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTwo girls walk past collapsed buildings in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip on 25 August 2026.Photograph: Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionGazaA year after the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, this is what our lives look like: no privacy, no peaceAkram Al-SouraniI look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselvesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.44 EDTShareEvery morning, I look at myself and my neighbours standing in the queue for water, and remember how each of us once had a life of our own, our privacy, our own toothbrush, our own home and our own bathroom. How we used to wash our faces and drink clean water without ever imagining that a day would come when these simple routines would become a battle with ourselves and with every drop of water. Even standing beneath a hot shower has become a dream postponed until further notice.A year has passed since theannouncement of the “ceasefire” in Gaza, yet the spectre of war, bombardment and death has never left our lives.War is not simply the bombing of buildings or the evacuation of a residential neighbourhood. There are small wars inside this one enormous war. The tent is a war. The surveillance drone – thezannana, as we call it, for its incessant buzzing – is a war. Queueing for water is a war. Waiting to use the toilet is a war. The death of privacy is a war. Thirty people crammed into a single room is a war.Every morning, the same question follows me: what will happen today? Will my children return from what remains of their school to what remains of our home, having walked along what remains of a street, when bombardment could take them from me at any moment?They walk long distances because transport is difficult and expensive amid fuel shortages, repeated border crossing closures and the trickle of essential supplies intoGaza. It is as though life itself is being rationed to us, drop by drop.In Gaza, waking up alive is not enough. You must also make sure that the place where you slept is still somewhere you can spend the following night. You must hope that your children can dream of an ordinary day – one in which obtaining a loaf of bread, an education or medical treatment is not an achievement worthy of celebration.As the Israeli bombs fell, my family committed an act of rebellion: we planted a garden in Gaza | Taqwa Ahmed al-WaiRead moreIt is as though the ceasefire never happened. The sounds of bombardment, explosions and surveillance drones have continued to accompany our days and nights. What remains of our homes and tents trembles – and so do our hearts.In Gaza, to be alive is to live on the edge of death. As though we are still trapped in October 2023, when the course of our lives was redrawn into a new geography, and evacuation became a matter of Israeli orders dropped from the sky on leaflets – orders to flee from one place to another, from one tent to another disappointment, from one dangerous patch of land to a corner that seemed slightly less dangerous.On the morning of Friday 13 October 2023, the skies over Gazarained down evacuation leafletsordering us to leave our homes and head south.We left the north, broken, and entered madness.We left, but we have never truly returned to ourselves. We lost the people we were before the war. We are no longer who we used to be. The war has turned us into strangers, unfamiliar even to ourselves.We left everything behind.We left the stairwell, the curtains and the windows. The sofas, the router, the 55in television, the pressure cooker on the stove, the unwashed dishes – and half a lemon that, for some ridiculous reason, we always insisted on keeping in the fridge door.We left behind conversations, arguments, disagreements, embraces and unfinished secrets. Stories told after dinner. A bunch of keys, and a never-ending chain of household troubles.We left our photo albums, our wedding pictures, and the hairstyle that irritated me on my wedding night because of all the hairpins; the clutter in the storeroom, the gas lighter, the bathrobe hanging behind the bathroom door, the dining table, the backgammon table, and the water, electricity and internet bills.And we left behind a precious set of drinking glasses, imprisoned in the display cabinet since 1997 on the charge of being “far too good to bring out for guests”.After the bombing, they ended up out in the street.And it turned out we had been wrong to punish our little boy for breaking a cup.We never imagined that we, too, would be broken.All of us were.Three years have passed, yet we still fear hearing again the announcement that changed our lives: “Leave your homes immediately and head south.”Three years of displacement, tents and fear. Three years in which school years have begun and ended without our children experiencing anything resembling a normal education.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the first time, school years are no longer measured in grades and certificates, but in the number of years children have spent displaced.Third year of tent school.It is as though the words I wrote years ago had been waiting for me in the present. As though I had written an early warning that I myself failed to take seriously.I once wrote, in my 2017 book What’s That:“A tent that lets us down.”And in a Facebook post that same year I wrote:“We are all beggars in the making.”I never imagined that the words I had written in satire would one day become the details of our daily lives.From Gaza to Khan Younis, to Rafah, to al-Mawasi, to al-Zawayda, to Deir al-Balah, from a tent to what remains of our home, we have arrived safely in the unknown.Our dreams have yet to arrive. Our hopes have yet to arrive. I fear they may have evaporated somewhere along the way.And today, a year after the announcement of the “ceasefire”, I am still standing in queues: for aid, for cooking gas, for water – and in the endless queue of those waiting for the unknown.I wait for my children to return from school, and I try to recover something of the life we left behind.The name of this chapter has changed. But fear has not changed its address.There is more to tell – if there is anything left of our minds, or our lives, to tell it.Akram Al-Sourani is a writer and poet from Gaza City, and the author of A Homeland Out of Coverage, Half-Baked Homeland and What’s ThatDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: A regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essential
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: A regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essential
Content: John Healey’s budget is expected to promise almost £20bn to public financial institutions, or PuFins.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey’s budget is expected to promise almost £20bn to public financial institutions, or PuFins.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesNils Pratley on financeJohn HealeyThe chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutinyNils PratleyA regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essentialTue 27 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTShareTwo winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy.The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and nowJohn Healeyis going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn.Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing.Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules. Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt.To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse.Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies ina reportlast week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-eraprivate finance initiativedid. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped.Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions.In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new. Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful.There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out.The line can appear blurry at times. This columnhas questionedthe £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”? Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising.Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans?To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’sfollow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities. In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell:last year’s return on equity was -2.6%but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful.But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in itsimpact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholder, the Treasury.The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.”That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundationarguesthat, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets.Explore more on these topicsJohn HealeyNils Pratley on financeBudgetEconomic policyEconomicscommentShareReuse this content

title: My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: John Healey (right) and Andy Burnham are understood to be planning to raise taxes on banks.Photograph: Ian Vogler/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey (right) and Andy Burnham are understood to be planning to raise taxes on banks.Photograph: Ian Vogler/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionBudget 2026My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hardPolly ToynbeeBankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their matchTue 27 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTShareVibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from cappingbus faresto that small but resonant sum of£45 VAT on average off electricity bills– get people talking, alongside bigger plans for anational care service,electoral reformand a possible journeyback to the EU.Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused,banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.UK profits from the country’s four biggest bankswere reportedly £13bnfor the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Financewrites to the chancellorsaying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries.Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him toscrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, andannounced the tower go-aheadonly after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists hisnet worth as $3.1bn, and hetook home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir,Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islamrecounts that episodeas told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.The bank payroll taxraised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?Officiallythe bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP;others suggest double that amount.Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take.Dimon visited No 10last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, fromthe 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTUC pollingfinds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studiesand Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so isemployment,growth,business investmentand average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest wayto raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyBankingBanking reformFinancial sectorcommentShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk says he has ‘cyber psychosis’. Do you too? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Whether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signs, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Whether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signs, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Time to put the phone down? Elon Musk speaks after Donald Trump’s ‘superintelligence’ reveal.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreenTime to put the phone down? Elon Musk speaks after Donald Trump’s ‘superintelligence’ reveal.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAOpinionElon MuskElon Musk says he has ‘cyber psychosis’. Do you too?Arwa MahdawiWhether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signsTue 27 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTShareIn the least surprising news you’ll hear all week, Elon Musk has said he’s not entirely right in the head. “I’ve got a little bit of cyber psychosis,” the world’s richest and most irritating manexplained during an eventthis month. “Maybe a lot actually.” Musk added that, over “various points this year”, he’s had “AI or SI psychosis probably half a dozen times”. SI, in case you missed the super-important memo, stands for “superintelligence” and it’s what Donald Trump wants everyone to call AI now, for reasons too stupid to explain.While the phrase SI is still being used 0nly by weaselly tech bros desperate for Trump’s approval, you’ll probably have heard the term “AI psychosis” bandied around a lot. On the most serious level, it refers todelusional thinkinginduced or exacerbated by sycophantic chatbots. People who have ploughed their life savings into a ridiculous business idea, for example, because computer code told them they were the next Jeff Bezos. But the phrase has also been used more jokingly to describe overexuberance around artificial intelligence, and that seems to be how Musk was using it. The comments about his self-diagnosed bouts of cyber psychosis came as the tech mogul waxed lyrical about how great AI music videos have become, and how he believes artificial intelligence now “understands beauty and harmony”.I don’t know if Musk gushing over the beauty and harmony of AI slop is down to cyber psychosis or possibly hiswidely reported enthusiasmfor the benefits of ketamine and psychedelics. But I can tell you that large swathes of Silicon Valley are dangerously high on their own supply of AI bullshit. And the sickness is rapidly spreading to the populace. So, I’m taking it on myself to help you spot a couple of signs that demonstrate someone has become over attached to AI or grown too credulous when it comes to the puffery around the industry.A sudden cigarette habit is one of the more unusual signals something is afoot. This month, Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankartold CBSthat numerous AI researchers “have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers” that they believe AI is going to cure cancer soon. Sankar provided no data to back up this extraordinary claim, which he said was emblematic of “this mass psychosis, social delusion” around AI. But tech executives don’t need to prove things any more, do they? They just makegrandiose statementsand watch the investor dollars roll in.Another signal your brain may have been fried by AI? An inability to interact with your small children without the help of a large language model. “I cannot imagine having gone through figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT,”OpenAI CEO and new dad Sam Altman saidon Jimmy Fallon last year. Try to imagine, Sam! People have been doing it for a while. Earlier this year, Altman also informed us that AI is a great way to bond with your kids. “cool use case of chatgpt work i heard last night: connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests,” Altmantweeted. “every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc.”While Altman’s parenting tip didn’t land well with normies, Marissa Mayer probably appreciated it. Mayer made her name (and tons of money) as the first female engineer at Google and the CEO of Yahoo; now she’s flogging an AI assistant called Dazzle. In anew interview with the New York Times, Mayer told a story about how, when her daughter Marielle was turning 10, her teacher wanted three bullet points about what made Marielle special. Mayer “felt overwhelmed”, and asked Dazzle for help. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer told the Times. I don’t know how much AI Kool Aid Mayer has drunk, but it’s clearly enough to have made her believe asking AI for insights about your kid is sweet, not downright dystopian.Unfortunately, I do not have the cure for AI psychosis. But as the gold rush continues, let me point you to a sobering reality check from American asset management firm Apollo Global Management. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype … [AI] has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,”stated an insight it published on Saturday. While AI is obviously a transformative technology, I suspect we’re in the middle of a bubble that’s about to burst. After all the mass exuberance, we’re due a very nasty comedown.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Defund Elon Musk | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine
Content: ‘Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink.’Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreen‘Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink.’Photograph: Matt Rourke/APOpinionElon MuskDefund Elon MuskRobert ReichNo private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in UkraineTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.19 EDTShareHe’s Exhibit A on why billionaire wealth should be taxed, why we must get big money out of politics, why billionaires shouldn’t be allowed to buy up major media, and why our government shouldn’t give them huge military contracts.I’m talking aboutElon Musk, of course.According to theWall Street Journal, Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine”. The decision “sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said”.Musk and Trump, the Journal noted, have both “expressed anger atUkrainefor attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices” – although the high prices are really due to Trump’s war in Iran.This month, Musk slowed “the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network … rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless”.According to the Journal, “Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.”Who gave Musk authority to slow his satellite service in the first place? Musk finally admitted this weekend that he had pulled the plug because, hewrote on Twitter/X: “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”So Musk can decide on hisownwhen a foreign country working alongside the United States against a brutal dictator can have access to vital US intelligence?Every time I list another of Musk’s outrages, someone says: “Yes, but he’s an innovator!”He’s not. As is made clear in Alex Gibney’s smart new documentary,Musk,Elondidn’t invent Tesla. He didn’t invent X. He got plenty of help foundingSpaceX.Musk is to innovation what Trump is to governing.We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro KhannaRead moreBoth are conmen. Both are megalomaniacs. Both love authoritarians and detest democracy. Neither believes in (or harbors an ounce of) empathy toward anyone. Both think nothing of corrupting governments for personal gain.Both spout bigoted filth all hours of the day and night to hundreds of millions of people.OK, let me just say it out loud: both Musk and Trump are loathsome human beings.Someday historians will come up with an explanation of how two such awful people could have become the two most powerful people in the US, if not the world (whatwasit about the US in the early 21st century?).But for now, the goal of all sane people must be to defund both and get them as far away from politics as possible.That will be difficult, to be sure. Musk has so far sunk roughly$445minto the 2026 midterm election cycle – all to help Republicans retain control of Congress. That makes him thelargest single known donorin the entire midterm elections.Will he expect a return on his investment?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHell, hespent a quarter of a billion dollarsin 2024 to help Trump win re-election and ended up with access to vast troves of government data, along withbillions of dollars’ worthof no-bid contracts with the Pentagon.His Starlink satellite system is now key to the military strategy of the United States as well as that of Ukraine. He was also rewarded with a chainsaw inaptly named “department of government efficiency”, which he used todestroy USAIDand slash other government agencies he doesn’t like.Musk has given at least$168mto Texas Super Pacs seeking to elect Republican Ken Paxton to the Senate, despite (or is it because of?) Paxton’slong recordof ethical lapses and legal controversies. Musk’s businesses are headquartered in Texas, so he needs friends there.Musk recentlypushed the false storyto his 242 million followers on X that James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, was absent from the campaign trail because he had suffered a mental breakdown and was receiving counseling at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Ohio.In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane MartinsonRead moreThat story has been thoroughly debunked. Security camera footageshows Talaricoat home, not at an Ohio mental health facility. (Meanwhile, according tothe Wall Street Journal, on New Year’s Eve 2024, Paxtonpartied in Dubai with his extramarital girlfriend and two fugitives from charges of about $300m in healthcare fraud in the US. One of the men donated $190,000 to Paxton, $25,000 of it after he was indicted.)The project of defunding Musk will probably have to wait until after 20 January 2029, when, let’s pray, we have a sane administration in Washington that will end all government contracts with him (his support for rightwing extremists around the world makes him a security risk), bust up his monopolies (a reinvigorated Federal Trade Commission and Federal Communications Commission will see to it), and impose a significant wealth tax on him.No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine.If Musk’s Starlink system has become so central to military strategy that its Pentagon contracts can’t be cancelled, it should be nationalized. (After I suggested this on my podcast last Saturday, Musk posted: “Stealing companies is a serious crime. Prison for Reich.”Butyoudon’t have to wait until Musk is officially defunded. Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink. And support politicians who promise to defund him.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsElon MuskOpinionDonald TrumpUkraineUS politicsEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm
Content: ‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAOpinionEuropeThe Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and TrumpEditorialIf ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harmTue 27 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTShareFollowing the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, shetoldone interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined theirvisionsof a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally,proposesslashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.View image in fullscreenAlice Weidel.Photograph: AFP/GettySimilar ideas have longcirculatedin far-right thinktanks. But they are now in the programmes of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany – Europe’s historic engines of integration. Ms Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland.Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight. Mario Draghi, the former head of the European Central Bank, haswarnedthat without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. But other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leaderspeakingwith the same sense of urgency.Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defence, the moves towards European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Xi Jinping andVladimir Putin(and any Maga successor to Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit.As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counter-arguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming. But it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms. For the time being, to paraphraseWB Yeats, the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
