title: The Guardian view on supporting carers: the DWP’s problem is deeper than IT | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A taper is much better than a cliff-edge. But problems with carer’s allowance should have been solved years ago
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A taper is much better than a cliff-edge. But problems with carer’s allowance should have been solved years ago
Content: ‘A Guardian investigation revealed that the Department for Work and Pensions failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid.’Photograph: Sopa Images/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘A Guardian investigation revealed that the Department for Work and Pensions failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid.’Photograph: Sopa Images/Rex/ShutterstockOpinionCarer's allowanceThe Guardian view on supporting carers: the DWP’s problem is deeper than ITEditorialA taper is much better than a cliff-edge. But problems with carer’s allowance should have been solved years agoTue 27 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTShareThereform of carer’s allowance– a benefit paid to people who spend 35 or more hours a week caring for a disabled relative – is overdue and welcome. The cliff-edge design that forces claimants in England and Wales to forfeit their entire payment if they breach an earnings limit of £204 a week by as little as a penny is wrong in principle and made much worse by the appalling way in which rules have been applied.AGuardian investigationrevealed that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid. This resulted in debts and hardship, and hundreds of criminal convictions for fraud. Carers in already difficult personal circumstances described feeling driven to desperation and illness by what one called a“catch-out culture”. Most claimants are women on low incomes; the allowance is £86.45 a week.The plan to replace this outdated, blunt tool with a taper is a good one. The disincentive to employment built into the existing system is perverse. Adults with caring responsibilities should be encouraged to do paid work in addition to their roles at home if they can. As with child benefit, the promised taper will mean that earnings over the threshold lead to a diminution rather than a loss of the allowance. Demands for repayment should be drastically reduced. Thousands of low-income households with disabled members will gain more freedom as a result.View image in fullscreenLouise Casey.Photograph: PADetails of the policy’s implementation have yet to be set out. But after years of delay and inaction, the main concern is timing. ADWP whistleblowerfirst raised the overpayment issue a decade ago, only for their complaint to be shut down. Successive Conservative governments did nothing despite a detailed 2020 report from the work and pensions committee. Finally, last November, Liz Sayce’s independent review led to the recruitment of extra staff and a new approach. Ministers committed to correcting past errors, including the way that claimants had been unlawfully blocked from averaging their earnings. Butprogress has been slow,and with the taper expected to be rolled out in 2030-31, the injustice of the current situation looks set to continue for several more years.The benefit system is complicated, and it is better to make changes properly than to rush through a botched job. But the overhaul of carer’s allowance should not be mistaken for an IT problem. The deeper issue is the ongoing failure to get to grips with the fundamental challenge of care in our society, and to take on board the extent to which millions of people’s lives are shaped by the needs of dependent adult relatives.Louise Casey has made it clear thather social care commissionwill deliver recommendations about what it is reasonable to expect of families, as well as the state. There are grounds to hope that her forthright style and years of experience, combined with Andy Burnham’s strong commitment to reform, will finally lead to a breakthrough. In the meantime, the DWP must do all it can to put right the wrongs done to carer’s allowance claimants. There has still been no satisfactory explanation about how such a punitive culture developed. But the new commitment to tapered support is an encouraging indication that the government is now moving in a more compassionate direction.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Lack of a ‘protective ring’ around care homes meant our loved ones died of Covid | Covid inquiry | The Guardian
description: Letters: Diane La Rosa and Teresa Pacey-Devlin on the deaths of their fathers during the pandemic. Plus more letters responding to the Covid inquiry from John Robinson, David Flood and James Townsend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Diane La Rosa and Teresa Pacey-Devlin on the deaths of their fathers during the pandemic. Plus more letters responding to the Covid inquiry from John Robinson, David Flood and James Townsend
Content: ‘Sadly, it comes as no surprise that Lady Hallett rejected Matt Hancock’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreen‘Sadly, it comes as no surprise that Lady Hallett rejected Matt Hancock’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PACovid inquiryLettersLack of a ‘protective ring’ around care homes meant our loved ones died of CovidDiane La RosaandTeresa Pacey-Devlinon the deaths of their fathers during the pandemic. Plus more letters responding to the Covid inquiry fromJohn Robinson,David FloodandJames TownsendTue 27 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTShareMy dad was in a care home when Covid hit in March 2020 and visits were stopped (UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry finds, 20 October). It was heartbreaking not being able to see him, and talking to him via phone was almost impossible. I couldn’t see how Covid wouldn’t spread to the home as there wasn’t any testing at that point. He was a sitting duck and there was nothing I could do.In late April 2020, when I had been calling all day, eventually someone answered and told me they were too busy to talk. The next day when I called, I was told Dad wasn’t feeling very well. I asked if there was Covid in the home: they were honest and said there was. I was distraught.I then received the inevitable call in the early hours next morning from the home, saying my father had been taken to hospital with suspected Covid. My conversation with the hospital was soul-destroying. They would make Dad as comfortable as possible, he wouldn’t be given oxygen and no resuscitation would be given. The only positive was that I’d be able to go in and see him when he was close to death – they would call me.In a way I felt as though I was one of the lucky ones, being with my father as he passed away, convulsing and gasping for his last breath. I will never forget it.Diane La RosaTottenham, LondonMy father died in a care home during Covid, surrounded by close family. For many weeks before that we couldn’t touch him or hold his hand. Restrictions were still in place, as others in government were partying. It was only when he was dying, and a kind nurse telephoned us to say he’d taken a sudden turn for the worse, that we all ignored the rules and rushed to the nursing home to be with him, speak to him, tell him he could let go – give him permission to take his last breath.Until then only my mother and I had spent any time with him, and that was 10 minutes in a cold segregation room where he looked at us blankly as a tear rolled down his cheek. All other times it was waving through the window of the care home to him. He had dementia and didn’t understand why his family was deserting him.As agency staff entered the care home – strangers to my dad and possibly carriers of the virus – we, his family, were locked out. We took the tests, we wore the PPE, we pleaded with the care home, we promised to be extremely vigilant; anything to allow us to see our loved ones while doing everything we could to safeguard them against the virus.Please supportGloria’s Law, which would give everyone a right to a care supporter when using health or care services. Allow care givers and loved ones access during any future pandemic so that people don’t die scared, lonely and alone.Teresa Pacey-DevlinBassingfield, NottinghamshireBoris Johnson apologised to mein parliament on 19 April 2022 for his partying in Downing Street while my wife and thousands of others were dying from Covid (Letters, 14 April 2022).Many of us had already suspected the unimaginable, that Johnson and the health secretary were prepared to let us older people die. Now we know the awful truth: there was no “protective ring”, no “ring of steel” around care homes, just a ring of lies.John RobinsonLichfieldSadly, it comes as no surprise that Lady Hallett rejected Matt Hancock’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic, saying it was “unfounded”. I was working as a nurse in a large acute hospital at the time of Covid, in particular within the interface between the NHS and social care. I kept a diary.This is what I noted on 31 March 2020: “So we are starting to see the fallout from poor policy/guidance from DH/NHSE. Discharge plans to care homes etc causing huge amount of understandable confusion and even possible cross-infection across the sector. Care home managers saying no to at risk patients ‘ready’ for d/c as too many unknown factors/risk in terms of Covid. Really is a mess. Watch this space as the impact in care home sector could be huge.”I look back with anger, sadness and shame at how our colleagues in the care sector and their residents/clients (and respective families) were treated. Never again, please.David FloodWimbledon, LondonThe Covid inquiry’s report on the care sector finds that about 5.8 million people were caring unpaid for a family member or friend during the pandemic. Many did so for months without a break, buying their own protective equipment and taking on medication, injections, dressings and end-of-life care at home with little or no training. In 2021, almost three in four had still not had a single break since the pandemic began.Yet none of the report’s eight recommendations is about them. Their experience gets a chapter section of findings, a short paragraph in the executive summary, and nothing the four governments must formally answer.The report is clear about why help failed to reach them: nobody knew who they were. There is no register of unpaid carers anywhere in the UK. A minister at the time told the inquiry the government had limited knowledge of who was caring. Northern Ireland resorted to leafleting every household.This is fixable. The government’s Pandemic Preparedness Strategy, published in March, already commits to identifying unpaid carers in England by digital means, and the report points to GP records and health apps as practical routes. What is missing is a deadline and someone accountable for meeting it.When ministers respond to this report, they should add the recommendation it lacks: that everyone caring for someone they love can be found, told what help exists and offered a break, well before the next pandemic arrives.James TownsendChief executive and co-founder, MobiliseHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Pablo Escobar tried to bomb me in Bogotá. To stop the cartels infiltrating Europe, we should legalise cocaine | Drugs trade | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to a Guardian investigation into trafficking, former British ambassador to Colombia Keith Morris says the ‘war on drugs’ has failed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to a Guardian investigation into trafficking, former British ambassador to Colombia Keith Morris says the ‘war on drugs’ has failed
Content: A French navy photograph of bales of cocaine seized earlier this month from an unflagged fishing boat in the Atlantic ocean.Photograph: Marine Nationale/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA French navy photograph of bales of cocaine seized earlier this month from an unflagged fishing boat in the Atlantic ocean.Photograph: Marine Nationale/AFP/GettyDrugs tradeLettersPablo Escobar tried to bomb me in Bogotá. To stop the cartels infiltrating Europe, we should legalise cocaineResponding to a Guardian investigation into trafficking, former British ambassador to ColombiaKeith Morrissays the ‘war on drugs’ has failedTue 27 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTShareI congratulate the Guardian on this investigation (Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’, 13 October). It has already prompted astrong call from the former Colombian vice-president Marta Lucía Ramírezfor effective international cooperation to counter the transnational criminal threat.I have followed the “war on drugs” pretty closely since I was the British ambassador toColombiain the heyday of Pablo Escobar, but I was still shocked to learn of the scale of the Latin American criminal presence in Europe, including supposedly political insurgents such as the Colombian ELN and various Farc dissident factions. The fivefold increase in the cocaine trade in the last decade has boosted organised crime on both sides of the Atlantic. It underlines dramatically the failure of the “war on drugs”.In 2001 you publishedan opinion piece by mesaying that this war was unwinnable and that state supervision of legalised drugs would be preferable. I argued that aggressive law enforcement had greatly damaged producer and transit countries without reducing the flow of drugs to consumer countries. Prohibition ensured that the incentive of high prices for cheaply produced drugs was simply too great. So it has remained.However, legalised cannabis regimes are now working in Canada, Uruguay and more than 20 US states, providing possible models for cocaine. The situation has been complicated by the development of extremely strong synthetic drugs, such as fentanyl. Of around80,000 drug overdose deathsin the United States in 2024, 22,000 were cocaine users, while 48,000 had used fentanyl. It strikes me that the availability of such dangerous drugs would make the alternative of legally controlled and safer cocaine worth an experiment, on top of the reduction of violence and corruption that legalisation should bring.I will soon be 92, and owe that to the good fortune that I and fellow members of our chamber of commerce board walked out of a meeting in Bogotá in January 1993, just 15 minutes before an Escobar-ordered car bomb destroyed our boardroom. I have an obligation to continue making this case.Keith MorrisAmbassador to Colombia, 1990-94Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Radio 4 Extra sustains a major part of our cultural heritage. Save it from the BBC cuts | Radio 4 Extra | The Guardian
description: Letter: Stephen McKenna argues against the axing of the station to cut the BBC’s costs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Stephen McKenna argues against the axing of the station to cut the BBC’s costs
Content: ‘The BBC’s radio archive is to our ears, as the National Trust is to our Sunday afternoon excursions.’Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The BBC’s radio archive is to our ears, as the National Trust is to our Sunday afternoon excursions.’Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyRadio 4 ExtraLettersRadio 4 Extra sustains a major part of our cultural heritage. Save it from the BBC cutsStephen McKennaargues against the axing of the station to cut the BBC’s costsTue 27 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareMy father was theactor TP McKenna, who died in 2011. A boon of his years in that great radio studio in the skies is the regular messages I get from friends who have heard him of late on BBC Radio 4 Extra in such programmes asBallylenonandBaldi. If I tune in myself, it’s as if he’s in the room with me.Of itself, that’s hardly a reason to save this important channel from plans to scrap it (BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next year, 20 October), and yet it is. Not to mention the astonishing roll call of British actors that could be cited, includingPaul Daneman,John Moffatt,Robert Hardy,Robert Lang,Richard Pasco,Norman Rodway,Anna Massey,Stephanie Cole,Elizabeth Spriggs, Joanna David, Maggie Steed, Melinda Walker,Geraldine McEwan, and the words of our finest writers from Alan Ayckbourn to George Bernard Shaw. Just a few out of so many.The fact is, the BBC’s radio archive is to our ears as the National Trust is to our Sunday afternoon excursions. It is a major part of our cultural heritage, and far too important to be stuffed away in some corner ofBBC Sounds. An all too pertinent reminder these days that there is hardly anyone remaining in the BBC’s management who was ever a part of its former culture.Stephen McKennaBlackheath, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Britain’s fridge disposal crisis and what to do about it | Environment | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountain
Content: Fridges and freezers at the former Mayton Wood recycling centre in Little Hautbois, Norfolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFridges and freezers at the former Mayton Wood recycling centre in Little Hautbois, Norfolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianEnvironmentLettersBritain’s fridge disposal crisis and what to do about itReaders respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountainTue 27 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareSam Wollaston (What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain, 21 October) highlights an urgent issue, but misses a key underlying driver: the reality of climate change and increasingly hot UK summers.Many standard UK fridge-freezers are only built to normal (N) ambient climate classes, rated to operate in temperatures up to +32C. During recent heatwaves, indoor temperatures in many homes regularly exceed this limit. Even subtropical (ST) rated units fail when ambient temperatures push past 38C. When ambient limits are exceeded, cooling systems fail, leading to compressor breakdown, spoiled food and premature appliance disposal.We need higher regulatory standards requiring manufacturers to produce more durable, resilient appliances rated for higher ambient temperature classes (such as Tropical T or SN-T). Until manufacturers are held to these standards, UK consumers will continue to be left with failing fridges and our landfill waste will keep growing.Alistair BeattieLondonThe problem of fridge disposal needs government action. A “polluter pays” levy should apply to all new fridges, and should go proportionally to local authorities responsible for waste management. They could use the levy to commission companies to recycle fridges in an environment-friendly way.Steve RowellSolihullThere is a simple solution when fridges and freezers are being thrown away simply because the owner wanted an “upgrade”. Appliances in working order can be given away to others via apps such as Olio and Freecycle, or community Facebook pages or WhatsApp groups. This is how I disposed of all my functional white goods when my house was renovated.Jacky RowlandLondonI have just had to buy a new fridge as I can’t find replacements for the door seals on the the old one. Fridges should be repairable. Now the old one, which still functions in a rattly sort of way, has to join the recycling queue simply because of a bit of perished rubber.Diana DalasiniMolesey, SurreyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘That was what you live for’: Fleetwood revel in ‘unbelievably special’ Arsenal win | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor reflected on celebrating his club’s incredible win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor reflected on celebrating his club’s incredible win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’
Content: The Fleetwood manager, Matt Lawlor, joined his players’ delirious celebrations.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Fleetwood manager, Matt Lawlor, joined his players’ delirious celebrations.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesCarabao Cup‘That was what you live for’: Fleetwood revel in ‘unbelievably special’ Arsenal winManager Matt Lawlor, born and raised in area, reflects on celebrating win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’Will Unwinat HighburyTue 27 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor, hailed the club’s victory as one for all football after his sideshocked the Premier League champions, Arsenal,on penalties in the Carabao Cup. The side 18th in League Two held their nerve in the shootout, Conor Haughey hitting the winner to reach the quarter-finals.The goalkeeper, Jay Lynch, was Fleetwood’s other hero, saving from Bruno Guimarães to set up the chance for victory. Aaron Loupalo‑Bi and Viktor Gyökeres ensured it finished 1-1 in normal time, butArsenalended up a man light after Max Dowman was shown a red card for reacting to a challenge.Fleetwood Town stun Arsenal on penalties: Carabao Cup fourth round – as it happenedRead moreAsked if Fleetwood’s win was the story of the season, Lawlor said: “Yeah, I hope so. Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and sanitised. And that to me there was that feeling that we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special. To be giving that to football fans, and especially Fleetwood fans, is unbelievably special. And yeah, something that I’m really proud of.”Lawlor was clearly emotional at full-time as many of the 4,000 home supporters streamed on to the pitch to celebrate beating a team 84 places above them. “I was trying to not cry and I didn’t. I’ve managed to hold it,” he said. “My family, my little boy here, we’re all local. I was turning around and people were screaming at me in the crowd and people that I knew and grew up with, that I went to school with or they’ve got a loose connection, and people that jumped out on to the pitch.“That’s really special and really emotional. To do something that special early in my career as well, it’s an emotional night. It is emotional. Emotional for the players, emotional for me.”This was Dowman’s second red card of the month, having been sent off for England Under-19s, providing a steep learning curve for the talented teenager. Mikel Arteta was clearly unimpressed. “When we prepare the context of the match, we were very clear on the things you expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was very clear,” said Arteta, who appeared to aim criticism at Dowman as he walked past him after being sent off.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupFleetwood TownArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows
Content: Manchester United managers past and present: Matt Busby (top left), Frank O'Farrell (bottom left), Tommy Docherty (third left), Michael Carrick (centre), David Moyes (third right), Erik ten Hag (bottom right) and Alex Ferguson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Popperfoto/Getty Images; PA; Tom Jenkins/The Guardian; Action Images; Shutterstock; ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester United managers past and present: Matt Busby (top left), Frank O'Farrell (bottom left), Tommy Docherty (third left), Michael Carrick (centre), David Moyes (third right), Erik ten Hag (bottom right) and Alex Ferguson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Popperfoto/Getty Images; PA; Tom Jenkins/The Guardian; Action Images; Shutterstock; ReutersManchester UnitedAn unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeurOnly Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadowsJohn BrewinTue 27 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShould any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it isManchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation ashis predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes andLisandro Martínez going off-pistein TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.View image in fullscreenAlex Ferguson shows off the team hat and scarf after his appointment as Manchester United manager in November 1986.Photograph: Gerry Crowther/Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesDocherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.Major honours won by Manchester United managersFerguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador untilSir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipend in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo, loose talk escaping to social media.Ferguson’s part inRonaldo’s disastrous return to Old Traffordevidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss.The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game, left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.View image in fullscreenThe Sir Matt Busby statue alongside the Manchester United club crest at Old Trafford.Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/ShutterstockA Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to theLouis van Gaaland José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, thathe was being replaced. His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho during his tenure as Manchester United manager, in November 2018.Photograph: Nigel Roddis/EPAUsing the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the facthe turned United down in 2013. The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leaveDavid Moyes, the immediate successorpainted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.Moyes’s reputation is another enhanced by failures that followed, including Mourinho’s grumpy, fractious tenure. When emerging reluctantly from his Lowry Hotel bolthole, the Portuguese reduced himself to mocking club history with “football heritage” rants. Such a scorched-earth policy was echoed by Ruben Amorim, whileErik ten Hag’s retention by Ineos in summer 2024was as confusing to Ten Hag as to everyone else.An unmanageable club? Busby and Ferguson showed it can be done, though the chance of another empire recedes the longer the vanity, plotting and self-interest that personify United continues. And for that, Busby and Ferguson deserve a share of the blame.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedAlex FergusonOle Gunnar SolskjaerJosé MourinhoLouis van GaalMichael CarrickfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Ballon d'Or | The Guardian
description: The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London
Content: 1:27Harry Kane ends England's 25-year wait for a Ballon d'Or winner – videoBallon d'OrKane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremonyBarney RonayThe England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in LondonTue 27 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTShareWell, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.Harry Kane claims men’s Ballon d’Or to end England’s 25-year wait for winnerRead moreNot just for Harry Kane, who isnow the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.11:25Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The LatestEven Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind,sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025,Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.View image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas and Harry Kane pose with their trophies at the end of the 2026 Ballon d’Or awards ceremony in London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAAnd the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.View image in fullscreenFrench Montana performs during Ballon d’Or award ceremony in London.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesBefore long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.View image in fullscreenThe hosts of the ceremony: Kate Scott and Thierry Henry.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlthough by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka delivers his speech after accepting the Sócrates award from Burna Boy.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Uefa/Getty ImagesIt is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-dayEnglandplayer. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane celebrates after scoring a penalty against Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s Champions League.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APAnd yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.Explore more on these topicsBallon d'OrHarry KaneEnglandBayern MunichTottenham HotspurcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia fight back in rollercoaster start to deciding Test against South Africa | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Decision to bowl first was almost disastrous but the hosts were dismissed for 329 after being 140-0 at lunch
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Decision to bowl first was almost disastrous but the hosts were dismissed for 329 after being 140-0 at lunch
Content: Mitchell Starc cleaned up the tail as Australia fought back in Cape Town.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMitchell Starc cleaned up the tail as Australia fought back in Cape Town.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesCricketAustralia fight back in rollercoaster start to deciding Test against South AfricaDecision to bowl first looked like backfiringBut hosts all out for 329 after being 140-0 at lunchGeoff LemonTue 27 Oct 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a time, it was heading up there with the worst. David Gower at Leeds in 1989, when Australia topped 600 and declared.Nasser Hussain in Brisbane, 2002, when Australia were 364 for two by the end of the day. Edgbaston 2005, where Englandlamped 407 from 80 overs. Those were the looming comparisons for captains deciding to bowl at the toss, after Pat Cummins did the same in the third Test at Cape Town, only for South Africa’s openers to smash 140 by lunch. Yet, by day’s end, Australia had taken 10 for a further 189, Mitchell Starc destroying the tail with four wickets in six balls, 329 all out constituting a serious Australian comeback.What a rollercoaster. The Australian setuphas looked frazzledon this tour: confused player selections for the squad, then for the XIs, confused shot selection in the middle, players bouncing around the order with nightwatch duties and injury absences. Here they chose to leave out their best player from the second Test, Scott Boland, for Nathan Lyon, andwere forced to leave outtheir best player of the last decade, Steve Smith, for Josh Inglis, as well as dropping Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster for Cameron Green and Cooper Connolly. The last time a touring Australian side made four non-disciplinary changes was in the West Indies in 1984.Madushanka stars as Sri Lanka thrash Pakistan to end England’s tri-series hopesRead moreSo it tracked that there was confusion in the decision by Cummins as well. He has been a bowl-first enthusiast relative to captaincy convention, this being the ninth time he has made that call in 25 opportunities, and perhaps was banking on there being more juice in the surface on the first morning than on the second afternoon. But with locals describing a Cape Town surface that is known to run easy, and on a morning of bright sunshine with plenty more predicted, surely the safest move was to try to build a score?That is what Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman did, Markram setting the tone with some early blows, then Ackerman following his lead until surpassing it.Starc and Josh Hazlewood bowled poorly, too short and too wide on too many occasions, and with no swing and no lateral movement from the pitch, Markram laid into front-foot drives, back-foot punches, and even a shockingly audacious smash from Hazlewood on the up. When Cummins came on to play enforcer, Markram pulled him for six. Lyon, the spinner, was bowling by the 12th over rather than waiting to influence day five.Before long, Ackerman took over. Happy to hook whenever the opportunity came, he cleared fine leg for six from Cummins and belted Lyon out of the arena over midwicket. When Starc returned for a later spell, Ackerman smashed 18 off one over, hitting four boundaries in a row. Australia were shambolic, Travis Head dropping one of the easiest catches of his life at cover, spliced to him by Markram from Starc, then Lyon letting a return catch go through in the first over after lunch. With the score on 158, South Africa were 13 short of the record opening stand against Australia for a team being sent in, and the tourists looked set for a dismal day.It was Lyon who found a way through. With Ackerman determined not to temper his approach on 95, he ran at Lyon only to be outfoxed, a wider and slower ball evading his bat to bring about his stumping. Markram also perished while forging on, pulling a Hazlewood ball that had bounced nowhere high enough out to long leg, the first of many false shorts to short balls that found the hands of a fielder. That opened the door for Lyon to bowl Temba Bavuma, past the defensive outside edge, and Connolly to get his first Test wicket by burrowing past Matthew Breetzke’s inside edge, lbw on review.David Bedingham had played beautifully, driving with precision, and finally reached 50 having been out for 46 and 49 earlier in the series. But he went no further, also caught at fine leg hooking, Hazlewood dancing over the boundary and back to complete it, followed by Wiaan Mulder top-edging a hook off Starc for nought. Wicketless for 158 had become 216 for six.So it was time for South Africa’s rollercoaster to climb up again. Marco Jansen, so often the Australians’ chief cause of frustration, took them on once more, flaying the ageing ball for another half-century after his match-turning 85in the second Test. With Ryan Rickelton alongside him, they added 95 in good time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the first over with the new ball brought about the rollercoaster’s death-drop finale. Now with cloud cover at the end of the day, the ball began to swing, and Starc went back to his roots. No wobble-seam, no bouncers, just left-arm, over the wicket, inswinging menace. Rickelton nailed on the back pad, fourth ball of the over, for 42. Jansen two balls later, trying to drive, curling back to kiss the outside of off-stump, bowled for 52.First ball of Starc’s next over, Gerald Coetzee was bowled off his pads, backing away from that inswing, and while Kagiso Rabada survived the hat-trick ball, he was smashed in line with leg-stump from the one that followed. South Africa had lost four wickets for two runs, Starc finished with six for 72 and a day of Test cricket containing almost everything one could ask for was called to a close. The jury might remain out overnight if asked to decide who should be happier. Look for a verdict later this week.Explore more on these topicsCricketAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamAustralia sportmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blow | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Steve Borthwick has lost two key England squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Steve Borthwick has lost two key England squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg
Content: Bath’s Guy Pepper (left) and Bristol’s Benhard van Rensburg will be sidelined for several weeks due to injury.Composite: CameraSport/Getty Images; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBath’s Guy Pepper (left) and Bristol’s Benhard van Rensburg will be sidelined for several weeks due to injury.Composite: CameraSport/Getty Images; Getty ImagesEngland rugby union teamEngland’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blowBath flanker Pepper injured ankle at Gloucester on FridayBristol’s Van Rensburg advised to rest after two concussionsRobert KitsonTue 27 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s head coach, Steve Borthwick, said he will be monitoring this weekend’s domestic Prem games with some trepidation. Already he has lost at least two potentially key squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg, with doubts still hanging over his first-choice fly-half, Fin Smith, andfresh injury uncertaintyemerging on virtually a daily basis.Pepper’s involvement always looked improbable from the moment he sustained a nasty-looking ankle injury against Gloucester last Friday. The young Bath flanker will be sidelined for several weeks, as will the Bristol centre Van Rensburg who has been advised to rest and recuperate after two heavy concussions within the past three months.The Breakdown | England need to unearth World Cup core despite derby friction and injury chaosRead moreSmith, meanwhile, is still being treated for thecalf problem he sustainedagainst Leicester last Saturday. Borthwick says it remains “unclear at this stage” whether the Northampton fly-half will be available to face Australia next week. Calf injuries and kicking are not a great combination and England also need their tactical hub to be at the heart of their preparations.Borthwick, accordingly, will effectively want to make a call by the end of this week although England are slightly helped by the fact the Wallaby fixture is on a Sunday rather than 24 hours earlier. “Typically I would name the team for a Sunday game around the Wednesday, so that would still be my aim,” said Borthwick. “But if Fin’s not available for selection we also have some quality fly-halves in George Ford and Marcus Smith.”The Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has also limped away from training in Bagshot with a leg injury that will now be assessed, but there ismore encouraging newsregarding Seb Atkinson (knee) and Manny Feyi-Waboso (hamstring), both of whom should be available to play for Gloucester and Exeter respectively this weekend.Borthwick’s preference would probably be for both players to be tucked up on their sofas but under the terms of the joint agreement between the Rugby Football Union and the clubs, the latter can pick their international players once they are cleared by England’s medical staff. “If they’re fit then they’re available for selection,” said Borthwick. “That then comes down to the head coach or director of rugby of the club.”Either way it is a tense time for the national management who are having to do without their customary full extra week of training because of the need to shoehorn the new Nations Championship finals weekend into the calendar. Rugby players need to play rugby but, invariably, it comes with an element of risk attached. “Certainly there is a part of me watching these games and hoping the players get through the 80 minutes and are fit and available for next week,” said Borthwick.The stakes are further heightened by next year’s looming World Cup, with Borthwick having pointedly reminded his players that only nine Tests remain before England’s World Cup preparations enter their final stages. The primary message is that, for those intending to be on the plane to Australia, performing at the requisite level starts now. “This series of games this autumn is the last opportunity we have playing southern hemisphere opposition before we’re at that World Cup,” said Borthwick.“I’m looking forward to seeing players compete and perform against this calibre of opposition. You look at the power many of these southern hemisphere teams have. That’s a different challenge. When they come into camp again on Monday night, having recovered from their games, all that matters is performing the way we want to against Australia.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorthwick also brushed aside suggestions of potential discord after the fractious East Midlands derby between Leicester and Northampton where several of his squad were at loggerheads. The RFU sought to try to dilute any notion of friction by issuing a photo of Ollie Chessum and Henry Pollock with their arms cheerfully around each other and Borthwick has not yet deemed it necessary to pull anyone aside.“I actually think it’s a real strength of the game to be able to compete like that in that kind of full-blooded encounter – and then they’re perfectly fine. It’s a strength of English rugby that the players have such pride in their clubs … in modern day sport I see that as a positive. But when you come in [here] it’s all about the England team.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamSteve BorthwickRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona fined £503 over their approach for Atlético Madrid star Álvarez | European club football | The Guardian
description: Atlético accused Barcelona of not notifying them in advance with the striker now rebuilding his reputation after summer chase
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Atlético accused Barcelona of not notifying them in advance with the striker now rebuilding his reputation after summer chase
Content: Julián Álvarez’s form for Atlético Madrid is winning back fan support.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJulián Álvarez’s form for Atlético Madrid is winning back fan support.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean club footballBarcelona fined £503 over their approach for Atlético Madrid star ÁlvarezAtlético accused Barcelona during summer chaseStriker now rebuilding his reputation with fansReutersTue 27 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona’s pursuit of Julián Álvarez came at a modest cost ⁠on Tuesday after the Spanish FA fined the club €602 (£503) following a complaint byAtlético Madridover contact ⁠with ​the striker.Atlético accusedBarcelonaof approaching the Argentine, whose contract runs until June 2030, ⁠without first notifying them in writing.The sanction falls under Article 133 of the federation’s regulations. Atlético ⁠also complained to Fifa, which declared it had no ​jurisdiction over the case.For ‌Álvarez, the repair ‌work has been rather more public.The striker scored Atlético’s ‌winner against Deportivo La Coruna on Saturday, finding the net for a second successive match as his side moved within two points of theLa Ligaleaders Barcelona, before apologising for expressing his desire to join their rivals.“It ‌was a mistake. I understand why the fans are angry. If I were a fan, ​I’d be angry too. Especially given how they’ve supported me since I arrived,” Álvarez said referring to an interview during the 2026 World Cup in which he said that ⁠he “wanted to fulfil his dream” of playing for ​Barcelona, triggering ​a transfer dispute that ​stretched through the summer transfer window.Frequently booed by ​the home ‌fans this ​season, Álvarez ​received a standing ovation from sections of the crowd after scoring on Saturday, a sign of a thawing relationship with the Metropolitano faithful.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBarcelonaAtlético MadridLa LiganewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexia Putellas a worthy Ballon d’Or winner but the limited shortlist illustrates flaws | Women's football | The Guardian
description: Neglect of African football and a third win for the Spanish great does little to challenge narrative that the prize is reserved only for players of the top nations
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Neglect of African football and a third win for the Spanish great does little to challenge narrative that the prize is reserved only for players of the top nations
Content: Alexia Putellas won a record-equalling third Ballon d’Or Féminin after 14 goal contributions in 11 Women’s Champions League appearances last season.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas won a record-equalling third Ballon d’Or Féminin after 14 goal contributions in 11 Women’s Champions League appearances last season.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersMoving the Goalposts newsletterWomen's footballAlexia Putellas a worthy Ballon d’Or winner but the limited shortlist illustrates flawsNeglect of African football and a third win for the Spanish great does little to challenge narrative that the prize is reserved only for top nations’ playersTom GarryTue 27 Oct 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a four-year wait, Alexia Putellas is the queen of women’s football once again. Receiving the Ballon d’Orfor a record‑equalling third timeto continue Spain’s domination of the award, the 32-year-old reinforces her status as one of the greatest players of all time.It was the sixth consecutive year in which the honour went to either Putellas or her international teammate Aitana Bonmatí, and it was symbolic of Putellas’s resurgence after her comeback from the anterior cruciate ligament injuryshe sustainedin 2022, her refusal to surrender her career to that setback, and her majestic rise back to the top.Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney RonayRead moreThe midfielder’s competition‑leading 14 goal contributions – eight goals and six assists – in 11 Women’s Champions League appearances last season,helping Barcelona to liftthe trophy, went a long way to her securing the most votes, as well as her starring role in Spain’s victory in theNations League finalslast December. Her new club, London City Lionesses, will rejoice in the prestige ofhaving the Ballon d’Or winnerin their squad but Putellas, who spent 14 years at Barcelona, made it clear whom she wanted to thank. As she said in her acceptance speech: “This prize is for Barcelona.”Barcelona collected a clean sweep of the night’s bigger awards, with Cata Coll taking the goalkeeper prize, Pere Romeu the coach award and Vicky López the young player award, as well as Ewa Pajor finishing second behind Putellas for the main honour and Clara Serrajordi finishing second in the young player vote. It was almost a perfect night for the European champions, until their president, Joan Laporta, spoke bizarrely about his belief that their men’s team could win the Champions League this season, appearing to have eyes only for the men’s game despite specifically accepting the award for the women’s club of the year.That slip aside, the glamorous ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night passed without the sexist controversythat tarnished the early yearsafter France Football belatedly added the women’s award for the first time in 2018. Progress has been made – the women’s game does now at least receive a prize for the same categories as the men, but the event still does not quite offer full equality. Specifically, there is still not quite parity in the lengths of shortlists. Why, for example, were 10 players nominated for the men’s young talent award, but only five for the women’s? It was the same for the goalkeeper awards.The live show also demonstrated a disappointing lack of women’s players presenting prizes, aside from Lucy Bronze who was on stage to hand López her prize. Putellas receiving the Ballon d’Or Féminin from Michael Owen – rather than, perhaps Mia Hamm, Birgit Prinz or Sun Wen – perhaps served as a reminder that there are very few former winners of the women’s prize for the organisers to choose from – only Ada Hegerberg, Megan Rapinoe, Putellas and Bonmatí – because it was introduced so late.View image in fullscreenVicky López speaks after winning the young player award.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APMany fans will also have felt it was a shame that the dates covered by the relevant voting period – 3 August 2025 to 19 July 2026, effectively for last season – were based clearly on the conclusion of the men’s World Cup this summer, and therefore did not includethis year’s rearranged Wafcon,which was held from 26 July to 16 August. Performances at that tournament will instead be taken into account for next year’s prizes. It meant, for example, that Cameroon’s Wafcon‑winning head coach, Valentine Nguele, was not nominated for the coach of the year award, and there was an overall dearth of African players recognised, aside from Temwa Chawinga becoming the first African player to finish in the women’s top 10. Arguably she deserved to be even higher.Putellas was a very worthy winner of the main prize, although some will feel it is a missed opportunity for a player from one of the countries less likely to succeed in major international competitions to be recognised, given that the Women’s World Cup next year will inevitably ensure that the annual awards nights focus on whatever happens in Brazil. Poland’s Pajor, for example, finished second after a tremendous campaign with Barcelona but she feels unlikely to go one better next year, simply because of her nationality.The same goes for Jamaica’s Khadija Shaw, who came third after firing Manchester City to their first domestic title in a decade – although the fact that she made the top three in spite of not playing Champions League football said a lot about how revered she is. Haiti’s Melchie Dumornay – the best player Moving the Goalposts had the pleasure of seeing play live in the 2025-26 season – finished fourth. Aged 23, her time may well come in the future, but it is most likely to be in an even-numbered year.If Putellas continues her form, it would take a brave person to bet against her retaining her crown next year, as Spain target a successful defence of the world title. A humble role model for the sport, it is a privilege watching her grace the pitch with her deft touches, leadership and creativity and being a three-time Ballon d’Or winner is no less than her storied career deserves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGet in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailmoving.goalposts@theguardian.com.This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. To get the full edition,visit this page and follow the instructions. Moving the Goalposts is delivered to your inboxes every Tuesday and Thursday.double quotation mark“We were asking for intensity, fight and playing for the fans – we have that on the pitch from the starters. I think they were amazing. Caitlin Foord was a fighter and a warrior on the pitch today.” – Renée Slegers praised her team afterExplore more on these topicsWomen's footballMoving the Goalposts newsletterBallon d'OrfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Police called to Florida soccer game after parents say three-year-old benched for being too good | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Police were called to remove the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game in Florida over the weekend
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Police were called to remove the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game in Florida over the weekend
Content: The incident happened in Florida over the weekend.Photograph: David Madison/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe incident happened in Florida over the weekend.Photograph: David Madison/Getty ImagesSoccerPolice called to Florida soccer game after parents say three-year-old benched for being too goodOrganizer says parents were causing disturbanceNo one arrested or made to leave game in FloridaGuardian sportTue 27 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice were called after a dispute involving the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game inFloridaover the weekend.The boy’s parentscan be heard on police body camerassaying their son, Nevada, had been kicked out because he was too good at soccer and was embarrassing the other children. However, an organizer at the game said Nevada had pushed other children and his parents had become argumentative when their son was taken out of the game.In police body camera footage the organizer of the event, who works for i9 Sports, a youth sports group, can be heard saying Nevada’s parents had caused a disturbance.“The kid is good. He’s great. Really good,” the organizer says in the footage. “He’s very advanced compared to the other ones, so he’s scoring a lot of goals. But he’s pushing the kids ... So, I try to tell him, don’t push; we want to play without pushing, right?”In audio of the 911 call, the organizer says Nevada’s mother was being “really, really disruptive, following me around and calling me names in front of this whole bunch of people.”Nevada’s parentsposted a clip of their sonat the event in which he can be seen dribbling around older children with ease. The video has since gone viral. Nevada cannot be seen pushing any other children in the footage posted by his parents.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. They’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” his mother says in the body camera footage. “First, they said he’s not passing, but nobody’s catching the ball when he’s passing.”The i9 Sports worker told police they were willing to give Nevada’s parents a refund if they left.“I just want him out. Immediately,” the organizer told police. “Just give me their names so I can give them their refund.”The Winter Park Police Department said the family agreed to leave the event and no one was arrested.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers,” the department wrote in a statement on its website. “No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park.”i9 Sports said it was reviewing the incident and had contacted Nevada’s family.“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” i9 Sports said in a statement. “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us.”One officer appeared to want to see more of Nevada though. “I kind of want to see him play. I bet he’s good,” he can be heard saying to another officer on body camera.Explore more on these topicsFootballFloridaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kylian Mbappé apologises after being dropped by Chinese brands for Mao Zedong comment | Kylian Mbappé | The Guardian
description: Kylian Mbappé has apologised for his ‘ill-judged’ comment about the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong, which has led to brands in China dropping the Real Madrid forward
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kylian Mbappé has apologised for his ‘ill-judged’ comment about the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong, which has led to brands in China dropping the Real Madrid forward
Content: Bottled electrolyte drinks endorsed by Kylian Mbappé before the sports drink company Dongpeng was one of two China brands to end deals with the footballer.Photograph: Liu Junfeng/VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBottled electrolyte drinks endorsed by Kylian Mbappé before the sports drink company Dongpeng was one of two China brands to end deals with the footballer.Photograph: Liu Junfeng/VCG/Getty ImagesKylian MbappéKylian Mbappé apologises after being dropped by Chinese brands for Mao Zedong commentVideo appears to show Mao Zedong called a ‘dictator’Dongpeng and Mengniu end deals with the playerAgence France-PresseTue 27 Oct 2026 07.54 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 02.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people inChinaand in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.Harry Kane claims men’s Ballon d’Or to end England’s 25-year wait for winnerRead moreSpain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.View image in fullscreenTwo Chinese brands have ended deals with Kylian Mbappé after he allegedly referred to Mao Zedong as a ‘Chinese dictator’.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageIn an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kanein the Ballon d’Or awardfor the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to Chinasuspending sponsorship deals with the NBAand pulling games off Chinese television for a year.Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”Explore more on these topicsKylian MbappéChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
Content: Mohmed Abdulkarim (left) and Nouman Essghir appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenMohmed Abdulkarim (left) and Nouman Essghir appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PAUK newsRAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court toldHelena HortonTue 27 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 05.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.Abdulkarim, of London, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service. He is accused of buying the vans used in the Fairford incident on the instruction of Ali.Essghir, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, after initially being arrested at the scene near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September and then re-arrested on 20 October. He is accused of visiting RAF Fairford and filming around the facility on a video call with Ali before returning a month later in the convoy of vans.Abdulkarim has been released on bail under conditions including the surrender of his passport, and Essghir has been remanded in custody. They will appear at the Old Bailey on 20 November.Prosecutor Louise Gray alleged the defendants were in contact with an individual known as Ali who is now believed to be abroad.She said that during the events of 27 September at the RAF Fairford base, five men who were arrested travelled in vans, parked and got out “and were told to do so by someone known as Mr Ali”.One of them, she said, had claimed they were told there was a bomb in the van and called 999.The court heard that the person calling stated that they were from London and that he was one of a group of five males. The caller told the police that they had been tasked to drive vans to the location for the purpose of a new business venture. When the vans arrived at the location, the organiser was in communication with them over the telephone.Gray alleged he then told them to park the vans and to walk away from them. After they did that, the organiser told them to run as he had planted a bomb in the van. The caller indicated that he and his colleagues had run away from the vans and were now calling the police for help.The defendants are believed to have known Ali for “a number of years”, she said.Essghir is accused of travelling to RAF Fairford on 22 August and contacting Ali.Abdulkarim is accused of buying mobile phones and collecting cash for Ali, as well as buying five vans including the three that were driven to RAF Fairford.The court heard he had known Ali for 10 years and it was claimed the latter had been linked to a drone incident at the Israeli embassy.Counter Terror Policing said they believed the foreign intelligence service involved in the case was Iranian.The assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said: “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat.“The public can help us with this, and as always I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national who was also arrested on 20 October on suspicion of aiding Iran’s intelligence service has been released without charge but remains on police bail after being arrested on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford. We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content
