title: ‘Well-known’ public figure in bid to stop publication of allegations of inappropriate sexual activities | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Individual seeks permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN to block claims, citing high risk of suicide
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Individual seeks permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN to block claims, citing high risk of suicide
Content: In written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a ‘wide-ranging and rigorous investigation’.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a ‘wide-ranging and rigorous investigation’.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesUK criminal justice‘Well-known’ public figure in bid to stop publication of allegations of inappropriate sexual activitiesIndividual seeks permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN to block claims, citing high risk of suicideMichael SavageMedia editorTue 27 Oct 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA “well-known individual” attempting to block two media outlets from publishing allegations about him has been accused of inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities with girls and young women, the high court has heard.The individual, referred to in court as PPT, is seeking a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies. His legal team argued that publishing them would “highly likely lead him to commit suicide”.In written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a “wide-ranging and rigorous investigation”.However, at the opening of a two-day trial, PPT’s legal team argued it was a “highly exceptional” case in which publishing was likely to lead to the death of the claimant.In a written submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team said that he suffered from “very severe mental health problems”.“It is important to understand that this drastic effect on the claimant is not from guilt of the wrongdoing alleged (which is denied) but because of shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of ‘trial by media’,” it stated.Sara Mansoori KC, PPT’s lead barrister, said that he had first attempted to commit suicide in May, when the Guardian and ITN contacted him to give him the chance to respond to the allegations. He was admitted to hospital that afternoon as a voluntary patient.The court was told PPT made a second attempt to take his life in July, “on that occasion absconding from a secure hospital to do so”.Submissions to the court by PPT’s legal team stated he is detained in a psychiatric hospital for his own safety and has no intention of returning to public life.The claimant is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life, article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment” and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.Setting out the claimant’s case, Mansoori pointed to medical evidence that PPT’s life would be endangered should the allegations be published.“It would be a travesty if the court didn’t step in to act in these circumstances,” Mansoori said.According to written submissions from the news outlets, they will argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never required a state to prevent publication of journalism in order to protect against the risk of suicide by an individual.The written submissions argue that any duties the state has towards PPT should come in the form of NHS mental health treatment and its powers under the Mental Health Act.The news outlets will set out their case to the court on Wednesday.An independent expert assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing stated that “community arrangements” would not be sufficient to manage the immediate suicide risk around the prospect of publishing the allegations.“Publication while the claimant remains in an inpatient psychiatric setting would be significantly safer in terms of reducing the likelihood of a successful suicide,” the expert concluded, according to a summary of his findings.“The expert does not conclude either that suicide is inevitable if publication occurs, or that psychiatric treatment can eliminate all risk,” the expert’s report states.Mr Justice Nicklin, the judge overseeing the case, opened the trial with a warning about online speculation over PPT’s identity.“That speculation has named several different individuals,” he said. “This is a difficult and important case. The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions, while respecting both the principle of open justice and the protective purpose of the orders already made.“I ask that the court be allowed to perform that task without further attempts to identify PPT or any other person whose identity is protected.”The trial continues.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceInjunctionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Parents inflicted fatal physical and sexual abuse on their baby, Warwick court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Michal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to death of 13-month-old Isabella Stasiak
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Michal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to death of 13-month-old Isabella Stasiak
Content: Isabella Stasiak’s parents were known to social services and the police, the court was toldPhotograph: Warwickshire policeIsabella Stasiak’s parents were known to social services and the police, the court was toldPhotograph: Warwickshire policeUK newsParents inflicted fatal physical and sexual abuse on their baby, Warwick court hearsMichal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to  death of 13-month-old Isabella StasiakNeha GohilMidlands correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 13-month-old girl was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of her parents before she was fatally injured by her mother, a court has heard.Michal Stasiak, 28, and Kinga Wydrzynska, 26, appeared at Warwick crown court on Tuesday, where they pleaded not guilty to 11 counts related to the death of Isabella Stasiak.Wydrzynska is charged with Isabella’s murder, while both parents have been charged with one count of causing or allowing the death of a child, four counts of causing or allowing serious physical harm to a child, two counts related to the sexual assault of a child and three counts of child cruelty.The court heard both parents were known to social services and the police.Isabella died in hospital after sustaining a series of injuries including a fractured skull and ribs, a broken arm and a burn to her entire face, the court was told.In her opening statement to the court on Tuesday, Annabel Darlow KC said emergency services were called to the Wydrzynska’s home in the early hours of 7 January 2025 where Isabella was found “grey and lifeless”.Medical experts later concluded Isabella died “because she suffered injuries consistent with a forceful direct impact to her head against a hard surface”, Darlow told the court.Darlow said Wydrzynska was the only adult present at the home when Isabella was found by police and the injuries were the “devastating culmination of systematic physical abuse”.“The prosecution say, by the time Isabella died, there was an entrenched pattern of abuse, neglect and mistreatment of the little girl of which both parents were entirely aware,” Darlow told the court.“Before she died, Isabella was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of both her mother and father,” Darlow added. “Neither defendant has ever provided any explanation for those injuries to their daughter.”Jurors were told Isabella was born in December 2023 and immediately taken into the care of social services. After being placed in emergency accommodation, Isabella was looked after by foster parents for four months before she was returned to her parents in April 2024 – nine months before her death, the court was told.Members of the jury were also told Stasiak was arrested by police for common assault after a report was made by Wydrzynska on 14 December 2024, less than a month before Isabella’s death.Wydrzynska made repeated attempts to withdraw the report, jurors were told. However, Stasiak was placed on police bail and prohibited from living at the family home or contacting Wydrzynska.In addition, the court was told police officers had attended the family home after a complaint was made by a neighbour in October 2024.Officers attended the property and were only responded to when the police threatened to force entry, Darlow said. Officers spoke to the parents and saw Isabella and “did not have any immediate safeguarding concerns” after the visit, the court was told.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts | Heat pumps | The Guardian
description: Boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £9,000 for sustainable alternatives, expected to be slashed in budget
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £9,000 for sustainable alternatives, expected to be slashed in budget
Content: ‘It’s going to damage us as a company,’ said Bill Tuck, operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford.View image in fullscreen‘It’s going to damage us as a company,’ said Bill Tuck, operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford.Heat pumps‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cutsBoiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £9,000 for sustainable alternatives, expected to be slashed in budgetMatthew PearceTue 27 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”But despite asurge in interestin cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to beslashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumpsas it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget.Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, the operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging.“Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.”Theboiler upgrade scheme(BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers.Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a“critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. The UKlags far behind other European countrieswith heat pump installation; Norway, the global leader, has 632 installed for every 1,000 households, while the UK has a paltry 3.5.View image in fullscreenJim Lacey: ‘The whole argument’s gone.’Jim Lacey, who has been installing renewables with his business JLN Plumbing & Heating for 20 years, said: “No one’s going to save the planet if it really hits their pocket.”“We can go in [to homes] now and go: ‘It’s a few hundred pound more than having a normal boiler, but you save so much on your energy usage.’ That whole argument’s gone.”Adam Killa, the founder of Ask Renewables in Burscough, Lancashire, saw what happens when subsidies are removed after the 2022 closure of theRenewable Heat Incentive, a scheme that paid households for generating clean heat.“As soon as that stopped, we went from doing six, seven, eight [installs] a week down to zero. The customers say: ‘Well, I know they’re good, but 15 grand – I can buy a new boiler for three grand. What’s the point?’While the government continues its drive to increase numbers of young people earning while learning, heat pump installers say cuts to the subsidy will put their apprentices – and the future of the industry – are at risk.View image in fullscreenAdam Killa: ‘Customers say: what’s the point?’“Unless we start bringing the young generation through, we’re going to have a huge lack of installers, repair engineers, and more importantly, heat pumps as well,” said Tuck.A nascent industry, installers fear manufacturers will go under too.According to the Heat Pump Association, about a third of heat pumps sold in the UK in 2024 were produced domestically.“This isn’t just down to us fitting the heat pumps, it’s the people delivering them, it’s the people manufacturing them, it’s all the associated trades that go with it that make the little bits, the little bobs, everything,” said Lacey. “There’s so many knock-on effects”James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the green thinktank Verdant, said removing money from green jobs and manufacturing would damage Andy Burnham’s mission to effectively reindustrialise Britain. “It’s at a point where his blank spot on climate is working hard against other things he wants to do,” he said.Lacey said that, while he had not thought the grant would last for ever, he had expected business and consumers to be weaned off gradually as the technology became more widespread and production costs fell. “But to suddenly axe some off the BUS grant or get rid of it completely is just catastrophic for all the work that we’ve put in so far,” he said.A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on budget speculation.“We remain committed to bringing down bills for families now, while investing in the clean, homegrown energy and warmer homes that will protect households from volatile fossil fuel prices for good.”Explore more on these topicsHeat pumpsBudget 2026Environment policyGasEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups  | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans
Content: Members of the Save Brick Lane campaign protested against the construction of an AI datacentre in the east London neighbourhood in June.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMembers of the Save Brick Lane campaign protested against the construction of an AI datacentre in the east London neighbourhood in June.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianDatacentres - UKUK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groupsInvestigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plansAisha DownGlobal technology reporterTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found.The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026.Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry.Kamila Kingstone, a campaign lead at the NGO, said: “The government totally failed at the most senior level to speak to environmental NGOs or community groups when developing its flagship policy on AI datacentres. This is despite the serious environmental implications of its plans.”Over 12 months, Spotlight on Corruption filed 40 freedom of information requests to 18 government agencies, seeking details of meetings and investment figures relating to the government’s policymaking on the growth zones, covering the period between July 2024 and June 2026.The investigation foundthat ministers, permanent secretaries and directors general involved in developing the policy met 137 businesses – some several times – to discuss Britain’s datacentre policy. By contrast, senior officials met only two community groups and no environmental organisations.View image in fullscreenApproval has been given for a £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, east London, to include a datacentre.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianOf the 38 senior officials who left government, nine were from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which has played a central role in shaping Britain’s AI strategy. These included a former minister for AI and intellectual property, a former AI adviser to the prime minister, a former director of AI opportunities, a deputy director of AI international policy and a head of AI engineering.AI growth zones were a groundbreaking policy under which the government promised to “turbochargethe economy” and create jobs bybuildingmassive datacentres across five regions – in Starmer’s words, “mainlining AI into the veins” of the country.The policy aimed to pave the way for Britain to build big datacentres, some of them larger than any datacentre that has been built in the country so far. These developments, often partnered with US tech companies, would supposedly bring in thousands of jobs.Investigationsby the Guardian have called the policy into question, suggesting that it rests on assumptions that do not hold up, financial figures that were not audited and exaggerated projections for job creation.In particular, the Guardian has shown there islittle realismbehind announced plans to power these developments, and claims that they will use purpose-built renewables. In fact, different government departmentsappear to divergeon how much electricity the UK’s datacentre plans will actually require – and what their environmental cost will therefore be.Meanwhile, there has been growing opposition to datacentres in Britain, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging fromAuchtertool, a rural village north of Edinburgh, toBrick Lanein east London.View image in fullscreenFourteen local campaigns rallied in September at Holyrood against datacentres planned in Scotland.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianChi Onwurah, the MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the growing backlash – and the far larger opposition in the US – was a warning that the government needed to seek greater community input.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is critically important that AI benefits communities and is also shaped by them,” she said. “I’ve been concerned about what we’ve seen in the US, where there’s a strong feeling that datacentres are being imposed without adequate consultation. We can see the backlash influencing the midterms. It’s really important that communities are involved in datacentres and AI growth zones and see the benefits.”Spotlight on Corruption’s investigation suggests that previous policy was largely shaped by conversations with business, and that the government “failed to take the environmental and social impacts [of datacentres] seriously”.While the government met a handful of civil society groups, these meetings were “held a few days before the launch of the policy, meaning they had no meaningful input”, according to the report.Finally, many further meetings between businesses and Starmer’s administration would not have been disclosed, said Spotlight on Corruption. This is largely because Starmer’s policy was led by a special adviser, Jade Leung, whose role was subject to far less stringent transparency requirements.Spotlight on Corruption also looked at how other countries – including Canada, Germany and Australia – developed policy. It found these countries consulted far more widely on introducing datacentres and had more stringent environmental criteria. It said the UK had “fallen behind equivalent jurisdictions” in developing an equitable strategy.A government spokesperson said: “We are clear that datacentres should create British jobs, strengthen supply chains and deliver benefits for the communities that host them, while prioritising clean power and using water responsibly – and meet with these companies to make sure that happens. We want to work closely with industry, local authorities, environmental groups and communities, and welcome opportunities to hear their views.“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes. We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKPlanning policyAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingFreedom of informationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Letter to PM argues series of wrong choices on North Sea oil, Heathrow, EVs and heat pumps will scupper net zero plans
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Letter to PM argues series of wrong choices on North Sea oil, Heathrow, EVs and heat pumps will scupper net zero plans
Content: Climate campaigners in London earlier this month protesting against the possible approval of drilling at the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenClimate campaigners in London earlier this month protesting against the possible approval of drilling at the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAEnvironment policyBurnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaignersLetter to PM argues series of wrong choices on North Sea oil, Heathrow, EVs and heat pumps will scupper net zero plansFiona HarveyEnvironment editorTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said.Big decisions onNorth Sea drilling, theexpansion of Heathrow airport,electric vehicles(EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers.But they should be considered in the context of their cumulative impacts rather than be taken separately by different government departments, according to Greenpeace andFriends of the Earth(FoE) in a letter to the prime minister.Taken together, the emissions resulting from approving drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, expanding Heathrow airport, watering down the UK’s EV targets and cutting heat pump grants would be 402m tonnes of CO2over the next 25 years, the letter says.The emissions would be greater than those of 106 coal plants running for a year, more than enough to prevent the UK meeting its carbon budgets and net zero.Doug Parr, chief scientist atGreenpeace, said: “The Burnham government is facing a series of big decisions over the next few months that could define its legacy on climate. This administration seems to get the urgency of cutting the emissions causing deadly heatwaves and droughts, but there’s a real risk they could still sleepwalk into reversing the strong progress the UK has made so far.”Last week, the governmentgave the go-ahead to drill the Jackdaw gasfield, despite warnings that it would create only 27 new jobs, fail to cut the cost of living, and add little to UK tax revenues. Now, the North Sea fossil fuel industry ispressing for a green lightto the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, which would produce higher emissions.Car manufacturers havelobbied hard for the government to water down its mandate to ensure all new car and van sales are electric by 2035, by allowing as many as half of sales to be petrol or diesel in 2030, which would mean falling far short of the current target of 80% electric by then. Given the long life of vehicles, this could produce future emissions equal to about 60% of the emissions from Rosebank,according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank.Airlines are also pressing for an expansion of Heathrow, which thechancellor, John Healey, strongly favoursin the belief that it could increase economic growth. Campaigners challenge this analysis, arguing the UK is already embarking on airport expansion at Gatwick.In his budget on Wednesday,Healey is also likely to cut the boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants to households installing heat pumps in place of gas boilers, despite thesavings on gas use that it representsand the slow speed of the transition to electric heating so far.Parr said: “Decisions about Rosebank, Heathrow expansion, electric vehicle targets or heat pump funding should not be rushed through or made in isolation – ministers need to be far-sighted and keep track of their cumulative impact on our climate. The carbon bill may take a while to turn up, but there’s hell to pay when it does.”If Burnham were to reject these high-carbon plans, the UK could build a cleaner, more equal and more prosperous society, added Imogen Dow, climate lead at FoE. Renewable energy couldbring down bills, particularly amid soaring oil and gas prices, and thenet zero economy has grown faster than the rest of the economy, according to the CBI.Dow said: “Delivering on our climate goals is not solely a win for the planet – it will alsostrengthen the economy, lower household bills, improve public health and protect the places we call home.“At a time when powerful vested interests are pushing the world towards climate catastrophe, it’s more important than ever that governments like the UK stand strong.”A government spokesperson said: “Reindustrialisation will never mean reneging on our climate obligations and net zero. Over the past two years, clean power has secured £110bn in announced investment and supported thousands of jobs through our record renewable energy auctions.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironment policyClimate crisisGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelsAutomotive industryOil and gas companiesProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events
Content: People watch waves from the Pacific Ocean crashing into a seawall amid powerful surf on 9 October in Long Beach, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople watch waves from the Pacific Ocean crashing into a seawall amid powerful surf on 9 October in Long Beach, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesEl Niño southern oscillationTrump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warnPresident has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather eventsGabrielle CanonTue 27 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US facesa cascade of hazardsfueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter.From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, cancelingcontracts and grants,and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025.The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices.This column chart shows the workforce losses at NOAA since 2015. In general, over the years losses and gains have been +/- 500 jobs until 2025 when there were over 2,000 jobs lost. This data comes from the Office of Personnel Management.The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has sent morale plummeting, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps.“The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central.That test could soon be coming.This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected tostrengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, landslides and flash floods.“Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said.Noaa plays a pivotal role in public safety and provides key insights and forecasts relied upon by a vast array of communities and industries, from weather shifts that could affect crop schedules, to emergency response preparations when hurricanes are brewing or fire conditions are aligning. The agency operates early warning systems for tsunamis, monitors seafood supply chains and provides ocean data needed for safe shipping and port operators.View image in fullscreenWaves crash into damaged homes as a powerful ocean surge and very high tides generated by Tropical Storm Rachel batter the southern California coastline on 11 October.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesWhile the losses are expected to have a profound effect on the American public, they will be felt globally, too. Scientists and forecasters around the world depend on Noaa satellites, studies and intelligence, including data-sharing arrangements that track severe weather across Europe, coordination for disaster response in the Caribbean, and deforestation monitoring and the effects of the climate crisis in the Amazon rainforest.“I worry about loss of life and about our inability to be protected at a time when we need our government the most,” said Monica Medina, who served as the principal deputy administrator of Noaa during the Obama administration.The risks are but a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. “If this is a real test” of a hotter, more precarious future, she added, “we’re going to flunk”.Budget and research cutsGaps in staffing, operations and engagement with the public are the top three concerns for Rick Spinrad, who spent three decades at the agency and served as Noaa administrator for the Biden administration.The agency was already shorthanded in those areas when Trump took office, according to Spinrad. But since January 2025, Noaa has lost more than 3,000 staffers, according to workforce data from the US office of personnel management that was last updated in August this year.It’s the biggest staffing drop in the last decade, and includes hundreds of people who lost their jobs during massive layoffs or who took incentives to retire or resign as the administration worked to systemically shrink the size of the federal government last year, along with those who left voluntarily.Some departments have been hit harder than others.The public affairs team that helps disseminate important information was roughly halved. Information technology management workers, who provide vital support for forecasting and data infrastructure among other things, were reduced by roughly 27%. The data showed a loss of more than 500 staffers across a range of science positions with only 46 new hires.There were also about 10% fewer meteorologists and meteorology technicians as the US went into autumn this year, even after theNational Weather Service rushed to staff upin theaftermath of the Trump administration’s massive 2025 layoffs.View image in fullscreenWorkers at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) Center for Weather and Climate Prediction headquarters in College Park, Maryland, on 5 December 2024.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe NWS analyzes and collects roughly 6.3bn observations each day. They release 1.5m forecasts and up to 50,000 warnings each year. Cracks have begun to show as the agencyhas tried to takes on its enormous and essential workload with fewer people.Staffers had towork double shiftsto keep some forecasting offices open, the Washington Post reported last September. Staffers who spoke to the Post at the time described an agency pushed to its limits.Only 40 meteorologists were added to the ranks across Noaa between January and August this year, with hundreds of vacancies across the country still open as a tumultuous winter approaches.Overall, the agency was able to bring on just 525 new hires since January 2025, leaving a gaping 2,500-person deficit.Already, staffing limitations have shown up in delayed or limited weather balloon launches that leftparts of the Great Plains unprepared for tornadoesand limited warnings to rural communities in Alaska, where more than 1,500 people were displaced by floods earlier this year. The NWS alsofailed to adequately provide multilingual weather alertsdue to staffing and funding cuts, the government accountability office (GAO) found, leaving 26 million people in the US at higher risk.“There has been this hollowing out – there’s no time to do anything other than the very basics,” said Dr Anna Zivian, a climate researcher and policy expert. “I suspect we haven’t seen the worst outcomes from the loss of capacity yet. You can’t pick up that kind of slack.”View image in fullscreenWaves batter the shoreline in Laguna Beach, California, during a period of high tides associated with El Niño on 26 October.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersMeanwhile, the Trump administration terminated dozens of grants representing a loss inmore than $28m in funding for states, cities, non-profits and universities, according to calculations from Grant Witness, an organization that tracks science-related grant making by the federal government. Climate research has been the most affected, according to their analysis, which found that the number of grant awards in fiscal year 2026 was 37% lower than the 2021-2024 average.Despite these concerns, the administration has outlined more plans to slash budgets and research capacity.Trump has proposed cutting$1.6bnin Noaa funding – a26%drop – for next year’s budget. While many of the cuts won’t make it through the budget process, they showcase how the president views the essential services the agency provides the American public and puts more pressure on the staff still working at Noaa.“People at Noaa are nervous,” Di Liberto said, adding that employees across the organization were afraid they would get in trouble if they said something that conflicted with the administration’s anti-climate narrative.“You want people doing their best work when we face these extremes,” he said. Denials of human-caused climate crisis coming from the top have only made their jobs harder, as scientists and forecasters work to put urgent information into context for the American public and others around the world.“It’s incredibly difficult,” Di Liberto said. “Imagine being told the number six doesn’t exist and then being asked to do math.”A missed learning opportunityAn El Niño year can be high risk, but it’s also an incredible chance to learn and prepare, offering a glimpse of what the world might expect as temperatures rise. In that regard, experts worry a shrunken Noaa is missing a vital research opportunity.“This El Niño is so useful in a sense of getting an understanding about where we stand for dealing with extreme weather around the world,” Di Liberto said. “Unfortunately we’re going to learn a lot this winter about our ability to deal with multiple extremes happening at the same time.”He and other experts have also expressed concerns that not enough has been done to ready communities for the coming hazards or capture important data that will inform the future. “When it comes to preparing for El Niño events – or any weather extreme – the preparation happens during the off season,” he said.During the last strong El Niño a decade ago, the agency deployed planes, weather balloons, unmanned aircraft and a research ship to collect data. This year, only “a handful of unmanned watercraft” will be deployed into the Pacific, NPR reported in September.View image in fullscreenProtesters gather outside the headquarters of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) in Silver Spring, Maryland, to protest job cuts at the agency.Photograph: Jay Mallin/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockTheTrump administration had also begun removing ocean monitoring systems that provide important data during El Niño, butrestored them after widespread outcryfrom scientists, fishers and public officials.Roughly $6bn has been shaved off an investment secured for weather satellites that would have propelled major advancements in future weather predictions. The sharp reduction couldcreate a gap in satellite coverage, according to an analysis from the government accountability office, severely disrupting data.Fundingfor a decade-long project to monitor the oceansusing autonomous robotic devices called biogeochemical-argo floats – part of a global effort – will also expire at the end of October.A Noaa spokesperson responded that efforts to monitor and collect data this year have built on past efforts by using “new, cutting-edge technologies” that were previously unavailable.“NOAA has never been more equipped to study, prepare for and respond to an ENSO event [El Niño southern oscillation event],” a Noaa spokesperson said in an emailed statement that highlighted updated modeling tools and the use of uncrewed systems. “These advanced capabilities have allowed NOAA to streamline resources and study this year’s El Niño more effectively than ever before.”Spinrad and other experts agreed that new technologies had helped advance data collection and improve forecasting ability.“We are more capable than we have been in the past because of the developments in the technology, the satellites that we’re flying, the observing systems that we’ve put in place,” Spinrad said. “But everything that this administration is doing suggests that we cannot and will not sustain those capabilities. So the real question is – are we at a turning point now?”This article was updated on 27 October 2026 to include a response from Noaa issued after publication and to add that an ocean monitoring program had been reinstated.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationTrump administrationOceansExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Change to carer’s allowance cliff-edge rule is not enough, victims say | Carer's allowance | The Guardian
description: Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with unjust overpayments still have to pay
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with unjust overpayments still have to pay
Content: Guy and Oksana Shahar, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were issued with a bill for more than £10,000 when Oksana earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGuy and Oksana Shahar, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were issued with a bill for more than £10,000 when Oksana earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCarer's allowanceChange to carer’s allowance cliff-edge rule is not enough, victims sayDigital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with overpayments will still have to payPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorTue 27 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,” says unpaid carer Guy Shahar of the government’s decision toabolish the notorious carer’s allowance cliff edge.But Shahar is angry that most carers hit with unjust overpayments in the past will still have to repay them, for all the promise of a different future. And he notes that the cliff edge remains in place for four more years, potentially catching out more carers.“They are effectively saying: ‘We know that the system was unfair but we will still punish you for having been the victim of an unfair system,’” he says.The chancellor is expected to announce the introduction of a new digital taper system into the carer’s allowance benefit in the budget, in effect ending a rule that has landed hundreds of thousands of carers with life-shattering financial penalties.Unpaid carers have broadly welcomed the move – and there is a general acknowledgment that ministers are moving positively, if slowly, to reform a system with inbuilt injustices and terrible management that birthed what became known as thecarer’s allowance scandal.But there is also disbelief that the new system – which must be built from scratch – will be live before 2030, and a feeling that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has a lot more to do to regain the trust of unpaid carers.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, says the cliff edge symbolises a ‘whole crazy system’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianShahar and his wife, Oksana, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were victims of the cliff edge. This rule meant that a carer who earns more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – will forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, now £86.45.A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40. Last year, the Shahars werelanded with a £10,000 repayment billfor relatively trivial earnings breaches dating back five years.Oksana had earned more than the allowed limit by just £1.92 a week on average while juggling caring with part-time minimum wage jobs. In some weeks, she was paid just 38p more than the carer’s allowance earnings threshold.Over the period, she earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed – but was duly issued with a bill for £10,130.45 – plus a £50 civil penalty. The Shahars are challenging the charge at tribunal but the stress is real and ongoing.Unpaid carer Elizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, is staggered that the taper system is years away: “We live in the age of tech; it is ludicrous it is going to take so long. They need to make it a priority.”Tait, a former teacher and now a private tutor and educational consultant whoended up with a bill for £1,623after unwittingly breaching the earnings threshold, says the carer’s allowance cliff edge symbolises a “whole crazy system”.Reforming carer’s allowance is essential but it needs to be part of a wider examination of the crucial role of unpaid care in propping up England’s social care arrangements, she says: “We care willingly and lovingly, and yet we end up a casualty of the system.”Andrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, is one of a handful of carers tochallenge a cliff edge penalty and win, successfully overturning a £4,600 overpayment at a tribunal in February 2025.View image in fullscreenAndrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, challenged the cliff edge penalty and won but says it cost her months of stress.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAs a result, she did not have to repay the money, although she suffered months of stress along the way. She welcomes the decision to introduce a taper but believes carers punished unfairly by draconian rules should be compensated.“People repaying overpayments should no longer have to, and they should be given back what they have already paid,” she says.Tucker recalls how for years she carefully monitored her monthly earnings from her part-time charity shop role to stay under the limit. Some weeks she would work six hours for nothing so as not to risk losing carer’s allowance.Even so, she was hit with an overpayment when DWP officials decided – unlawfully – that she could not average her earnings over a one-year period.There is raw bitterness among carers about the cliff edge, she says. “My friend is paying back their overpayment at £10 a month. She went £12.50 over as a result of receiving holiday pay. She always tells me: ‘I hope I die before I have paid it all back.’”Explore more on these topicsCarer's allowanceBudgetCarersSocial careState benefitsBenefitsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand told police he led a ‘very promiscuous’ life, trial hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Comedian accused of sexual offences against six women said consensual encounters were ‘unfavourably reframed decades later’
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Comedian accused of sexual offences against six women said consensual encounters were ‘unfavourably reframed decades later’
Content: Russell Brand leaving Southwark crown court in London on Tuesday. He denies all seven charges against him.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand leaving Southwark crown court in London on Tuesday. He denies all seven charges against him.Photograph: James Manning/PAUK newsRussell Brand told police he led a ‘very promiscuous’ life, trial hearsComedian accused of sexual offences against six women said consensual encounters were ‘unfavourably reframed decades later’Emine SinmazTue 27 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand told police he had led a “very promiscuous” life and consensual sexual encounters had been “unfavourably reframed decades later”, his trial has heard.The 51-year-old comedian blamed the allegations on “defamatory and fictitious” media reports. He said in a statement that he had had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios and kissed hundreds of people in public while trying to be “friendly, consensual and warm”.Brand is accused of seven offences against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Wearing a grey suit and pale blue shirt, he sat in the dock on Tuesday as his statements to police were read to Southwark crown court in London.The jury was told Brand was interviewed four times between November 2023 and July 2025, when he read prepared statements in which he insisted he had “never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity”.“I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I have spent years openly denouncing,” he said in his first statement on 16 November 2023.Referencing joint reporting by Channel 4, the Times and the Sunday Times, Brand added: “On 16 September 2023, a defamatory and fictitious documentary was broadcast in conjunction with the publication of two national newspapers containing false, anonymised allegations which led to unprecedented media reporting.“Subsequently, both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which resulted in further encounters being invented or reimagined.”Addressing an allegation that he had touched an MTV worker’s breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her in 2004, he said he did not recall meeting the woman.“At no point would I have touched [her] breasts unless it was consensual,” he said. “I have had consensual sex in toilet cubicles during parties. I have never forced anyone into a toilet and I have never forced my penis into anyone’s mouth.”In a statement on 14 December 2023, Brand said he did not remember the women who had come forward to accuse him.But he added: “It is entirely possible that I may have encountered them and that we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that has since been reimagined.”Brand described aspects of his past celebrity lifestyle, saying: “My engagement with interested members of the public was friendly, consensual and warm. There was often physical contact. At live shows, press events, junkets and book signings I did my best to be accessible, non-discriminatory and loving. I spent a lot of time at these events.“I have shared kisses with hundreds of members of the public during press events and photos of many such kisses, in front of hundreds of people, are available online. Everything I did in public once I was famous could be photographed or recorded and end up in the tabloids – I was aware of this.“I routinely made provocative jokes or comments both with members of the public and during live performances and broadcasts.”He also went on to detail his promiscuity, saying: “I did on occasion find reasons for leaving, or for asking partners in casual sexual encounters to leave, shortly after the experience had concluded.“I had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios often with people I had just met. The way of life that I have described, the magnitude of the promiscuity, deceptively rendered in recent media attacks, accompanied by advertisements for complainants, have caused consensual encounters to be unfavourably reframed decades later.”Brand gave similar statements to police in his subsequent interviews on 17 January 2024 and 17 July 2025. In response to police questions after each statement, Brand said: “I have nothing further to add at this time.”Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: Retailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacks
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Retailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacks
Content: UK supermarkets say they have good supplies of the long-life products that households have been advised to keep for emergencies.Photograph: Sam Oaksey/AlamyView image in fullscreenUK supermarkets say they have good supplies of the long-life products that households have been advised to keep for emergencies.Photograph: Sam Oaksey/AlamyEmergency planningBottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile adviceRetailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacksSarah ButlerTue 27 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households toprepare for emergencies.Retailers have reported a jump in sales of items linked to preparation for emergencies such as extreme weather or cyber-attacks. The Be Ready campaign was launched last week with the aim of persuading households to lay in supplies to last 72 hours.Maplin said sales of torches had almost quadrupled and sales of power banks and radios had doubled. One brand of emergency wind-up radio sold out on Friday.The specialist technology retailer said sales would have been higher but it was low on stock, particularly for power banks after a summer of heatwaves and the fallout from the Iran war. Home security camera sales were up 130%.Ollie Marshall, the managing director of Maplin, said: “Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics – a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank.“These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it’s encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously.”The grocery chain Iceland said sales of tinned products were up 40% over the weekend and it had also seen strong sales of bottled water. A spokesperson said: “It’s clear consumers have listened to the government’s message. Our supplies of these products remain healthy.”The online grocer Ocado said demand for some products was up and it would “continue to work with suppliers to ensure there is stock for customers to gradually add items to their shops”.Several major supermarkets said they had seen no material change in demand in tinned goods and that the cooler, stormy weather was more likely to influence demand for soups and beans.Jim Bligh, food policy director at the British Retail Consortium, said:“While some retailers have seen a small uptick in sales for some products, food availability remains strong and retailers remain well stocked with all essential products.”The boom in interest for relatively unusual gadgets helped specialist outdoor and “prepper” sites.Zaid Al-Mufti, founder of survival kit seller EvaQ8, said over the weekend it had sold out of items including a make of wind-up radio and water purification tablets. He said the company had sold about 300 radios compared with the usual 15.Long-life dried food was also in high demand but Al-Mufti did not expect this to last.“History has shown us people’s attention span doesn’t last long,” said Al-Mufti who keeps a “grab bag” with emergency gear in his car after time spent in earthquake-prone California where such precautions are normal. “The one time demand lasted was during Covid and we also saw demand when Russia invaded Ukraine.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJosh Pringle, co-founder of the online store Sgt Prepper, said business had been 10 to 15 times busier than usual last weekend, particularly focused on wind-up radios and long-life food including tins that last for 25 years.“I have never seen it like this before.” he said, saying the site’s larger wind-up radio had sold out and he was having to hunt for different brands because his supplier did not have enough stock.While the number of people buying radios and water purification tablets remains relatively low, many more households have been adding tins of food to their weekly shop.Retail industry insiders said supermarkets had been well prepared for a surge in food and drink sales and had good supplies of the long-life groceries recommended by the government.While pictures of empty shelves and queues have appeared on social media, industry sources warned against reading too much into the posts.“Inevitably some people will post pictures online of an empty shelf of water, beans or other products, however the likelihood is that just out of shot is a whole load of alternatives of a different brand available for everyone,” one insider said.Explore more on these topicsEmergency planningNatural disastersCybercrimeSupermarketsClimate crisisFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser | University of Oxford | The Guardian
description: Student supporters of Reform UK at Oxford college have organised evening with Nathan Cofnas discussing DEI
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Student supporters of Reform UK at Oxford college have organised evening with Nathan Cofnas discussing DEI
Content: Jason Arday died in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJason Arday died in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesUniversity of OxfordOriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuserStudent supporters of Reform UK at Oxford college have organised evening with Nathan Cofnas discussing DEIChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe University of Oxford’s Oriel College has been urged to cancel an event featuring Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas that has been organised by student supporters of Reform UK.Arday, 41, wasfound dead in Augustafter resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship. He had faced intense media scrutiny afterCofnas made unproven accusationsof plagiarism against him and said there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims.Cofnas, a blogger and academic who has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, is expected to appear at an event called “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: Is DEI undermining higher education?” at Oriel’s Harris lecture theatre on 17 November.The event has been organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society (OURS), a student group set up this year to support Reform UK.Oxford campaign groups, British academics, members of the public andOxfordalumni have signed an open letter urging Oriel to “withdraw its facilities from the event”.The signatories say the event “risks creating a hostile and exclusionary environment for students, particularly those of ethnic minorities” and “risks undermining Oriel’s role as a world-class educational institution” in 2026, the year of the 700th anniversary of its royal charter.The letter accuses Cofnas of using his platform to assert discriminatory beliefs, and claims his blogging played a significant role in the coverage Arday faced.View image in fullscreenNathan Cofnas is a blogger and academic who has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixDays before Arday’s death, Kehinde Andrews, the author and the UK’s first professor of Black studies,told the GuardianArday was facing a “dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge”.Responding to news of the Oriel event, Andrews said in a post online that it was “despicable and disgusting”.Oriel College said in a statement: “Oriel College is committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive. We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination.“The college considers events booked by students who are committee members of registered societies according to our code of practice on freedom of speech. When an event is permitted, this does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers.“When considering booking requests, the college takes seriously the security implications of events and the safety of its members.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a post on X, OURS claimed: “Nathan Cofnas and the event organisers have been subjected to a disturbing torrent of online hostility.”In a statement, OURS said that since it was a registered student society at the University of Oxford, constituent colleges “are under a legal obligation to host events like ours”.It added: “The Reform Society is committed to hosting Nathan Cofnas, and allowing attendees at the event to engage in respectful dialogue with the same.“We find it strange that the University of Oxford or any of its constituent colleges should receive reputational damage in respect of this event. The decision to host Nathan Cofnas was made solely by the committee of the Reform Society, and responsibility for the event rests exclusively with the same.”Cofnas was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of OxfordJason ArdayReform UKHigher educationUniversitiesOxfordEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m at New York auction | New York | The Guardian
description: Sale makes ‘Jodi’, a smaller relative of T rex, the ‘second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction’, Sotheby’s says
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Sale makes ‘Jodi’, a smaller relative of T rex, the ‘second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction’, Sotheby’s says
Content: The skeleton of ‘Jodi’, a Nanotyrannus that lived alongside T rex at the end of the Cretaceous, about 67m years ago, displayed at Sotheby's, on 13 October in New York City.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenThe skeleton of ‘Jodi’, a Nanotyrannus that lived alongside T rex at the end of the Cretaceous, about 67m years ago, displayed at Sotheby's, on 13 October in New York City.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APNew YorkRare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m at New York auctionSale makes ‘Jodi’, a smaller relative of T rex, the ‘second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction’, Sotheby’s saysAnna BettsandJenna AmatulliTue 27 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus, a smaller relative of the Tyrannosaurus rex, sold at auction inNew Yorkthis week for $47.3m, making it one of the world’s most expensive fossils.The skeleton,named “Jodi”after the person who found the remains in 2019, sold at Sotheby’s on Tuesday for $47.3m, “after a twelve-minute bidding battle that saw six bidders compete online and over the phones, before ultimately selling on the phone”, Sotheby’s said in a statement.Sotheby’s initially estimated that the skeleton would sell for $6m to $9m. Tuesday’s result makes “Jodi” the “second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction”, Sotheby’s noted. The buyer has not yet been identified publicly.The skeleton, which wasunveiledat a Manhattan auction earlier this month, was discovered by Jodi Pierson in 2019 on her privately owned land in the Hell Creek Formation in Garfield County, Montana, near the town of Jordan. According to Sotheby’s, the skeleton measures 19.6ft long from nose to the tail, and around 9.6ft tall on the armature, “comprising approximately 191 fossil bone elements”.In a statement on Tuesday, Cassandra Hatton, vice-chair and worldwide head of science and natural history at Sotheby’s, thanked the team who assisted in the efforts to “excavate and save ‘Jodi’”.“Their passion and expertise have been fundamental to Jodi’s story,” Hatton said. “From the discovery and excavation, their commitment to understanding and preserving this remarkable specimen has helped bring us to this moment, a testament to the fact that we can all make major contributions to science. This exceptional result is a wonderful recognition of that work, and of the enduring fascination with the Nanotyrannus.”“Jodi” is one of only “three substantial Nanotyrannus skeletons known to science, and the first to come to market since the genus was confirmed last fall”, per Sotheby’s. Judging from the overall size and degree of bone development, “it can be determined that the skeleton belonged to an adult individual”, according to a description on Sotheby’s website.Sotheby’s described the nanotyrannus as “a fast, highly specialized carnivorous tyrannosaurid that lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Cretaceous, about 67 million years ago”. It added that “previously hypothesized by some to be adolescent T rex, Nanotyrannus has been shown to have over 150 morphological differences that distinguish it from its much larger cousin”.The sale and cost of the fossil has prompted criticism from some in the science community.Thomas R Holtz Jr, author and principal lecturer on vertebrate paleontology at the University of Maryland, said that as a “tyrannosaur researcher”, his “concerns about the sale of Jodi are the same general concerns about all these multimillion-dollar sales of fossils.“At the same time this sale went on, some museums are closing (the Academy of Natural Sciences at Drexel in Philadelphia) or being threatened with closure (the Sternberg Museum of Natural History at Fort Hays State University) because of cost overruns literally only 1/10th that of the final cost of Jodi.“So a person really interested in paleontology could do vastly more good by supporting the ongoing operations of multiple museums than the sale of one specimen. And indeed, the total cost of excavation, preparation, and mounting of a skeleton like this is probably on the order of $1m at most, possibly much less. So a well-funded museum would be able to gather multiple good skeletons for the price of this one ‘trophy.’”He also emphasized that “potentially scientifically significant fossils” like Jodi “can be lost to research and the public when they are in private hands”.“Now maybe the as-yet unidentified purchaser will donate it to a museum or similar institution, where the public can see it and where scientists now and in future generations can measure the bones, take samples and scans of the fossils, and apply current analytical procedures (as well as procedures no one has dreamed of yet) to help us better understand the biology of these ancient animals. But if it simply graces the lobby or ballroom of one of some billionaire’s mansions, unseen and unaccessible to all but their friends, servants and so forth, it is effectively lost to both the public and the scientific community. In fact, at that point, it is no different than if it had just been left in the ground,” he said.Linda Ivany, a professor of evolutionary paleoecology at Syracuse University, echoed similar sentiments to the theNew York Times: “These amazing fossils should stay in the public sphere for scientists to study, for children to be awed and inspired, and for everyone to be able to marvel at worlds long past and what we can learn from them.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorkDinosaursFossilsEvolutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster
Content: The first episode of Elon Musk’s AI-generated Odyssey. The seven-minute instalment was made by London-based Wonder Studios.Computer-generated: Grok ImagineView image in fullscreenThe first episode of Elon Musk’s AI-generated Odyssey. The seven-minute instalment was made by London-based Wonder Studios.Computer-generated: Grok ImagineElon Musk‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmTesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbusterDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 27 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.Having criticisedthe hit moviein the summer, the tycoon said he would useGrok Imagineto make a “historically accurate” adaptation.The initial results have been released on X in the form of aseven-minute episodemade in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.Musk hadobjected to Nolan’s casting choices– such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.View image in fullscreenThe Greeks make land. The team behind the first episode said they would seek to make improvements in the second episode.Computer-generated: @ImagineThe first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take onHomerare supporters of the summer blockbuster.Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeter Bradshaw’s review in the Guardiangave it one star, saying: “Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver.”The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the last episode we make is radically better than the first,” he said.Wonder has also worked with Google DeepMind to produce an AI-generated video for the Lewis Capaldi trackSomething in the Heavens.Explore more on these topicsElon MuskAI (artificial intelligence)Christopher NolanHomerThe OdysseyGrok AIXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table | Italy | The Guardian
description: Fifteen establishments join trial scheme to encourage parents and children to talk while dining out
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Fifteen establishments join trial scheme to encourage parents and children to talk while dining out
Content: Restaurants taking part in the pilot scheme in Sardinia will give families a ‘reunion kit’ to spark conversation.Photograph: Awakening/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRestaurants taking part in the pilot scheme in Sardinia will give families a ‘reunion kit’ to spark conversation.Photograph: Awakening/Getty ImagesItalySardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the tableFifteen establishments join trial scheme to encourage parents and children to talk while dining outAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 27 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of restaurants in Sardinia are banning families from using smartphones and other devices at the table in a quest to encourage conversation.The initiative, calledA tavola senza schermior At the table without screens, is being spearheaded by Anna Cau, the children’s ombudsman for the Italian island. It is part of a campaign to curtail excessive screen use among children and inspire interaction during meals.Parents and their children will be required to put their phones away when dining at any of the 15 restaurants that have volunteered to participate in the scheme during a one-month pilot exercise beginning next week.Cau, a former juvenile magistrate, said: “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others.“We need real-world settings that strengthen and accommodate the lives of both adults and children. This initiative is a small step within a broader philosophy that guides my approach to this highly complex issue.”After families hand in their devices, restaurant staff will give them a “reunion kit” containing games and drawings. The kit, which has been designed by the Italian federation of paediatricians, is aimed at helping under-18s start conversations with their parents, such as sharing stories about their day.The kit includes a brochure outlining the risks of digital overexposure and tips on managing social media use at home.“The restaurants will offer an alternative activity in the form of a game which is intended to foster interaction,” said Cau. “Obviously, the games are structured with time limits within the context of a restaurant lunch or dinner.”Cau worked on the scheme with the Sardinian wing of Fipe-Confcommercio, an association uniting the catering, tourism and entertainment sectors.Emanuele Frongia, president of the federation on the island, said the 15 restaurants had readily agreed to participate. The plan is to expand the initiative on a voluntary basis.“Restaurants play a vital role in fostering the intimacy that families rediscover when they dine out,” said Frongia. “Yet we increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices. Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.”Explore more on these topicsItalySocial mediaRestaurantsMobile phonesChildrenTablet computersDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: DNA links serial killer Ted Bundy to 1974 murder of Utah girl | Utah | The Guardian
description: Discovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that year
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Discovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that year
Content: Ted Bundy at his murder trial in Miami, Florida, in 1979.Photograph: Ken Hawkins/AlamyView image in fullscreenTed Bundy at his murder trial in Miami, Florida, in 1979.Photograph: Ken Hawkins/AlamyUtahDNA links serial killer Ted Bundy to 1974 murder of Utah girlDiscovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that yearUwa Ede-OsifoTue 27 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe notorious serial killer Ted Bundy has been found responsible, through DNA evidence, for the murder of a 17-year-oldUtahgirl who went missing in 1974 before her nude body was found days later, state authorities announced at a Tuesday news conference.The breakthrough in the investigation of Melissa Ann Smith’s death comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed in April that Bundy had killed another Utah girl, 17-year-old Laura Ann Aime, in 1974.Bundy had confessed tokillingLaura during a string of admissions he made before being executed in 1989 for two of his murders.Laura was last seen during a Halloween party, before being found dead and severely beaten in late November 1974.It was not until this year, though, that new DNA testing backed Bundy’s account.Bodily fluid extracted from Laura’s body was a match to Bundy’s known DNA profile, law enforcement officials said then.That discovery put into motion the closure of Smith’s homicide investigation.The Y-STR DNA profile recovered from Laura’s body was a genetic match to one found from Melissa’s body.“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence, even when decades have passed,” said the Salt Lake county sheriff, Rosie Rivera, on Tuesday. “We have the ability to take a look at these cases again and again.”Between 1974 and 1978, Bundy went on a violent rampage, sexually assaulting and killing at least 30 women across the American west and Florida.“The voices and cherished memories of Melissa Ann Smith and Laura Ann Aime and others involved in these cases ring louder than the hate and sedition of the one that took their lives,” said Mike Reynolds, a sergeant with the Utah county sheriff’s office, on Tuesday. “With every case closure may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out.”Explore more on these topicsUtahUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’ | Business | The Guardian
