description: Administrator BTG says 738,144 firms struggling as calls grow for more support for private sector in budget
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Administrator BTG says 738,144 firms struggling as calls grow for more support for private sector in budget
Content: The hospitality industry has been hit hard this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe hospitality industry has been hit hard this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyBusinessNumber of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’Administrator BTG says 738,144 firms struggling as calls grow for more support for private sector in budgetLauren AlmeidaTue 27 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector inWednesday’s budget.There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004.The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively.The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866. Struggling food and drug retailers rose by more than 7% to 19,269, according to BTG, which is one of the UK’s biggest insolvency practitioners and changed its name from Begbies Traynor in February.The growing strain on UK companies comes as the chancellor,John Healey, prepares to give his first budget on Wednesday, against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East disrupts the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.The chancellor has vowed to use the budget to provide households and businesses with more“breathing space”.Mark Fry, the chief executive of BTG, said British businesses were “battling a combination of rising employment costs, inflationary pressures, higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs.“Crucially, these pressures are not only affecting small businesses’ ability to operate, but also larger businesses’ ability to compete on a global stage,” he said.A freedom of information request by BTG also found that British businesses still owed £27.3bn in arrears toHMRCin VAT, corporation tax and PAYE at the end of August.About £24bn has been recovered since arrears reached a peak of £51.3bn during the Covid pandemic, compared with a pre-pandemic total of £11.4bn.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“With £27.3bn owed to HMRC, high levels of recovery activity and record financial distress across the economy, many companies are approaching this budget from a position of financial weakness rather than strength,” Fry said.“We hear from businesses that structural hurdles, weight of red tape, employment legislation and the tax burden alongside high interest and energy costs will need to be tackled if this is to be a budget for business.”Last week the prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised that his government would “slash red tape” for businesses, with plans to make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses.Explore more on these topicsBusinessJohn HealeyHospitality industryConstruction industryReal estateFood & drink industryBudget 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes | HSBC | The Guardian
description: As John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profits
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: As John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profits
Content: HSBC’s global HQ is on London but it has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHSBC’s global HQ is on London but it has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianHSBCHSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxesAs John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profitsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK overtax increases expected to be announcedin Wednesday’s budget.HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad.HSBC on Tuesday revealed a 32% rise in third-quarter profits to $9.6bn (£7.2bn), alongside plans to give $2.7bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.Lobby groups have for months warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills, with the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, saying he could evenscrap plans for a new £3bn London headquartersif Britain became “hostile” to banks.A handful of wealthy businesspeople have already said they are leaving the UK, with some criticising Labour’s tax policies.The Guardianrevealedearlier this month that the chancellor, John Healey, was planning to tax Britain’s banks in Wednesday’s budget. He is likely to reverse the previous Conservative government’s cuts to the bank surcharge.“Irrespective of what happens on taxes, we are there to support our customers, and that is what we will do,” she told journalists during a media call on Tuesday. “We are very comfortable, we are domiciled in the UK and we remain in the UK. So that question is just not on the table,” Kaur said.HSBC has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits, and has twice been pushed to shift or split its operations in reaction to UK policies.That includes in 2015, when growing regulatory burdens and a new bank levy led HSBC to considershifting its headquarters out of London to Hong Kong. The Conservative government later scaled back the levy to cover only UK-based assets, in a boon to HSBC.HSBC later faced pressureto separate the bank’s profitable Asian businessfrom the rest of its operations in 2022, amid anger that the UK had forced the bank to cancel its dividend during the first Covid lockdown.Kaur gave broad backing to Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying the bank was “very encouraged by the government’s growth agenda”, adding that the bank would “just have to see how businesses and customers react”.The lender’s profit in the July to September quarter was boosted by higher interest rates, lower loan losses and smaller legal provisions compared with last year. However, its UK-listed shares fell 5.4% on Tuesday, causing it to lose its status as the biggest company on the FTSE 100.Kaur speculated that investors may have expected stronger forecasts for net interest income – which is the difference between what banks charge for loans versus what they pay out in deposits.HSBC’s net interest income rose to $9.3bn in the third quarter, up from $8.8bn a year earlier. That metric has been a flashpoint for groups campaigning for a UK bank tax, including the Trades Union Congress, which said bank profits have been driven by higher interest rates rather than their own improving performance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, HSBC said its net interest income grew in the third quarter as a result of hedging strategies and a growth in deposits in Hong Kong, while UK deposits stayed flat.TheTUCgeneral secretary, Paul Nowak, said HSBC’s results still showed banks could comfortably shoulder higher taxes. “Some in the finance lobby have tried every which way to stop tax rises in the budget. But these results make it blatantly obvious banks can afford to contribute more.”Abhijay Sood, an economist at the New Economics Foundation thinktank, said HSBC’s strong profits would be “difficult news to swallow for households struggling with rising mortgage costs”.He added: “Like other big banks, its profitability has depended on keeping interest rates on savings accounts low, and a stealth subsidy from taxpayers via the Bank of England due to quantitative easing.“While the rumours of a bank tax change in the budget are welcome, it is unlikely to go far enough …“The chancellor should go further by clawing back the stealth subsidy, and use this to fund inflation-busting investment and keep the essentials of life affordable for ordinary people.”Explore more on these topicsHSBCBankingBudget 2026BudgetTax and spendingTUCTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards
Content: The 92-page document released on Monday talks about Anthropic’s explosive growth and the risks AI has brought to the business.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe 92-page document released on Monday talks about Anthropic’s explosive growth and the risks AI has brought to the business.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersAnthropicExplainerFour takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filingThe AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguardsJohana BhuiyanTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropichas filedto go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.Here are some of the key takeaways from Anthropic’s lengthy S-1.Anthropic reveals rapid revenue gains and larger losses in stock market filingRead more1.Explosive and expensive growthHere’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence.Anthropic brought in $16.3bn in revenue and lost $80bn in just the first half of 2026, though much of that was due to a $72.4bn one-off charge. In 2025, the company brought in $4.585bn and lost roughly $33.9bn, per the filing.Column chart showing quarterly filings from Anthropic from Q1 2025 to Q2 2026. While revenues are increasing quarter over quarter, net losses are increasing at a faster rate.Securing computing power accounts for the vast majority of Anthropic’s costs. The company spent nearly $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of this year, up from $2.3bn in the same period last year.Anthropic, unlike OpenAI, has made it clear that its customers are largely other businesses. “Frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest,” the company executives wrote in the filing.The company said its top five customers account for 25% of its business – which makes it risky business.2.‘A country of geniuses in a datacenter’Anthropic says there is considerable potential for AI to reach levels of intelligence that would be akin to what its executives called “‘a country of geniuses in a datacenter’ – millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionize every area of human endeavor: software, physics, math, biology, medicine, finance, economics, commerce, robotics, military and intelligence capabilities”. Noticeably, the company mentioned military capabilities despite being embroiled in a standoff with the Trump administration over its refusal to limit restrictions on the way the Department of Defense could use Claude.The company highlighted four specific categories of opportunity at the start of the filing: Acceleration of progress in biology and medicine; economic growth; spreading said growth globally; and streamlining government services (such as social services and medical programming).The company said it was already working with several pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and improved the process for clinical trials, which is “cutting the time it takes to write clinical trial reports from months to minutes”.The company’s executives claim they have also made biological discoveries with Claude, including a “molecular machine” that has the “potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool”. One purported use case: gene editing.3.AI ‘safeguards are incomplete’The company discusses risks in two contexts: the dangers that AI itself poses to society and human beings, and the ways Anthropic’s business could go awry.Risks that AI poses were broken down into four main categories: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. While Anthropic put a great deal of emphasis on the guardrails it has implemented to block attempts to misuse its models, it also includes one big caveat later in the filing: those safeguards may not work.Anthropic’s most capable models are capable of providing “meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote in the filing.The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended”.Already, Anthropic has detected what it believes is the first documented case of a large-scale cyber-attack with little human intervention. The company believes a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated a Claude code tool “into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”, per the prospectus.The company said it recognized AI may be used by authoritarian governments to “deepen repression” and develop “high-tech surveillance states”. Anthropic presented less of a defense or potential safeguard against those uses and instead said it was committed to working with “free societies to provide a counterweight to authoritarian abuse and to promote freedom and democracy”. The firm seems to suggest that its work with what it describes with scant details as “free societies” will cancel out in some way the AI-enabled repression of authoritarian regimes.The company had a falling out with the Trump administration after the firm said it would not change its restrictions to allow its models to be used to build domestic surveillance or autonomous lethal weapons.4.92 pages of financial riskAnthropic goes into detail in laying out 92 pages of risks to its business. Investors are making sense of a type of company that is fairly new to the public market in a highly competitive space with everything to lose.The company acknowledges that much of its success is tied to its top executives and whether they stay at the firm, being able to edge out its main competitors Google and OpenAI, navigating the tumultuous regulatory landscape around AI and datacenters and surviving any public relations fallout over its AI models being used to do things they are not supposed to do, likecreate bioweapons.The company’s focus on enterprise customers means that if any of its top buyers leave, the company could take a huge hit.Anthropic’s structure as a public benefit corporation – which is a designation for a for-profit company that balances financial interests with achieving a stated social good – may make it harder to achieve its short – or medium-term financial goals, the company said. The firm is obliged to report on its progress in meeting its public benefit goals in the same way it has to report its financials.There’s also all the risk related to any AI-enabled catastrophic event – the sort of doomsday scenario Anthropic employees have been warning about. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for a pause on AI development to ensure firms are developing it responsibly to avoid any such catastrophe. In addition to the public harm and potential fallout over a scenario where Claude went rogue, Anthropic said they worry they will be subject to a great deal of liability, especially considering insurance options for AI are still evolving.“We may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses,” the filing reads.The bedrock of Anthropic’s AI infrastructure is concentrated in the US, making it extremely vulnerable to regulatory changes, power grid constraints, natural disasters and opposition to AI or datacenters. The filing specifically calls out datacenter moratoriums that have been passed or are being considered as among the big issues they are concerned about.“We are expanding our data center capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration risks,” the filing reads.The company, which says a big part of its value proposition is its talent, also said it worries about US immigration policies affecting its ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. The Trump administration has targeted H-1B visas, a tool tech firms have come to rely on to attract and hire from the global pool of tech and engineering talent.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)Internet IPOsTechnology sectorChatbotskey takeawaysShareReuse this content

title: Tom Skerritt obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: US actor who often played authority figures and was admired for his film roles in Alien, Top Gun and A River Runs Through It
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: US actor who often played authority figures and was admired for his film roles in Alien, Top Gun and A River Runs Through It
Content: Tom Skerritt as Captain Dallas in Alien, 1979.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarView image in fullscreenTom Skerritt as Captain Dallas in Alien, 1979.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarMoviesObituaryTom Skerritt obituaryUS actor who often played authority figures and was admired for his film roles in Alien, Top Gun and A River Runs Through ItAnthony HaywardTue 27 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lean, rugged US actor Tom Skerritt, who has died aged 93, was described by one screenwriter as “a character actor trapped in a leading man’s body”. He took significant roles as authority figures in the films Alien, Top Gun and A River Runs Through It before landing star billing in the 1990s TV family drama Picket Fences, as a sheriff trying to keep the peace in a rural Wisconsin town plagued by violent – and bizarre – crimes.Skerritt’s breakthrough had come in the 1970 filmM*A*S*H, directed byRobert Altman. He played Augustus “Duke” Forrest, a US army surgeon in the Korean war exuding southern charm at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital. Along with his fellow surgeons, Benjamin Franklin “Hawkeye” Pierce (played by Donald Sutherland) and “Trapper” John McIntyre (Elliott Gould), Duke displayed cynicism and irreverence towards his superiors.But Skerritt’s character was not transferred to the TV series that followed. While some sources reported that the actor had no faith in the film working as a half-hour sitcom, the writerLarry Gelbart, who adapted the novel for the small screen with Gene Reynolds, explained they wanted characters they felt could generate storylines, adding: “Trapper John just seemed more colourful than Duke.”Skerritt remained prolific in character roles in films and on TV until coming to worldwide attention as the doomed Captain Dallas, in charge of the commercial space tug Nostromo, in the sci-fi horror movieAlien(1979), which made a star of Sigourney Weaver.View image in fullscreenTom Skerritt as a father trying to bond with his sons in A River Runs Through It, 1992.Photograph: Columbia/Kobal/ShutterstockHe initially turned down the role, but changed his mind when he heard that it was to be directed by Ridley Scott, whose debut film, the Napoleonic wars drama The Duellists (1977), he regarded as a “classic … a painting from beginning to end”.Skerritt appeared alongside another actor reaching star status, Tom Cruise, inTop Gun(1986), directed by Ridley’s brotherTony Scott. He played Mike “Viper” Metcalf, mentoring the fighter pilot Pete “Maverick” Mitchell (Cruise) in the elite US navy school.His own slow-burn rise to stardom was boosted by his part in A River Runs Through It (1992) as the Presbyterian minister who finds a bond with his sons (Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt) through fly-fishing. It provoked the Hollywood Reporter to observe that “he has one of his richest roles in years as their emotionally cut-off father”.The film, directed byRobert Redford, came out at the same time as Picket Fences (1992-96) was launched. This time, Skerritt was playing a warm, loving father, Jimmy Brock, a small-town sheriff married to Jill (Kathy Baker), a psychiatrist, with three children, in Rome, Wisconsin. “We’re the ones with whom the audience might most relate to – because all these other folks are crazy!” he said.The quirky and daring storylines included cows’ udders exploding, animal sacrifice and date rape and tackled taboo subjects such as euthanasia, abortion, incest and homophobia – groundbreaking for peak-time US television at the time.Skerritt’s performance won him a Primetime Emmy award as outstanding lead actor in a drama series and he was kept firmly in the public eye during the programme’s four runs. “I’ve never really been comfortable with celebrity,” he said, while admitting that Jimmy Brock was another role he had initially turned down before being won over by the storylines. When the series ended, he returned to guest roles on TV and supporting parts in films in a hard-working career in which he portrayed almost 200 screen characters.View image in fullscreenTom Skerritt, centre, in the 1970 film of M*A*S*H*, with Elliott Gould, left, and Donald Sutherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamySkerritt was born in Detroit,Michigan, to Roy Skerritt, a business executive, and his wife, Helen (nee Maybee). On leaving Mackenzie high school, he served in the US air force as a classification specialist (1951-55) before studying English, first at Wayne State University, then at UCLA (the University of California Los Angeles), where he took up acting. The director Denis Sanders and his brother, the producer Terry Sanders, spotted Skerritt in a stage production of The Rainmaker and cast him as a soldier in War Hunt (1962), alongside Redford.Dozens of one-off TV roles followed such as My Three Sons (in 1963), Wagon Train (in 1964) and The Fugitive (two parts, in 1966 and 1967) before his appearance in M*A*S*H meant he was switching between the big and small screens.He was a motorcycle cop in the film Harold and Maude (1971), choosing to be credited as Martin Bormann (the name of Hitler’s private secretary). “We did silly things in those days,” he explained.Skerritt then playedShelley Duvall’s father, a mechanic, in Thieves Like Us (1974), reuniting him with Altman; Shirley Maclaine’s husband, a retired ballet dancer, in The Turning Point (1977); a Vietnam veteran in the cult classic Up in Smoke (1978), alongside Cheech Marin and Tommy Chong; and Sally Field’s good-hearted husband, also the father of Julia Roberts, in Steel Magnolias (1989).On TV, he was Kirstie Alley’s suave former boss, Evan Drake, in the sixth series of Cheers (1987-88), Joe Kennedy in Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis (2000) and General William Westmoreland in Path to War (2002). He played Field’s husband again, this time deceased and appearing in flashback, in the first three series ofBrothers & Sisters(2006-09).Skerritt’s first two marriages ended in divorce. He is survived by his third wife, Julie (nee Tokashiki), whom he married in 1998, and their daughter, Emi, as well as by Andy, Dan and Erin, the children of his first marriage, to Charlotte Shanks, and Colin, the son from the second, to Sue Oran.Thomas Roy Skerritt, actor, born 25 August 1933; died 21 October 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmUS taxationDetroitMichiganobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama | Television | The Guardian
description: The Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new light
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new light
Content: Relationship/romance … Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani in the Disney/Hulu series The Dropout.Photograph: Beth Dubber/APView image in fullscreenRelationship/romance … Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani in the Disney/Hulu series The Dropout.Photograph: Beth Dubber/APTelevisionElizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV dramaThe Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything  documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new lightHannah J DaviesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are surprise smash hits, and then there’s You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s documentary-cum-psychodrama about the disgraced US entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes. It arrived in US cinemas with much buzz: this was, after all, an A24 production, helmed by one of TV’s leading performance-art pranksters. But You Can See Everything has surpassed all expectations to become an undeniable hit, and is nowthe highest-grossing US documentary in 15 yearsjust two weeks after its release.Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, it is a surreal and masterly epic; at a press screening in London, the audience appeared to be alternately spellbound by its comedic elements and repulsed by the sheer grossness of some of its characters. That grossness, it should be mentioned, doesn’t pertain only to Holmes, who was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison (this has since beenreduced several times) for defrauding investors, after the collapse of her sham blood-testing startup Theranos). It has also – perhaps unsurprisingly – led audiences towards other media inspired by Holmes’s downfall. Journalist John Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood,has returned to the bestseller lists; the ABC News podcast The Dropout, hosted by Rebecca Jarvis reported a900% surge in listeners; whiletheDisney/Hulu TV seriesof the same name enjoyed a700% bump in viewers, and is now ranked #47 on IMDb’s “Most popular TV shows” list, despite having been released in 2022.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreAs Holmes mania abounds, I decide to fire upthe podcast, a show I listened to when it was released in 2019. Unlike You Can See Everything – which explores whether Holmes can convince us of her innocence, as much as whether she is innocent – The Dropout podcast takes us back to her halcyon days, when she was named America’s youngest self-made billionaire. This was a time when her Steve Jobs-esque black turtlenecks, apparently bogus baritone voice and talent for wooing super-rich investors was a large part of the story (the first episode is titled Myth-Making).But it wasn’t just about Holmes the person – it was about what her company did (or rather, didn’t do) and offered a stark reminder that the claims that she made never matched reality. In one episode, we hear Holmes declare that it is possible to run “any lab test from a drop of blood from a finger”, juxtaposed with a clip from a deposition hearing where she is asked just how many tests her machine was capable of carrying out: “I-I-I don’t know exactly what the number was … I think there were probably tens of tests …” (If this sounds like a straightforward lie, Holmes offers her own explanation of her claims in You Can See Everything.)View image in fullscreenA masterly epic … Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24The TV adaptation of The Dropout recycles the story that the podcast so thoroughly investigated, albeit with a little more artistic licence (Holmes dances like a robot to Lil Wayne, and there’s an entire plot point that’s reverse-engineered to incorporate the Katy Perry song Firework). It’s entertaining, sure: I find myself strangely captivated by the stilted professional relationship/romance between Holmes (Amanda Seyfried) and Sunny Balwani (Naveen Andrews), 19 years her senior, who are obsessed with one another but suggest a cold indifference, too (see also: a real-life text exchange between Holmes and Balwani, where she wrote: “You are the breeze in the desert for me. My water. And ocean. Meant to be only together tiger,” to which Balwani replied: “OK”).But for the first few episodes at least, The Dropout is mostly like watching a campus drama that occasionally morphs into an episode of Law and Order. Seyfried is great – all bulging, marble-like eyes, unsettling jaw placement and off-kilter speech patterns – but there is a sense that this is an almost meme-esque endeavour, gleefully ripped from the headlines (You Can See Everything does, in its own way, ask whether that might have indeed been the case). At the end of episode one, Elizabeth stares at her finger, and – deus ex machina – the idea for Theranos arrives.But The Dropout series, like the podcast before it, was built on inescapable facts and what the Guardian described at the time of release as the“gut-twisting mental gymnastics”of it all – the technological inadequacies of Theranos’s equipment; the surveillance culture that meant employees felt they couldn’t speak out; the third-party machines the company used in place of its own hardware; false positives for HIV, cancer and other serious conditions. It might sound facile, but it’s a reminder of the sheer weight of what Holmes’s company did, and of her ability to fight off the most legitimate of concerns. It touches, too, on the suicide of Ian Gibbons, the company’s former chief scientist, who took his own life before he was due to testify against the company. It would be irresponsible to lay the blame for this death solely on Theranos. But it’s clear, amid the jacked-up comedy, that there was plenty of pain for its writers to mine.Holmes’s story first gripped the world during what was a big moment for scammers, from thephoney heiress Anna DelveytoFyre festival, with its schadenfreude-inducing story of influencers stranded in the Bahamas under disaster relief blankets. In the years since, the conversation around such grifts has become less cut and dried: Delvey has gonefull-on media caricature, while – conversely – many Fyre attenders were revealed to have been normies who got their tickets on Groupon.Aptly, perhaps, for a moment that was so focused on untruths, the narrative of the “golden age of the grift” is now being rewritten again, in real time. Fielder and Oppenheim have done something daring and brilliant with You Can See Everything, incorporating anew era of technofascismand AI in the process, and meeting Holmes not as a Silicon Valley sweetheart but as a mother and soon-to-be-convict. But the facts – be it on TV or on a podcast – remain as unsettling as ever. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” says Holmes in the film. And yet so much of it is hard to ignore.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderAmanda SeyfriedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arnie & Barney review – dimwit ant double-act from Maya the Bee are on mission to entertain | Movies | The Guardian
description: From the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holiday
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: From the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holiday
Content: Tiresome ant-ics … Arnie & Barney.View image in fullscreenTiresome ant-ics … Arnie & Barney.MoviesReviewArnie & Barney review – dimwit ant double-act from Maya the Bee are on mission to entertainFrom the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holidayCatherine BrayTue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1912 in Germany, antisemitic writer Waldemar Bonsels published The Adventures of Maya the Bee, which later became a 1970s anime series in Japan called Maya the Honey Bee, and was later dubbed into English a couple of times, including for kids TV channel Nickelodeon in the 1990s anda bunch of films between 2014 and 2021. Still with us? Recurring characters from the show include Arnie and Barney, a pair of dimwit ants, and now, at long last, they have their own spin-off movie.The film opens very muchin media res, with a young female bee flying through outer space clutching a small pig and droplet of water the size of her head. She’s being pursued aggressively by a handful of wasp-type creatures and a narrator solemnly intones: “Sometimes the most unlikely heroes … become legends.” The bee then stops next to a couple of red ants and asks what they’re doing. They are the narrators, they explain, but this his is all soon revealed as fantasy – the pair of ants are telling a story to a larger platoon of ants. Some exposition follows about the ants’ mission: to find fresh water.This is fine as far as it goes, perhaps, but what a précis can’t convey is quite how staggeringly ugly and uninteresting the whole endeavour is. It starts with the character design: it’s hard to imagine any but the most aesthetically starved children embracing this ant pair. Boy are they a chore to spend time with, both visually and in terms of the lacklustre script. Even if you are struggling for entertainment options you might want to do the kids a favour and skip this one.Arnie & Barney is in UK cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFilm adaptationsFamily filmsTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tribute | Matthew Perry | The Guardian
description: This intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelming
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelming
Content: ‘Just please make me famous’ … Matthew Perry.Photograph: courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreen‘Just please make me famous’ … Matthew Perry.Photograph: courtesy of NetflixTV reviewMatthew PerryReviewThe One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tributeThis intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelmingLucy ManganTue 27 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“God, you can do whatever you want to me, just please make me famous.” So prayedMatthew Perrywhen he was a young unknown actor auditioning in LA, enjoying the partying and the friendships but struggling to find work. Many have offered up such a fervent wish, of course; few have had both sides of it fulfilled in such a spectacular way as the man who became part of one of the most successful sitcoms in television history and who died after relapsing into drug addiction in 2023 at the age of just 54.The three-part, three-hour documentary – titled, perhaps inevitably, The One About Matthew Perry – charts the whole of the actor’s rise and fall. It is an exhaustive but never (quite) exhausting film. Three hours is a long time, for sure, to tell what is in essence a sad but very simple tale, and some tiny trims could undoubtedly have been made, but it avoids tedium because of the quality of the interviews and the interviewees. The latter include his half-sister Mia and his best friends since his first days in LA, Roger Castillo and David Pressman. They all talk about the brother and the man with such love and such despair at the addictions he could not beat that it becomes at points not just a moving tribute to Perry but also to the thousands upon thousands of addicts and the people who love and despair of them, but whose stories don’t make international headlines.View image in fullscreenFriends, from left: Jennifer Aniston, David Schwimmer, Courteney Cox, Matt LeBlanc, Lisa Kudrow and Matthew Perry.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyPerry’s parents divorced when he was a baby and he lived with his mother in Canada but flew frequently to California (his memoir details his terror, at five, of making the trip alone with a strap reading “Unaccompanied minor” around his head) to see his father, the actor John Bennett Perry. Mia was born to John and Matthew’s stepmother when Matthew was 16 and it is clear from family photos and video footage that they adored each other from the beginning. She talks about “Matty” and the good times they shared and the bad times he put her through with the warmth and grief that is the mark of the truly loved – and the loving ones left behind.His friends do likewise. So too do a handful of ex-girlfriends. Normally the presence of exes not only makes you fear the worst but delivers it too, but here there is no mud slung, no sense of producers glorying in a “find” who turns out to have nothing to say. They all give fond, eloquent accounts of the man they knew – focusing, like Mia, on the good things but not skipping over the bad stuff and his failings, paying us and him the courtesy of providing a portrait of the man entire.After a childhood that may have been slightly peripatetic but seems to have been loving and essentially stable, Perry – the class clown from an early age – went out to LA to see if he could parlay his comic talents into a career. It worked. Director William Richert saw him making a group of companions laugh in a restaurant and cast him as River Phoenix’s best friend in A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon, which I think makes Matthew Perry, however unexpectedly, the Lana-Turner-in-Schwab’s-drugstore of the 90s, though as he noted in an interview with another friend, Kevin Pollak, years later (for a laugh – always for a laugh): “It would have been a better story if anyone had seen the movie.”Then, in 1993, a script for a new show calledFriendsLike Us began circulating. By the time Perry got a call to audition, he was already knew the lines because so many of his peers had asked him to help prep for theirs; this guy in it, Chandler, was so like him they felt Matty could really help.The programme gives the phenomenon of Friends its due but, like the decision to keep mawkishness at bay, rises above expectations by not dwelling on it or letting it overwhelm the subject – even if, at points in real life, it did the man.Then come the years of addiction – to booze first, then pills, then the ketamine that initially promised to lift his depression but which eventually killed him – and the many, many efforts to get sober. They are described in his memoir, but it is here that you see the pain on his family and friends’ faces as they remember his and their frustration as each attempt ended, never more than a year later, in relapse. Mia notes in her interviews that their father supported his son through everything, probably partly out of guilt for not being fully around as a parent in his childhood, and that he would have loved to have contributed to this film but that he is now too ill to do so. It’s a mixture of honesty and an evocation of a close, if complicated, family background that characterises all her contributions.It remains at heart a simple, sad story. But this unexpectedly candid, thoughtful, genuinely intimate film gives it nuance and depth, and gives a voice to wider sorrows – including what a shame it was that Perry could not enjoy his talent or appreciate the joy it gave as fully as his audiences always did.The One About Matthew Perry is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsMatthew PerryTV reviewFriendsDocumentaryTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Big Baby review – a screenwriter’s nightmares become reality in a meta-horror misfire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Spider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn characters
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Spider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn characters
Content: ‘There are flashes of something great here’ … Big Baby.Photograph: ShudderView image in fullscreen‘There are flashes of something great here’ … Big Baby.Photograph: ShudderMoviesReviewBig Baby review – a screenwriter’s nightmares become reality in a meta-horror misfireSpider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn charactersCatherine BrayTue 27 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn this slasher directed by Michael Cummings, AKA Powerman 5000 singer Spider One, Adam Lewis (Brandon Scott) is a screenwriter who spends too much time fretting about what the film reviewers he claims to despise think about his work, and not enough time writing. It’s a little hard initially to get a handle on exactly where this writing really sits: are we meant to believe he’s a misunderstood genius, or are the reviewers, in fact, correct? When Big Baby opens, Adam’s most recent film is being negatively reviewed by a couple of blowhards on a horror podcast, then he later gets grouchy with his all-too patient and supportive girlfriend (Krsy Fox) when she dares to imply he may never win an Academy Award. It emerges he’s aiming for a career something like Jordan Peele’s, but figures he’s not above trying for something more in the Sean S Cunningham oeuvre.For the first half of Big Baby, a pattern develops: Adam attempts to write, or search for inspiration, only to be haunted by a vision or dream about a slasher villain in a baby mask. Scott, as it happens, is a decent actor and does good work in the dialogue-free scenes, but the words themselves are a problem: it’s would-be smart material that hangs the character out to dry as a self-aggrandising, touchy killjoy and it’s hard to see why most of the people in his life would want to stay in touch. Scott’s charisma helps, but can’t completely counteract an unprepossessingly drawn character.In the horror movie roadmap, Big Baby lives a few degrees south of the likes of meta-slasher Wes Craven’s New Nightmare, and a little west of John Carpenter’s delirious In the Mouth of Madness. This is the kind of horror where in-universe script and reality bleed into each other. Unfortunately, it’s not sharp and tightly delineated enough for the former, while not sufficiently insane for the latter.For its first half, Big Baby is too often bogged down trying for character development: close to 90% of every conversation is about Adam and his anxieties, while the girlfriend character, played with a certain spark by Fox, doesn’t seem to have anything much going on in her own life. It’s a frustrating film, because there are flashes of something great here, but in the final analysis, Big Baby crawls rather than walks.Big Baby is on Shudder and AMC+ from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: We, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop Oil | Movies | The Guardian
description: The levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’
Content: Close to the action … We, The HatedPhotograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenClose to the action … We, The HatedPhotograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewWe, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop OilThe levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’Cath ClarkeTue 27 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Hated” is not putting it too strongly. The strength of feeling againstJust Stop Oil, as caught by this documentary, is really disturbing. It’s filmed from inside the climate group’s protests, and as activists block roads, furious drivers hurl abuse. “Have a wash you fucking idiots!” “Middle class wankers!” It gets physical, too – punching, kicking and dragging. One man appears to drive his van at protesters. Another walks along a line of them, pouring water over their heads, one by one.Film-maker Rich Felgate could not be closer to the action; his girlfriend, Indigo Rumbelow, is an activist. “Don’t look at the camera. I’m a fly on the wall,” he tells her at their shared house, where books about the suffragettes and Gandhi are on the shelves. On the streets, activists glue themselves to roads and fasten their necks together with bike locks. In October 2022, campaigners notoriously lobbedtomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers. At one road shutdown an angry driver shouts: “You’re children.” But they’re not all young; a vicar in late middle age with Parkinson’s quickly takes his medicine before he’s cuffed.The group’s strategy is to stay disruptive, stay in the news. We watch Just Stop Oil spokespeople appear on TV in increasingly hostile interviews. Their argument is that the planet is in crisis, there is no time to lose. Piers Morgan et al tell them their message is lost in the tactics. And it does look like that: by targeting infrastructure that hits ordinary people after protests aimed directly at the fossil fuel industry don’t work, Just Stop Oil throws away goodwill generated towards protesters acting on their consciences. Still, they claim a victory when Labour wins the election in 2024, pledging no new licences for gas and oilfields. (It seems that last week’sgo-ahead for the Jackdaw North Sea gasfielddoes not break that pledge, since it already holds a licence.)As Just Stop Oil actions escalate, Rumbelow and other activists are arrested and jailed,handed down the longest-ever prison sentencesin England for nonviolent protest. When the credits roll, you have to wonder who the real vandals are..We, the Hated is in UK cinemas from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsJust Stop OilProtestreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not my pain. There’s a responsibility in that’: Thea Gilmore on writing songs from anonymous confessional voicemails | Music | The Guardian
description: After tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousands
Author: Shaun Curran
Headline: After tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousands
Content: ‘People know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place’ … Thea Gilmore.Photograph: Carsten WindhorstView image in fullscreen‘People know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place’ … Thea Gilmore.Photograph: Carsten WindhorstMusicInterview‘It’s not my pain. There’s a responsibility in that’: Thea Gilmore on writing songs from anonymous confessional voicemailsShaun CurranAfter tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousandsTue 27 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘This project has changed my whole thinking,” Thea Gilmore says of her new endeavour,The Echo Line. “What am I getting from it? All of humanity.” Disillusioned with the numbers-chasing music industry and wanting a break from her personal songwriting after releasing 22 folk-orientated albums since 1998, the 46-year-old is “putting people back at the centre of it. I’ve said enough about me.”Community building has been key to the Oxford singer-songwriter’s work since debut Burning Dorothy, released when she was just 18, through to her 00s breakthrough albums Avalanche and Harpo’s Ghost all the way to her most recent studio album, 2023’s Thea Gilmore: a body of work that has won Gilmore admiration from Bruce Springsteen, Richard Thompson and collaborator Joan Baez.But The Echo Line goes even further. Akin to a musical iteration of Nick Cave’s interactive fan advice column The Red Hand Files, Gilmore invites people to leave her an anonymous voicemail or written message viaThe Echo Line websiteabout anything they want – hopes and dreams, fears and confessions, triumphs and tribulations – to which people have obliged with bravery and honesty in their thousands. Gilmore then writes a song inspired by one or more messages and uploads it to the website for a limited time only.When it was launched in January, Gilmore was unsure if anyone would call, or even notice – she currently has no management, label or press team – but received 150 messages within two days. The fourth and latest song of the project He Walks Like War was listened to more than 10,000 times before it was taken down. Songs initially remained available for just one week – “music is so disposable and available all the time, I wanted to see what happened if I took it away again” – though demand for He Walks Like War meant Gilmore relented and kept the song up for several weeks.View image in fullscreen‘Listening is a powerful act’ … Thea GilmoreEven as the community grows, Gilmore listens to and reads every message. “Listening has become increasingly undervalued in my lifetime. But it’s a powerful act. People more and more feel very alone. And I think what they’re getting from this is they know they’re actually being listened to, with no judgement.” The anonymity is key. “It’s really important to the integrity of the project that people know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place.”She admits she wasn’t quite prepared to receive such emotional messages. Certain themes recur: grief, loss and heartbreak; estrangement, especially from parents; messages about children, both pride and worries; the overwhelm of the modern world and distrust of elites. Many tell stories of overcoming adversity; one message detailed surviving an intruder attack at home (“like a Tarantino script”). But there are joyful ones too, including Gilmore’s personal favourite: a message about the interconnectivity of mushrooms as they grow in the ground. “In my bonkers songwriter brain, I’m like: that’s what this whole thing is about! We’re all connected, just like fungus.”The trust placed in her, she says, is a delicate gift. “As a songwriter you feel emboldened in some respects because they obviously think I can do a good job with their story,” she says. “But it is really tough. Because it’s not my pain. You’re making sure you do other people’s lives justice. There’s a weight of responsibility in that.”The Echo Line’s first three songs, beautiful examples of Gilmore’s spectral balladry, are incredibly moving. Blood Bike is an amalgamation of three messages: a blood bike worker delivering neonatal breast milk to hospitals, an overworked NHS nurse and a mother whose daughter was born prematurely. “They’re human stories that show we’re all connected, and this light went on – I was like: this is exactly what I wanted this to be.”‘Shane was rascality personified’: the Pogues on their late frontman, anti-Irish prejudice and the feud over Fairytale of New YorkRead moreThe second song, Silvie, tells the story of a relationship from 30 years ago tragically cut short by a road accident. The contributor was forbidden by their partner’s family to say a proper goodbye and the pain lingers. “That person’s message started ‘I don’t talk much about Silvie anymore’,” Gilmore says. “Those words just sat on top of your heart like a weight.”A long-distance relationship conducted entirely online inspired The Lines (Greg), a non-traditional courtship that ended tragically with Greg’s death by suicide. Even though the messenger is now happily married, “they felt they couldn’t talk about it or explain to people that it had been so important to them. And I really wanted to honour that in a song, that some of the most transformative relationships can be outside the bounds of what society says you can do.”The gnarlier He Walks Like War came after an influx of different types of messages from people across the political spectrum: disillusionment and anger at the billionaire class, tech bros and insidious algorithms dividing society. “You can see the same frustrations in completely different types of people. There are a lot of people out there who feel completely disenfranchised.”With The Echo Line now open 24/7, Gilmore is currently working on the next song, to be released by the end of October. “A very happy song, one of the most beautiful stories framed in the most beautiful way.” She has big ambitions for The Echo Line, including gallery events and live shows. “I would love to see this grow. For me, this is a sort of project that when I die, I’ll be like: that’s what I was meant to do.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockFolk musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: LPO/Gardner review – Mark Simpson’s piano concerto leaves its audience panting | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Pianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping up
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Pianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping up
Content: Music with the volume dialled up … Tamara Stefanovich, Mark Simpson and Edward Gardner with the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Julian GuideraView image in fullscreenMusic with the volume dialled up … Tamara Stefanovich, Mark Simpson and Edward Gardner with the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Julian GuideraClassical musicReviewLPO/Gardner review – Mark Simpson’s piano concerto leaves its audience pantingRoyal festival hall, LondonPianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto, with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping upAlexandra CoghlanTue 27 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Restless and impassioned.” “Very fast.” “Explosive, with abandon!” Before a note of Mark Simpson’s new Piano Concerto has sounded, it’s clear from the movements that this is music with the volume dialled up: louder, faster, bigger, fiercer. And it’s no idle promise. We open in a landslide of sound and barely draw breath for half an hour. This is a concerto that leaves the audience panting – let alone the soloist.Simpson’s music is larger than life. The British composer and clarinettist (who famously won both BBC Young Musician and BBC Young Composer of the Year back in 2006, aged just 17) plays with big forces and sounds at their extremes – whether that’s a barrage of percussion or extremes of register – and is rarely far from the kinetic twitch of nervous energy.His Piano Concerto – premiered here by soloist Tamara Stefanovich with Edward Gardner and theLondon Philharmonic Orchestra– shows no fear of the genre’s historical greats. An opening volley of virtuosity from the soloist could be Rachmaninov or Tchaikovsky, but arrives thickly encrusted with orchestral weight, barely audible through the layers.View image in fullscreenSeizing the fleeting opportunities for lyricism … soloist Tamara Stefanovich.Photograph: Julian GuideraThroughout this first movement we must excavate through sound to find the piano, which finally breaks free in a quicksilver central scherzo that sees it dancing with tuned percussion, rippling briefly above the orchestra in glinting passagework. The finale introduces a new vein of introspection, but once again extremity prevails as the pianist explores the outer reaches of the keyboard, goading the orchestra on to ever more athletic feats. Stefanovich wrestled bodily with Simpson’s demands, assertive and uncompromising, seizing the fleeting opportunities for lyricism, while Gardner and his band mostly kept up.Did the Simpson take all the rehearsal time? The framing works – Dorothy Howell’s pleasant, French-accented tone-poem Lamia and Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird – should have been all drama, all colour. But there was a workaday quality to the Stravinsky, a lack of tension to the pacing, a lack of precision to the woodwind solos and brass ensembles. Everything was there – villain Kashchei’s brooding evil, delicate princesses, the dazzling, darting Firebird itself – but in grayscale, waiting for that spark that turns Kansas into fairytale Oz.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Philharmonic OrchestraEdward GardnerMark SimpsonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiver | Biography books | The Guardian
description: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered
Content: Michael Gambon in 2016.Photograph: Roger Askew/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMichael Gambon in 2016.Photograph: Roger Askew/REX/ShutterstockBook of the dayBiography booksReviewMichael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiverFrom the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unansweredKathryn HughesTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the south-east London suburbs embellished his CV with entirely fabricated theatrical experience. It was a gamble, but it worked. In 1962 he made his professional debut as the Second Gentleman in Othello. The following year he was hired by Laurence Olivier for the brand new National Theatre.Gambon carried on telling tall tales long after there was any need. Some were self-aggrandising: he had been a dancer with the Royal Ballet, worked as a nuclear physicist and auditioned for James Bond. To be fair, this last one was half-true – producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli had once called him in for a chat. Others were absurdities for the sake of it: he was thinking of buying a house in Hanoi, his mother had operated cranes in Dublin. Occasionally, the lies were intended to save his skin. Terrified of being sacked for turning up late yet again to rehearsal at the National, he claimed that his mother had died in the night. She went on to live for another 49 years. More often, he lied to make other people laugh, claiming that he had worked with the Russian director Dmitri Shagyerarsoff.Gambon’s compulsion to invent and conceal presents obvious challenges for Jasper Rees, the veteran stage and showbiz journalist who interviewed the actor several times before his death in 2023 and reports always coming away feeling puzzled. Rees’s authorised biography draws on the archive held by Gambon’s wife, Anne, a woman whose existence was unknown to most of his colleagues. For years Gambon had a relationship with the NationalTheatreadministrator Lyn Haill and was later photographed with set designer Philippa Hart, with whom he had two sons. Yet, apart from a brief period in the early 1970s, he remained in the marital home in Kent. That marriage lasted 61 years, and Anne and their son Fergus accompanied Gambon to Buckingham Palace when he was knighted in 1998.Rees largely leaves his subject’s private life tactfully alone, focusing instead on the origins of Gambon’s talent for deflecting scrutiny. He belonged to no obvious cohort or peer group. Unlike Tom Courtenay and Albert Finney, he had not attended drama school. Unlike Ian McKellen and Derek Jacobi, he had not made his way to Cambridge on a scholarship. Instead he emerged from working-class London-Irish amateur dramatics, where his practical skills were useful for building sets. This delight in making and tinkering remained with him throughout his life: in his home workshop he once built an exact replica of an antique pistol that he’d been asked to restore by a West End dealer, “so really I’m a faker”.Rees cross-references Gambon’s tall tales with other actors’ archives and draws on more than 100 new interviews, including conversations with Eileen Atkins, Penelope Wilton, Brian Cox and Simon Russell Beale. He also uses the archive of New York Times critic Mel Gussow, whose collection of interviews with Gambon appeared in 2004. The result is probably as near as anyone will get to a definitive account of Gambon’s life and career, although you would not want to bet on one or two of the actor’s misdirections slipping through undetected.View image in fullscreenMichael Gambon (left) and Brian Cox worked together on a 1968 prodction of Othello.Photograph: PRDespite being chosen by Olivier for the nascent National, Gambon initially failed to progress much beyond spear-carrying. His thuggish good looks – he was over 6ft tall, barrel-built, with a face of fleshy menace – made him useful as background colour. His unfamiliarity with the classical and modern repertory, not to mention the demands of iambic pentameter, left him ill-equipped for more demanding roles. Only after leaving in 1967 in search of better parts did his potential emerge. Most notably he played Tom in the London opening of Alan Ayckbourn’s The Norman Conquests.Gambon’s return to the National in 1978 saw him triumph in Pinter’s new play Betrayal and a revival of Brecht’s The Life of Galileo, which established him as a leading stage actor. In 1986, his performance in the BBC’s The Singing Detective made him a household name. Although he was reportedly not the first choice, the part of Dennis Potter’s Philip Marlow could have been written for him. Confined to a hospital bed by psoriatic arthritis and heavily bandaged, Marlow escapes his anguish by imagining parallel lives. He becomes a private detective and nightclub crooner, inhabiting a world of femmes fatales and Nazi spies, while revisiting a childhood scarred by his parents’ sexual unhappiness. Gambon plays a man who assumes multiple identities but never escapes himself.He liked to give the impression that he never planned anything, simply accepting the next job that came up. Perhaps that was true: there were certainly some poor choices along the way. For the moment, though, Gambon made the most of his newfound stardom. The following year, he played Eddie Carbone in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge. Miller was enchanted: “This guy can really disappear into a role.” The Guardian wrote that it showed “Michael Gambon shaking hands with greatness”.Rees devotes perhaps too much of this nearly 600-page book to Gambon’s mischief on stage and screen. His interviewees recall fart machines, water bombs and ad libs designed to throw fellow actors off their lines. The stories are often funny, but their cumulative effect is less comfortable. Was Gambon merely an antic fool, or was he a bit of a sadist? Rees leaves the verdict to his witnesses. Penelope Wilton recalls that the water pistols “got very tedious”.During RSC rehearsals Eileen Atkins remembers him saying, “I don’t bother with matinees, I just say the words”, which made her furious. He also lost interest once a production had peaked. After the triumphant opening of A View from the Bridge, he began, says co-star Michael Simkins, to “gently destroy it”. His performances deteriorated and the anticipated New York transfer never materialised.Gambon’s gradual decline makes for painful reading. In his late 50s he began to struggle with lines, flubbing them or improvising in ways that were no longer funny. Prompt boards were introduced, followed by “earwigs”, tiny earpieces through which a prompter fed him lines. This worked best on screen, where performances could be patched together from multiple takes, as happened in the Harry Potter films, where Gambon took over as Dumbledore after Richard Harris’s death. On stage, the difficulties became increasingly hard to conceal. Rees reveals that Gambon was diagnosed with dementia, something which he always denied, perhaps because he had watched his mother ravaged by the disease. It is at this late stage that we begin to glimpse the vulnerability and terror of exposure that lay beneath decades of blustery bravado.Rees avoids a conventional cradle-to-grave structure by following each main chapter with an interlude devoted to an aspect of Gambon’s character or career that might otherwise get lost in the narrative. One explores his beautifully elegant hands, evident in his wand work in Harry Potter; another his love of fast cars, memorably displayed on Top Gear’s Star in a Reasonably Priced Car segment, when he almost overturned a family saloon.Rees’s chief challenge is to convey what made Gambon such a great actor. He collates the testimony of colleagues and the verdicts of critics, but neither quite captures the alchemy of a performance. Nor can the actor’s wildly conflicting qualities be assembled into a single coherent character. This unresolved tension is not a failure of the biography so much as its most fitting conclusion: one suspects it is exactly the way that Gambon would have liked it.Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). title: Time Being by Jude Cook review – a smart existential tale of midlife | Books | The Guardian
description: A fatal mistake sparks this juicy melodrama, in which a philosophy professor navigates the guilt of being a survivor
Author: James Smart
Headline: A fatal mistake sparks this juicy melodrama, in which a philosophy professor navigates the guilt of being a survivor
Content: Moral maze … Jude Cook.Photograph: Sarah RaymondView image in fullscreenMoral maze … Jude Cook.Photograph: Sarah RaymondBooksReviewTime Being by Jude Cook review – a smart existential tale of midlifeA fatal mistake sparks this juicy melodrama, in which a philosophy professor navigates the guilt of being a survivorJames SmartTue 27 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat if, battered by cancer and cancer treatment, you decided to end your life? And what if it went wrong and you lived, but a friend died in your place? Would you tell the police the truth? Or reason that there’s no point punishing your grieving, bruised self any further, especially when – in the first bit of good news you’ve had for years – you learn that your treatment may finally be working?It’s the kind of moral question that London philosophy professor Esther Luck loves throwing at her students. But Jude Cook’s third novel makes the dilemma bracingly personal. As it opens, Esther, who has ovarian cancer, is waiting in a toilet cubicle on the fifth floor of her university building – the only one without CCTV – for the arrival of her dodgy French ex, Michel. He has agreed to shoot through the door and end her misery. But someone else arrives first. Laura is the department’s fragrant superstar, with her BBC presenting gig and handsome barrister husband. She finds an empty stall, Michel gets the wrong door, and Esther is left guilty, panicked and alone on the loo as Laura’s blood pools on the floor.The setup may feel like a Tarantino subplot, but Cook is here less for the violent drama than the existential questions that follow. His debut, Byron Easy, saw a poet mull over his frustrated life on a train, while its successor, Jacob’s Advice, followed two cousins as they discussed Europe, identity and terrorism. True to form, Time Being does not take long to hunker down with Esther’s thoughts.Having given a lecture on autopilot and deflected police questions, she sits in her Crouch End flat and walks in the nearby park, alone with her guilt and sorrow. Steroids have left her heavy and listless; radiotherapy has given her permanent nerve damage and agonising cystitis. She is crushed by her menopause and has few friends. Her career once offered fulfilment and security; now the philosophy department faces savage cuts, and an academic who can barely function is right in the firing line.double quotation markYou don’t have to like the protagonist to share her dread at the trauma she endures and the brutal decisions she facesBut the police investigation seems to be going nowhere fast, and chinks of light appear in Esther’s purgatory: good news from her doctor, an unexpected romance, a chance of a book deal. Esther finds herself hammering out Every Grain of Sand, an introduction to philosophy that’s also a memoir. It is, says her agent, “a book I just know women will identify with”. And for all her misery, Esther’s eye for the world is wonderfully vivid throughout. The new year finds “spring crouching under the churned soil”, while on a rare holiday to a country house hotel, Esther opens her eyes to the stars and basks in the universe.Yet nothing is entirely untainted. One October morning, she visits her mother’s grave under “a blaze of majestic bronze and apricot” foliage to find freshly painted swastikas on the stones of the Jewish cemetery. The police may seem no closer to solving Laura’s murder, but they return every few months to ask leading questions and sit thoughtfully in Esther’s book-lined office. And can the wild, charismatic Michel simply have vanished?Like any good philosopher, Esther ponders it all: is life “just one damn thing after another”; is she a “temporal husk of flesh, or something else”? She turns to Boethius, Kant, Arendt, Weil and De Beauvoir, but finds little solace. Indeed, Time Being’s philosophical asides end up feeling like its flimsiest part. The rest of the book is better and more focused, and while the juicy melodrama of Laura’s murder and the bleak mundanity of an unhappy life may seem an uncomfortable marriage, Cook ultimately brings his strands together with confidence.Throughout, it’s the details and feelings that power Time Being: the heavy silence of the clinic’s waiting room, the happy buzz of an unexpected date, the practised rhythm of a lecture. Esther is a fine and acutely observed creation, at times thoroughly sympathetic, at others grimly evasive, and all the more credible for it: you don’t have to like her to share her dread at the trauma she endures and the brutal decisions she faces. The result is a fine portrait of a wounded midlife, as seasons shift and hope and happiness roll by, glorious but fleeting, like clouds in a turbulent sky.Time Being by Jude Cook is published by Salt (£10.99).
