title: The Master Builder review – false swagger and queasy infidelity propel Ibsen’s big-drop drama | Stage | The Guardian
description: David Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignore
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: David Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignore
Content: Hicks is almost antic, and Binder is marvellous … left to right: Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) and Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenHicks is almost antic, and Binder is marvellous … left to right: Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) and Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianStageReviewThe Master Builder review – false swagger and queasy infidelity propel Ibsen’s big-drop dramaArcola theatre, LondonDavid Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignoreArifa AkbarTue 27 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis outing of Henrik Ibsen’s play, translated by playwright David Edgar, is reassuring afterLila Raicek’s oddly conceived West End version last year starring Ewan McGregor– as well intentioned as its feminist revisionism might have been.Edgar’s is more faithful to the original in form and spirit (although he compresses three acts into two), and its strengths lie in drawing out the psychological aspects of the ageing, anxious master builder at its centre, whose fall from the heights of worldly acclaim is both real and symbolic in a play that blends both those realms together.Halvard Solness (Greg Hicks) is determined to keep his place in the world but also plagued by midlife insecurity – and the protege Ragnar Brovik (Ryan Wichert) whom he perceives to be snapping at his heels – when he is confronted by Hilde Wangel (Louisa Binder), a young woman who has come to claim the “kingdom” he promised her in an encounter when she was 13.Edgar deftly draws out the intimacies and tensions between characters in this curious story, with its enigmatic ending and its growing sense of otherworldliness. Except there is nothing otherworldly to the production: director Mehmet Ergen gives the characters a solidity in his modern-dress production.View image in fullscreenIntimacies and tensions … (from left) Sally George (Aline Solness), Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel), Peter Guinness (Doctor Herdal) and Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThis world is recognisable, with Hilde real and a symbol of his past – or a consequence of it. She brings memories Solness claims to have forgotten and you can read the #MeToo subtext in his amnesia. It is queasy to hear about the kisses he gave her as a girl, and queasier still to feel the flirtation now between them.Hicks is animated, almost antic, as a man at the height of his worldly pomp who is inwardly unravelling. Binder is marvellous as Hilde, almost swaggering as she runs rings around him. Sally George, too, is very believable as Solness’s wife, Aline, forever grieving the death of their twin children and well able to see her husband’s emotional infidelities with the women that float around him, including office assistant Kaja (Jade Williams).Yet the drama still hits against the limits of Ibsen’s strange and static story: you do not quite know if Solness is to be admired or condemned, and what of Hilde’s final triumphalism as she sees him fall from his tower? The puzzle of the ending might be the workings of fate, the personal cost of success, or an Icarus-like comeuppance for a middle-aged man in thrall to a younger woman. This production does not feel like a tragedy. You do not feel for Solness, or his fall. But then, were you ever supposed to?AtArcola theatre, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreHenrik IbsenArcola theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours | Architecture | The Guardian
description: A low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to star
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: A low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to star
Content: High lights … the glowing polycarbonate ventilation shaftofthe new Yard theatre near the Olympic site.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightView image in fullscreenHigh lights … the glowing polycarbonate ventilation shaftofthe new Yard theatre near the Olympic site.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightArchitectureOur loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighboursA low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to starOliver WainwrightTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but thelegacy of the sporting spectaclerolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of theYard theatre. Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – andIan McKellen set to star in the next show.View image in fullscreenWill the actors’ knees be able to take it? … the concrete stage.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates ofPractice Architectureto conjure anad hoc auditoriumon a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard intoa mixed-use district. That project never materialised, but executive director Ashleigh Wheeler and her team succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (community infrastructure levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.View image in fullscreenSpell it out … the theatre’s name in the multicoloured recycled brickwork.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work ofTakero Shimazaki, a Tokyo-born Londoner who wasshortlisted for the Stirling prize last yearfor an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. It reads like a collage of its context: a shed clad with corrugated fibre-cement sheeting, rising from graffiti-covered warehouse walls on one side and framed by a new brick gable end on the other. The bricks include subtle shades of blue, yellow and magenta, in a nod to the previous printworks, while the name of the theatre is spelt out in the brickwork, recalling the faded factory signs of the area. In keeping with the waste-not ethos, theseK-Briqs, manufactured in Scotland, are unfired and made of 95% construction waste, recycling 16 tonnes of waste that would have otherwise gone to landfill and saving the equivalent of 3.5 tonnes of CO2that regular bricks would have emitted.There is a grandeur to the new theatre’s form. With its central tower and symmetrical pitch roof, Shimazaki says the Yard was inspired by Palladian churches to bring a sense of permanence, as if the building might have been here far longer than it has. “The Yard was interested in the idea of permanence in theatre, and fakery in architecture,” he says. “And how to build something grownup with not much money.” Mirrored panels in some of the windows bring a theatrical touch, while bright pink guttering and yellow coping blend with the local street art vernacular. Miraculously, for now, the new brickwork remains graffiti free.View image in fullscreenOne of the first shows …for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf–Photograph: Philip VileEntering through big double doors – emblazoned with “open me up now” – you find a large open foyer and cafe, with walls and banquettes in rich shades of burgundy, while a glossy blue bar is framed with bands of teal and green, recalling a Josef Albers painting. Gold-painted columns add a touch of theatrical bling, which will be cranked up a notch next year when a vestibule is installed. Designed by artistEd Atkins, it will usher theatregoers through a dramatic ruched silver curtain. The loos add further sparkle, inspired by thebathroom at the Villa Necchi Campiglio in Milan, with glossy black tiles, shiny brass fittings and coloured lino floors – “a little bit of economical opulence”, as Shimazaki puts it.So what of the theatre itself? A central staircase leads up through a dark passage to the new auditorium, where the architects had to strike a tricky balance. “We wanted to retain what people loved about the old space,” says Miller, “and evolve what wasn’t as functional.” It has the same bare bones quality as before, with an exposed back wall built with bricks salvaged from the site, a concrete stage (actors’ knees won’t thank them), and curved, raked seating in the manner of an amphitheatre. The plastic cafe seats were upgraded for upholstered communal benches.“Epic and intimate at the same time” was the brief, and Shimazaki has risen to the challenge, creating a 250-capacity space – more than double the previous theatre – that is at once cosy and grand. Continuing the fakery theme, the cast concrete-looking seating structure is actually cement particle board, while banks of radiators hidden below the seats keep bums warm while aiding the passive stack ventilation system. As before, what you see is what you get: there are no wings, no fly tower, nowhere for the actors to hide. “We wanted to amplify the sense of liveness,” says Miller. “After all, that’s what makes theatre unique.” It still feels raw – although performers now benefit from the luxury of dressing rooms, tucked beneath the seating, saving them from dashing to beat the audience to the loos in the interval.View image in fullscreenInspired by Palladian churches … the corrugated fibre-cement claddingPhotograph: Philip VileAround the other side of the building, the graffitied warehouse offices are being transformed into a youth hub by Jeremy Deller and architect educators Matt+Fiona, alongside local schoolchildren. It’s part of an Arts Council-fundedseriesthat has also seen an Antony Gormley figure appear on the roof – visible from the elevated platform of Hackney Wick station – with further commissions and community collaborations in the works.Fit for a king: Ian McKellen to play Lear at newly rebuilt Yard theatre in east LondonRead moreThe ad hoc ingenuity on show puts what is emerging across the other side of the park into sharp relief. One of the biggest components of the Olympic legacy is the “cultural quarter” ofEast Bankin Stratford, a £1.1bn colossus that houses branches of the V&A, Sadler’s Wells theatre, BBC studios, University of the Arts London and University College London, soon to be garnished with towers of unaffordable flats. The presence of these institutions is welcome – but despite the big budgets, top architects and endless design review panels, the results feel less than world class.It is a cumbersome beast, designed by committee and airlifted in from on high, begat from the loins of mayors hungry for legacies. The Yard, by contrast, shows how a young, agile team with a fraction of the resources can achieve so much, building a project that feels truly grown from its place.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureTheatreYard theatreGreen buildingHackneyLondonOlympic legacyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more | Macklemore | The Guardian
description:
3Arena, Dublin
Several unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: 3Arena, DublinSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon
Content: Macklemore performing on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Zoe RainView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Zoe RainMacklemoreReviewMacklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more3Arena, DublinSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia NixonAlexis PetridisTue 27 Oct 2026 00.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organising this concert,” offers a member of Kneecap, one of several unannounced guests who have turned up for the first European date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour. It’s a characteristically two-fisted approach to the matter in hand from a band who have seldom shied away from controversy, but it has more than a grain of truth in it.The events of the last six weeks are quite something, and perhaps not what Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, had in mind when he led efforts to pressurise Sheeran toremove Macklemore from his summer US tour, after the rapper made a speech about Palestine on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore was duly removed from the tour, but the rapper saw his profile rise dramatically as a result – in fairness, he was hardly unknown, but his biggest hits are a decade old – whileevery other artist on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity. Sheeran’s tour limped on amid much opprobrium, while Macklemore was able to translate the publicity into a tour of his own, in noticeably bigger venues than he played on his last European tour, with proceeds donated to organisations assisting Palestinians. Dublin’s 13,000-capacity 3Arena is sold out, as is every other date on the tour.Accordingly, a certain infectiously giddy excitement attends the event itself: the audience receive everything – speeches from activists; video messages from actors Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon and the Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas, among others; sets of Arabic-themed dance music from Palestinian American DJ Habibeats; and an appearance by longstanding political US hip-hop duo Dead Prez.View image in fullscreenKneecap performing on the Free Palestine tour.Photograph: Zoe RainThey go nuts for Lina Makoul, the first Palestinian to win the Israeli equivalent of The Voice: her brief set opens with a wordless vocal protesting censorship and ends with a song admonishing late-stage capitalism that comes complete with a glancing reference to Guy Debord’s La Société du spectacle, which really isn’t what one would expect from a TV talent show winner. They receive Beoga, the County Kerry folk band who performed on Sheeran’s Galway Girl, but left the singer’s tour alongside Macklemore, like returning heroes. It turns out they’re founding members of an organisation called Irish Artists For Palestine, which does rather beg the question of what Sheeran thought they might do under the circumstances. “You don’t fuck with the Irish, lads,” offers drummer Eamon Murray.There’s something very striking about the fact that the local artists who’ve heeded Macklemore’s call to help out are evidently committed to the cause behind it: you never get a sense of anyone rocking up in order to grab brownie points or reflected glory. Backed by a string section, Hozier’s performance is heavy on audience-pleasing hits – Take Me to Church, Too Sweet – and takes in a rendition of a remarkable 19th-century folk ballad called The Prayer of Shields, which he apparently learned from Ian Lynch of Lankum. Thescreens behind him display a QR code that links to a petition in support of 55 students from Gaza who have not had their visas approved to study inIreland. He goes down a storm, but the real bedlam is caused by Kneecap, who know a thing or two about how controversy can impact an artist’s profile. Their brief set opens with a film that proceeds in a frantic blur of images – The Troubles, Sinéad O’Connor ripping up the pope’s photo on Saturday Night Live – causes an outbreak of moshing and ends with DJ Próvaí struggling to maintain his balance in the midst of the audience: it’s splenetic, chaotic and remarkably powerful.View image in fullscreenFans outside 3Arena in Dublin before Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour gig.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesWhen Macklemore finally appears, it’s hard to miss the effect of recent events upon him, not least because his opening track, Chant – a 2022 single about his struggle with addiction – now sounds remarkably like a defiant comment on them: “This is my moment … you can’t take my voice from me.” He has a point: he’s been writing about Palestine since 2024’s Hind’s Hall, but as he rolls out his old hits – Thrift Shop’s hymning of limiting one’s spending rather than splurging in grandstanding rapper style; Same Love’s backing for same-sex marriage – a fresh sense of energised purpose about his approach is hard to miss. Between songs, he assiduously shifts attention from himself to the cause he’s advocating, but notes that the show itself “makes me feel glorious”. Understandably so: he mentions that he’s “called up a lot of people in the last six weeks” and notes that Kneecap and Hozier were the first to agree to perform alongside him, which makes you wonder how successful his efforts have been elsewhere. But in Dublin at least, the Free Palestine show feels like a worthwhile triumph.Macklemore’sFree Palestine tourgoes to Paris on 29 October and London on 30 OctoberThis article was amended on 28 October 2026 to correct a photo caption.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreRapPop and rockIrelandlive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary! | US theater | The Guardian
description: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy
Content: ‘But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.’Photograph: Shaun VadellaView image in fullscreen‘But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.’Photograph: Shaun VadellaUS theaterInterview‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary!Owen MyersThe RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedyTue 27 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlaska may be starring in the most subversive comedy in American theater today, but she carries herself with the poise of a 40s movie star. On a brisk September afternoon, the actor, comedian and RuPaul’s Drag Race alumnus is in a small rehearsal room in New York’s midtown, sipping hot tea from a flask while perched on a hard-shell travel case. She sits bolt upright, as if she has spent her life balancing books on her head.Oh, Mary! review – Cole Escola’s gloriously deranged historical rompRead moreIt has been a madcap time for the actor as she prepares to play Mary Todd Lincoln in a new touring production of Cole Escola’s Tony award-winning comedyOh, Mary!. She is amid a few weeks of rehearsals in the city before the show’s four-month sprint across the US. When I ask how she is handling the upheaval from her Los Angeles home, she smiles indulgently. “I mean, I would go to the planet Remulak for this show,” she says, referencing the home planet of theConeheads. “I didn’t even think about it. I was just like, ‘Let’s make this happen.’”Alaska (AKA Alaska Thunderfuck 5000, born Justin Honard) is on the brink of her biggest career moment yet and is determined to make every moment of it count. Since competing in season five of RuPaul’s Drag Race in 2013, the self-described “extraterrestrial phenomenon from the planet Glamtr0n” has released five electro-pop albums with titles like Anus and Vagina, taken to the high seas for drag-themed cruises and co-written and performed in the off-Broadway hit Drag: The Musical, produced byLiza Minnelli. Her live performances showcase the art of drag at its high-concept creative peak; a recentperformanceof Taylor Swift’s The Fate of Ophelia was a delightfully dizzying hurricane of hairstyles, props, frills and feathers, with three costume changes in as many minutes.View image in fullscreenAlaska and Wesley Taylor in the first national tour of Oh, Mary!Photograph: Evan Zimmerman/MurphyMadeWith Oh, Mary!, Alaska is stepping away from nightlife stages and into the shoes of a character already played by actors including Maya Rudolph, Jane Krakowski and Jinkx Monsoon as well as Escola. A London production opened in 2025, while a live-recorded special of the show will air on HBO next year. The character of Mary Todd Lincoln, in Escola and director Sam Pinkleton’s vision, is stifled by her duties, drinks to escape the unbearable company of her (closeted) husband, and longs to return to the life as a cabaret star that she gave up to be first lady.Director Pinkleton first encountered Alaska over a decade ago when she played Nomi Malone in aShowgirls tributeshow at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre. “It was electric,” he tells me. “I was like, ‘This person is a star; you can’t take your eyes off her.’”Pinkleton cast Alaska in a 2021Los Angelesproduction of Head Over Heels, which reimagined the Broadway musical as a queer rave. “I couldn’t believe how much she cared and how great she was technically,” he says. “I have since worked with a lot of drag queens, and I’ve had exclusively great experiences because they are really hard workers. You know, they make everything happen on their own.”‘Bodies, pornography and disgust’: did 2 Girls 1 Cup change the way a generation thinks about sex?Read moreAfter an initial Zoom workshop with Pinkleton and Escola this March, Alaska was offered the role of Mary this summer. She was particularly struck by the purity of the character’s ambition, even as she resorts to increasingly bizarre tactics to get back on the cabaret stage where she belongs. “This isn’t a comedy show to me,” Alaska says. “This is deathly serious. It’s very real, and I think that’s why so many people can step into the role and make it seem like it’s written for them.“I feel like I can make sense of this role,” she adds. “I can’t name any other role where I feel like I make sense. I mean, being a weird drag queen person, queer-bodied person existing in society … that’s exactly what I felt like when I grew up.”Raised in Erie, Pennsylvania, she was a shy and watchful kid. “I wish that I had the confidence to be like, ‘You know what? I am something and I do deserve more than like being scared to go out of my fucking room,’” she says. “It wasn’t until many years later, when I discovered theater and drag, that I was able to find that in myself. But it is a feeling of like, ‘Fuck, I can’tbe.’”She was introduced to the world of performance while on school trips: she caught a touring production of The Phantom of the Opera while in Canada, and saw a version of Cats at SeaWorld. (“Maybe they should do Oh, Mary! on water skis in Florida,” she muses.) She was especially drawn to the over-the-top femininity of film characters like Jessica Rabbit and Michelle Pfeiffer’s Catwoman. “Not real people”, she notes.As a theater major at the University of Pittsburgh, she starred in a 1922 Czech expressionist drama called The Insect Play (she played a murderous wasp) as well as in Brecht’s Mother Courage and Her Children. Importantly, the program taught every aspect of mounting a production, including directing, playwriting, set design and costume – crucial skills for a drag superstar in the making.After a few years of gigging around LA, Alaska won a slot on RuPaul’s Drag Race season five. For many fans, it’s still the best season, with a cast that also included Jinkx Monsoon (now aBroadwaystar in her own right) as well as much-loved comedy queens Detox and Alyssa Edwards. Alaska was the rare queen that could do it all; she finished as runner-up and after the season aired in 2013, she found herself as one of the most famous drag queens in America. “It was being shot out of a fucking cannon. I was in my late 20s, but still mentally I was still a child.”Alaska and her then-partner Sharon Needles (who had won season four ofDragRace) went from being broke and scraping together money for a 12-pack of beer to being the most famous drag queen couple in America. “Our lives changed a lot really fast, and we made every single mistake that you can make,” she says. “There was no gameplan. There was no roadmap. We suddenly had money and we never had a fucking penny before. It wasdo every drug,drink every thing.”After reading a book by the Buddhist nun Pema Chödrön, who she says “does a really good job of talking about meditation and consciousness in a way that a dumb American can understand”, Alaska became sober for two and a half years. These days, she has a more moderate relationship with alcohol, which has set her up to be in fighting shape for Oh, Mary! “The rehearsal has been really intense,” she says. “It’s like doing cardio every day. Which is great, because I hate cardio.”Despite its financial successes in New York (Oh, Mary! was the first show of the 2024-25 season to recoup its costs), the show is perhaps not the most natural choice to tour a politically divided country, with dates in smaller cities including Hartford, Connecticut, and Saint Paul, as well as Los Angeles and Boston. “I think it’s pretty great,” Alaska says. “It’s going to be interesting because there are going to be people seeing the show who don’t go see Broadway shows all the time. I’m excited to shock people.“I mean, it would even be important even if we didn’t have a piece of shit in the Oval Office,” she says. “But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.”View image in fullscreenJohn-Andrew Morrison and Alaska in Oh, Mary!Photograph: Evan ZimmermanThe pipeline from drag superstar to grande dame of theatre hasn’t always been so well established, and Alaska credits Jinkx Monsoon’s arc from Drag Race to Broadway as an inspiration. “She’s slammed open so many doors for so many people,” Alaska says. “And she continues to do so. I’m glad to walk right through, honey.”Does she face stereotypes because of her background in drag? “It’s definitely better now. I mean, I’ve been doing drag for almost 20 years. On a Hollywood set, a dog would get better treatment than a drag queen. And that’s not even an exaggeration. That’s hard, and that shit still exists and still happens.”I’m curious if Drag Race feels far away to Alaska now. It’s been 10 years since she was crowned the winner of All Stars season two. “Yes and no”, she says. “My job as a podcaster is talking about Drag Race. I still work with all the girls from Drag Race all the time. Yes, it’s in the past, but still it’s very much a part of my life. I wish I was more in that universe, but they won’t fucking invite me. So if they read this, maybe they could call me. I would love to have been inStop! That! Train!” So RuPaul and the film’s producers never got in touch? “No”, she says crisply. That’s a shame. “I agree.”That comedy film seems like small potatoes when compared with the plans Alaska is hatching. After Oh, Mary! wraps, she will embark on her 50-date, 50-stateRevolution Tourthis March, taking in the length and breadth of the country from Fayetteville to Fargo. Even an A-list pop star would balk at such an ambitious schedule. “I know,” she smiles. “This is just something that my fiance and I have wanted to do for a while. There’s a lot of states that we just haven’t been to, let alone gotten to do drag in.“There are gay people everywhere, and they don’t often get to go out to a drag show,” she says, as if casting her mind back to the Catwoman-obsessed kid growing up in rural Pennsylvania. But isn’t it a logistical nightmare? Alaska throws her head back and laughs.“Well”, she says, “nobody has told me no!”Alaska is in the touring production ofOh, Mary!until 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsUS theaterDragPop and rockTheatreRuPaulBroadwayOff-BroadwayinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies | Neil Young | The Guardian
description: The musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song again
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song again
Content: Neil Young pictured in 2019.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APView image in fullscreenNeil Young pictured in 2019.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APNeil YoungNeil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at ralliesThe musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song againLaura SnapesTue 27 Oct 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeil Young is suing Donald Trump’s political action committee Trump 47 Committee Inc for $10m (£7.47m) over alleged copyright infringement of his song Rockin’ in the Free World after the US president used it as walk-up music in recent midterm election rallies.It is the second time that Young has filed against one of Trump’s organisations over his unlicenced use of the song. He first did so in 2020, against the corporation Donald J Trump for President Inc. Trump settled, promising, according to Young’s suit, that his organisation “would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young”.Filed on Monday in the US district court for the eastern district of Virginia, the suit states that Trump’s ongoing use of the song meant that Young, a very vocal critic of the president, “has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J Trump in any way”.Neil Young: Rockin’ in the Free World – videoTrump’s administration has not yet responded to the suit.Young’s case outlines how diametrically opposed his 1989 song is to Trump’s values, calling it “a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten.“The lyrics pain vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNeil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes goldRead moreLawyers for Young cite the playing of the song at the president’s rally in Ohio on 12 October but state that it has been played “numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections”. Young also seeks an injunction against further public performances.Young’s anti-Trump stance is clear: he has repeatedly damned the president in writings on his website and in 2025released a protest song about his administration, Big Crime. “Don’t need no fascist rules / Don’t want no fascist schools / Don’t want soldiers walking on the streets,” Young sings. “Got to get the fascists out / Got to clean the White House out … no more money to the fascists, the billionaire fascists.”In the past 12 months, the Trump presidency has amped up its strategy oftrolling leftwing musicians– including Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter and SZA – by using their songs to soundtrack ICE propaganda or clips about Trump’s strategy in Iran. In August, Taylor Swift had her song August removed from a video celebrating the Trump presidency.Explore more on these topicsNeil YoungDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cheer up, Scrooge! The merriest Christmas theatre shows, from musketeers to a penguin party | Christmas shows | The Guardian
description: The festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella
Content: Wrongdoings, reckonings and redemption … Stuart Bowman as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol at the Royal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenWrongdoings, reckonings and redemption … Stuart Bowman as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol at the Royal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicChristmas showsCheer up, Scrooge! The merriest Christmas theatre shows, from musketeers to a penguin partyThe festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s CinderellaArifa AkbarTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Little Night MusicRoyal Exchange theatre, Manchester, 5 December to 30 JanuarySelina Cartmell is sending in the clowns this Christmas, directing Stephen Sondheim’s fairytale musical about mismatched couples. Originally inspired by an Ingmar Bergman film, it has some of the most exquisite songs of Sondheim’s magnificent oeuvre and is choreographed by former Strictly judge Arlene Phillips.The Three MusketeersRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, 28 November to 9 JanuaryBuckle up for some swashbuckling: the RSC’s version of D’Artagnan’s duelling adventures alongside Athos, Porthos and Aramis is co-produced with Told By an Idiot, a company known for its visual comedy. It is billed as a “wild” new adaptation of Alexandre Dumas’s novel and features an international company of performers.Honk!Barn theatre, Cirencester, 21 November to 3 JanuaryIn George Stiles and Anthony Drewe’s musical drama for all ages, Ugly is a plucky wee duck, teased by siblings and friends alike for his idiosyncratic looks. We find him undertaking a perilous wild goose (duckling?) chase in his quest to discover the beautiful drake within.View image in fullscreenTate Masuku goes walking in the air with Andrew Ashton as the Snowman.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe SnowmanBirmingham Repuntil 1 November, thenPeacock theatre, London, 21 November to 3 January 2027Raymond Briggs’s gorgeous snowman goes walking in the air again ina new version of the Christmas classic, about an unlikely friendship that takes delightful flight. Featuring Howard Blake’s timeless score, it is now directed and choreographed by Will Tuckett and features puppets designed by Tahra Zafar, who recreated Michael Bond’s Paddington Bear for the West End musical.The Merry Adventures of Maid MarianSherman theatre, Cardiff, 27 November to 2 JanuaryThe Robin Hood story is relocated and respun to place a female outlaw at its centre. Now it is Maid Marian of south Wales, whose resistance against the king’s men will be accompanied by familiar faces from the legend. Performed by a band of actor-musicians and directed by Lee Lyford.AntarcticaPolka theatre, London, 27 November to 17 JanuaryHere’s a south pole show filled with icy wildlife, from tripping penguins to cheeky albatrosses. There are clowns, puppets and the promise of some magical surprises in this tale of what lies at the bottom of our planet. A winter wonderland for children, aimed at three- to seven-year-olds.View image in fullscreenHappy anniversary … Hannah Kremer and Rory Macleod in Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella.Photograph: Johan PerssonMatthew Bourne’s CinderellaTouring from 16 NovemberAmid the season’s flurry of fairytale princesses in glass slippers isMatthew Bourne’s 30-year-old ballet, twirling back for an anniversary tour. Set during the second world war, it situates the romance in blitz-torn London. Hannah Kremer and Katrina Lyndon share the role of Cinders, who meets an RAF pilot. The show travels to 17 venues over 24 weeks.Robin Hood and the Merry MandemTheatre Royal Stratford East, 21 November to 2 JanuaryAnother spin on the heroic outlaws of Sherwood folklore. This Robin Hood hails from E15 and hits east London in a hoodie, along with his merry band of “mandem”. Nottinghamshire’s forest is swapped for housing estates, retail jungles and the Central Line commuter rush as Robin’s men take from the undeserving rich to give to the area’s poor.The Reluctant DragonMarlowe theatre, Canterbury, 5 December to 3 JanuaryA child befriends a flamboyant, poetry-reciting dragon and embarks on an intrepid campaign to save it from a slayer who mistakes it for a fire-breathing fiend in Kenneth Grahame’s book. A David and Goliath story in reverse, now told as a musical family show.Santa’s First ChristmasUnicorn theatre, London, 14 November to 3 JanuaryThe elves want old Saint Nicholas to take five from shimmying up and down chimneys and drink in some yuletide spirit himself in this adaptation of Mac Barnett’s book. Directed and choreographed by Olivier award-winner James Cousins, it has songs by Harry Blake.The Jungle BookNational Theatre, London, 13 November to 6 FebruaryThe National Theatre’s Christmas shows have hit the mark in recent years. This one reimagines Rudyard Kipling’s classic tale of Mowgli and friends’ adventures through the mangroves of the Sundarbans. It’s adapted by Anupama Chandrasekhar and staged by the NT’s artistic director, Indhu Rubasingham, with puppetry by Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell.The Further Adventures of Peter Pan: The Return of Captain HookGrand Opera House York, 5 December to 3 JanuaryJust when we thought Neverland was safe! Captain Hook strikes back in this continuation of JM Barrie’s story about the pirate’s feud with the forever young leader of the Lost Boys. Here it comes in the form of a pantomime, complete with songs and aerial stunts.Miss Bennet: Christmas at PemberleyPark theatre, London, 2 December to 10 JanuaryThe hot new takes on Pride and Prejudice keep on coming. This festive permutation by playwrights Lauren Gunderson and Margot Melcon finds the Bennets reuniting at the family estate, and centres on bookish middle sister, Mary, and aChristmasvisit from Lord Arthur de Bourgh.A Christmas CarolRoyal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh, 28 November to 3 JanuaryWhat’s Christmas without this classic about moral wrongdoings, ghostly reckonings and redemption, featuring the stingy Ebenezer Scrooge? Charles Dickens’ Victorian London is swapped for Edinburgh in the Lyceum’s production, adapted by Deborah McAndrew and directed by James Brining. It might be comfy Christmas fare, but it still contains resonant messages for our times about the duty to be charitable.Explore more on these topicsChristmas showsChristmasTheatreDancePanto seasonMusicalsSherman theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content
