title: Houseplant hacks: should plants rest in the dark over winter ? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: Some do need a rest to complete their growth cycle, but for others this hack could be stressful
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Some do need a rest to complete their growth cycle, but for others this hack could be stressful
Content: Cacti will benefit from a cooler, lower-light rest in winter.Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCacti will benefit from a cooler, lower-light rest in winter.Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: should plants rest in the dark over winter ?Some do need a rest to complete their growth cycle, but for others this hack could be stressfulGynelle LeonTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemWinter plant advice is full of contradictions. Rest your plants; don’t rest your plants. Move them to a cooler spot; keep them warm. One common tip is to put certain houseplants in a dark, cool spot, to mimic natural dormancy and give them the rest they need.The hackSome plants need a period of reduced light, cooler temperatures and minimal watering to complete their growth cycle. Forcing this dormancy by moving them somewhere darker and cooler in winter is said to result in stronger growth, better flowering and a healthier plant come spring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouseplant hacks: Are windowsills too cold for plants in winter?Read moreThe methodMove cacti and succulents to a cool, dark place from around October to March. Reduce watering dramatically, stop feeding entirely and keep them between 5C and 10C if possible.The testI moved some cacti to an unheated room for winter and put some in total darkness. In spring, the ones with low light were compact, firm and pushed out new growth quickly. The ones in total darkness etiolated (became unnaturally long, pale and weak).The verdictDormancy works for the right plants. Cacti will benefit from a cooler, lower-light rest in winter, though they don’t like total darkness. Tropical plants will simply get stressed.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: CurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need it | Skincare | The Guardian
description: With six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devices
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: With six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devices
Content: Seen the light: our tester found the Series 3 comfy and reported fewer breakouts after four weeks.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSeen the light: our tester found the Series 3 comfy and reported fewer breakouts after four weeks.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSkincareReviewCurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need itWith six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devicesThe best LED face masksSarah MatthewsTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCurrentBody’sLED maskshave long been my favourite. They’re comfortable, simple to use and effective. My previous favourite, the now-discontinuedCurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask, offered five treatments that used different light wavelengths to address multiple skin concerns. The company’s latest mask, the new Series 3, has the most detailed customisable treatments I’ve ever seen.This isn’t the first LED mask I’ve tried that allows its user to select different treatments for different areas of the face. TheLustre Renew Pro Facewearallows you to choose from two treatments across four different zones, with 16 possible combinations. The Series 3 takes this much further, allowing you to choose between six light wavelengths across 125 light points on the mask. If you stick to one wavelength per light point, that’s 6125combinations available. That number is longer than I can reasonably comprehend, so allow me to call its level of customisation endless.At £499.99, it certainly isn’t cheap, but it’s the same price as its less-advanced predecessor. Having tested my custom treatment for six weeks, my results were just as good as I had hoped, with the same excellent coverage I’ve come to expect from CurrentBody LED masks. Once you’ve got over the price, there’s very little to grumble about here, given that theDr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Procosts almost as much and has no personalisation, and cheaper masks such as theSilk’n LED face mask Procan’t pinpoint precise areas of the face. For anyone looking for the best LED mask money can buy, this is a safe bet.View at CurrentBodyView at AmazonHow I testedView image in fullscreenAny changes to the condition, texture and appearance of our tester’s skin were noted after two months of using the LED mask.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI’ve tested 18 LED masks, considering overall efficacy, comfort levels and ease of use – all things that help make consistent treatments enjoyable. I alwayscheck comfort levels by testing how well the eye guards block out the light from the mask, how easy the straps are to adjust and how comfortable the mask is to wear when lying down, sitting up and moving around.I also assess how straightforward the mask’s controls are. This was especially important for this mask, which required me to download an app. If it’s going to take up space on my phone, it had better be flawless.The test also involved noting the condition, texture and appearance of my skin before and after two months of use. I tested the four preset treatments for four nights each to get a quick idea of how they affected my skin, but since personalised treatments are the star of the show here, I used a customisable treatment for the rest of the test. Having tested LED masks before, I was hoping to at least maintain, or, ideally, build on the improvements I’d seen previously.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAll the kit: the Series 3 comes with adjustable straps, removable eye guards and a touchscreen controller.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView at CurrentBodyView at AmazonLet’s not beat around the bush: LED therapy, AKA photobiomodulation, looks a lot like pseudoscience. Scepticism is understandable, so as part of my LED mask testing for the Filter, I spoke to four independent dermatologists, anti-ageing experts and facialists. Their overall outlook on the tech was positive, particularly with regard to managing mild acne, reducing inflammation and firming skin. They advised choosing a mask from a reputable brand that bolsters its claims with clinical studies, and doing consistent treatments alongside agood skincare routine. Or, if you’re already inconsistent with skincare,consider whether you really need an LED maskfirst.The mostconcrete evidencefor LED therapy is in the blue, red and infrared wavelengths, used for acne, ageing and wound healing. There is growing interest in green and yellow light for brightening and calming redness.Small studiescommissioned by CurrentBody reported modest reductions of 4.1% in pigmentation with green light and 8.6% in redness with yellow light, compared with a 37.1% reduction in forehead wrinkle volume with deep near-infrared light.The Series 3 has 750 LEDs spread across 125 light points on the face. This is more light points than any previous CurrentBody mask, allowing for greater light coverage. For context, the Shark CryoGlow has more light points (160), although it lacks the range of wavelengths on offer here, with 480 individual LED light sources across three wavelengths. Some entry-level masks offer fewer light points, sometimes under 100, which tend to garner less effective results. In the Series 3, each light point has six LEDs: red, blue, near-infrared, deep near-infrared, yellow and green. Unlike all other masks I’ve tested, which mostly concentrate the most deeply penetrating deep near-infrared light around the eyes and mouth, the Series 3 offers full-face coverage, meaning it can tackle deep wrinkles anywhere you fancy.View image in fullscreenReady, set, glow: the controller offers four preset treatments, including Advanced Anti-Ageing.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThere are four preset 10-minute treatments: Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Brighten & Balance, and Complexion Corrector. These combine near-infrared light with a different visible light wavelength to achieve their results and work like those offered on theMulti Light Therapy mask.As mentioned, the star of the show here is the customised treatments, where users can pick out wavelengths with reckless abandon in the app. Helpfully, each colour is labelled with a brief description of its aims: “clear breakouts” for blue light, “calm redness” for yellow and so on. These can be positioned anywhere on the face and combined to create a treatment that’s unique to your needs. And, since you can save up to 10 custom treatments on the mask and more in the app, it also gives users the flexibility to target breakouts or dark spots precisely where they pop up, while continuing with other treatments elsewhere.But if free salad bars have taught me anything, it’s that people are likely to overdo it if left unsupervised. That’s why CurrentBody has developed MyDose, which automatically calculates the optimum dosage for your chosen light wavelengths. In theory, this means you can safely customise treatments without compromising on results.The Series 3 also has CurrentBody’s Veritace certification. Every mask undergoes quality control tests in which each of the 750 LEDs is tested to ensure it emits the specified wavelength and power output required before it’s shipped out to you. The mask comes with its own NFC card that lets you view the results; it’s reassuring to have this kind of transparency for a mask that costs this much.CurrentBody Series 3 specificationsPrice:£499.99Recommended use:3-5 times per weekSettings:Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Complexion Corrector, Brighten & Balance, plus near-infinite customised optionsLightwavelengths:red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1072nm), blue (415nm), green (532nm), yellow (590nm)Treatment time:10 minutesSuitable for:all skin types, but darker tones should take care with blue lightBattery life:13 usesCharging time:4.5 hoursContents:mask, three straps, two removable eye guards, Veritace card, charging cable, storage bagWhat we loveView image in fullscreenA personal touch: the Series 3 lets users customise the light wavelengths across different areas of the face.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianLike the Series 2 that came before it, the Series 3 is made from flexible silicone that fits comfortably without digging in, and has a chin strap that offers more coverage than other masks. Its straps are adjustable at four points – two on either side of the head – plus there’s an overhead strap that can stop the mask from slipping down on smaller heads. I also found the eye guards did a fantastic job of blocking out the mask’s light during treatment, as I was able to see clearly enough to read or potter around in dim lighting with no issues.The results from my tests were fantastic. As expected, given the Multi Light Therapy mask’s near-identical treatments, each of the preset treatments performed well. However, the real selling point for me was the personalised treatments.View image in fullscreenPaint by numbers: the app lets you select different light wavelengths for individual points on the maskLike many withPCOS/PMOS, I get hormonal breakouts and hair growth on my chin and upper lip. For a while, I have been worried that using red light in these areas would make this more pronounced, as red light has been shown tostimulate scalp hair growth. With the Series 3, I chose not to use red light in those areas, and instead used blue light on my acne-prone chin, with red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared everywhere else. I also threw in a sprinkling of yellow light on my cheeks to tackle redness.Given my hatred for beauty tech apps, which are often full of ads, useless subscriptions and grating tech problems, I was glad to find the CurrentBody app refreshingly simple. The app pops up with an illustration of the light points on the face, ready for you to select which of the six light options you would like to shine from each point. The six light options can be applied using a paintbrush, fill bucket and eraser, which made it feel a lot like using a simplified version of Microsoft Paint. The whole process took about five minutes.I was most relieved to see that, once my personalised treatment had been saved to the device, I never had to open the app unless I wanted to tweak my treatment. There’s space for up to 10 personalised modes on the mask’s controller, on top of the four preset modes, and if for some reason you want more options than that, you can store more treatments on the app. There’s also the option to share treatments with others using a code (mine’s RYPGJ, if you’re feeling nosy).After six weeks of using my personalised treatment, my skin looked calmer, with less redness on my cheeks, fewer breakouts on my chin and a healthier overall appearance. Mission accomplished. I was also pleased that the mask lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments before needing a recharge. If you’re short on time, you can’t reduce the treatment time, but I’d be reluctant to mess around with the treatment length too much anyway, as this would add too many variables to the automatic dosing.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenA fiddly fit: the Series 3’s manual could be clearer about how to attach the straps.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI can’t complain about the results on this mask, but it does have a few nitpicky problems. Namely, the chin strap makes it impossible to pack flat when travelling, as opposed to flat silicone LED masks. Its nose flap left a tiny red mark on my nose for a few minutes after treatments, and to my frustration, CurrentBody’s instruction manual does a poor job of explaining how to add the straps.View image in fullscreenShortcomings: the controller’s smaller clip makes it harder to attach securely to clothing.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianFurthermore, unlike the Series 2, the controller comes with a small built-in touchscreen to accommodate its more complex treatments. While this is intuitive to use, I found the screen easy to jog accidentally mid-use, which would often pause my treatment. At 190g, the controller is also bulkier than before, and its clip is about an inch shorter, which makes it harder to carry around or clip securely on to clothing.I also found the battery life indicator a touch unreliable. Occasionally, the mask died before it got the chance to flag up red low-battery levels. This didn’t happen every time, and the charge always lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments, but it was frustrating nonetheless.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWarranty and repairsLED therapy is safe and comfortable for most people, but it’s always best to be cautious. CurrentBody recommends doing a skin sensitivity test before starting treatment, and offers a full refund if your skin becomes red or itchy after 24 hours, provided you return the mask within 14 days. For those who keep the mask, there is also a two-year warranty that covers manufacturing faults.Should I buy the CurrentBody Series 3 LED face mask?View image in fullscreen‘The top LED mask I’ve tested.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIf you have the money, absolutely. The CurrentBody Series 3 fits comfortably, has a generous battery and is the only one with anti-ageing deep near-infrared light all over the face. With this level of customisation available, it’s easily the top LED mask I’ve tested.This mask is particularly good for those with areas of their skin where one flat treatment won’t cut the mustard. For example, if you just want to fade one dark spot using green light, or treat a localised breakout using blue light, this mask gives you the flexibility to do that. This is a rare instance where I think the app is genuinely worthwhile, too. I didn’t dread booting it up every time I wanted to make an adjustment, and I love that the mask remembers my personalised treatments.That said, if you aren’t battling deep wrinkles and don’t have problematic skin, you might be better off with a moreaffordable LED mask.View at CurrentBodyView at AmazonCurrentBody Series 3 vs …Silk’n LED face mask ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£259 at Lookfantastic£259 at BootsAt about half the price of the CurrentBody Series 3 at the time of writing, the Silk’n LED face mask Pro is an obvious competitor. It has a silicone fit that blocks light well and coverage under the chin. And, if you think a wired controller will bother you, this is controlled and charged via a small, light battery pack that clips on to the mask itself, making it completely wireless. Treatments are all 10 minutes, and the mask had a lovely calming effect on my skin.That said, it offers no personalisation and far fewer deep near-infrared lights, which are positioned exclusively around the mouth, eyes and across the forehead. I also found the mask’s controls harder to get used to. The seven treatments, many of which look similar at first glance, are controlled via a button on the battery pack, which doesn’t give you any information about the treatment selected. To check which lights are being used, you’ll need to read the instructions and memorise how many presses it takes to get to your desired treatment. This shouldn’t be a huge problem, but it does somewhat hinder usability.Lustre Renew Pro FacewearView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£399 at Boots£399 at AmazonThis is the only other customisable LED mask I’ve tested. It’s not perfect, with a far less comfortable fit thanks to a heavy battery pack stuck on the forehead and a smaller-than-average size, but the lower price and simpler customisation options could clinch it for some.This mask has two preset treatment options – Energise and Revitalise – which use blue, red and near-infrared light. While you can use either as a full face treatment using the mask’s button, boot up the app and you’ll be able to select areas of the face for each treatment. Rather than offering pinpoint precision, like the CurrentBody Series 3, these areas span the eyes, nose, forehead, and cheeks and chin.I found these treatments effective at calming my skin, but I didn’t find the app or connection as simple as the CurrentBody, since I had to load the app up every time I wanted to personalise the treatment. If you won’t use the app either, you’d be better off buying the Silk’n option above, which is cheaper, more comfortable and includes deep near-infrared light in its anti-ageing treatments.Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWear ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£372 at Lookfantastic£465 at Cult BeautyIf 10-minute treatments feel like too much of a commitment, the Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWear Pro requires only three minutes a day, making it perfect for those who are time-poor but rich in other aspects. The lights are bright, the fit is supremely comfortable, and it’s wireless, so you don’t need to faff around with a controller.I was initially sceptical about this mask’s performance, given its shorter treatment times, but the combination of red, deep red, near-infrared, amber and blue lights helped give my skin a smoother, clearer and brighter appearance. For an effective LED mask without bells, whistles or any fancy app-based extras, this is a brilliant, if expensive, choice.For more:The best LED face masks that are worth the hypeI tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 timesSali Hughes’s favourite anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)Explore more on these topicsSkincareThe FilterBeautyGadgetsWearable technologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fresh isn’t always best: six easy ways to make better pasta, according to Julia Busuttil Nishimura | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: The Australian cookbook author shares her simple but effective techniques to improve your midweek pasta – and why you should be generous with olive oil and salt
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Australian cookbook author shares her simple but effective techniques to improve your midweek pasta – and why you should be generous with olive oil and salt
Content: How to make better pasta. Credit:  Armelle HabibAustralian food and drinkFresh isn’t always best: six easy ways to make better pasta, according to Julia Busuttil NishimuraThe Australian cookbook author shares her simple but effective techniques to improve your midweek pasta – and why you should be generous with olive oil and saltGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailJulia Busuttil NishimuraTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTSharePasta is a well-loved staple in the kitchen. It’s something that many of us fall back on when we don’t know what to cook or don’t feel like anything too fussy. But if your pasta sauce is a little too watery, or lacks that oomph of restaurant dishes, there are a few simple tricks and techniques that can take your simple midweek dinner to new and delicious heights.1. Fresh isn’t always bestThree simple vegetarian spring pasta recipes from Julia Busuttil NishimuraRead moreWhile some might see fresh pasta as superior, true pasta lovers know that dried pasta has a very important role in Italian kitchens. There are many sauces that are simply better served with dried varieties, such as all of the Roman sauces:amatriciana,carbonara,cacio e pepeandalla gricia. Plus, dried pasta is very economical and a handy pantry staple. Look for dried pasta with a rough surface, perfect for sauce-catching, and a pale yellow colour, which indicates the pasta was dried low and slow, resulting in better texture and flavour.2. Be generous with the olive oilIf a sauce is olive oil-based, such as aglio olio or alle vongole, or tomato-based, be generous with the extra virgin olive oil you use in the beginning. Particularly with an oil-based sauce, olive oil not only brings flavour, but also helps to emulsify the sauce once that pasta water meets the pan. Topping your finished dish with more extra virgin olive oil to finish is also highly recommended.View image in fullscreenJulia Busuttil Nishimura’s new cookbook is Simple Pleasures: Recipes to Fall in Love With Every Day.Photograph: Pan Macmillan Australia3. Cook sauce low and slowWhen adding base aromatics for a sauce, make sure your pan and oil are only just warm, rather than very hot. Ingredients like chilli, garlic, onion and even parsley stalks added to a cold or warm pan with oil will slowly release their flavours and yield much more depth than cooking quickly over a high heat can achieve. Garlic, in particular, can become bitter and acrid if cooked over a too-high heat.View image in fullscreen‘The starchy pasta water helps loosen and emulsify the sauce, so it clings to the pasta in the most pleasing way.’Photograph: Armelle Habib4. As salty as the sea?When I lived in Italy, one of the first things I learned was just how important it is to salt the pasta water. Cooking pasta in unseasoned or underseasoned water results in, well, underseasoned pasta. But how much salt is too much salt? You’ve probably heard people say the water should be “as salty as the sea”, which if you ask me, is far too salty. I never measure, but if you want to, around one-and-a-half to two teaspoons of salt per litre is a good place to start.5. Keep that precious pasta waterSo your pasta is boiling (I like to cook mine for a couple of minutes fewer than the packet directions, and always taste mine towards the end of the cook time to make sure it’s al dente). Don’t tip that perfectly seasoned, now starchy, pasta water down the drain! Instead, keep the pot on the stove, scoop the pasta out either with a sieve for short shapes, or tongs for long ones, and place it directly into the pan with the sauce, which should now be at a fairly high heat. Have a ladle or a mug handy and scoop out some of that precious pasta water into the pan. Finish cooking the pasta in the sauce, adding more pasta water as needed. The starchy water helps both loosen and emulsify the sauce, so it clings to the pasta in the most pleasing way.If making a sauce that doesn’t require any heat, for example a pesto, place the cooked pasta in a large bowl with the dressing or condiment, add splashes of reserved pasta water and combine until the sauce is glossy and coats the pasta.View image in fullscreen‘Some pasta dishes are simply better without a heaping of parm’ … Spaghetti with fish and saffron.Photograph: Armelle Habib6. No cheese, please!View image in fullscreenAll pasta dishes need grated parmesan, right? Well, I’m no absolutist, but some pasta dishes are simply better without a heaping of parm. Pecorino is the preferred cheese for certain dishes – I especially prefer it when making something with spring vegetables or lamb or those aforementioned Roman pasta sauces. Pecorino is a salty and sharp sheep’s milk cheese which is very commonly used in Lazio, in central Italy, and surrounding regions. I love how it builds a bold sauce when cooked with a handful of ingredients, and also cuts through the richness of ingredients like lamb and guanciale.Generally fish and cheese don’t mix in Italian cooking – there are some exceptions, most notably mozzarella and anchovy or mussels with pecorino in Puglia, however using a strong cheese like parmigiano reggiano or pecorino with seafood is very uncommon. According to Hippocrates and ancient medicine, cheese and fish eaten together was said to poison the body. But I would just say that the flavour of strong cheese overpowers the sweet brininess of seafood and fish. Instead, try crunchy fried breadcrumbs scattered atop your next plate of seafood pasta.Julia Busuttil Nishimura’s cookbook,Simple Pleasures: Recipes to Fall in Love With Every Day, with photography by Armelle Habib, is available now through Pan Macmillan Australia, $44.99Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkItalian food and drinkPastaFoodShare

title: Fritters and chocolate cake: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for cooking with pumpkin | Food | The Guardian
description: Quick, simple finger food that children will love for Halloween: pumpkin and carrot fritters, plus a pumpkin chocolate slice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Quick, simple finger food that children will love for Halloween: pumpkin and carrot fritters, plus a pumpkin chocolate slice
Content: Thomasina Miers’ pumpkin and carrot fritters with green chilli and coriander relish.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ pumpkin and carrot fritters with green chilli and coriander relish.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.FoodFritters and chocolate cake: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for cooking with pumpkinQuick, simple finger food that children will love for Halloween: pumpkin and carrot fritters with a chilli-coriander relish, and pumpkin baked into a dark chocolate sliceThomasina MiersTue 27 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt would be lazy to write, with a rueful shake of the head, thatHalloweengets bigger every year. Halloween ishuge. I have seen it grow, vicariously, through my children year on year and, despite previously approaching it with a Scrooge-like attitude, something in me has shifted. Perhaps it’s simply the pleasure I see light up in all toddlers through to teens; they can’t get enough of the fandango of dressing up, mixed with its unmistakable, irresistible sprinkle of wickedness. So now I am in. Last year, we had 60 14-year-olds dancing the night away, and I wish I’d made them the recipes here, both of which play on the deliciously sweet, wonderfully savoury nature of pumpkin, that most brilliant of Mexican fruit. Quick, utterly delicious and the perfect finger food. Happy Halloween!Pumpkin and carrot fritters with green chilli and coriander relish (pictured top)Delightfully crisp, rich in flavour and delicately spiced, these are simple to throw together but look and taste spectacular, especially with the zippy relish for dipping.Prep15 minCook40 minMakes14,to feed4-6 as a starter200g squash or pumpkin wedges(delica, crown prince, butternut), peeled200g carrots, scrubbed clean2 tsp olive oil8 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped2 tsp coriander seeds2 tsp cumin seeds1 tsp ground cinnamonSalt and black pepper2 fat garlic cloves, peeled and finely grated or minced15g ginger, peeled and finely grated or minced120g gram flourNeutral oil, for fryingGreek yoghurt, to serveFor the relish1-2 green chillies, to taste, stalks discarded, then roughly chopped (remove the pith and seeds first if you prefer less heat)1 bunch corianderJuice of 1 lime1 tbsp apple cider vinegar1 tsp runny honey1 garlic clove, peeled and roughly chopped1 shallot, peeled and finely choppedCoarsely grate the pumpkin and carrot, then wrap them in a clean tea towel or kitchen paper, and squeeze hard to push out any excess moisture.Put a frying pan on a medium heat, add the oil and spring onions, and cook, stirring, for two to three minutes. Grind the coriander and cumin seeds in a mortar, then add to the pan with the cinnamon and a few generous pinches of salt, and cook for a few minutes more. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook, stirring all the time, for a couple of more minutes. By now, the onions will have softened and the mixture will be smelling irresistibly fragrant. Tip the lot into a large bowl, then add the grated pumpkin and carrots, and the gram flour. Season with a little more salt and plenty of black pepper, then mix to combine.To make the relish, set aside half the chopped chilli, then put the rest in a food processor with all the remaining relish ingredients and a tablespoon of cold water. Blend to a smooth sauce, then taste, season with salt and pepper, and add more chilli, if need be, or more lime juice for acidity.Heat 2cm of neutral oil in a medium pan until hot. Scoop out rounded dessertspoons of the pumpkin mixture and, using your hands, shape them into round patties; wet your hands with cold water to stop the mix sticking. Working in batches, slide the patties into the hot oil and fry for a few minutes on each side, until golden and crisp. Keep the cooked fritters in a warm oven while you fry the rest.Serve the hot fritters with the relish and scoops of yoghurt on the side.Pumpkin, cardamom and dark chocolate sliceView image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ pumpkin, cardamom and dark chocolate slice.Part blondie, part sponge cake, these delicious slices are full of sweet nuttiness from the squash, the gentle scent of cardamom and rich chunks of dark chocolate that melt in the mouth.Prep10 minCook1 hr 20 minServes9250g squash or pumpkin(delica, crown prince, butternut would all work), or 200g pumpkin puree200g unsalted butter200g soft brown sugar2 large eggs250g plain flour, or a mix of plain and emmer, einkorn or spelt2 tsp baking powderFine sea salt12 green cardamom pods, bashed to open and seeds crushed100g dark chocolate, roughly choppedFlaky sea saltIcing sugar and ground cinnamon, to serveHeat the oven to 180C fan (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line a 20cm square baking tin with greaseproof paper.Cut the pumpkin/squash into a couple of wedges, remove and discard the seeds, then arrange the wedges on a baking tray. Sprinkle with a few teaspoons of water, then roast for 25-30 minutes, until completely soft. Scoop the flesh into a bowl, then mash with a fork until mostly smooth – don’t worry about any small lumps here or there, because they add a pleasing texture to the slices. You want 200g cooked flesh.Melt the butter in a small pan and cook over a medium heat until the solids begin to brown and toast. Once smelling nutty and delicious, take off the heat and add the sugar, stirring until it melts. Tip the brown butter mix into a large bowl, add the cooled pumpkin puree and stir to combine. Whisk in the eggs one at a time, until smooth.Sieve the flour and baking powder into a second bowl, season with a generous pinch of fine sea salt and add the ground cardamom seeds. Gently stir half the dry ingredients into the wet, then stir in the rest of the flour mix. Stir in the chopped chocolate, making sure there are no pockets of flour remaining, then pour into the prepared tin. Bake for 25-30 minutes, until springy to the touch.When the tin comes out of the oven, sprinkle over some flaky sea salt, then leave to cool completely. Remove from the tin and cut into squares. If you like, dust the slices with a little icing sugar scented with a pinch of cinnamon to serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodStarterDessertSnacksVegetablesHalloweenCakerecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was so sick’: is running a marathon while on a GLP-1 a bad idea? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: As the weight-loss drugs become more common, some runners find the side-effects challenging. Here’s what experts say
Author: Lauren Gould
Headline: As the weight-loss drugs become more common, some runners find the side-effects challenging. Here’s what experts say
Content: GLP-1s are more accessible now than when they first came on the market, said Meghann Featherstun.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGLP-1s are more accessible now than when they first came on the market, said Meghann Featherstun.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesWell actually‘I was so sick’: is running a marathon while on a GLP-1 a bad idea?As the weight-loss drugs become more common, some runners find the side-effects challenging. Here’s what experts sayWomen: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed?Lauren GouldTue 27 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeri M, a marathoner in her 50s, knew the race would be terrible.This feeling couldn’t be chalked up to inexperience. Keri, who asked us to omit her full name due to the sensitive subject matter, has completed dozens of half marathons and four full marathons.She ran the 2024 Philadelphia marathon fast enough to earn a coveted spot in this year’s Bank of America Chicago race, one of the eight world marathon majors.But this half marathon felt different. It was the first time she had raced on a GLP-1. Less than a week beforehand, she had taken her first 2.5mgstandard starting doseof tirzepatide, commonly sold under the names Mounjaro and Zepbound, for weight loss.Throughout the race, Keri felt nauseous, struggling to keep down the energy gels many endurance runners rely on for fuel.“After that half marathon, I was so sick,” she said. Keri had a “severe” reaction to the 2.5mg dose and, in hindsight, wishes that she had started at a lower dose.The number of people taking GLP-1s to lose weight has grown from3% to 11% in the past two years. A 2026 cohortstudyfound that 15 times more people use them for non-FDA-approved reasons compared with five years ago. The study also found that 35% of users are not considered overweight according to the BMI chart.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Meghann Featherstun, an Ohio-based registered sports dietitian, has worked with multiple marathon runners who use GLP-1s; they are more accessible now than when they first came on the market and fewer clinical criteria are required for a prescription, she said.Some experts, such as Heidi Skolnik, a fellow of the American College of Sports Medicine and author of Your GLP-1 Game Plan, believe it’s possible to run longer races while taking GLP-1s.“If you can eat enough to fuel your workouts and your runs and drink enough, then go for it. Good for you. But if you can’t, then don’t. Then you’re working against your health and wellbeing,” she said.Midlife is the perfect time to start trail running – here’s how to get into itRead moreGLP-1 side-effects such as nausea and loss of appetite can negatively affect running performance. Some athletes use strategies such as microdosing to achieve their weight loss goals while still training for half and full marathons. In one subreddit, “Zepbound athletes”, users exchange advice for training and performance while on the drugs, such as skipping doses and how to get enough fuel for races.Some researchers, such asEmily Lundstrom, an assistant professor of clinical physical therapy who studies low energy availability, believe endurance athletes focused on performance should wait until they have finished preparing for a race to use a GLP-1. “Even microdosing is not a good idea,” she said.As the number of people who take GLP-1s for weight loss grows, so has the controversy surrounding these drugs.When Serena Williams, a decorated female tennis player, became a spokesperson for Ro, a telehealth company that sells GLP-1s, it opened upa debateover who should take these drugs and if they have a place in sports. Some accused her ofpromoting thinnessand unnecessary weight loss. Others argued that her openness may help reduce the shame surrounding GLP-1s.Yetdespite the pushback,runners relate to her journey.Steve, a 44-year-old from Oregon, who asked to be identified by only his first name because of the deeply personal topic, has always considered himself active. Even when he wasn’t training for a long-distance race, he went for casual runs, boxed and lifted weights.Around the age of 41, he started gaining weight.“No matter how hard I trained, no matter how much I tracked my macros and stayed on plan, I just kept gaining weight,” he said. He noticed Williams had a similar story ofturningto a GLP-1 because she couldn’t reach her desired physique through diet and exercise.Steve started a tirzepatide compound in July 2026 and soon began training for an October half marathon. Initially, runs didn’t feel great. Five miles usually came easy, but now required multiple breaks and spiked his heart rate higher than usual.Steve cut his 2.5mg dose in half after four weeks, a tip he saw on Reddit. He can now train without a heart-rate spike. “I don’t feel as exhausted any more,” he said. His weight loss has stalled, but he said it wouldn’t be worth taking the drug if he couldn’t train properly on it.Dr Melanie Jay, a professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said GLP-1s can cause a two to 10bpm increase in resting heart rate, but further increases are possible during exercise. However, Jay noted that there weren’t many studies on how the second generation of GLP-1s (such as the tirzepatide Steve takes) affect exercise and heart rate. Other common side-effects of GLP-1s are gastrointestinal, including nausea and constipation, which Jay said can improve with time.Long-distance runners should exercise caution when it comes to these drugs, saidClaire Shorenstein, a board-certified sports dietitian.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Typically, I would not want someone to be on a GLP-1 while actively training for a marathon or any other type of endurance event,” she said.Because marathoners and other endurance athletes are already at risk for underfueling, Shorenstein says taking a GLP-1, which suppresses appetite, can lead to a chronic state of low energy availability, where the body doesn’t have enough energy left for “all the other functions that our body needs so that we can stay alive and be healthy”.Low energy availability is not permanent, but over time, it can causeRelative Energy Deficiency in Sport(Reds), which may reduce bonedensityanddecrease immunity. In women, it can causehypothalamic amenorrhea(loss of the menstrual cycle). Reds is treated throughadequate nutritionand exerciseadjustments.“I was definitely at risk for Reds because I was underfueling,” said Keri, the runner who was training for the 2026 Chicago Marathon. She has stopped and restarted her GLP-1 use during training, due to harsh side-effects, weight gain and appetite loss. “I’m not doing another dose until after the marathon,” she said.Kylie Keeton, a 32-year-old based in Texas, lost 170lb without a GLP-1. However, when she increased her running mileage, she noticed the number on the scale began to rise. Despite feeling “super embarrassed” about it, she decided to try semaglutide at the end of 2025 and eventually switched to a tirzepatide.But side-effects such as nausea made it hard to hit her mileage, and she had to drop out of a half marathon.Keeton felt torn about whether to continue taking the drug. It was hard to decide whether weight gain or not being able to run was worse, she said. Keeton tried various strategies to integrate GLP-1 use with her fitness practices, such as breaking up her weekly dose into two smaller doses.But this is not recommended because “it is not how the drug was studied in any of the clinical trials”, saidDr Nidhi Kansal, who specializes in GLP-1 treatments at Northwestern Medicine.Kristy Baumann, a Minnesota-based registered dietitian who works with endurance runners, said she doesn’t personally see clients take doses in this way. However, she notes athletes should time their doses after a long run or race day: if you take it the day before, “you’d have a greater chance of GI issues”, she said.Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?Read moreEventually, Keeton stopped taking the drug. She had lost about 5lb in six months of taking GLP-1s and didn’t think it was worth continuing given the expense. Now she can run without feeling nauseous and hopes to improve her personal record by 45 minutes at the 2026 BMW Dallas Marathon.Overall, there is little research on using GLP-1s while long-distance running. The experts I spoke to expressed caution over energy levels and dosage tweaks, and urged users to heed any adverse symptoms or difficulties. The only thing that’s clear is that long-distance runners who use GLP-1s can have varying experiences.Nikki Thornton, a 47-year-old marathon runner based in Taree, Australia, started a GLP-1 in 2023 to lower her blood sugar levels, which were reaching pre-diabetic ranges,and lose weight. At first, Thornton noticed she struggled to run more than 5km (about 3 miles). Eventually, completed thesweltering Sydney Marathon, but experienced gastrointestinal issues. “It was the worst one I’ve ever done,” she said.About six months after starting a GLP-1, she said her body adjusted. In 2025, she improved her Sydney Marathon time by three hours.While Featherstun, the sports dietitian from Ohio, works with marathon runners on GLP-1s, she said they rarely stay on them for long.“Every single person who’s been on it, I’ve got an email from them. ‘I’m done with it. I’m off it. I can’t handle this.’ So I do think it’s a really tricky combination,” she said.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyMarathon runningWeight-loss drugsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz | The Guardian
description: Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid
Author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Headline: Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid
Content: ‘[Seed oils] are high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy’, writes Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘[Seed oils] are high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy’, writes Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralNutritionAre seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them?Gideon Meyerowitz-KatzRandomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acidRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.46 EDTShareIf you’ve been online lately, you’ve probably been bombarded with the discourse about seed oils. Once a completely innocuous food that no one really talked about, they have become the enemy of the moment. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services in the US, hascalled them “toxic”and vowed to act against them. There are countless activewear-clad influencers online saying that nothing harms your health more than these products.Which is odd, because theAustralian dietary guidelinessay seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines andmost experts– why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.”So why the hubbub online?Inflammation claims ‘not supported by evidence’Seed oils are a group of cooking oils that are, unsurprisingly, extracted from seeds. They’re generally quite highly refined – although you can get less refined versions of many of them – and include canola oil, sunflower seed oil, rice bran oil, soya bean oil and corn oil. Most of the time vegetable oil is composed of seed oils – it’s often a mixture of sunflower seed and canola oils.Vitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep? | AntiviralRead moreThe concerns about seed oils boil down to one thing: inflammation. It is asserted that the omega-6 fatty acids contained in most seed oils such as linoleic acid can be harmful in large doses and may cause the body to become more inflamed over time. This isn’t entirely crazy – there issome evidencefrom rodent studies that omega-6s cause inflammation, and that having too many of themcan havelong-term negative outcomes.The problem, of course, is that lab rats and mice aren’t people. Very high levels of omega-6s can cause liver dysfunction and gut issues in rats but that doesn’t mean that a bit of sunflower seed oil is going to destroy your intestines.Data from humans doesn’t really show this connection. People who eat more linoleic acid havesubstantiallylowerrisksof cardiovascular disease than those who eat less. Studies looking at supplementing seed oils in people’s dietshave shownno major impacts – and sometimes even modest benefits – compared with placebos.Human studies also don’t support the inflammation link. Randomised trials of omega-6sdo not showan increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acids. Arandomised crossover studyin which the same people were randomly given either omega-3 or omega-6 fatty acids found that there was no difference in how they affected inflammatory markers. Evidence fromcareful analysesof genetics and causality in humans show little indication that omega-6 fatty acids are inflammatory. As Wu puts it, the pro-inflammatory effects of omega-6 fatty acids are “not supported by evidence”.Scaremongering ignores the scienceOn the other hand, we know that animal fats are probably bad for you. They contain high levels of low-density lipoprotein – bad cholesterol – which goes on to clog arteries and cause heart attacks. Ball notes: “Replacing saturated fats, such as those in butter, with unsaturated fats in oils like canola and sunflower can lower LDL cholesterol, an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease.”In other words, the scientific perspective is simple: seed oils are fine. They’re high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy, and if you’re eating them to replace saturated fat then they’re probably going to improve your health. So why are there crazy-eyed men yelling at canola oil in the supermarket aisle on Instagram?Magnesium is essential for health. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep? | AntiviralRead moreThe story here is mostly about dietary fads. Favourite diets online now are quite high in animal fats. If you’re promoting your new book about keto diets, it’s not great for sales if everyone thinks that eating too many steaks is going to give them heart disease. Yes, there were some scientific concerns but those have been largely disproven in the literature already.There are a lot of people scaremongering about seed oils online, which makes sense. You get a lot more attention for yelling that we’re all being poisoned than by calmly explaining the science. I doubt the furore about seed oils is going away any time soon.But from a health perspective you’re probably better off eating seed oils than any other fats. You should limit consumption, because too many calories is not great, but whether you’re frying, making mayonnaise or whatever, it’s likely that the healthiest choice is a seed oil of some kind.Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of WollongongAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: ‘The view from the Mournes was CS Lewis’s idea of Narnia’: how Northern Ireland inspired a magical kingdom  | Belfast holidays | The Guardian
description: Ahead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imagination
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ahead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imagination
Content: Dunluce Castle, which some scholars believe inspired CS Lewis’s Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Photograph: Shawn Williams/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenDunluce Castle, which some scholars believe inspired CS Lewis’s Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Photograph: Shawn Williams/Getty Images/iStockphotoBelfast holidays‘The view from the Mournes was CS Lewis’s idea of Narnia’: how Northern Ireland inspired a magical kingdomAhead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imaginationGraham LittleTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the gable walls of the tough, working-class streets of east Belfast, the mystical beasts of Narnia vie for brick space with balaclava-wearing loyalists. The murals of the city have long projected the power of paramilitaries, but in recent years they have also begun to reflect the more positive contributions made by other local people, including the authorCS Lewis.Lewis was born in Dundela in 1898 in an attractive terrace house that has sadly since been demolished to be replaced by rather unattractive flats. But elsewhere in this part of the city, the Lewis connection is being built on and celebrated.CS Lewis Squareis in the Holywood Arches neighbourhood and has a short walking trail featuring metal sculptures of Mr and Mrs Beaver, Mr Tumnus and other beloved characters from The Chronicles of Narnia. The centrepiece is a gigantic Aslan, towering over all from atop a circular mound.View image in fullscreenA CS Lewis mural in east Belfast.Photograph: Stephen Barnes NI/AlamyAbout 15 minutes’ walk away, St Mark’s church on the Holywood Road is the proud custodian of a much smaller lion that may have inspired Lewis’s creation of Aslan. His grandfather,the Rev Thomas Hamilton, ministered here, living in the rectory for 13 years, and his front door was decorated with a beautiful brass lion’s head doorknob. The original has been removed for safekeeping, but an exact replica attracts thousands of Lewis pilgrims each year.Leafy Circular Road, half a mile away, is where the Lewis family moved in 1905 to a large, redbrick house that, back then, was on the outskirts of the city. The road has since been subsumed by the growth of the town, but remains the realm of the prosperous. The house, called Little Lea, is privately owned, but can be seen from the iron gates at the end of the drive.“To a child, it seemed less like a house than a city,” Lewis wrote of the family home in his autobiography, Surprised By Joy. “I am a product of long corridors, empty sunlit rooms, upstairs indoor silences, attics explored in solitude.”View image in fullscreenThe Aslan sculpture in CS Lewis Square, east Belfast.Photograph: Radharc Images/AlamyLittle Lea appears in the opening two Narnia books, first when a boy exploring a large attic in The Magician’s Nephew finds a way into another world, and then in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe when a game of hide and seek leads a group of inquisitive children to that same magical world a generation later.Although it was close to east Belfast’s industrial heartland, it was also just a fence clamber away from the fields, hills and woodland glens that fringed the city like a vast adventure playground. As children, Lewis and his elder brother Warnie seem to have had a freedom to wander that would terrify modern parents. They would trek for hours up into the hills between Belfast and Strangford Lough, and travelling that way today still evokes a sense of romantic escapism.double quotation markIt is easy to imagine, as Lewis wrote in an essay, that a ‘giant might raise his head over the next ridge’ of the Mourne mountainsThe Belmont Road takes you up, climbing dramatically out of the city and into the expansive high ground that towers over Belfast, Bangor and Newtownards. There are many viewpoints up here. Lewis didn’t record the exact spot that inspired the following ethereal description of the views he loved, but for this writer, the crags of theWhitespots country parkon the hill above Newtownards are a pretty good bet, especially as this place also chimes loudly with his descriptions of the stone table on which Aslan was sacrificed in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.View image in fullscreenMussenden Temple on the north coast of Co Derry.Photograph: Ballygally View Images/Getty Images“Looking south with a little east in it, a different world,” he writes in Surprised By Joy. “And having seen it, blame me if you can for being a romantic. For here is the thing itself, utterly irresistible, the way to the world’s end, the land of longing, the breaking and blessing of hearts. You are looking across … the plain of Down, and seeing beyond it the Mourne Mountains.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLewis once told Warnie that the view from the Mournes above Rostrevor looking down over Carlingford Lough was his idea of Narnia. The statement is now stencilled on a bench at a viewpoint in the town’sKilbroney forest park. Sitting there, in the majesty of this area, it is easy to imagine, as Lewis later wrote in an essay, that a “giant might raise his head over the next ridge”.Rostrevor is an hour’s drive south of Belfast, and an hour’s drive in the other direction will take you to the equally spectacular north coast, where Lewis holidayed with his mother as a young child. There’s an ongoing debate among Lewis scholars and his many passionate fans about whether it wasDunluce CastleorDownhill Demesnethat inspired Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Netflix unveils first trailer for Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s NephewRead moreThe ruins of Dunluce perch precipitously on the coast east of Portrush, while Downhill Demesne, near Castlerock, contains what remains of the old Downhill House but also the iconic Mussenden Temple, which much better fits the description of Cair Paravel looking “like a great star resting on the seashore”.Lewis was writing his autobiography at the same time he was producing the seven Chronicles of Narnia. The experiences and landscapes he was remembering for his memoir very likely bled into the creation of his magical kingdom. And so the heavenly, pastoral landscapes of Narnia on the murals of east Belfast might feel familiar even to those locals who haven’t read the books or watched the screen adaptations. The wholesome images of his imagination being sandwiched between paintings glorifying terrorism is an unusual setting for a tribute to the world’s most famous Christian apologist, but perhaps in Belfast, as in Narnia, good will win in the end.The first ofNetflix’snew The Chronicles Of Narnia adaptations,Narnia:The Magician’s Nephew, will be released in cinemas on12 February 2027and onNetflixon 2 April.
