title: ‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big tech | Technology | The Guardian
description: From apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attention
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: From apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attention
Content: ‘Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,’ said a computer science student at Duke.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,’ said a computer science student at Duke.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesTechnology‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big techFrom apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attentionGen Z voters: tell us what is guiding your vote in the US midterm elections?Jenna ZazaTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNelissa Moukoudi, 19, a university student in Canada, noticed a shift once she joinedInstagramand TikTok.“My social life completely plummeted and it felt like my life was only [using] social media and school,” she said.Tired of fighting for self-control, Moukoudi downloaded Opal, an app that forces users to solve math problems before reopening distracting apps. It is one of a growing number of companies in the sprawlingdigital detoxindustry that is enticing users – ideally paying ones – by promising to keep them off their devices. The industry isvaluedat nearly $1bn and is estimated to grow to nearly $8bn by 2035.Many of these companies are hoping to capitalize on gen Z’s growing weariness about the devices and social media platforms they grew up with.Nearly 60%of gen Z respondents identified as having a social media addiction in an April poll, and athirdof the generation said they had deleted some of those apps, according to a 2025 survey.It’s the age of regret: gen Z grew up glued to their screens, and missed the joy of being human | Gaby HinsliffRead moreThe shift has also been driven by growinganger at tech platformsthat have left some in gen Z feeling as if they are being exploited for profit.Gen Z “was basically optimized for dopamine by very smart systems”, said Kenneth Schlenker, 39, a former product marketer at Google and co-founder of Opal. “But this generation is also realizing what they don’t want and are trying to change how the system impacts them.”Some are turning to new devices entirely. Kendall Schrohe, 23, a founding partner of the Attention Studio, a consulting firm advising parents and policymakers on responsible tech, said that she traded her smartphone for aLight Phone, which sells for $349 and includes minimal smartphone features.“These big tech platforms have been hurting people for years, and we are just now feeling the impacts of it,” Schrohe said. “Our generation were the guinea pigs to big tech, and our suffering and addiction to these apps were profited off of.”Shreya Nallamothu, 19, a computer science student at Duke University, created her own DIY “Brick”, a device to block selected apps, using $8 near-field communication (NFC) tags that she bought online.“Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,” Nallamothu said. “Often the tech companies’ best interests aren’t in the users’ best interests.Social mediahas gotten away from what good technology can do, and people have noticed.”double quotation markThe doomscrolling economy is not one that we need to keep participating inHan Choi, 26Research that Nallamothu conducted in high school helped convince state senators in Illinois toadvancea recent bill to prevent parental exploitation of children on social media and the state to pass a law forcing parents tocompensate their kids.New event-focused apps are also trying to capitalize on the pivot away from social media. Pie (People I Enjoy), an app highlighting local events including bar pop-ups, 5K runs and concert meetups, grew 150% in a single month – jumping from 120,000 users in July to 300,000 in August.Co-founder Nadya Okamoto describes Pie as an in-person, active social network.“I think of social media as this passive consumption of content, but Pie is separate from that,” Okamoto said. “Users are actively networking and building your social circle.”‘It made my day more meaningful’: the Japanese gen Zers attempting a two-hour limit on smartphone useRead moreCo-founder Andy Dunn, who also founded menswear brand Bonobos, added: “Everything about the product is designed to make you want to go and be in community with those people. It gives you so much more agency.”The price of using such digital detox apps can vary. An Opal subscription costs $99.99 a year, while Brick, a physical block that phone users tap to lock and unlock apps, costs $59. Shift, an app that promises to turn a smartphone into a so-called “dumbphone” that can only make calls or send texts, charges a one-time $150 payment.That is one reason why convincing gen Z digital detoxers to pay for a new app could be tricky. Like approximately 95% of Opal’s 10 million customers, 75% of whom are gen Z, Moukoudi said she is using the free version. “I am not going to pay for an app just to reclaim my life,” the university student said.For some, simply deleting apps does the trick. Han Choi, 26,deletedallsocial media appslast year to spend more of his time on trivia nights and workouts.“People are rejecting the systems that have been put in place by people who stand to profit off our compliance,” Choi said. “Thedoomscrollingeconomyis not one that we need to keep participating in.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologySocial mediaYoung peopleSmartphonesMobile phonesInstagramTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pest I’ll never forget: the rats stood six or seven deep on the lawn beside my dormitory | Life and style | The Guardian
description: All it took was one or two careless teenage girls giving the vermin a taste of their snacks and they became the most well-fed animals imaginable
Author: Bim Adewunmi
Headline: All it took was one or two careless teenage girls giving the vermin a taste of their snacks and they became the most well-fed animals imaginable
Content: ‘The rats began to stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator.’Composite: Guardian design; Nynke van Holten; Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The rats began to stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator.’Composite: Guardian design; Nynke van Holten; Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetLife and styleThe pest I’ll never forget: the rats stood six or seven deep on the lawn beside my dormitoryAll it took was one or two careless teenage girls giving the vermin a taste of their snacks and they became the most well-fed animals imaginableBim AdewunmiTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve written a fair amount about my boarding school years inNigeriain the 90s, but never about the rats that accompanied my school experience. Picture it: thousands of girls from across the country, each bearing a suitcase or two of a term’s worth of “provisions” – cornflakes, sugar cubes, powdered milk, hot chocolate powder, and so on. All it took was one or two careless girls giving the rats a taste of the exotic and they became among the most well-fed rats in the country, enjoying a steady stream of delicious teenage-girl snacks.I will never forget the sight of rats – six or seven deep – congregating at dusk on the scraggly lawn next to my dormitory, like an illegal gathering of political dissidents. They were large (what with their rich diet), thick tails twitching, noses pushed together, damn near whispering. At first, they would scatter when humans approached. Then we had to clap and stomp to get them to shift. Like the proletariat, the rats began to understand their power, and stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator. If this sounds like the beginning of a highbrow horror, that’s how it felt.Stories circulated – rats that seemed irritated and bemused when you shouted at them; rats that strolled rather than scurried. The most fantastical stories came from people who alleged they’d woken up to a rat nibbling on their toes, and that the rats were dastardly enough to blow cool air,between bites, to soothe their victims back to slumber. I have a specific memory of being actively chased by the two large rats I’d disturbed when I went to fetch a bucket of water one night. I remember telling that story, still breathless, to wide-eyed roommates. A friend in another house came back to her dorm one evening to find a mother rat and her newborn pups – pink and devoid of fur – under her pillow.These rats were of course in their own habitat, perfectly at home, and adapting to our unwelcome presence.Wewere the interlopers, with our classrooms and dormitories, and daily assemblies and annual sports days. I can now recognise that dealing with a certain kind of pest is a fact of life in places where nature has not yet been completely decimated. The rats were the price of a kind of freedom. But years later, post-pandemic lockdown, when the rats attempted to colonise New York, I had searing flashes of the rats of my childhood. Yup, still traumatising.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pest I’ll never forgetMammalsAnimalsNigeriaAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military | Sexual harassment | The Guardian
description: In 2021, the young soldier took her life after being sexually assaulted by a sergeant major, then sent thousands of messages by her line manager. She was just 19. Five years on, Leighann McCready is still searching for answers
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: In 2021, the young soldier took her life after being sexually assaulted by a sergeant major, then sent thousands of messages by her line manager. She was just 19. Five years on, Leighann McCready is still searching for answers
Content: Beck and McCready at Beck’s passing in parade.Photograph: Centre For Military Justice/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBeck and McCready at Beck’s passing in parade.Photograph: Centre For Military Justice/AFP/Getty ImagesSexual harassmentThe life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the militaryIn 2021, the young soldier took her life after being sexually assaulted by a sergeant major, then sent thousands of messages by her line manager. She was just 19. Five years on, Leighann McCready is still searching for answersAnna MooreTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Leighann McCready phoned her 19-year-old daughter, Jaysley Beck, on 15 December 2021, she got no reply, but brushed away her worries. “Jays always, always answered her phone, but it was early, eight in the morning,” she says. Beck, an army soldier in the Royal Artillery, had been at a party the night before at her Wiltshire barracks. She was probably asleep.It was a busy time, the Christmas countdown. Soon, Beck was expected to be back home in Cumbria, where her parents – McCready and Anthony Beck – own a village pub. McCready had already bought matching Christmas pyjamas for Beck and her older sister Emilli to wear on the day.Beck had been preparing for the holidays, too. She had been Christmas shopping two days earlier, calling and consulting throughout the day with her mum, who was transferring the cash to cover it all. She’d bought presents for herself and her sister: a Gucci bag, a belt and a purse. For her dad, she’d bought tickets for a James Blunt concert for the two of them to attend together in February. At the end of the spree, Beck had messaged her mum: “We’re two so lucky girls aren’t we, Mum? Thank you, thank you, thank you. I love you with all my heart!”View image in fullscreenJaysley Beck.Photograph: Family Handout/PADespite all this, as the hours passed that Tuesday in December, with still no word from Beck, McCready began to feel a deep foreboding. She knew that, in the preceding weeks, her daughter had been struggling through a strange and intense period of escalating harassment from her line manager. With this in mind, Emilli offered to call one of Beck’s friends at the barracks, who assured them that Beck was probably fast asleep. “He said he was five minutes away and he’d go and wake her,” says McCready. “That five minutes just seemed like forever. I continued ringing Jays’ phone – until somebody else answered it. The voice said: ‘Hello, can I ask who I’m speaking to?’ And I just knew. They didn’t even have to tell me.”Gunner Beck had taken her life, alone in her bedroom. Her suicide threw a spotlight on the British army and the treatment, safety and protection of female recruits. For the last five years, ever since Beck’s death, McCready has fought for answers and accountability. She has found some, but believes there is still far more to uncover. At every step – theservice inquiry,the inquestand a subsequent police investigation – McCready has been in the public eye, talking to the press, advocating for her daughter. Now, she features in a Stacey Dooley documentary, Death in the Barracks, which follows the family’s continued search for justice. She still can’t quite believe that any of it is real.View image in fullscreenLeighann McCready and a picture of her daughter, Jaysley Beck, at home in Oxen Park, Cumbria.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“Grief is not what you see on TV, where you instantly fall to the floor and break down in tears,” says McCready, who has worked for 30 years in the care sector, much of it as an end-of-life nurse. “The moment I found out, I automatically went from being a mum, a partner, a daughter, to quite literally feeling as if I was putting my uniform on. It was about protecting a family and guiding them. No matter how many interviews I do or how many times I see Jays’ photo in the news, it doesn’t register. That isn’t my daughter – and this isn’t my life. I call it my ‘invisible uniform’ and I have never taken it off.”Beck had joined the army at 16. “As a child, I used to call her my baby muck-magnet,” says McCready. “She was a cheeky little chops – pulling out her pigtails, collecting snails. She loved helping her dad with DIY. You always knew when Jays was around.” Aged 15, she’d returned from a school careers day intent on joining the army. McCready wasn’t keen. “I hadn’t expected that in a million years,” she says. “I thought it was a phase, but she was determined. She put her heart and soul into it. I remember her running round the village wearing backpacks weighted with bricks to build her strength up. She was only tiny – probably a size six in clothes.”After Beck’s initial military training, her family attended her passing in parade at Army Foundation College Harrogate. “It was magical,” says McCready. “I was a proud mum.”Beck settled happily into army life – but in her final six months, that changed. In July 2021, at a training exercise, Beck wassexually assaulted by Michael Webber(then 39, married, and a battery sergeant major). She escaped, then spent the night hiding in her car. When Beck reported the incident to senior officers, she was advised not to be “a female troublemaker”, and was urged to think of Webber’s career, and his family. Eventually, after she reported it a second time, Webber was asked to write Beck a letter of apology. He was promoted shortly afterwards. This meant that, three months later, when her line manager, bombardier Ryan Mason, 32, began showing an obsessive interest in Beck, she had no faith in any complaints process, and nowhere to turn.McCready had known all this as it happened. “Jays told me everything,” she says. Her daughter had even shared Mason’s messages on a family WhatsApp – he sent more than 4,600 in two months. The family had tried to advise and support her, but they were hundreds of miles away, and military protocol was a strange, sealed world. “When she was assaulted by Michael Webber, she’d said: ‘Get off me, sir.’” says McCready. “I remember my first reaction was: ‘How, Jays, did you call him “sir”?’ Some of it was over my head.”View image in fullscreenMcCready (second right) speaking to the media outside the Wiltshire and Swindon coroner’s court in Salisbury, after the inquest.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAIn the days after Beck’s death, as their home filled with military personnel, McCready became determined to bring all she knew to light. “Jays was not going to be another statistic. She was not another ‘sudden passing’,” she says.“I was not a ‘grieving mum’. You have to be stronger than that,” she continues. “I had to keep going for Jays and also for Emilli. What would she do if I broke? She’d crumble, she wouldn’t be far behind me.” Christmas was days away, so McCready asked Emilli how they should spend it. Should they even get a tree? “Emilli said: ‘Lets do the tree, and let’s still go to Auntie’s as planned for Christmas Day.’ So that’s what we did,” says McCready. “It didn’t feel right, but nothing would have felt right. I printed up a big picture of Jaysley and asked if I could put it in the tree so she’d be watching.” McCready didn’t touch any alcohol – in fact, she hasn’t had a drop since losing her daughter. “I don’t want alcohol to affect my emotions,” she says. She doesn’t watch TV either. “I don’t think it’s good for my mindset. I remember trying to settle down one night – I think it was [with] Gogglebox – and the first thing that was shown was a mortuary. I couldn’t turn it off quick enough.”Her “invisible uniform”, her years in end-of-life care, guided all her decisions in those first weeks. “I knew I needed to be kind to my mind, to bubble-wrap it and protect it,” she says. “I chose not to see Jays after her passing and I don’t regret it. I know from my work that it’s just a shell left behind, and do I want to see my daughter’s shell? Instead, I can close my eyes and she’s that happy little girl – she’s smiling, she’s singing, she’s running round the block with her backpack on. I didn’t deal with the coroner – I didn’t want to know details.”What she did want, instantly and urgently, was to visit Beck’s room in Larkhill garrison. She had to push for access. “I was told I was not allowed, so we had a meeting. I explained how much I needed this moment. I wanted to lie on my daughter’s bed. I wanted to know the last bit of music she played – Jays loved music, we always shared songs and playlists. What was the last bit of laundry she put in her laundry basket? How do her clothes smell?”View image in fullscreenBeck (left) with her sister, Emilli, (centre) and McCready.Photograph: Family handoutThe family were finally allowed entry on 28 December, although they were initially informed that they had to be accompanied. “I said: ‘Absolutely not.’” McCready had another motive, too. “I needed to gather as much information to find out what happened,” she says. “I wanted the letter of apology from Michael Webber – I knew exactly where she’d filed it. I wanted her smart watch and her laptop. I got all of them. I did want her phone, too – but Wiltshire police had already taken that.” Months later, when the police had done nothing with the phone, McCready returned to Wiltshire to collect it, having argued successfully that she had paid for it – so it was in fact hers, not Beck’s.“Not only had I put my invisible uniform on, in my mind, I was also becoming a detective,” McCready says. “I sat down with a roll of wallpaper and I did a timeline.” She also found a lawyer throughthe Centre for Military Justice. “We’ve been on this journey together and we’ve had to push for every single inquiry and investigation since.”There have been some answers. After the inquest, the coroner’s summing-up report found Mason’s “intolerable harassment” and “the daily barrage of messages, calls and face-to-face encounters” to have been a significant factor in Beck’s suicide. As her line manager, Beck found Mason possessive and manipulative, setting the rota so that they were always together. He said that he loved her, composed messages that ran to essays, called her at night and engaged in lengthy conversations, sometimes until 4am (when she had to be up at 6am).On 7 December 2021 – a week before Beck’s death – Mason and Beck had been staying in a hotel for a recruitment event when Beck left suddenly in the night, after calling a friend while in tears, who drove over and took her back to barracks. At the inquest, giving evidence, Mason said that he did not know the reason for Beck’s sudden departure that night. (He left the army the day after the recruitment event.)The summing-up also found that the earlier mishandling of Beck’s sexual assault complaint against Webber had left her “with a feeling of injustice but, more importantly, [a loss of] faith in her ability to complain effectively”. After the inquest, Webber was charged with sexual assault and, last October,pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to six months.View image in fullscreen‘There are still so many unanswered questions’ … McCready at her home in Cumbria.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianOther factors were identified as “significant” by the coroner, foremost Beck’s “turmoil” around her intimate relationships. In November 2021, she had separated from her long-term boyfriend – although the two remained friends. She’d then embarked on an affair with a married sergeant. She was a 19-year-old girl, says McCready, making some mistakes and finding her way – and none of this explains why her daughter, who had never reported any mental health problems, should so suddenly end her life.“Truth be told, there are still so many unanswered questions,” says McCready, “but I’m trying not to let them into my head. It won’t change anything for Jays. Instead, I’m trying to focus on changing things for the next people.” She welcomes MoD plans to tackle “unacceptable behaviours” in the military, including a Violence Against Women and Girls taskforce and a tri-service team, covering the army, navy and RAF, which will take serious complaints out of the single chain of command.View image in fullscreen‘For me, she’s still here’ … McCready and Beck.Photograph: Family handout“It’s going in the right direction,” she says, “but it’s not enough. The reporting system has to be independent, separate from the army. I’m still contacted daily by soldiers, veterans and their families who have their own stories of rape, assault, bullying, harassment – and it’s not just females.” She hopes the Dooley documentary will encourage more to come forward, and she’s in the process of establishing a formal organisation, Jaysley’s Voice, to advocate on their behalf.Meanwhile, Christmas – that most difficult anniversary – is coming. This year, McCready and Anthony are flying out to Thailand to meet Emilli and her partner, who now live in Australia. “We’ve promised each other that we’ll always be together at Christmas,” says McCready. “Emilli went travelling 10 months after we lost Jaysley, so we’ve met her in Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Bali. She keeps us busy, living the best life possible, which is exactly what Jays would have wanted for her. She’d have wanted that for all of us.”Sometimes, McCready wonders if she has left any time and space for grief. She has rarely cried, she says, and opted against counselling. Could it all come crashing down? “I do ask: ‘Is this it?’” she says. “What am I waiting to feel like? Am I in denial?” Usually, though, she prefers to believe that Jaysley is close by, holding her together, protecting her from the worst of it, still on guard. “Maybe she’s saying: ‘This is how it will be for you, Mum, I’m not going to let you be hurt,’” says McCready. “For me, she’s still here.”Stacey Dooley: Death in the Barracks screens Tuesday 27 October at 9pm on BBC Three; 10.40pm on BBC One; and iPlayerIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsSexual harassmentBritish armyEnglandMilitaryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump shows off tanker with ‘1m barrels of oil’ and floats Venezuela as 51st state | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President at Texas campaign rally hails deal struck with post-Maduro government as ‘greatest oil victory in history’
Author: Auzzy Byrdsell
Headline: President at Texas campaign rally hails deal struck with post-Maduro government as ‘greatest oil victory in history’
Content: Trump at the rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday, with the tanker in the background.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump at the rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday, with the tanker in the background.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump shows off tanker with ‘1m barrels of oil’ and floats Venezuela as 51st statePresident at Texas campaign rally hails deal struck with post-Maduro government as ‘greatest oil victory in history’Auzzy ByrdsellTue 27 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 19.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump suggested Venezuela would become the 51st state of the United States on Tuesday as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “one million barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months afterdeposingits president.At a campaign rally in Corpus Christ, Texas, Trump touted aUS oil dealwith Venezuela, which the US attacked in January, capturing its long-serving leaderNicolás Maduro.Trump claims the agreement –struck with the South American country’s interim government, which is backed by Trump’s administration – will cover “billions” of barrels of oil.Venezuela “will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe some day soon it’ll become a prosperous 51st state,” Trump said at the podium on Tuesday. “That’s possible.”Venezuela is on a growing list of countries and territories Trump has spoken of acquiring, including Greenland, Canada and Mexico.With tens of millions of Americans set to vote in next week’s midterm elections, Trump’s aggressive foreign policy – including his controversial war on Iran, and tariffs on goods from much of the world – have challenged his popularity, according to opinion polls, with his approval ratings falling to record lows.But on Tuesday, the president sought to point to the Venezuela operation as an example of his success. US fuel prices, which surged after the start of the Iran war, piling pressure on Americans’ cost of living, “will soon come plummeting down”, he claimed in a social media post.“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” he said at the rally, pointing out the ship off the Texan coast. “The oil provided is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.”Moments before Trump took the stage in Texas, heclaimedon his Truth Social platform: “By unleashing Energy Dominance from Alaska, all the way down to Venezuela, I have made the Western Hemisphere the Energy Capital of the World.”The deal has also drawn skepticism as critics complained that the Trump administration has not pushed a transition to democracy in Venezuela, where elections have not been held since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence.The urgency of the oil agreement stems from Trump’s opting into the war with Iran in February. Gas prices have shot up nationwide after Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpVenezuelaAmericasOilUS foreign policyRepublicansUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday.Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro speaks to the media in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday.Photograph: Lucas Neves/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBrazilFlávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports sayFar-right senator en route to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to LulaTiago Rogeroin Brasília andTom Phillipsin São PauloTue 27 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right senatorFlávio Bolsonarohas reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”.A report by the news websiteMetrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like.Brazilis their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fledBrazilafter losing on Sunday.A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in BrazilRead moreBolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60 million votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives | Toronto | The Guardian
description: Tightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad Bradford
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Tightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad Bradford
Content: Mayor Olivia Chow delivers a speech after being re-elected for a second term in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 26 October.Photograph: Mert Alper Dervis/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMayor Olivia Chow delivers a speech after being re-elected for a second term in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 26 October.Photograph: Mert Alper Dervis/Anadolu/Getty ImagesTorontoOlivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressivesTightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad BradfordLeyland Ceccoin TorontoTue 27 Oct 2026 16.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mayor ofToronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressive councillors.The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13-percentage-point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared with his 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. On Monday night, she thanked her supporters and Bradford.“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”Chow, 69, haslong been a fixtureof the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what shereceived in 2023.Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms-related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers and other vulnerable institutions.In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in afierce battleover the city’s bike lanes.Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan,a well-known advocatefor unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on the city council.Explore more on these topicsTorontoCanadaAmericasCity mayorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US military says strike on alleged drug vessel in eastern Pacific kills five people | US military | The Guardian
description: US military says it carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug-trafficking boat in latest attack in region
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US military says it carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug-trafficking boat in latest attack in region
Content: A screenshot from a video shows an alleged narco-trafficking vessel in the Pacific Ocean on 27 October 2026.Photograph: US Southern Command via XView image in fullscreenA screenshot from a video shows an alleged narco-trafficking vessel in the Pacific Ocean on 27 October 2026.Photograph: US Southern Command via XUS militaryUS military says strike on alleged drug vessel in eastern Pacific kills five peopleUS military says it carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug-trafficking boat in latest attack in regionGuardian staff and agenciesTue 27 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ⁠military ⁠saidon ​Tuesday ⁠it killed ⁠five ​people ‌after ‌an airstrike on a ‌suspected drug-trafficking vessel in ​the ⁠eastern Pacific.Tuesday’s strike was among more than 70 such attacks since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second presidency, according to media tallies. title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll | China | The Guardian
description: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Content: Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBeijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesChinaChinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its tollLack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boomAmy Hawkinsin BeijingTue 27 Oct 2026 00.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.3:48Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainerUS bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agenciesRead moreThe fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.The US hasbanned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to beconsidering a banon Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down onrobotics– also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.View image in fullscreenHumanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockChina’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude,filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPOthat could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.This week thetop officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.Explore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk | Japan | The Guardian
description: US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
Content: A US navy jet lands at Kadena air base in Okinawa, Japan. The US military has banned vehicles made by China’s BYD at the base.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA US navy jet lands at Kadena air base in Okinawa, Japan. The US military has banned vehicles made by China’s BYD at the base.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesJapanUS bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ riskUS military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxisJustin McCurryin TokyoMon 26 Oct 2026 22.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chineseelectric vehiclemaker BYD over security concerns, the US military inJapansaid on Tuesday.The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island ofOkinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at otherUS militaryfacilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflationRead moreThe restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involvingChina,RussiaorNorth Korea.Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.View image in fullscreenA US military plane takes off at Kadena air force base on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa.Photograph: Issei Kato/ReutersThe move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companiesHuaweiand ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.China has imposed similar restrictions on US-madeTeslavehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as theworld’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehiclesin 2025.It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market,Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.With ReutersExplore more on these topicsJapanUS foreign policyUS militaryAsia PacificUS national securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Coalition MP calls for rethink of pre-poll voting amid heightened security concerns in wake of Haines incident | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Queensland MP Garth Hamilton says he has ‘witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental’
Author: Tess Ikonomou
Headline: Queensland MP Garth Hamilton says he has ‘witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental’
Content: Questions are being raised over the security environment at pre-polling places in the midst of heightened risk to politicians, staff and voters.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenQuestions are being raised over the security environment at pre-polling places in the midst of heightened risk to politicians, staff and voters.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPAustralia newsCoalition MP calls for rethink of pre-poll voting amid heightened security concerns in wake of Haines incidentQueensland MP Garth Hamilton says he has ‘witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental’Follow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastTess IkonomouTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Coalition MP has called for a rethink of pre-poll voting at federal elections, including potentially shortening the amount of time booths are open, amid concerns of threats to voters and volunteers.Security risks to politicians and their staff have been front and centre this week, as parliament returned after the alleged attack onHelen Haines, which left the independent MP in a serious but stable condition after both her legs were amputated.The LNP member for the Queensland electorate of Groom, Garth Hamilton, said the risk of having members of the public and volunteers lined up at booths near car parks or roads needed to be assessed.Albanese promises ‘swift response’ on MP safety as he mulls panic buttons for politiciansRead more“I’ve had three elections and I’ve witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental, one wasn’t,” Hamilton said on Tuesday.“The threat is already there, the potential is already there in a heightened environment.”Pre-polling booths usually open one to two weeks before an election. The Toowoomba-based politician said the length of the pre-polling period, the allocation of resources at centres and the role of postal voting were all measures that could be considered to lower the risk to voters and staff.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here“What we obviously want is not in any way to restrict anybody’s access to democracy, but we also want to make sure that it’s done in a safe way,” Hamilton said. “There’s a reasonable conversation to be had on the shape of pre-poll in Australia, if these threats are increasing, and that’s what we’re hearing from the AFP.”Australians are increasingly choosing to vote early ahead of polling day. More than 9m votes, or 56%, were cast at early voting centres, according to theAustralian Electoral Commission’s 2025 election report.It is understood Jerome Laxale, a Labor MP who chairs the parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election, raised safety and his committee’s interim report on the issue at a caucus meeting on Tuesday.The report recommends the electoral commission reviews the resourcing requirements and duration of pre-poll voting to ensure adequate arrangements are in place, noting the rising number of people opting to cast their ballot early.The AEC advised the committee that shortening the pre-poll period would not decrease early voting, but would instead “compress the growing demand into a shorter period and increase operational risks, such as queues and shortages of appropriate venues”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLaxale, who has represented the NSW seat of Bennelong since 2022, said it was incumbent on the parliament to provide a safe and welcoming atmosphere at a polling booth.“Democracy doesn’t collapse, it just crumbles,” he said.“If people go, ‘you know what? I don’t want to deal with that. I’m not going to vote,’ then that has a snowball effect, which will undermine and erode our democratic process. Voting has to be safe and secure.”Submissions to the inquiry detailed neo-Nazis turning up to booths with speakers, volunteers being bullied and harassed and voters leaving polling centres in tears.The independent MP Monique Ryan said candidates, volunteers, and campaign workers facing threats of violence should be given clear guidance for how they might engage with federal and state police.“We need to go back to democracy sausages and bake sales, not voters feeling intimidated and harassed as they approach polling booths,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsAustralian politicsHelen HainesLiberal National partyLabor partyIndependentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Frontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuation
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Frontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuation
Content: A woman beneath anti-drone nets stretched over a street in Kherson during a local ceasefire on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APView image in fullscreenA woman beneath anti-drone nets stretched over a street in Kherson during a local ceasefire on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APUkraineOleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with PutinFrontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuationLuke HardingandPjotr SauerTue 27 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlocal ceasefirein a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians.The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troopsrecaptured Kherson in autumn 2022.Map of frontline in KhersonWitnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation.Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call withVladimir Putinabout efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia,Ukraineand the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump,requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid.Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council ofEurope.View image in fullscreenPeople board a bus in Kherson during a local ceasefire on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APBetween 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, andmany people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it.Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles.Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia.Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.“People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press.The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russiabombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire.View image in fullscreenA building damaged by an overnight Russian missile strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe bridge remains closed to traffic, but some commuters walked across it to get to work. Writing on social media,Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote.The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole.European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, given Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a candidate.View image in fullscreenLeft to right: Alexander Stubb, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Jonas Gahr Støre in Oslo on 20 October.Photograph: Heiko Junge/EPAThe divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said.She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.”Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process.This month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces.Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in aninterview with ABC News. He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer | Glaciers | The Guardian
description: Extreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identity
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Extreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identity
Content: Slovenia's Mount Triglav, pictured on 19 October 2026 after the last of the glacier had melted.Photograph: Anton Melik Geographical InstituteView image in fullscreenSlovenia's Mount Triglav, pictured on 19 October 2026 after the last of the glacier had melted.Photograph: Anton Melik Geographical InstituteGlaciersSlovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summerExtreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identityAjit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe final ice patch has vanished from Slovenia’s Triglav glacier, the latest Alpine casualty of Europe’s scorching summer.The once mighty ice mass lost 93% of its surface area between 1983 and 2003, shrinking to cover less than a hectare of overheated rock, but went on to surprise researchers who feared its imminent demise, clinging on to the mountain for two more decades.In the last five years, which includes Europe’s three hottest years on record, the remaining ice has melted to a handful of isolated pockets, with the final remnant of the main body measuring just a few metres by the end of summer. New photos of the mountainside – taken either side of snowfall this month – confirm that no ice remains.View image in fullscreenThe last piece of the Triglav glacier, pictured on 2 October.Photograph: Borut Živulovič/ReutersMatija Zorn, director of the Anton Melik Geographical Institute, said Mount Triglav “holds a central place in Slovenian national identity” and the demise of the glacier represents the loss of an important data source and indicator of climate change.“Every year I knew that the ice was going to be less and less,” he said. “But I was shocked every year [by] how much less ice was up there.”‘Planetary destruction on fast-forward’: witnessing the disappearance of Indonesia’s ‘eternity glaciers’Read moreFierce heatwaves made hotter by carbon pollution have ravaged the Alps and reduced big white glaciers to what scientists have called “moonlike” rock deserts. Last month, Swiss glaciologists found thatnearly a fifth of the country’s ice had disappeared in the last five years, with a 5.5% drop in volume in 2026.In Slovenia, home to the south-eastern tip of the Alps, the Triglav glacier suffered most of its decline in the last century. Historical photographs and documents suggest the glacier covered about 40 hectares in the mid-1800s. By 1946, when scientists conducted the first formal measurements, its area had shrunk to just 14 hectares.Zorn, who first took measurements at the glacier in 2001, said the rate of change was surprising even in the decades in which the glacier defied expectations. The spot at which he had to put on crampons to prevent slipping jumped back year after year as the glacier receded.Aerial map view of the Triglav glacier and surrounding mountains“The melting is incredible,” he said. “In 2002 … we took a core of ice out for some geochemical analysis and it was like 5 metres [deep]. The next year, I was standing on the same spot … not on ice, but on rock.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTriglav appears on Slovenia’s flag.Illustration: WikimediaTriglav is Slovenia’s highest peak, a cultural touchpoint that every person in the country of skiers and climbers is expected to climb at least once. Although the glacier has vanished, scientists have found ice in the caves beneath Triglav as its retreat has exposed new shafts. A second glacier on the Skuta mountain has also shrunk and thinned, but the remaining patch of ice is better shaded than Triglav and is expected to hold out for a few more years.View image in fullscreenGlaciers in the French Alps are also melting fast as a result of climate change.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesMay heatwaves, deaths, ruined harvests: study of Europe’s summer paints grim picture for the futureRead moreWestern Europe suffered through its hottest summer on record this year, causingat least 50,000 estimated heat deathsand costly secondary effects that ranged from failed harvests to power plants being forced to shut down. Scientists are still assessing the damage done to ecosystems.Miha Pavšek, a glaciologist and mountain guide, said “nature is changing in front of our eyes” but people were not yet taking it seriously.“With the melting of the glacier, a part of me is also going away,” said Pavšek, who has a photograph of his parents there in 1957. “There are some things that humans thought were eternal.Glaciersare obviously not.”Explore more on these topicsGlaciersExtreme heatMountainsSloveniaEuropeClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kyiv hopes for ‘new momentum’ in peace talks after Finnish and Norwegian leaders’ call with Putin – as it happened | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre held ‘substantive’ call with Russian president on peace negotiations, but faced sceptical reactions from some European leaders
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre held ‘substantive’ call with Russian president on peace negotiations, but faced sceptical reactions from some European leaders
Content: 11.27 EDTSybiha confirms Putin phone call was 'coordinated' with Ukraine as Kyiv hopes for 'new momentum' in peace talksUkraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has confirmed the Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin was coordinated withUkraine, saying it was “the right approach” to any engagement with Putin.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha‎ looks on prior to a meeting his Finnish counterpart Valtonen in Helsinki, Finland.Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPASpeaking alongside Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministers in Helsinki, Sybiha said:“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process. This call was, as it was mentioned, coordinated with us, and this is the right approach. …I will say this once again, Ukraine wants to end this war.We have doable proposals and solutions. We are ready for partial ceasefires and a full end to hostilities. Of course, everything needs to be fair. We will not take any one-sided steps.”Sybiha said thatUkraine was looking for “a new momentum” in peace talks with Russia,and to “define new role forEuropein our peace efforts.”“So president Zelenskyy shared with his vision which signals our friends should convey directly to the Putin, and these signals were conveyed. Ceasefire … and another signal meeting with Putin. We are ready to meet with him. …Probably the only way to get …. new quality in our talks is a meeting at the level of president Zelenskyy and Putin.”He later said that the negotiators can only discuss things up to a certain level, butkey decisions can only be made by the heads of states.He also added thatKyiv was “ready for the trilateral meeting” in the UAE next month,and “we will use every opportunity to bring peace closer.”He alsowelcomed the limited ceasefire in Oleshky,saying it could “pave the way for other steps in the peace process as a confidence-building measure.”Butconceded that “the reality on the ground in Ukraine remains very tough”as a result of relentless Russian strikes.ShareUpdated at11.32 EDT

title: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Business secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Business secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’
Content: The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said the ‘British people are the people who will decide this’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said the ‘British people are the people who will decide this’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PABrexitUK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summitBusiness secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 27 Oct 2026 05.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movementRead more“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”19:01What makes Andy Burnham think we can rejoin the EU? | Politics WeeklyReynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands arewary about reopening the argumentsfor free movement or rejoining the EU.TheLabourMP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”Cabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EURead moreThe Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago,Andy Burnhamsays to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”Burnham made his plea for an“honest discussion” about freedom of movementin an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then?
