I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyJonathan ReynoldsAndy BurnhamLabourEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions | Italy | The Guardian
description: Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings
Content: Soldiers from Italy’s Julia Alpine brigade work to make a first world war bomb safe before removing it.Photograph: Julia Alpine brigadeView image in fullscreenSoldiers from Italy’s Julia Alpine brigade work to make a first world war bomb safe before removing it.Photograph: Julia Alpine brigadeItalyMelting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitionsItalian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightingsAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.View image in fullscreenSoldiers from Italian army’s Julia Alpine brigade at work.Photograph: Julia Alpine brigadeMore than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.View image in fullscreenA soldier with some of the munitions recovered.Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade“It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMelting ice reveals first world war relics in Italian AlpsRead moreA wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”Explore more on these topicsItalyFirst world warGlaciersClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape | Israel | The Guardian
description: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing
Content: Gadi Eisenkot, right, may have to negotiate with Mansour Abbas, left, of Ra’am to form a coalition.Composite: AlamyView image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, right, may have to negotiate with Mansour Abbas, left, of Ra’am to form a coalition.Composite: AlamyIsraelAnalysisRise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeJulian Borgerin NazarethExit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governingIsraeli elections: live updatesTue 27 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTShareThe big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or handBenjamin Netanyahua roadmap to political survival.In the wake ofTuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.The exit polls gave a narrow lead to Eisenkot’s opposition bloc over Netanyahu’s governing coalition and its supporters, though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party.Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seatsRead moreIf confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role.Eisenkot will argue that he commands the bigger overall bloc and has the better chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election”.However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.1:49Israeli candidates cast their votes in consequential election – videoNegotiations with the Joint List, with 10 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.“Laying down conditions won’t work with the Joint List,” Shbita said. “We will negotiate as equals because we need each other.”In the absence of an agreement with one or both of the Palestinian groupings, it is possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.Is this the end for Benjamin Netanyahu? – podcastRead moreIt would be an unstable solution, making another election more than likely. That would provide Netanyahu the opportunity to rally support among conservative Israeli Jews and claim to have been vindicated in his campaign slogan, “the Right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.Netanyahu has looked beaten before over his three decades at or near the top, and staged a comeback each time with the aid of his unparalleled tactical skills as a dealmaker. No one is yet ruling out another breathtaking political escape. But this time, if he does bounce back, he would owe his resurrection to his avowed political enemies for dropping him a lifeline rather than make historic compromises across Israel’s deep racial divide.Speaking from the Joint List victory party in Nazareth in the early hours of Wednesday, one party official said: “The Zionist opposition will have to choose between supremacy and building democracy.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats | Israel | The Guardian
description: Early indications suggest it will be some time before the shape of new government and who will lead it is clear
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Early indications suggest it will be some time before the shape of new government and who will lead it is clear
Content: Members of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party react to the exit polls.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party react to the exit polls.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesIsraelIsrael election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seatsEarly indications suggest it will be some time before the shape of new government and who will lead it is clearIsrael election – live updatesRise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeEmma Graham-Harrisonin Tel Aviv,Julian Borgerin Jerusalem andPeter BeaumontTue 27 Oct 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s election appeared to have delivered no clear winner on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters.Exit polls published on Tuesday evening suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin,edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party.The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called, but represents a sharp electoral rebuke to Netanyahu.1:49Israeli candidates cast their votes in consequential election – videoAfter a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis.The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition.While Eisenkot could theoretically assemble a majority by forming a government with the Arab parties, he ruled that out before the election.The exit polls – if they prove accurate – suggest a struggle for either Likud or Eisenkot’s Yashar to find a road to a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud’s projected showing, not for the first time, appears to have defied predictions in the run-up to the vote.What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s historyRead moreHowever, the ​stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu’s favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity. What is clear, however, is that Netanayhu no longer has a claim to a mandate with his political fate hanging in the balance.Opposition figures were quick to cast the exit polls as a defeat for Netanyahu, with former prime minister Yair Lapid saying: “Netanyahu’s bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse. The public has told them to get out.”For his part Eisenkot called the exit polls a vote of “no-confidence in Netanyahu. If these are the final results, it’s a complete victory for Israel’s mainstream majority. I’ll work immediately to enact the will of the nation, to change Netanyahu’s government … as soon as possible.”The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee. The prime minister had suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee that said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.Tuesday’s election, which drew the highest turnout in 50 years, had been framed as a referendum on nearly 17 years of unbroken rule byBenjamin Netanyahu, who has most recently overseen three years of unprecedented conflict, instability and growing international isolation.With more than 7 million people eligible to vote, by 6pm voter turnout was 77.1% – a rise of about 9% on the previous election – with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting. There were also reports of tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad who had arrived to vote in recent days, with many still arriving at Ben Gurion airport to cast their ballots on Tuesday.Voting was heavy in a number of major cities, including Tel Aviv and Haifa, which some analysts had suggested would benefit the opposition, with long queues to vote in some locations. That pattern was repeated in Israeli-Arab towns, many of which have a long history of boycotting elections.View image in fullscreenIsraeli-Arab voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth.Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty ImagesAs polls opened on Tuesday, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition allies launched what critics condemned as a scare campaign to encourage their supporters to turn out, with the familiar racist tactic of warning that large numbers of Israeli Arabs would be voting. Netanyahu made a similar claim to rally support in 2015.In a recorded message to voters, Netanyahu suggested Arabs and the left were trying to steal the election and Likud claimed suspected irregularities at hundreds of polling stations used by Israeli Arabs.Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin make up about 20% of the country’s population.That prompted Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, to say Netanyahu was laying the ground to challenge the result.View image in fullscreenA Likud election poster at a polling station in Jerusalem.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images“Netanyahu has returned to his familiar tricks, lies and fearmongering to mobilise voters,” he said. “The same lies we saw in previous election campaigns.”Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023 – an event that many blamed on Netanyahu’s failings – Israel has devastated Gaza with the loss of more than 74,000 Palestinian lives, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners have also attracted international opprobrium for Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank, where violent Jewish settlers have been accused of pogroms against Palestinians and ethnic cleansing.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian family walk past campaign posters for Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in Beit Kahil in the West Bank.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesDespite the many issues confronting the country, much of the focus in the campaign has been on the contrasting characters of the two main party leaders – the machiavellian, grandstanding Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption, against Eisenkot, the unpolished former IDF chief of staff who rose from humble origins.The campaign, unusually febrile even by Israeli standards, included a struggling Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.On Tuesday, encouraging ultra-orthodox voters, Netanyahu – who has long elided his personal and political survival with that of Israel – returned to his apocalyptic language. “The Jewish state is on the brink of ruin,” he said.In the midst of a major trial for corruption, which has been moving at a glacial pace through the courts, Netanyahu has appeared rattled by the challenge mounted against him by an array of centre-right parties whose unifying pitch has been “anyone but Netanyahu”.“This is a very moving and fateful moment,” he told journalists after voting, saying he believed the Arab parties that could make or break the election were “receiving massive, truly massive support … heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers”.Despite tonight’s results, the complexity of Israel’s fragmented political system, with many parties jostling and horse trading, means that it will probably be some time before the shape of any future government – and who will lead it – is clear.All of which has amplified the importance of Israeli Arab parties, which could emerge as potential kingmakers.“Our vote will change the government,” the head of the Islamist Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, said while voting, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are “not even people”, said “it will be Mansour Abbas’s government” if Netanyahu and his allies lose.Underlining the sense of a country at a defining crossroads, an editorial in the left-leaning Haaretz publication had exhorted Israelis to vote, which they didin huge numbers.“Israel cannot afford another four years under Netanyahu,” it said. “It has exhausted its reserves. The erosion of its diplomatic credit has reached dangerous proportions, and its tired citizens are at the very limits of what they can bear.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Legacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbers | Israel | The Guardian
description: Bereaved families tell voters to remember the victims while others have flown thousands of miles to cast their ballots
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Bereaved families tell voters to remember the victims while others have flown thousands of miles to cast their ballots
Content: Religious Israelis walk past a polling station in Bet Shemesh on Tuesday. Turnout is expected to shatter records.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReligious Israelis walk past a polling station in Bet Shemesh on Tuesday. Turnout is expected to shatter records.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelLegacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbersBereaved families tell voters to remember the victims while others have flown thousands of miles to cast their ballotsEmma Graham-Harrisonin Efrat,Julian Borgerin Nazareth andQuique Kierszenbaumin JerusalemTue 27 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElection day inIsraelbegan with a protest by some of the voters with most at stake. Bereaved families of those killed in the 7 October attacks held a minute of silence at 6.29am, the moment when Hamas launched its onslaught just over three years ago.They gathered in a Tel Aviv plaza that has become known as “hostages square” because it was the centre of demonstrations demanding the return of more than 200 captives fromGaza. Holding pictures of their loved ones, they stood in silence then called on voters to remember the losses and betrayals of that day when deciding on the next government.“Three years after the massacre, our loved ones will not be voting today. Go out and vote – remember them at the ballot box. This is what these elections are about,” the group said.They are not explicitly backing any political party, but one of their key demands is a state commission of inquiry into the attacks.Benjamin Netanyahuhas resisted this and it has become a rallying point for the opposition parties trying to unseat him as prime minister.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, casts his vote in Herzliya. He said Benjamin Netanyahu had led the worst government Israel had known.Photograph: Shir Torem/ReutersNetanyahu’s strongest challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, started the day by visiting communities attacked on 7 October. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here,” said the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party.Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”.As the day wore on, it became clear that voter turnout was shattering all records and among those lining up at polling stations were tens of thousands of Israelis who live overseas.View image in fullscreenA polling station in the Jewish settlement of Efrat in the West Bank.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianA bipartisan “Fly&Vote” initiative was set up to support those who wanted to return because electoral law only allows voting in person. While not everyone coming back was opposed to the government, anecdotal evidence suggested many were opposition supporters who held the view that Israel faced an existential choice.Monica Moria, 58, and her husband, Ron, flew in to Tel Aviv from Barcelona. They took a train to a kibbutz where she is registered to vote and she cast her ballot for the most leftwing of the Jewish Israeli parties, the Democrats.She said: “It feels like Israel has lost its way, there are deep divisions and hatreds that will be very difficult to heal. The idea is to bring a political change so that we can bring Israeli society together again. I want to be optimistic, but I am also afraid.”Kobi Mizrahi, 35, who has been completing a PhD in New York, paid more than $1,600 (£1,200) to come back to Israel for just a few days and vote.He said: “Given the fact that it feels like a ‘now or never’ moment, where if we lose these elections to the Bibi coalition this might be the turning point we can’t come back to, I felt like I have to do anything in my power to help.”View image in fullscreenYuval Schwarzfuchs, right, flew all the way from Rio de Janeiro to vote for the Joint List in Jerusalem.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianYuval Schwarzfuchs, 26, travelled from Rio de Janeiro via Ethiopia to vote for the Palestinian-led Joint List. “For me, its about equality for all,” he said. “I did what I had to do.”He came to the Jerusalem polling station wearing a T-shirt with an image of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the leftwing president of Brazil, who defied the polls to win re-election at the weekend.In the settlement of Efrat near Jerusalem, Shani, 19, had come to the polling station with her parents, to cast her vote for the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich.She is part of a large cohort of first-time voters who are more rightwing than older generations and may help bolster support for Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners.More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel).Shani said she chose Smotrich, a settler himself, for his promises to expand Israel’s footprint in occupiedPalestine. “Smotrich is pushing forward with settlement expansion and improving security,” she said.Her mother, kindergarten teacher Rivka, also voted for Smotrich, and said her priority was to return Netanyahu’s coalition to office.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian family walks past election campaign posters in Beit Kahil in the West Bank on Tuesday. Palestinian parties in Israel may hold the balance of power in what is expected to be a tight result.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images“The right must win, because otherwise there is a chance of a Palestinian state, which will be very bad for Jews,” she said.Spiralling attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinians, and the growing threat of sanctions on settlement goods and construction, were not a key election issue for voters in Efrat who spoke to the Guardian.The Palestinian Israeli vote is a critical camp in this election, representing about a fifth of eligible voters. Their votes are expected to go to either Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, or Joint List, an electoral alliance of Palestinian-Israeli parties.Even if the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot wins more seats than Netanyahu’s coalition, it is not expected to win an outright majority. It has also ruled out going into coalition with the Palestinian Israeli parties, which could well hold the balance of power.Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the leading party in the Joint List coalition, thinks Eisenkot’s approach may change after the elections.“He cannot sit down [in coalition] with Netanyahu, and he won’t want to go back to another round of elections, so we think he can be flexible,” he said.View image in fullscreenArab voters who are Israeli citizens cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth, Israel. Turnout was high in the city.Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty ImagesIn Nazareth, the largest Palestinian-majority town in Israel, the turnout at polling stations has been noticeably higher than at recent elections, although still below the average Jewish turnout across the country. A surge of evening voting was expected here as people came home from work.At the headquarters of the Joint List, the most pressing concern was the spoiler tactics of far-right election monitors at predominantly Palestinian polling stations.“They can say that they want to check all the voter numbers and identity and everything, so they can slow things down, so that people wait a long time and give up. That’s their intention,” said Shbita.At worst, these ploys have slowed the process down so that it took half an hour to vote, rather than a couple of minutes, he added.Shbita said voters were sufficiently motivated to overcome such obstacles. “It is the first time for a long time that a government has stayed in office for its full term, four years,” he said.“We are talking about one of the worst governments when it comes to Arab society. We feel racism at all levels of Israeli society, in hospitals, in buses, in public transportation, in the media. So people understand that today we have the opportunity to change the government.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineGazaBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Fears grow for Iranian athletes on death row as mountaineer latest to be hanged | Global development | The Guardian
description: Two sportspeople have been executed in the past month and at least six more face the same fate, says activist group
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Two sportspeople have been executed in the past month and at least six more face the same fate, says activist group
Content: Mountaineer Ali-Sina Mostafavi was executed earlier this month for taking part in protests against the Iranian government.Photograph: Ali-Sina Mostafavi/Iran Human RightsView image in fullscreenMountaineer Ali-Sina Mostafavi was executed earlier this month for taking part in protests against the Iranian government.Photograph: Ali-Sina Mostafavi/Iran Human RightsRights and freedomGlobal developmentFears grow for Iranian athletes on death row as mountaineer latest to be hangedTwo sportspeople have been executed in the past month and at least six more face the same fate, says activist groupSupported byAbout this contentEd AaronsTue 27 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFears are growing for more Iranian athletes facing execution after mountain climber Ali-Sina Mostafavi became the latest in a string to be killed by the regime.Mostafavi – who documented his ascents of some of the world’s highest peaks, including Mount Everest – was executed on 14 October having been arrested in April after the anti-government protests a few months earlier. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, at the start of October, and the mixed martial arts fighterGholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hangedin May.NowHuman Rights for Sport– a group of former Iranian athletes based in Oslo that has been documenting the growing number of cases – has warned that at least six more are facing execution after having their sentences upheld by Iran’s supreme court. They include the swimmer Ali Pishevarzadeh and the footballer Ehsan Hosseinpour, who were both arrested during the January protests, and Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani – a boxer arrested in 2020 for taking part in protests a year earlier. He saw his request for a retrialrejected last year.View image in fullscreenBoxer Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani – arrested for protesting in 2019 – is among those facing imminent execution, warns Human Rights for Sport.Photograph: Iran Human RightsAnother MMA fighter, Benyamin Naghdi, equestrian athlete Taraneh Rahimi and the climber Maryam Siri have also been condemned to death this year.Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media postRead moreHuman Rights for Sport said six athletes have already been executed in cases linked to the January protests or earlier political charges.Dr Zohreh Abdollahkhani of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The Iranian sporting community is under enormous pressure. For one of those sentenced to death, we managed to raise attention and awareness through other organisations and they halted his execution. But it was only temporary and I’m very concerned about all of them.”Human Rights for Sport believe that athletes have been targeted to send a message to the wider community, with the deaths of prominent sportspeople often given widespread coverage in the state-run media. They include Navid Afkari Sangari – a wrestler who was executed in September 2020.View image in fullscreenWrestler Navid Afkari Sangari was executed in September 2020.Photograph: UN Watch“He was a role model and very famous in the whole community. What happened to him was also a warning to the whole population: look what we can do to someone like this,” Abdollahkhani said.Mostafavi’s death sentence was upheld by the supreme court at the end of September and he is believed to have been subjected to physical violence during his detention in Kerman before being transferred to solitary confinement. He was accused of being an “armed agent of the American-Zionist enemy” and was arrested forallegedly opening fire on civilians in Azadi Squarein Kerman on 24 March and taking part in January’s protests. Mostafavi’s family are thought to have been summoned to the prison hours before his execution.View image in fullscreenMountaineer Ali-Sina Mostafavi before his detention.Photograph: Ali Sina Mostafavi/FacebookAbdollahkhani said that making contact with those facing the death sentence is a challenge, as some members of their families are also being targeted by security services.“In one case, his sister and brother-in-law have been arrested and the whole family’s phone lines are under surveillance. So it’s simply impossible to make direct contact,” she said.Overall, Human Rights for Sport has found that217 Iranian athletes were killedby direct gunfire in January, and more than 100 others detained. Four members of the European parliament also wrote to Fifa before the World Cup concerning Iranian athletes facing execution but Abdollahkhani said they received no response.“Fifa is aware of the concerns raised regarding the situation of Iranian athletes and thanks all stakeholders for their continued collaboration and dedication to raising awareness of these critical matters,” a spokesperson for football’s governing body said.Abdollahkhani also criticised the International Olympic Committee (IOC), saying changes in staffing had made it difficult to raise cases through its human rights and safeguarding structures. The IOC disputed her account, saying it had “fully functioning human rights and safeguarding teams”. It said it was deeply concerned about athletes affected by events in Iran but lacked the authority, as a non-governmental organisation, to change a sovereign country’s laws or political system.“Within our remit, we work tirelessly with all stakeholders of the Olympic movement, including national Olympic committees and international federations, to support the creation of a safe sporting environment for all athletes. We will continue to work with our Olympic stakeholders to support all athletes globally through sports diplomacy, and we remain in touch with the Olympic community of Iran.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomIranMiddle East and north AfricaCapital punishmentArab and Middle East unrestSport politicsTransnational repressionnewsShareReuse this content

title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India | World news | The Guardian
description: Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothing
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothing
Content: Rubio Central AsiaUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio, left, shakes hands with India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, right, before their meeting in Mumbai, India, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Kylie Cooper/Pool Photo via AP)Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenRubio Central AsiaUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio, left, shakes hands with India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, right, before their meeting in Mumbai, India, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Kylie Cooper/Pool Photo via AP)Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/APThis Is IndiaWorld newsWhat Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on IndiaRubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothingDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 27 Oct 2026 05.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace,Milan Vaishnavhas spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US.Vaishnav has describedTrump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio speaking to the media in the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai last Wednesday.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTrumpthe deal-makerAhead of Rubio’s visit,several commentatorsnoted the secretary of state’s“unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav.Pakistan’s standingin Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.But, after coming to power the second time,Trump thanked the countryfor its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomedAsim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.In arecent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.The way forwardDespite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without acomprehensive trade dealbeing reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’sH-1B visa and green card restrictionshave disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as“deeply offensive”. Furthermore,Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary,Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenOne of the images of the recent protests, which the artist Raihan Vadra was asked to remove from his show at Bikaner House in Delhi.Photograph: Raihan VadraStudent protests| Bikaner House, one of Delhi’s premier arts venues, asked visual artist Raihan Vadra to remove from his show more than 70 photographs that featured recent student protests. Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were“inconsistent”with its policy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFashion| Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted aDiwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled ahigh-jewellery collectioninspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.Air pollution| Emergency measures, including a ban on coal-fired tandoors in restaurants and restrictions on diesel generators, have come into effect in Delhi, asair quality dropped to the poor categoryat the onset of the annual pollution season.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenA scene from Flowers of Acacia, directed by Anmol Sidhu, which features in the Dharamshala international film festival.Photograph: PRFilm-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annualDharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenEnvironmental activists have been protesting against the felling of trees, such as these marked for removal in a park in Versova, Mumbai.Photograph: Alamy7,633That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according tothe Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenPrarthna Singh captured the rkivecity menswear line through a female gaze.Photograph: Prarthna SinghPrarthna Singhhas consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photographrkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me.One image shows a pair of handsholding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaDonald TrumpMarco RubioUS politicsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’ | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferred
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferred
Content: John Healey prepares for the budget in the kitchen of his Downing Street flat.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryView image in fullscreenJohn Healey prepares for the budget in the kitchen of his Downing Street flat.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryBudget 2026Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’Healey hopes to give ‘hope for the future’ but only modest policies are expected with important decisions deferredPippa CrerarandHeather StewartTue 27 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.The budget, which will be interpreted as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, is nevertheless expected to be a relatively modest affair as Healey grapples with stark fiscal realities, putting off important decisions on tax and spending until next year.“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellorRead moreHealey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.The chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran conflict, but changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily.In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families before a steep rise in typical energy bills in January; while pledging energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was keen to see the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – abolished. The move would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, and the cost would be picked up by those who use more.Industry experts fear further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture is likely to bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, in a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected toend the carers’ allowance cliff edge, which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence a week. Healey is also expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.But while he is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – Healey is expected to wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.Consumer confidencehas fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distresshas hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for younger people under the age of 21 after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs but prompting accusations that Labour had broken a manifesto pledge.He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for their retirement by shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost to middle-earners.You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the booksRead moreTo help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised toraise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyUK cost of living crisisEnergy billsBudgetTax and spendingHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban | Vaping | The Guardian
description: Three-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research finds
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Three-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research finds
Content: It is thought to have been the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.Photograph: Tim Parker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is thought to have been the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.Photograph: Tim Parker/Getty ImagesVapingAI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes banThree-quarters of all responses were machine-generated in failed attempt to stop bill from passing into law, research findsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorTue 27 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.The Department ofHealthand Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”More than 6m vapes and pods discarded weekly in UK despite single-use ban, study findsRead moreAzzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”Explore more on these topicsVapingHealth policyAI (artificial intelligence)HealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rape | UK news | The Guardian
description: Mark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assault
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Mark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assault
Content: Mark Tyrell, pictured in 2024, was based in the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, where the convicted rapists Wayne Couzens and David Carrick both worked.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenMark Tyrell, pictured in 2024, was based in the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, where the convicted rapists Wayne Couzens and David Carrick both worked.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.UK newsFormer Met officer who worked with Wayne Couzens found guilty of rapeMark Tyrrell, who was in same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, also guilty on three counts of sexual assaultNadeem BadshahTue 27 Oct 2026 16.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Change to carer’s allowance cliff-edge rule is not enough, victims say | Carer's allowance | The Guardian
description: Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with unjust overpayments still have to pay
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with unjust overpayments still have to pay
Content: Guy and Oksana Shahar, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were issued with a bill for more than £10,000 when Oksana earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGuy and Oksana Shahar, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were issued with a bill for more than £10,000 when Oksana earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCarer's allowanceChange to carer’s allowance cliff-edge rule is not enough, victims sayDigital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with overpayments will still have to payPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorTue 27 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,” says unpaid carer Guy Shahar of the government’s decision toabolish the notorious carer’s allowance cliff edge.But Shahar is angry that most carers hit with unjust overpayments in the past will still have to repay them, for all the promise of a different future. And he notes that the cliff edge remains in place for four more years, potentially catching out more carers.“They are effectively saying: ‘We know that the system was unfair but we will still punish you for having been the victim of an unfair system,’” he says.The chancellor is expected to announce the introduction of a new digital taper system into the carer’s allowance benefit in the budget, in effect ending a rule that has landed hundreds of thousands of carers with life-shattering financial penalties.Unpaid carers have broadly welcomed the move – and there is a general acknowledgment that ministers are moving positively, if slowly, to reform a system with inbuilt injustices and terrible management that birthed what became known as thecarer’s allowance scandal.But there is also disbelief that the new system – which must be built from scratch – will be live before 2030, and a feeling that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has a lot more to do to regain the trust of unpaid carers.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, says the cliff edge symbolises a ‘whole crazy system’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianShahar and his wife, Oksana, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were victims of the cliff edge. This rule meant that a carer who earns more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – will forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, now £86.45.A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40. Last year, the Shahars werelanded with a £10,000 repayment billfor relatively trivial earnings breaches dating back five years.Oksana had earned more than the allowed limit by just £1.92 a week on average while juggling caring with part-time minimum wage jobs. In some weeks, she was paid just 38p more than the carer’s allowance earnings threshold.Over the period, she earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed – but was duly issued with a bill for £10,130.45 – plus a £50 civil penalty. The Shahars are challenging the charge at tribunal but the stress is real and ongoing.Unpaid carer Elizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, is staggered that the taper system is years away: “We live in the age of tech; it is ludicrous it is going to take so long. They need to make it a priority.”Tait, a former teacher and now a private tutor and educational consultant whoended up with a bill for £1,623after unwittingly breaching the earnings threshold, says the carer’s allowance cliff edge symbolises a “whole crazy system”.Reforming carer’s allowance is essential but it needs to be part of a wider examination of the crucial role of unpaid care in propping up England’s social care arrangements, she says: “We care willingly and lovingly, and yet we end up a casualty of the system.”Andrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, is one of a handful of carers tochallenge a cliff edge penalty and win, successfully overturning a £4,600 overpayment at a tribunal in February 2025.View image in fullscreenAndrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, challenged the cliff edge penalty and won but says it cost her months of stress.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAs a result, she did not have to repay the money, although she suffered months of stress along the way. She welcomes the decision to introduce a taper but believes carers punished unfairly by draconian rules should be compensated.“People repaying overpayments should no longer have to, and they should be given back what they have already paid,” she says.Tucker recalls how for years she carefully monitored her monthly earnings from her part-time charity shop role to stay under the limit. Some weeks she would work six hours for nothing so as not to risk losing carer’s allowance.Even so, she was hit with an overpayment when DWP officials decided – unlawfully – that she could not average her earnings over a one-year period.There is raw bitterness among carers about the cliff edge, she says. “My friend is paying back their overpayment at £10 a month. She went £12.50 over as a result of receiving holiday pay. She always tells me: ‘I hope I die before I have paid it all back.’”Explore more on these topicsCarer's allowanceBudgetCarersSocial careState benefitsBenefitsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
Content: Mohmed Abdulkarim (left) and Nouman Essghir appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenMohmed Abdulkarim (left) and Nouman Essghir appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PAUK newsRAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court toldHelena HortonTue 27 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 05.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.Abdulkarim, of London, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service. He is accused of buying the vans used in the Fairford incident on the instruction of Ali.Essghir, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, after initially being arrested at the scene near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September and then re-arrested on 20 October. He is accused of visiting RAF Fairford and filming around the facility on a video call with Ali before returning a month later in the convoy of vans.Abdulkarim has been released on bail under conditions including the surrender of his passport, and Essghir has been remanded in custody. They will appear at the Old Bailey on 20 November.Prosecutor Louise Gray alleged the defendants were in contact with an individual known as Ali who is now believed to be abroad.She said that during the events of 27 September at the RAF Fairford base, five men who were arrested travelled in vans, parked and got out “and were told to do so by someone known as Mr Ali”.One of them, she said, had claimed they were told there was a bomb in the van and called 999.The court heard that the person calling stated that they were from London and that he was one of a group of five males. The caller told the police that they had been tasked to drive vans to the location for the purpose of a new business venture. When the vans arrived at the location, the organiser was in communication with them over the telephone.Gray alleged he then told them to park the vans and to walk away from them. After they did that, the organiser told them to run as he had planted a bomb in the van. The caller indicated that he and his colleagues had run away from the vans and were now calling the police for help.The defendants are believed to have known Ali for “a number of years”, she said.Essghir is accused of travelling to RAF Fairford on 22 August and contacting Ali.Abdulkarim is accused of buying mobile phones and collecting cash for Ali, as well as buying five vans including the three that were driven to RAF Fairford.The court heard he had known Ali for 10 years and it was claimed the latter had been linked to a drone incident at the Israeli embassy.Counter Terror Policing said they believed the foreign intelligence service involved in the case was Iranian.The assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said: “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat.“The public can help us with this, and as always I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national who was also arrested on 20 October on suspicion of aiding Iran’s intelligence service has been released without charge but remains on police bail after being arrested on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford. We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: DNA links serial killer Ted Bundy to 1974 murder of Utah girl | Utah | The Guardian
description: Discovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that year
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Discovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that year
Content: Ted Bundy at his murder trial in Miami, Florida, in 1979.Photograph: Ken Hawkins/AlamyView image in fullscreenTed Bundy at his murder trial in Miami, Florida, in 1979.Photograph: Ken Hawkins/AlamyUtahDNA links serial killer Ted Bundy to 1974 murder of Utah girlDiscovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that yearUwa Ede-OsifoTue 27 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe notorious serial killer Ted Bundy has been found responsible, through DNA evidence, for the murder of a 17-year-oldUtahgirl who went missing in 1974 before her nude body was found days later, state authorities announced at a Tuesday news conference.The breakthrough in the investigation of Melissa Ann Smith’s death comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed in April that Bundy had killed another Utah girl, 17-year-old Laura Ann Aime, in 1974.Bundy had confessed tokillingLaura during a string of admissions he made before being executed in 1989 for two of his murders.Laura was last seen during a Halloween party, before being found dead and severely beaten in late November 1974.It was not until this year, though, that new DNA testing backed Bundy’s account.Bodily fluid extracted from Laura’s body was a match to Bundy’s known DNA profile, law enforcement officials said then.That discovery put into motion the closure of Smith’s homicide investigation.The Y-STR DNA profile recovered from Laura’s body was a genetic match to one found from Melissa’s
