Content: Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb scores a first-quarter touchdown against the Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Monday night.Photograph: Kathryn Riley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb scores a first-quarter touchdown against the Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Monday night.Photograph: Kathryn Riley/Getty ImagesNFLEagles’ nightmare season deepens as Cowboys hand Philadelphia fifth straight lossPrescott throws three touchdowns in Dallas victoryJavonte Williams rushes for career-high 155 yardsEagles fall to 2-5 amid Jalen Hurts injury absenceAgenciesTue 27 Oct 2026 00.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDak Prescott threw for 212 yards and three touchdowns, two to CeeDee Lamb, and theDallas Cowboysbeat Philadelphia 38-21 on Monday night to hand the Eagles their fifth straight loss.Javonte Williams ran for a career-high 155 yards and a touchdown, and the Cowboys (3-4) remained in contention for the NFC East title. The New York Giants lead the division at 4-2-1.“We say the division’s right in front of us. It is as long as we win,” Prescott said after the game. “And if you lose another game, then you’re probably checking to see what New York’s doing. You’re probably checking and watching the other teams more than we should. So yeah, I mean you got to win games, got to win division games. How big of a game this was, understanding how much they’re hurt on their offensive side, yeah, huge road win for us.”The Eagles (2-5) are spiraling into a disaster of a season with their longest skid since 2016.Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs. Tanner McKee provided little encouragement that he can turn the season around, completing 23 of 35 passes for 211 yards with one touchdown and one interception.Prescott finished long drives with scores that McKee was unable to match.With Dallas trailing 21-20 late in the third quarter, Lamb hauled in his second touchdown on a beautiful 16-yard floater from Prescott in the corner of the end zone. Prescott ran in the two-point conversion for a 28-21 lead.Brandon Aubrey kicked field goals of 55, 27 and 24 yards. The final kick extended Dallas’ lead to 31-21. Williams capped the scoring and the first 150-yard rushing game by a Dallas player since Ezekiel Elliott in 2018 with a two-yard touchdown. The Cowboys finished with 204 yards rushing.McKee had a pass intercepted by linebacker DeMarvion Overshown late in the fourth quarter.McKee orchestrated the Eagles’ first touchdown drive in the third quarter this season when they ran almost 10 minutes off the clock and he hit rookie Makai Lemon for a four-yard touchdown and a 21-20 lead.The Eagles didn’t score again and are running out of time to salvage their season.The Cowboys got a field goal on the opening drive, and the Eagles came right back and made it 7-3 on Saquon Barkley’s eight-yard touchdown run. Barkley returned after missing the last two-plus games with a hamstring injury and had 37 yards rushing on the drive.Barkley entered with 36 yards rushing all season. He still seemed bothered by the hamstring and had to visit the sideline medical tent. Barkley also missed long stretches getting treatment for his back on the sideline and finished with 62 yards on seven carries.Prescott threw touchdown passes of nine yards to Lamb and 21 yards to George Pickens that helped the Cowboys stretch their lead to 20-14 at half-time. Pickens’ catch was particularly impressive, as he escaped tight coverage by safety Andrew Mukuba in the back of the end zone and dragged his left foot sideways for the score.At half-time, Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie was inducted into the team’s Hall of Fame.Lurie bought the Eagles on 6 May 1994, and since the turn of the century they have been one of the top franchises in football. The Eagles are one of three teams to play in four Super Bowls since 2004 and have won the only two titles in franchise history under Lurie’s ownership.Lurie was flanked by Eagles Hall of Famers including Brian Dawkins and Donovan McNabb and gave a brief speech. However, unlike other Hall of Fame inductees, Lurie did not hold a pre-game news conference. Coach Nick Sirianni remained the only team representative addressing Hurts’ condition since he was injured.Explore more on these topicsNFLDallas CowboysPhiladelphia EaglesUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Arise, Sir Harry? Downing Street hints at Kane knighthood after Ballon d’Or win | Harry Kane | The Guardian
description: Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, praising the footballer’s ‘extraordinary achievement’ as the first English winner of the Ballon d’Or in 25 years
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, praising the footballer’s ‘extraordinary achievement’ as the first English winner of the Ballon d’Or in 25 years
Content: 1:27Harry Kane ends England's 25-year wait for a Ballon d'Or winner – videoHarry KaneArise, Sir Harry? Downing Street hints at Kane knighthood after Ballon d’Or winAndy Burnham sends congratulations to England captainBayern player is first Englishman to win award since 2001Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 27 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, ­praising the England captain’s “extraordinary achievement” as the first Englishwinner of the Ballon d’Orin 25 years.The prime minister’s spokesperson saidAndy Burnhamsent praise and congratulations to the England captain, who was announced as the men’s winner of football’s most prestigious individual award at a ceremony on Monday night.Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney RonayRead moreNo 10 said it hoped it would be the prelude to a trophy to celebrate withEngland“before too long” – alluding to hopes of an England win when the country co-hosts the European Championship in 2028 with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.11:25Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The LatestThe Bayern Munich player is the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.“The PM would like to congratulateHarry Kaneon winning the Ballon d’Or,” the spokesperson said. “To be the first Englishman to win it in 25 years is an extraordinary achievement, and what a moment to do it here at home.“Seventy years after Sir Stanley Matthews won the inaugural award, it caps a remarkable season and Harry continues to set a brilliant example to young players across the country, and the PM knows the whole nation will be incredibly proud of him. And, hopefully, there’s another trophy to celebrate with England before too long.”Asked whether Burnham would like to see Kane receive a knighthood, she said: “I think everyone would agree, Harry Kane has given an enormous amount to English football, and this is a very special moment for him and the country, but, as ever, I’m not going to pre-empt the honours process.”Kane received the award at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night, beating Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal. He is the fifth English player to win the award, the list also including Kevin Keegan and Sir Bobby Charlton.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham cannot decide whether to hand Kane a knighthood, but ministers and departments can make recommendations to the honours committee, as can private individuals. The sport committee includes the presenter Sue Barker and the chief executive of the Football Foundation, Robert Sullivan.Kane holds an MBE, awarded after England’s success in reaching the semi-finals in the 2018 World Cup. Players are often not awarded knighthoods until after retirement. The former England captain Sir David Beckham received his knighthood last year, as did the former England player and manager Sir Gareth Southgate.Before those awards, the most recent was the former Scottish player and Liverpool manager Sir Kenny Dalglish. Owen, also a former Liverpool player, has not received a knighthood, and nor did Keegan, the former Newcastle player and manager who was also England’s captain and manager.Explore more on these topicsHarry KaneBallon d'OrEnglandAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona fined £503 over their approach for Atlético Madrid star Álvarez | European club football | The Guardian
description: Atlético accused Barcelona of not notifying them in advance with the striker now rebuilding his reputation after summer chase
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Atlético accused Barcelona of not notifying them in advance with the striker now rebuilding his reputation after summer chase
Content: Julián Álvarez’s form for Atlético Madrid is winning back fan support.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJulián Álvarez’s form for Atlético Madrid is winning back fan support.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean club footballBarcelona fined £503 over their approach for Atlético Madrid star ÁlvarezAtlético accused Barcelona during summer chaseStriker now rebuilding his reputation with fansReutersTue 27 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona’s pursuit of Julián Álvarez came at a modest cost ⁠on Tuesday after the Spanish FA fined the club €602 (£503) following a complaint byAtlético Madridover contact ⁠with ​the striker.Atlético accusedBarcelonaof approaching the Argentine, whose contract runs until June 2030, ⁠without first notifying them in writing.The sanction falls under Article 133 of the federation’s regulations. Atlético ⁠also complained to Fifa, which declared it had no ​jurisdiction over the case.For ‌Álvarez, the repair ‌work has been rather more public.The striker scored Atlético’s ‌winner against Deportivo La Coruna on Saturday, finding the net for a second successive match as his side moved within two points of theLa Ligaleaders Barcelona, before apologising for expressing his desire to join their rivals.“It ‌was a mistake. I understand why the fans are angry. If I were a fan, ​I’d be angry too. Especially given how they’ve supported me since I arrived,” Álvarez said referring to an interview during the 2026 World Cup in which he said that ⁠he “wanted to fulfil his dream” of playing for ​Barcelona, triggering ​a transfer dispute that ​stretched through the summer transfer window.Frequently booed by ​the home ‌fans this ​season, Álvarez ​received a standing ovation from sections of the crowd after scoring on Saturday, a sign of a thawing relationship with the Metropolitano faithful.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBarcelonaAtlético MadridLa LiganewsShareReuse this content

title: João Pedro out for ‘a few weeks’, reveals Alonso; Donnarumma gets Maresca’s backing | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The Chelsea manager’s return to Anfield is marred by update on Brazilian’s thigh problem.
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The Chelsea manager’s return to Anfield is marred by update on Brazilian’s thigh problem.
Content: João Pedro picked up the thigh problem during training before last weekend’s defeat by Tottenham.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenJoão Pedro picked up the thigh problem during training before last weekend’s defeat by Tottenham.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAManchester CityJoão Pedro out for ‘a few weeks’, reveals Alonso; Donnarumma gets Maresca’s backingChelsea manager making latest Anfield returnAndoni Iraola upbeat before Carabao Cup tieJacob Steinberg,Jamie JacksonandAndy HunterTue 27 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.Alonso’s Liverpool return hit by João Pedro injury layoffXabi Alonso will celebrate if Chelsea score at Liverpool tonight, but the manager’s attacking plan will have to change with João Pedro likely to be out until after the international break with a thigh injury.João Pedro picked up the problem during training and faces an extended layoff after missing last Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at home by Tottenham. It is a major blow for Alonso, whose side struggled without the Brazil striker.Chelsea will have to adjust when they visit Liverpool in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup and Alonso revealed that João Pedro would probably not be back until the end of November at the earliest.“He has an injury on his thigh and he is going to be out for a few weeks,” Alonso said. “Let’s see how many. We don’t want to predict on that, but he’s not ready for the next games.”Alonso clarified that João Pedro would “probably” be out until after next month’s international break, meaning he will not be available for Brazil after missing the last camp with a knee issue. For Chelsea, the question is how to play without the former Brighton forward. There was surprise at Alonso’s decision to play without a recognised striker and overlook Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Welbeck is pushing to start against Liverpool.It will be an emotional evening for Alonso, who won the Champions League with Liverpool as a player in 2005. This will be his third game back at Anfield as an opposition manager – he lost with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid last season – and he will not hold back if Chelsea score.“Of course I will celebrate,” the Spaniard said. “With full respect because my warmth with Liverpool was there as a player. But now, I am in a different role, I need to support my team, I need to support my club, I fight for my club and if we score, I will celebrate with whole respect.Alonso, who travels to Anfield without the suspended Cole Palmer, was considered by Liverpool when Jürgen Klopp stepped down in 2024. “At that time I was at Leverkusen and I was aware of the situation, but I decided to stay,” he said. “That was my decision at the time.” Alonso said he never held talks with Liverpool, who instead appointed Arne Slot.Liverpool sacked Slot last summer and replaced him with Andoni Iraola. Alonso, available after losing his job at Real Madrid last January, had already agreed to join Chelsea. He has made a promising start at Stamford Bridge, but doubts over his approach flared against Spurs, who had 68.5% possession.Alonso was a passing midfielder who played for Pep Guardiola. He was asked whether he valued possession or saw the game in a different way. “You evolve, you adapt,” Alonso said. “You want to have possession. Knowing the context, knowing what we are building, I think that we have room for improvement in that part. I think we need to play more confidently with the ball.”2.Maresca: ‘He’s a strong character’Enzo Maresca has given his backing to Gianluigi Donnarumma after the goalkeeper’s costly errors in Manchester City’s recent defeats by Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.Donnarumma was at fault for Nicolas Jackson’s game-winning strike at Villa Park on Saturday, the forward’s long-range shot squeezing under the Italian’s body and leading to City’s first league defeat of the season. Against PSG in the Champions League this month, Donnarumma was at fault for Désiré Doué’s and Maghnes Akliouche’s goals as City lost 4-2 against the holders.“As a football player or manager, when you don’t get results or make some mistakes, it’s normal. It’s a consequence,” Maresca said. “Gigio since we started is doing well. Like any manager or player making some mistakes, it’s part of the season.“They [footballers] play so many games and minutes that sometimes it’s impossible not to make mistakes. He’s a strong character. He knows that when he makes a mistake, he doesn’t need us to tell him – sometimes it’s so clear so they recognise this.”Marc Guéhi has been in uneven form, too. The defender was culpable for Jackon’s opener on Saturday. He also conceded a late penalty in the previous weekend’s 3-2 win against Ipswich and made an early mistake that led directly to Lamine Yamal scoring for Spain against England in the Nations League last month.“I am completely happy with Marc,” Maresca said. “The way he reacts is fantastic, he is a top guy. He is one of the captains, he is a leader and I love Marc. Same as Gigio, when they make some mistakes it is recognised.”Donnarumma will be rested for Brighton’s visit in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. Maresca said: “After the Villa game we gave five players three days off to recover the energy: Erling [Haaland], Rúben [Dias], Elliot [Anderson], Gigio and Josko [Gvardiol]. They are all on holiday. Three days off, energy, go, come back with full energy then we go again.”Geronimo Rulli will again deputise for Donnarumma against Brighton.JJ3.‘You have to earn the right to belong,’ says IraolaAndoni Iraola has claimed he is only at the start of the process of showing he belongs at Liverpool but feels a connection with the Anfield crowd is growing.The Liverpool head coach was more animated than usual after Sunday’s defeat of in-form Brighton as his team recorded a fourth successive victory and first Premier League home win on his watch. “It was a performance that united the team and the crowd,” said Iraola, who was tasked with rebuilding that bond when he replaced Arne Slot in the summer.Liverpool host Chelsea in the Carabao Cup last-16 on Wednesday and Iraola insists their recent improvement is only the start.“I said it since the first day: you have to earn the right to belong and you only get it with good performances, with wins, and this will take time,” he said. “But I am glad because I felt the other day the supporters helped us a lot and they were enjoying it the same as we were. I think the players had a very likable performance in terms of they gave everything, we were blocking everything, we were tackling, we were fighting, we were winning duels, we were making the runs in behind and those things you want to see and everyone wants to see. I enjoyed it.“I would say [it is just a] start. Still we need more wins, we need more performances so we need more time.”Iraola is hopeful Florian Wirtz will be available to face Chelsea despite being forced out of the Brighton win with an ankle problem. Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz remain doubtful and Iraola said there would be changes with Arsenal visiting in the Premier League on Sunday.“Against Chelsea, Arsenal, Crystal Palace definitely, we have some games where we have less time to rest than the opposition but you have to adapt. Sometimes it is to your benefit, sometimes it goes against you like this week. You have to be ready for this.”AHExplore more on these topicsManchester CityLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pierre Sage given more time by Crystal Palace but remains under pressure | Crystal Palace | The Guardian
description: Pierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Pierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure
Content: Pierre Sage retains the support of his Crystal Palace squad but is facing the sack after only 12 games in charge.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenPierre Sage retains the support of his Crystal Palace squad but is facing the sack after only 12 games in charge.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPACrystal PalacePierre Sage given more time by Crystal Palace but remains under pressureFrenchman’s future was in doubt after bad start to seasonHe could be sacked if Palace lose at Spurs on SaturdayEd AaronsTue 27 Oct 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure and could be dismissed if they lose against Tottenham on Saturday.The Frenchman’s position was in serious doubt after another poor performance in the2-0 defeat against Newcastleat the weekend. That followed a5-0 thrashing against Brightonwhen Sage was warned that he could be dismissed if results did not improve quickly.Donnarumma’s Manchester City mistakes are normal, insists MarescaRead moreHowever the club’s chair, Steve Parish, has decided not to act given the tight turnaround in Palace’s schedule: the side face Fulham at Craven Cottage in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, before their trip to Tottenham in the Premier League. But Sage, who attended the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London on Monday evening, is understood to have been left in no doubt that the meeting with Spurs on Saturday is crucial to his future.Palace are 17th and have conceded 19 goals in eight Premier League matchesthis season – the highest in the division. But, it is understood, Sage retains the support of his squad, with two leading players having sent him messages saying that they still have faith he can turn things around.Palace’s hierarchy are said to be split over whether to fire the former Lens manager after only 12 games in charge, with some in favour of bringing in Thomas Frank or Sean Dyche to steady the ship. The former Wolves manager Rob Edwards has also been mentioned as a potential contender.There is sympathy for Sage at boardroom level given that Axel Disasi – who was signed on loan from Chelsea to replace the key defender Maxence Lacroix – has only just returned from a three-match suspension. There were also signs of improvement in the 2-2 Europa League draw at Besiktas in midweek, with Sage believed to have been delighted with Jean-Philippe Mateta’s response since returning from injury. The France striker is in the final year of his contract butfailed in an attempt to have it ruled invalidby an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are concerns about Ismaïla Sarr, however, who missed the defeat against Newcastle after a recurrence of the groin injury that ruled him out earlier in the season. The Senegal forward has made no secret of his disappointment after Palace rejected a bid from Liverpool in the summer and Sage needs the club’s player of the year last season back on the pitch if they are to recover from a poor start to life after Oliver Glasner.Explore more on these topicsCrystal PalacenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That was what you live for’: Fleetwood revel in ‘unbelievably special’ Arsenal win | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor reflected on celebrating his club’s incredible win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor reflected on celebrating his club’s incredible win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’
Content: The Fleetwood manager, Matt Lawlor, joined his players’ delirious celebrations.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Fleetwood manager, Matt Lawlor, joined his players’ delirious celebrations.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesCarabao Cup‘That was what you live for’: Fleetwood revel in ‘unbelievably special’ Arsenal winManager Matt Lawlor, born and raised in area, reflects on celebrating win with ‘people that I knew and grew up with’Will Unwinat HighburyTue 27 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor, hailed the club’s victory as one for all football after his sideshocked the Premier League champions, Arsenal,on penalties in the Carabao Cup. The side 18th in League Two held their nerve in the shootout, Conor Haughey hitting the winner to reach the quarter-finals.The goalkeeper, Jay Lynch, was Fleetwood’s other hero, saving from Bruno Guimarães to set up the chance for victory. Aaron Loupalo‑Bi and Viktor Gyökeres ensured it finished 1-1 in normal time, butArsenalended up a man light after Max Dowman was shown a red card for reacting to a challenge.Fleetwood Town stun Arsenal on penalties: Carabao Cup fourth round – as it happenedRead moreAsked if Fleetwood’s win was the story of the season, Lawlor said: “Yeah, I hope so. Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and sanitised. And that to me there was that feeling that we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special. To be giving that to football fans, and especially Fleetwood fans, is unbelievably special. And yeah, something that I’m really proud of.”Lawlor was clearly emotional at full-time as many of the 4,000 home supporters streamed on to the pitch to celebrate beating a team 84 places above them. “I was trying to not cry and I didn’t. I’ve managed to hold it,” he said. “My family, my little boy here, we’re all local. I was turning around and people were screaming at me in the crowd and people that I knew and grew up with, that I went to school with or they’ve got a loose connection, and people that jumped out on to the pitch.“That’s really special and really emotional. To do something that special early in my career as well, it’s an emotional night. It is emotional. Emotional for the players, emotional for me.”This was Dowman’s second red card of the month, having been sent off for England Under-19s, providing a steep learning curve for the talented teenager. Mikel Arteta was clearly unimpressed. “When we prepare the context of the match, we were very clear on the things you expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was very clear,” said Arteta, who appeared to aim criticism at Dowman as he walked past him after being sent off.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupFleetwood TownArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blow | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Steve Borthwick has lost two key England squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Steve Borthwick has lost two key England squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg
Content: Bath’s Guy Pepper (left) and Bristol’s Benhard van Rensburg will be sidelined for several weeks due to injury.Composite: CameraSport/Getty Images; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBath’s Guy Pepper (left) and Bristol’s Benhard van Rensburg will be sidelined for several weeks due to injury.Composite: CameraSport/Getty Images; Getty ImagesEngland rugby union teamEngland’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blowBath flanker Pepper injured ankle at Gloucester on FridayBristol’s Van Rensburg advised to rest after two concussionsRobert KitsonTue 27 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s head coach, Steve Borthwick, said he will be monitoring this weekend’s domestic Prem games with some trepidation. Already he has lost at least two potentially key squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg, with doubts still hanging over his first-choice fly-half, Fin Smith, andfresh injury uncertaintyemerging on virtually a daily basis.Pepper’s involvement always looked improbable from the moment he sustained a nasty-looking ankle injury against Gloucester last Friday. The young Bath flanker will be sidelined for several weeks, as will the Bristol centre Van Rensburg who has been advised to rest and recuperate after two heavy concussions within the past three months.The Breakdown | England need to unearth World Cup core despite derby friction and injury chaosRead moreSmith, meanwhile, is still being treated for thecalf problem he sustainedagainst Leicester last Saturday. Borthwick says it remains “unclear at this stage” whether the Northampton fly-half will be available to face Australia next week. Calf injuries and kicking are not a great combination and England also need their tactical hub to be at the heart of their preparations.Borthwick, accordingly, will effectively want to make a call by the end of this week although England are slightly helped by the fact the Wallaby fixture is on a Sunday rather than 24 hours earlier. “Typically I would name the team for a Sunday game around the Wednesday, so that would still be my aim,” said Borthwick. “But if Fin’s not available for selection we also have some quality fly-halves in George Ford and Marcus Smith.”The Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has also limped away from training in Bagshot with a leg injury that will now be assessed, but there ismore encouraging newsregarding Seb Atkinson (knee) and Manny Feyi-Waboso (hamstring), both of whom should be available to play for Gloucester and Exeter respectively this weekend.Borthwick’s preference would probably be for both players to be tucked up on their sofas but under the terms of the joint agreement between the Rugby Football Union and the clubs, the latter can pick their international players once they are cleared by England’s medical staff. “If they’re fit then they’re available for selection,” said Borthwick. “That then comes down to the head coach or director of rugby of the club.”Either way it is a tense time for the national management who are having to do without their customary full extra week of training because of the need to shoehorn the new Nations Championship finals weekend into the calendar. Rugby players need to play rugby but, invariably, it comes with an element of risk attached. “Certainly there is a part of me watching these games and hoping the players get through the 80 minutes and are fit and available for next week,” said Borthwick.The stakes are further heightened by next year’s looming World Cup, with Borthwick having pointedly reminded his players that only nine Tests remain before England’s World Cup preparations enter their final stages. The primary message is that, for those intending to be on the plane to Australia, performing at the requisite level starts now. “This series of games this autumn is the last opportunity we have playing southern hemisphere opposition before we’re at that World Cup,” said Borthwick.“I’m looking forward to seeing players compete and perform against this calibre of opposition. You look at the power many of these southern hemisphere teams have. That’s a different challenge. When they come into camp again on Monday night, having recovered from their games, all that matters is performing the way we want to against Australia.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorthwick also brushed aside suggestions of potential discord after the fractious East Midlands derby between Leicester and Northampton where several of his squad were at loggerheads. The RFU sought to try to dilute any notion of friction by issuing a photo of Ollie Chessum and Henry Pollock with their arms cheerfully around each other and Borthwick has not yet deemed it necessary to pull anyone aside.“I actually think it’s a real strength of the game to be able to compete like that in that kind of full-blooded encounter – and then they’re perfectly fine. It’s a strength of English rugby that the players have such pride in their clubs … in modern day sport I see that as a positive. But when you come in [here] it’s all about the England team.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamSteve BorthwickRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick given chance to save job as he stays for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick will remain in charge for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea on Saturday despite two wins in 12 games this season
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick will remain in charge for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea on Saturday despite two wins in 12 games this season
Content: Michael Carrick arriving at Manchester United’s training ground on Tuesday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick arriving at Manchester United’s training ground on Tuesday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAManchester UnitedCarrick given chance to save job as he stays for Manchester United’s game at ChelseaJason Wilcox has driven decision to stand by head coachUnited would have to pay Newcastle about £3m for HoweJamie JacksonTue 27 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.David Squires on … Manchester United’s latest crisis and dirty laundryRead moreThe decision by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar Berrada, the chief executive, can be viewed as a surprise given United’s dire form. Sunday’s abject 3-0 league homedefeat by Bournemouthfollowed last Wednesday’s equally poor4-1 reverse at Comoin the Champions League. Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.Yet Wilcox, who has driven the retaining of Carrick, wants to give the 45-year-old a chance to change form and morale. Whether Carrick could survive another poor performance and result at Stamford Bridge is in the balance.United host Roma in the Champions League three days later, then Aston Villa in the league the following Sunday before a two-week international window, which would offer a longer period for the board to assess the situation.Carrick’s reprieve may be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him.View image in fullscreenEddie Howe is the preferred choice of Manchester United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAUnited will have to pay Newcastle about £3m in compensation if they want Eddie Howe. He isWilcox’s prime candidateif a change is made and the 48-year-old wants the job at Old Trafford. When he left Newcastle at the end of July a deal was struck on the remaining terms of his contract which means the club would be due compensation.United would also have to pay Newcastle a minor sum for Howe’s staff, headed by his assistant, Jason Tindall.Manchester United’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, has been pushing the case of Julian Nagelsmann, the 39-year-old former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedEddie HoweMichael CarrickNewcastle UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Jay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-Z | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description: Rapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in California
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Rapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in California
Content: Jay-Z, pictured performing in Paris last month. The rapper, who produces the Super Bowl halftime show through his company Roc Nation, is headlining it in 2027.Photograph: ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJay-Z, pictured performing in Paris last month. The rapper, who produces the Super Bowl halftime show through his company Roc Nation, is headlining it in 2027.Photograph: ABACA/ShutterstockJay-ZJay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-ZRapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in CaliforniaSian Cainand agenciesMon 26 Oct 2026 22.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter years of producing theSuper Bowlhalf-time show, Jay-Z has announced that the 2027 headline act will be none other than himself.After days of speculation, the NFL, Apple Music and Jay-Z’s company Roc Nation announced on Monday night that the rapper will be the featured performer for the half-time festivities at the Super Bowl LXI on 14 February at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.“From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” said the 56-year-old rapper in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”Roc Nation has partnered with theNFLsince 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl half-time show, beginning with Shakira and Jennifer Lopez’s performance at Super Bowl LIV in 2020.At the time, Jay-Z said he had told the NFL commissioner, Roger Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.”Goodell said on Monday that the NFL had wanted Jay-Z to perform for years.Jay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzyingRead more“When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him,” he said. “I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”Monday’s announcement came a week after reports first emerged that Jay-Z would perform, with some observers speculating that it was unlikely due to his lack of recent hits. Jay-Z’s last solo album, 4:44, was released in 2017 while his last collaborative album was made with his wife, Beyoncé, in 2018, performing together as the Carters.He just closed his Jay-Z 30 concert tour over the weekend at the SoFi Stadium, after performing several dates in New York and London.Born Shawn Carter, Jay-Z has won 25 Grammy awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife,who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalogue includes the albums Reasonable Doubt, The Blueprint and The Black Album, and hit songs such as Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem), 99 Problems and Empire State of Mind, his collaboration with Alicia Keys.His 1996 debut, Reasonable Doubt, was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.Jay-Z’s career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.Bad Bunny performedat last season’s Super Bowl in February, bringing on special guests including Lady Gaga, Ricky Martin, Jessica Alba, Karol G, Cardi B, Young Miko, and Pedro Pascal.The Puerto Rican superstar’s songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours after the show.Past Super Bowl half-time show headliners includeKendrick Lamar,Rihanna, theWeeknd, Michael Jackson, the Who, Madonna, Coldplay and the Blues Brothers.Associated Press contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsJay-ZSuper BowlUS sportsNFLShareReuse this content

title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster
Content: The first episode of Elon Musk’s AI-generated Odyssey. The seven-minute instalment was made by London-based Wonder Studios.Computer-generated: Grok ImagineView image in fullscreenThe first episode of Elon Musk’s AI-generated Odyssey. The seven-minute instalment was made by London-based Wonder Studios.Computer-generated: Grok ImagineElon Musk‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmTesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbusterDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 27 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.Having criticisedthe hit moviein the summer, the tycoon said he would useGrok Imagineto make a “historically accurate” adaptation.The initial results have been released on X in the form of aseven-minute episodemade in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.Musk hadobjected to Nolan’s casting choices– such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.View image in fullscreenThe Greeks make land. The team behind the first episode said they would seek to make improvements in the second episode.Computer-generated: @ImagineThe first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take onHomerare supporters of the summer blockbuster.Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeter Bradshaw’s review in the Guardiangave it one star, saying: “Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver.”The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the last episode we make is radically better than the first,” he said.Wonder has also worked with Google DeepMind to produce an AI-generated video for the Lewis Capaldi trackSomething in the Heavens.Explore more on these topicsElon MuskAI (artificial intelligence)Christopher NolanHomerThe OdysseyGrok AIXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic accelerates – for the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarity | Technology | The Guardian
description: The AI industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the ride
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: The AI industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the ride
Content: Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, earlier this year.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, earlier this year.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersTechScape newsletterTechnologyAnthropic accelerates – for the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarityThe AI industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the rideThis was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives.Sign up to receive it here.Blake MontgomeryTue 27 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToday in tech, we’re discussingAnthropic’s astronomic growth, how a settlement over social media safety dented Meta’s revenue, and Lula’s accusations of interference againstMeta.Anthropic acceleratesAnthropic filed for an initial public offering on the US stock market on Monday, ahead of what it slated to be one of the biggest debuts in financial history. The company withheld a valuation from its filing with US financial regulators, but investors and analysts are valuing theAIfirm at north of $1.5tn.The numbers are jaw-dropping and speak to the speed of the AI boom.Anthropicwas founded in 2021. That’s only five years ago, yet already it has grown to a valuation bigger than 98% of the top companies on the US stock market.Anthropic detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (a yearly increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026, mostly due to a one-time $72.4bn charge. It lost $36bn the year prior.Anthropic’s initial public offering will rock the US stock market and probably global markets as well. The infusion of at least a trillion dollars in value is likely to influence investor appetites for every kind of technology stock. That a company of that magnitude can be spun up in five years speaks to the breakneck pace of AI development and financing. Despite calls to slow down from Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, the artificial intelligence industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the ride.Such rapid growth demonstrates an upside for company founders for now. They can build a business that creates life-changing, globe-spanning wealth in just half a decade.For the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarity. Anthropic, a company that could determine the direction of the entire US economy, is going public before a baby born in its founding year has started kindergarten.Read more:Anthropic reveals rapid revenue gains and larger losses in stock market filingMeta pays outView image in fullscreenThe Meta logo.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersSettlements over the safety of social networks are growing so large that Meta is reporting significant drags on its business.In August, the biggest social media company in the world agreed to a $17bn settlement with dozens of state attorneys general to put claims it had endangered children to rest without admitting guilt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a quarterly earnings report last week, issued the same afternoon as a judge ordered the company to pay the state of New Mexico $25bn, Meta reported net income significantly below Wall Street analysts’ expectations because of a payment towards the settlement with attorneys general, this one $9.9bn.The dent in Meta’s business is a sign that child safety activists are succeeding. In the Los Angeles social media addiction lawsuit that took place earlier this year, lawyers for the plaintiff made it clear they’re intent on making it untenable for Meta to operate the current version of Instagram. They want to render endangering children, which they believe Meta is doing, too expensive to continue. They hope to push the company to the point where business as usual is untenable because of the financial risks of safety.Activists can’t celebrate yet, though. Despite the hefty payments, Meta still reported a 26% increase in quarterly revenue up to $64.6bn.The arresting blue eyes of Elizabeth Holmes‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesElizabeth Holmes is back in the spotlight: why can’t we look away?The wider TechScapeAnthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in USThe datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battleMeta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansioniPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handsetMicrosoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cutsUkraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictionsExperts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hackingExplore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterAnthropicnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims | Home Office | The Guardian
description: Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group
Content: AI is being trialled in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall FoI requests, the report says.Photograph: Gary E Perkin/AlamyView image in fullscreenAI is being trialled in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall FoI requests, the report says.Photograph: Gary E Perkin/AlamyHome Office‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claimsTasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights GroupDiane TaylorMon 26 Oct 2026 20.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI has been embedded across theHome Officein near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating thehostile environment first envisaged by Theresa Mayas home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”Explore more on these topicsHome OfficeImmigration and asylumAI (artificial intelligence)Facial recognitionData protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big tech | Technology | The Guardian
description: From apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attention
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: From apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attention
Content: ‘Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,’ said a computer science student at Duke.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,’ said a computer science student at Duke.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesTechnology‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big techFrom apps that block distractions to stripped-down phones, young people are finding ways to unplug from platforms they say profit from their attentionGen Z voters: tell us what is guiding your vote in the US midterm elections?Jenna ZazaTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNelissa Moukoudi, 19, a university student in Canada, noticed a shift once she joinedInstagramand TikTok.“My social life completely plummeted and it felt like my life was only [using] social media and school,” she said.Tired of fighting for self-control, Moukoudi downloaded Opal, an app that forces users to solve math problems before reopening distracting apps. It is one of a growing number of companies in the sprawlingdigital detoxindustry that is enticing users – ideally paying ones – by promising to keep them off their devices. The industry isvaluedat nearly $1bn and is estimated to grow to nearly $8bn by 2035.Many of these companies are hoping to capitalize on gen Z’s growing weariness about the devices and social media platforms they grew up with.Nearly 60%of gen Z respondents identified as having a social media addiction in an April poll, and athirdof the generation said they had deleted some of those apps, according to a 2025 survey.It’s the age of regret: gen Z grew up glued to their screens, and missed the joy of being human | Gaby HinsliffRead moreThe shift has also been driven by growinganger at tech platformsthat have left some in gen Z feeling as if they are being exploited for profit.Gen Z “was basically optimized for dopamine by very smart systems”, said Kenneth Schlenker, 39, a former product marketer at Google and co-founder of Opal. “But this generation is also realizing what they don’t want and are trying to change how the system impacts them.”Some are turning to new devices entirely. Kendall Schrohe, 23, a founding partner of the Attention Studio, a consulting firm advising parents and policymakers on responsible tech, said that she traded her smartphone for aLight Phone, which sells for $349 and includes minimal smartphone features.“These big tech platforms have been hurting people for years, and we are just now feeling the impacts of it,” Schrohe said. “Our generation were the guinea pigs to big tech, and our suffering and addiction to these apps were profited off of.”Shreya Nallamothu, 19, a computer science student at Duke University, created her own DIY “Brick”, a device to block selected apps, using $8 near-field communication (NFC) tags that she bought online.“Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,” Nallamothu said. “Often the tech companies’ best interests aren’t in the users’ best interests.Social mediahas gotten away from what good technology can do, and people have noticed.”double quotation markThe doomscrolling economy is not one that we need to keep participating inHan Choi, 26Research that Nallamothu conducted in high school helped convince state senators in Illinois toadvancea recent bill to prevent parental exploitation of children on social media and the state to pass a law forcing parents tocompensate their kids.New event-focused apps are also trying to capitalize on the pivot away from social media. Pie (People I Enjoy), an app highlighting local events including bar pop-ups, 5K runs and concert meetups, grew 150% in a single month – jumping from 120,000 users in July to 300,000 in August.Co-founder Nadya Okamoto describes Pie as an in-person, active social network.“I think of social media as this passive consumption of content, but Pie is separate from that,” Okamoto said. “Users are actively networking and building your social circle.”‘It made my day more meaningful’: the Japanese gen Zers attempting a two-hour limit on smartphone useRead moreCo-founder Andy Dunn, who also founded menswear brand Bonobos, added: “Everything about the product is designed to make you want to go and be in community with those people. It gives you so much more agency.”The price of using such digital detox apps can vary. An Opal subscription costs $99.99 a year, while Brick, a physical block that phone users tap to lock and unlock apps, costs $59. Shift, an app that promises to turn a smartphone into a so-called “dumbphone” that can only make calls or send texts, charges a one-time $150 payment.That is one reason why convincing gen Z digital detoxers to pay for a new app could be tricky. Like approximately 95% of Opal’s 10 million customers, 75% of whom are gen Z, Moukoudi said she is using the free version. “I am not going to pay for an app just to reclaim my life,” the university student said.For some, simply deleting apps does the trick. Han Choi, 26,deletedallsocial media appslast year to spend more of his time on trivia nights and workouts.“People are rejecting the systems that have been put in place by people who stand to profit off our compliance,” Choi said. “Thedoomscrollingeconomyis not one that we need to keep participating in.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologySocial mediaYoung peopleSmartphonesMobile phonesInstagramTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups  | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans
Content: Members of the Save Brick Lane campaign protested against the construction of an AI datacentre in the east London neighbourhood in June.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMembers of the Save Brick Lane campaign protested against the construction of an AI datacentre in the east London neighbourhood in June.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianDatacentres - UKUK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groupsInvestigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plansAisha DownGlobal technology reporterTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found.The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026.Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry.Kamila Kingstone, a campaign lead at the NGO, said: “The government totally failed at the most senior level to speak to environmental NGOs or community groups when developing its flagship policy on AI datacentres. This is despite the serious environmental implications of its plans.”Over 12 months, Spotlight on Corruption filed 40 freedom of information requests to 18 government agencies, seeking details of meetings and investment figures relating to the government’s policymaking on the growth zones, covering the period between July 2024 and June 2026.The investigation foundthat ministers, permanent secretaries and directors general involved in developing the policy met 137 businesses – some several times – to discuss Britain’s datacentre policy. By contrast, senior officials met only two community groups and no environmental organisations.View image in fullscreenApproval has been given for a £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, east London, to include a datacentre.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianOf the 38 senior officials who left government, nine were from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which has played a central role in shaping Britain’s AI strategy. These included a former minister for AI and intellectual property, a former AI adviser to the prime minister, a former director of AI opportunities, a deputy director of AI international policy and a head of AI engineering.AI growth zones were a groundbreaking policy under which the government promised to “turbochargethe economy” and create jobs bybuildingmassive datacentres across five regions – in Starmer’s words, “mainlining AI into the veins” of the country.The policy aimed to pave the way for Britain to build big datacentres, some of them larger than any datacentre that has been built in the country so far. These developments, often partnered with US tech companies, would supposedly bring in thousands of jobs.Investigationsby the Guardian have called the policy into question, suggesting that it rests on assumptions that do not hold up, financial figures that were not audited and exaggerated projections for job creation.In particular, the Guardian has shown there islittle realismbehind announced plans to power these developments, and claims that they will use purpose-built renewables. In fact, different government departmentsappear to divergeon how much electricity the UK’s datacentre plans will actually require – and what their environmental cost will therefore be.Meanwhile, there has been growing opposition to datacentres in Britain, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging fromAuchtertool, a rural village north of Edinburgh, toBrick Lanein east London.View image in fullscreenFourteen local campaigns rallied in September at Holyrood against datacentres planned in Scotland.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianChi Onwurah, the MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the growing backlash – and the far larger opposition in the US – was a warning that the government needed to seek greater community input.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is critically important that AI benefits communities and is also shaped by them,” she said. “I’ve been concerned about what we’ve seen in the US, where there’s a strong feeling that datacentres are being imposed without adequate consultation. We can see the backlash influencing the midterms. It’s really important that communities are involved in datacentres and AI growth zones and see the benefits.”Spotlight on Corruption’s investigation suggests that previous policy was largely shaped by conversations with business, and that the government “failed to take the environmental and social impacts [of datacentres] seriously”.While the government met a handful of civil society groups, these meetings were “held a few days before the launch of the policy, meaning they had no meaningful input”, according to the report.Finally, many further meetings between businesses and Starmer’s administration would not have been disclosed, said Spotlight on Corruption. This is largely because Starmer’s policy was led by a special adviser, Jade Leung, whose role was subject to far less stringent transparency requirements.Spotlight on Corruption also looked at how other countries – including Canada, Germany and Australia – developed policy. It found these countries consulted far more widely on introducing datacentres and had more stringent environmental criteria. It said the UK had “fallen behind equivalent jurisdictions” in developing an equitable strategy.A government spokesperson said: “We are clear that datacentres should create British jobs, strengthen supply chains and deliver benefits for the communities that host them, while prioritising clean power and using water responsibly – and meet with these companies to make sure that happens. We want to work closely with industry, local authorities, environmental groups and communities, and welcome opportunities to hear their views.“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes. We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKPlanning policyAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingFreedom of informationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards
Content: The 92-page document released on Monday talks about Anthropic’s explosive growth and the risks AI has brought to the business.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe 92-page document released on Monday talks about Anthropic’s explosive growth and the risks AI has brought to the business.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersAnthropicExplainerFour takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filingThe AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguardsJohana BhuiyanTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropichas filedto go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.Here are some of the key takeaways from Anthropic’s lengthy S-1.Anthropic reveals rapid revenue gains and larger losses in stock market filingRead more1.Explosive and expensive growthHere’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence.Anthropic brought in $16.3bn in revenue and lost $80bn in just the first half of 2026, though much of that was due to a $72.4bn one-off charge. In 2025, the company brought in $4.585bn and lost roughly $33.9bn, per the filing.Column chart showing quarterly filings from Anthropic from Q1 2025 to Q2 2026. While revenues are increasing quarter over quarter, net losses are increasing at a faster rate.Securing computing power accounts for the vast majority of Anthropic’s costs. The company spent nearly $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of this year, up from $2.3bn in the same period last year.Anthropic, unlike OpenAI, has made it clear that its customers are largely other businesses. “Frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest,” the company executives wrote in the filing.The company said its top five customers account for 25% of its business – which makes it risky business.2.‘A country of geniuses in a datacenter’Anthropic says there is considerable potential for AI to reach levels of intelligence that would be akin to what its executives called “‘a country of geniuses in a datacenter’ – millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionize every area of human endeavor: software, physics, math, biology, medicine, finance, economics, commerce, robotics, military and intelligence capabilities”. Noticeably, the company mentioned military capabilities despite being embroiled in a standoff with the Trump administration over its refusal to limit restrictions on the way the Department of Defense could use Claude.The company highlighted four specific categories of opportunity at the start of the filing: Acceleration of progress in biology and medicine; economic growth; spreading said growth globally; and streamlining government services (such as social services and medical programming).The company said it was already working with several pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and improved the process for clinical trials, which is “cutting the time it takes to write clinical trial reports from months to minutes”.The company’s executives claim they have also made biological discoveries with Claude, including a “molecular machine” that has the “potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool”. One purported use case: gene editing.3.AI ‘safeguards are incomplete’The company discusses risks in two contexts: the dangers that AI itself poses to society and human beings, and the ways Anthropic’s business could go awry.Risks that AI poses were broken down into four main categories: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. While Anthropic put a great deal of emphasis on the guardrails it has implemented to block attempts to misuse its models, it also includes one big caveat later in the filing: those safeguards may not work.Anthropic’s most capable models are capable of providing “meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote in the filing.The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended”.Already, Anthropic has detected what it believes is the first documented case of a large-scale cyber-attack with little human intervention. The company believes a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated a Claude code tool “into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”, per the prospectus.The company said it recognized AI may be used by authoritarian governments to “deepen repression” and develop “high-tech surveillance states”. Anthropic presented less of a defense or potential safeguard against those uses and instead said it was committed to working with “free societies to provide a counterweight to authoritarian abuse and to promote freedom and democracy”. The firm seems to suggest that its work with what it describes with scant details as “free societies” will cancel out in some way the AI-enabled repression of authoritarian regimes.The company had a falling out with the Trump administration after the firm said it would not change its restrictions to allow its models to be used to build domestic surveillance or autonomous lethal weapons.4.92 pages of financial riskAnthropic goes into detail in laying out 92 pages of risks to its business. Investors are making sense of a type of company that is fairly new to the public market in a highly competitive space with everything to lose.The company acknowledges that much of its success is tied to its top executives and whether they stay at the firm, being able to edge out its main competitors Google and OpenAI, navigating the tumultuous regulatory landscape around AI and datacenters and surviving any public relations fallout over its AI models being used to do things they are not supposed to do, likecreate bioweapons.The company’s focus on enterprise customers means that if any of its top buyers leave, the company could take a huge hit.Anthropic’s structure as a public benefit corporation – which is a designation for a for-profit company that balances financial interests with achieving a stated social good – may make it harder to achieve its short – or medium-term financial goals, the company said. The firm is obliged to report on its progress in meeting its public benefit goals in the same way it has to report its financials.There’s also all the risk related to any AI-enabled catastrophic event – the sort of doomsday scenario Anthropic employees have been warning about. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for a pause on AI development to ensure firms are developing it responsibly to avoid any such catastrophe. In addition to the public harm and potential fallout over a scenario where Claude went rogue, Anthropic said they worry they will be subject to a great deal of liability, especially considering insurance options for AI are still evolving.“We may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses,” the filing reads.The bedrock of Anthropic’s AI infrastructure is concentrated in the US, making it extremely vulnerable to regulatory changes, power grid constraints, natural disasters and opposition to AI or datacenters. The filing specifically calls out datacenter moratoriums that have been passed or are being considered as among the big issues they are concerned about.“We are expanding our data center capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration risks,” the filing reads.The company, which says a big part of its value proposition is its talent, also said it worries about US immigration policies affecting its ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. The Trump administration has targeted H-1B visas, a tool tech firms have come to rely on to attract and hire from the global pool of tech and engineering talent.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)Internet IPOsTechnology sectorChatbotskey takeawaysShareReuse this content

title: AI-driven disinformation running rampant on social media before US midterms, experts warn | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Social media companies including Meta have pulled back on efforts to protect voters from election-meddling lies
Author: George Chidi
Headline: Social media companies including Meta have pulled back on efforts to protect voters from election-meddling lies
