Content: People cast their votes on the first day of early voting in New York City on Saturday.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APView image in fullscreenPeople cast their votes on the first day of early voting in New York City on Saturday.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APUS midterm elections 2026AI-driven disinformation running rampant on social media before US midterms, experts warnSocial media companies including Meta have pulled back on efforts to protect voters from election-meddling liesGeorge ChidiTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood ofAI-driven disinformation ahead of November’sUS midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are probably “slipping through the cracks”.As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.While the backlash against Facebook after theCambridge Analytica scandalprompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election ofDonald Trumpin 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.Anatomy of a lie: James Talarico got the flu – sending rightwing midterm misinformation machine into overdriveRead moreArtificial intelligence hasmade it easier than everto launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a formerFacebookdata engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in big tech. Operatives playing dirty tricks can get around content moderation rules “because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through”, she said.Campaigns fromPennsylvaniatoTexashave been scrambling to respond to lies that have surfaced, and spread rapidly, online. Unlike previous elections, they find themselves in a quandary: who, exactly, do they turn to when fabrications and falsehoods propagate?Meta Platforms, the Facebook and Instagram owner, and X did not respond to requests for comment.YouTube, owned by Google, said all its users are subject to the same guidelines.James Talarico, the high-flying Democrat running for US Senate in Texas, took time off from campaigning earlier this month to recover from the flu. But many social media feeds hosted another – false – reason for his absence: that he was supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio.The claim was a complete fabrication, pushed by arightwing “provocateur”who published a deceptively edited phone call with a hospital staffer. Talarico’s campaign released security-camera video showing him at home in Texasand the candidate publiclyclarifiedhe had never even been to Ohio.But the lie circulated – and was stoked – for several days.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico, a Senate candidate, speaks to attenders at the Voto Latino ‘Ready, Go, Vote,’ rally on Sunday in Weslaco, Texas, before the midterm elections.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/APThe Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas (DDIA)trackedits propagation, and how the misinformation mutated as it was picked up by conservative Spanish-language media. What began as aviral lieabout Talarico being hospitalized in Ohio became a false claim in Spanish that he had attempted suicide.‘I don’t talk politics with anyone’: Georgia voting official on the pressure faced by election workersRead moreThe case “illustrates a recurring challenge in countering election disinformation”, DDIA’s researchers wrote. Lies evolve and shift as they spread, “making the original correction insufficient to address every version of the story”.Social media platforms enforce their terms of service “more congruently” in English than other languages including Spanish, according to Roberta Braga, the founder and executive director of DDIA.“There’s a lot less guardrails in place from the companies to deal with Spanish language, especially now that they’ve walked back a lot of their own investments in content moderation, and they’ve moved toward doing community-centered content moderation, like Community Notes-style things,” said Braga. “Now that they’re using AI to do a lot of the content moderation, even more is likely slipping through the cracks.”Ken Paxton, Talarico’s Republican opponent in Texas, also launched a campaignadvertearlier this yearusingAI-generated footage of Talarico – a Presbyterian seminarian – supposedly rewriting the Bible.“I think Texans are fed up with these kind of lies in our politics,” Talaricotold NBC Newsin September. “These AI deepfake ads don’t add anything to our civic discourse. They don’t do anything to elucidate the choice that’s in front of voters.”Online hit squads behind election disinformation once operated on the fringes. Today, their work may be amplified by official government sources.When viral posts on X and rightwing blogs claimed that an undocumented immigrant arrested in central Pennsylvania was an active field worker and canvasser for Democrat Janelle Stelson’s congressional campaign, staffers set thetruthsprinting, trying to to catch up witha lie.View image in fullscreenDemocratic candidate Janelle Stelson speaks at a campaign event on 23 September in York Haven, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Marc Levy/APAs they did, however, anofficial statementfrom the Department of Homeland Security amplified the claim. “It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public,”declared Charles Wall, the deputy director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the campaign released records showing that the immigrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, had no paid position on the campaign, despite an initial police incident report stating that Igbojekwe claimed to be a campaign worker. They hold the claim provably false.Can AI equalize political campaign ads – or will it remain a tool for spreading lies?Read moreThe campaign of Stelson’s opponent, Republican congressman Scott Perry,continues to run adswith the claim.The Stelson campaign sent cease-and-desist letters to the media. A Fox News reporter took down a post onXabout the indecent exposure arrest. Activists at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington launched a complaint accusing the DHS of violating the Hatch Act, which limits the political activities of government employees.“Trump has made clear that heintendstointerferein the elections,” said Nora Benavidez, a civil rights and free speech attorney with Free Press, a non-profit advocating for media independence. Trump “has leveraged agencies across the federal government, whether it’s the US Postal Service or DHS – you name it”, she added.Stelson’s campaign has yet to complain directly to the social media platforms: Meta’s Facebook, Elon Musk’s X, Google’s YouTube or others. But a spokespersonsaidthe campaign “continues to consider every legal avenue to fight the false claims in Perry’s ads”.The dominant social media platforms do have clear rules – based on specific, limited definitions – on how to handle misinformation driven by AI during election campaigns.Meta requires advertisers to disclose the use of synthetic images and AI-generated content with election ads, and enforces automated labeling on AI-generated images identified through Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) metadata. It also bans posts and ads that misrepresent voting dates, locations or legal requirements, as well as threats of violence.But the company does little active moderation of political commentary, beyond the exclusion of unsolicited political content from its recommended posts. Ananalysisby Free Press noted that Meta had narrowed its historical restrictions in 2023 to allow debate around the legitimacy of past election cycles.In 2023, YouTube alsostoppedremoving content that falsely claimed the 2020 election or other past US presidential elections were marred by “widespread fraud, errors or glitches”, stating that the removals had curbed misinformation, but also had a chilling effect on political speech.“All users” of YouTube, including political candidates and campaigns, “are subject to the same community guidelines … and have access to the same public reporting tools,” according to the platform.State attorneys general step up plans to counter Trump’s meddling in midtermsRead moreIt defines election misinformation narrowly, however: content that misleads voters about the time, place, means or eligibility requirements for voting or false claims that could materially discourage voting are banned. Claims that a candidate on the ballot is somehow ineligible, or calls to hack a polling site’s computers or incite violence at election locations, are also forbidden. “We also review government requests closely to determine if content should be removed because it violates a law or our policies,” YouTube’s spokesperson wrote in response to inquiries.Google has alikeness detection systemand allows civic leaders to request removal of a video when an AI-generated image falsely depicts their words or deeds. But a direct lie that falls outside these lines could propagate without intervention.Instead of relying on takedowns, Google prefers to amplify authoritative news outlets and election boards in search queries and underneath high-stakes civic videos via contextual “information panels”.X, formerly known as Twitter, abandoned internal safety reviews after its acquisition by Musk,replacingit with the crowdsourced “Community Notes” program. Its civic integrity policy bars false information about how to vote and suppression schemes. The platform also supposedly restricts synthetic media designed to mislead, though experts argue that the policy amounts to little without enforcement.“When you stop being able to focus on content because the AI will just slightly tweak it until it gets through, you have to focus on what are the systems of distribution,” Haugen said. “What are the biases? What are the ways we have feedback systems, cycles, that allow the community to provide feedback, that allows it to be damped down?”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US politicsDigital mediaSocial mediaElection interferenceMetaYouTubenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll | China | The Guardian
description: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Content: Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBeijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesChinaChinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its tollLack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boomAmy Hawkinsin BeijingTue 27 Oct 2026 00.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.3:48Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainerUS bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agenciesRead moreThe fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.The US hasbanned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to beconsidering a banon Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down onrobotics– also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.View image in fullscreenHumanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockChina’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude,filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPOthat could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.This week thetop officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.Explore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: CurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need it | Skincare | The Guardian
description: With six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devices
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: With six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devices
Content: Seen the light: our tester found the Series 3 comfy and reported fewer breakouts after four weeks.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSeen the light: our tester found the Series 3 comfy and reported fewer breakouts after four weeks.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSkincareReviewCurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need itWith six light wavelengths and almost endless ways to combine them, CurrentBody’s latest sets a new standard for red light therapy devicesThe best LED face masksSarah MatthewsTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCurrentBody’sLED maskshave long been my favourite. They’re comfortable, simple to use and effective. My previous favourite, the now-discontinuedCurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask, offered five treatments that used different light wavelengths to address multiple skin concerns. The company’s latest mask, the new Series 3, has the most detailed customisable treatments I’ve ever seen.This isn’t the first LED mask I’ve tried that allows its user to select different treatments for different areas of the face. TheLustre Renew Pro Facewearallows you to choose from two treatments across four different zones, with 16 possible combinations. The Series 3 takes this much further, allowing you to choose between six light wavelengths across 125 light points on the mask. If you stick to one wavelength per light point, that’s 6125combinations available. That number is longer than I can reasonably comprehend, so allow me to call its level of customisation endless.At £499.99, it certainly isn’t cheap, but it’s the same price as its less-advanced predecessor. Having tested my custom treatment for six weeks, my results were just as good as I had hoped, with the same excellent coverage I’ve come to expect from CurrentBody LED masks. Once you’ve got over the price, there’s very little to grumble about here, given that theDr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Procosts almost as much and has no personalisation, and cheaper masks such as theSilk’n LED face mask Procan’t pinpoint precise areas of the face. For anyone looking for the best LED mask money can buy, this is a safe bet.View at CurrentBodyView at AmazonHow I testedView image in fullscreenAny changes to the condition, texture and appearance of our tester’s skin were noted after two months of using the LED mask.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI’ve tested 18 LED masks, considering overall efficacy, comfort levels and ease of use – all things that help make consistent treatments enjoyable. I alwayscheck comfort levels by testing how well the eye guards block out the light from the mask, how easy the straps are to adjust and how comfortable the mask is to wear when lying down, sitting up and moving around.I also assess how straightforward the mask’s controls are. This was especially important for this mask, which required me to download an app. If it’s going to take up space on my phone, it had better be flawless.The test also involved noting the condition, texture and appearance of my skin before and after two months of use. I tested the four preset treatments for four nights each to get a quick idea of how they affected my skin, but since personalised treatments are the star of the show here, I used a customisable treatment for the rest of the test. Having tested LED masks before, I was hoping to at least maintain, or, ideally, build on the improvements I’d seen previously.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAll the kit: the Series 3 comes with adjustable straps, removable eye guards and a touchscreen controller.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView at CurrentBodyView at AmazonLet’s not beat around the bush: LED therapy, AKA photobiomodulation, looks a lot like pseudoscience. Scepticism is understandable, so as part of my LED mask testing for the Filter, I spoke to four independent dermatologists, anti-ageing experts and facialists. Their overall outlook on the tech was positive, particularly with regard to managing mild acne, reducing inflammation and firming skin. They advised choosing a mask from a reputable brand that bolsters its claims with clinical studies, and doing consistent treatments alongside agood skincare routine. Or, if you’re already inconsistent with skincare,consider whether you really need an LED maskfirst.The mostconcrete evidencefor LED therapy is in the blue, red and infrared wavelengths, used for acne, ageing and wound healing. There is growing interest in green and yellow light for brightening and calming redness.Small studiescommissioned by CurrentBody reported modest reductions of 4.1% in pigmentation with green light and 8.6% in redness with yellow light, compared with a 37.1% reduction in forehead wrinkle volume with deep near-infrared light.The Series 3 has 750 LEDs spread across 125 light points on the face. This is more light points than any previous CurrentBody mask, allowing for greater light coverage. For context, the Shark CryoGlow has more light points (160), although it lacks the range of wavelengths on offer here, with 480 individual LED light sources across three wavelengths. Some entry-level masks offer fewer light points, sometimes under 100, which tend to garner less effective results. In the Series 3, each light point has six LEDs: red, blue, near-infrared, deep near-infrared, yellow and green. Unlike all other masks I’ve tested, which mostly concentrate the most deeply penetrating deep near-infrared light around the eyes and mouth, the Series 3 offers full-face coverage, meaning it can tackle deep wrinkles anywhere you fancy.View image in fullscreenReady, set, glow: the controller offers four preset treatments, including Advanced Anti-Ageing.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThere are four preset 10-minute treatments: Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Brighten & Balance, and Complexion Corrector. These combine near-infrared light with a different visible light wavelength to achieve their results and work like those offered on theMulti Light Therapy mask.As mentioned, the star of the show here is the customised treatments, where users can pick out wavelengths with reckless abandon in the app. Helpfully, each colour is labelled with a brief description of its aims: “clear breakouts” for blue light, “calm redness” for yellow and so on. These can be positioned anywhere on the face and combined to create a treatment that’s unique to your needs. And, since you can save up to 10 custom treatments on the mask and more in the app, it also gives users the flexibility to target breakouts or dark spots precisely where they pop up, while continuing with other treatments elsewhere.But if free salad bars have taught me anything, it’s that people are likely to overdo it if left unsupervised. That’s why CurrentBody has developed MyDose, which automatically calculates the optimum dosage for your chosen light wavelengths. In theory, this means you can safely customise treatments without compromising on results.The Series 3 also has CurrentBody’s Veritace certification. Every mask undergoes quality control tests in which each of the 750 LEDs is tested to ensure it emits the specified wavelength and power output required before it’s shipped out to you. The mask comes with its own NFC card that lets you view the results; it’s reassuring to have this kind of transparency for a mask that costs this much.CurrentBody Series 3 specificationsPrice:£499.99Recommended use:3-5 times per weekSettings:Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Complexion Corrector, Brighten & Balance, plus near-infinite customised optionsLightwavelengths:red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1072nm), blue (415nm), green (532nm), yellow (590nm)Treatment time:10 minutesSuitable for:all skin types, but darker tones should take care with blue lightBattery life:13 usesCharging time:4.5 hoursContents:mask, three straps, two removable eye guards, Veritace card, charging cable, storage bagWhat we loveView image in fullscreenA personal touch: the Series 3 lets users customise the light wavelengths across different areas of the face.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianLike the Series 2 that came before it, the Series 3 is made from flexible silicone that fits comfortably without digging in, and has a chin strap that offers more coverage than other masks. Its straps are adjustable at four points – two on either side of the head – plus there’s an overhead strap that can stop the mask from slipping down on smaller heads. I also found the eye guards did a fantastic job of blocking out the mask’s light during treatment, as I was able to see clearly enough to read or potter around in dim lighting with no issues.The results from my tests were fantastic. As expected, given the Multi Light Therapy mask’s near-identical treatments, each of the preset treatments performed well. However, the real selling point for me was the personalised treatments.View image in fullscreenPaint by numbers: the app lets you select different light wavelengths for individual points on the maskLike many withPCOS/PMOS, I get hormonal breakouts and hair growth on my chin and upper lip. For a while, I have been worried that using red light in these areas would make this more pronounced, as red light has been shown tostimulate scalp hair growth. With the Series 3, I chose not to use red light in those areas, and instead used blue light on my acne-prone chin, with red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared everywhere else. I also threw in a sprinkling of yellow light on my cheeks to tackle redness.Given my hatred for beauty tech apps, which are often full of ads, useless subscriptions and grating tech problems, I was glad to find the CurrentBody app refreshingly simple. The app pops up with an illustration of the light points on the face, ready for you to select which of the six light options you would like to shine from each point. The six light options can be applied using a paintbrush, fill bucket and eraser, which made it feel a lot like using a simplified version of Microsoft Paint. The whole process took about five minutes.I was most relieved to see that, once my personalised treatment had been saved to the device, I never had to open the app unless I wanted to tweak my treatment. There’s space for up to 10 personalised modes on the mask’s controller, on top of the four preset modes, and if for some reason you want more options than that, you can store more treatments on the app. There’s also the option to share treatments with others using a code (mine’s RYPGJ, if you’re feeling nosy).After six weeks of using my personalised treatment, my skin looked calmer, with less redness on my cheeks, fewer breakouts on my chin and a healthier overall appearance. Mission accomplished. I was also pleased that the mask lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments before needing a recharge. If you’re short on time, you can’t reduce the treatment time, but I’d be reluctant to mess around with the treatment length too much anyway, as this would add too many variables to the automatic dosing.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenA fiddly fit: the Series 3’s manual could be clearer about how to attach the straps.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI can’t complain about the results on this mask, but it does have a few nitpicky problems. Namely, the chin strap makes it impossible to pack flat when travelling, as opposed to flat silicone LED masks. Its nose flap left a tiny red mark on my nose for a few minutes after treatments, and to my frustration, CurrentBody’s instruction manual does a poor job of explaining how to add the straps.View image in fullscreenShortcomings: the controller’s smaller clip makes it harder to attach securely to clothing.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianFurthermore, unlike the Series 2, the controller comes with a small built-in touchscreen to accommodate its more complex treatments. While this is intuitive to use, I found the screen easy to jog accidentally mid-use, which would often pause my treatment. At 190g, the controller is also bulkier than before, and its clip is about an inch shorter, which makes it harder to carry around or clip securely on to clothing.I also found the battery life indicator a touch unreliable. Occasionally, the mask died before it got the chance to flag up red low-battery levels. This didn’t happen every time, and the charge always lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments, but it was frustrating nonetheless.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWarranty and repairsLED therapy is safe and comfortable for most people, but it’s always best to be cautious. CurrentBody recommends doing a skin sensitivity test before starting treatment, and offers a full refund if your skin becomes red or itchy after 24 hours, provided you return the mask within 14 days. For those who keep the mask, there is also a two-year warranty that covers manufacturing faults.Should I buy the CurrentBody Series 3 LED face mask?View image in fullscreen‘The top LED mask I’ve tested.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIf you have the money, absolutely. The CurrentBody Series 3 fits comfortably, has a generous battery and is the only one with anti-ageing deep near-infrared light all over the face. With this level of customisation available, it’s easily the top LED mask I’ve tested.This mask is particularly good for those with areas of their skin where one flat treatment won’t cut the mustard. For example, if you just want to fade one dark spot using green light, or treat a localised breakout using blue light, this mask gives you the flexibility to do that. This is a rare instance where I think the app is genuinely worthwhile, too. I didn’t dread booting it up every time I wanted to make an adjustment, and I love that the mask remembers my personalised treatments.That said, if you aren’t battling deep wrinkles and don’t have problematic skin, you might be better off with a moreaffordable LED mask.View at CurrentBodyView at AmazonCurrentBody Series 3 vs …Silk’n LED face mask ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£259 at Lookfantastic£259 at BootsAt about half the price of the CurrentBody Series 3 at the time of writing, the Silk’n LED face mask Pro is an obvious competitor. It has a silicone fit that blocks light well and coverage under the chin. And, if you think a wired controller will bother you, this is controlled and charged via a small, light battery pack that clips on to the mask itself, making it completely wireless. Treatments are all 10 minutes, and the mask had a lovely calming effect on my skin.That said, it offers no personalisation and far fewer deep near-infrared lights, which are positioned exclusively around the mouth, eyes and across the forehead. I also found the mask’s controls harder to get used to. The seven treatments, many of which look similar at first glance, are controlled via a button on the battery pack, which doesn’t give you any information about the treatment selected. To check which lights are being used, you’ll need to read the instructions and memorise how many presses it takes to get to your desired treatment. This shouldn’t be a huge problem, but it does somewhat hinder usability.Lustre Renew Pro FacewearView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£399 at Boots£399 at AmazonThis is the only other customisable LED mask I’ve tested. It’s not perfect, with a far less comfortable fit thanks to a heavy battery pack stuck on the forehead and a smaller-than-average size, but the lower price and simpler customisation options could clinch it for some.This mask has two preset treatment options – Energise and Revitalise – which use blue, red and near-infrared light. While you can use either as a full face treatment using the mask’s button, boot up the app and you’ll be able to select areas of the face for each treatment. Rather than offering pinpoint precision, like the CurrentBody Series 3, these areas span the eyes, nose, forehead, and cheeks and chin.I found these treatments effective at calming my skin, but I didn’t find the app or connection as simple as the CurrentBody, since I had to load the app up every time I wanted to personalise the treatment. If you won’t use the app either, you’d be better off buying the Silk’n option above, which is cheaper, more comfortable and includes deep near-infrared light in its anti-ageing treatments.Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWear ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£372 at Lookfantastic£465 at Cult BeautyIf 10-minute treatments feel like too much of a commitment, the Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWear Pro requires only three minutes a day, making it perfect for those who are time-poor but rich in other aspects. The lights are bright, the fit is supremely comfortable, and it’s wireless, so you don’t need to faff around with a controller.I was initially sceptical about this mask’s performance, given its shorter treatment times, but the combination of red, deep red, near-infrared, amber and blue lights helped give my skin a smoother, clearer and brighter appearance. For an effective LED mask without bells, whistles or any fancy app-based extras, this is a brilliant, if expensive, choice.For more:The best LED face masks that are worth the hypeI tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 timesSali Hughes’s favourite anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)Explore more on these topicsSkincareThe FilterBeautyGadgetsWearable technologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween | Games | The Guardian
description: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Content: Night moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionView image in fullscreenNight moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionGamesEight great new indie horror games for HalloweenWhether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching seasonKeith StuartTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTis almost All Hallows’ Eve and naturally, the thoughts of all good video game players are turning to horror. 2026 has already been a bloody good year for the genre withResident Evil RequiemandSilent Hill: Townfallleading the rabble. But this autumn sees a festering surge of indie horror releases, featuring everything from cursed card games to Nazi-hunting penguins. Here are eight terrifying titles we think you should sample while jack-o-lanterns burn and spirits walk the moonlit streets.Allogloom (PC)View image in fullscreenShady story … Allogloom.Photograph: Galactic GhostlyMixing dark fairytales with classic point-and-click adventure gameplay, Allogloom follows a young girl who must leave her isolated village alone to hunt for her lost mother. The game’s eerie picture book aesthetic and doll-like characters have the feel of a 1970s Czech animation, making for a surreal and disquieting experience.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival (PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox)View image in fullscreenComing for more … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThis latest extension of Barker’s seminal horror novella The Hellbound Heart received mixed reviews, but then so did the Hellraiser films, and they were largely awesome. You play as Aidan, looking to rescue his girlfriend from the nightmarish realm of the Cenobites and their S&M obsessed followers. Gory, kinky and ridiculous it is quite literally a hell of a ride.Grease Trap 99 (PC)View image in fullscreenFrying to fright … Grease Trap 99.Photograph: James MuirheadYou’re working in a quiet Scottish takeaway, frying and serving fish, chips and pizza, when your boss asks you to start serving a “special” dish. But what is it, and what’s that strange gurgling noise coming from the cellar? Created by lone developer James Muirhead with dialogue in Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig), this is more of a short interactive horror movie than a game, but its glitch-ridden, low-poly visuals and dark humour keep you serving until the gruesome finale.Hunter’s Moon (PS5)View image in fullscreenDark tale … Hunter’s Moon.Photograph: Twin SwansBased on the real-life witch-hunts of the 17th century, this atmospheric immersive adventure has you playing as a young woman accused of devilry and now running for her life through woods, rivers and abandoned mines as her hunters pursue. Poetic and strangely beguiling, fans of the classic folk horror movie Witchfinder General, will feel oddly at home.The Killing Stone (PC, PS5, Xbox)View image in fullscreenFeast of occult delights … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionFans of deck-building card battlers are spoiled for choice these days, but The Killing Stone is the perfect choice forHalloween. Set in a remote 17th-century mansion, you must play an ancient card game against the devil to win back the soul of your beloved mistress. The set-up is familiar but there are lovely occult touches, and you get to explore the gloomy house in first-person between bouts, leaning its dark lore. An engrossing fireside treat.Penguin Colony (PC)View image in fullscreenShivers … Penguin Colony.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerA Nazi base in the desolate Antarctic is beset by Lovecraftian entities, driving its inhabitants to madness. But in a neat twist, you play as a penguin observing the chaos and exploring the wilderness, discovering weird obelisks and winding labyrinths as the cosmic horrors threaten your colony.Read our review.Silver Pines (PC, PS5, Xbox, Switch 2)View image in fullscreenCurious case … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17On the trail of a missing singer, troubled private investigator Red Walker finds himself in an abandoned town, but quickly discovers he is far from alone. Influenced by Twin Peaks, Silent Hill and Alan Wake, this haunting 2D adventure is rich in atmosphere and crammed with intriguing puzzles.Read our review.Tenebris Somnia(Switch,PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox)View image in fullscreenUnrest room … Tenebris Somnia.Photograph: New Blood InteractiveWhen a young actor visits her estranged boyfriend, she discovers that his apartment has been trashed and he’s nowhere to be seen. Where is he and what are those weird symbols daubed on the wall? Heavily inspired by early 90s point-and-click adventures as well as interactive movie games such as Night Trap, Tenebris Somnia mixes beautiful pixelated visuals and FMV sequences to eerie effect.Explore more on these topicsGamesXboxPCPlayStationPlayStation 5Nintendo Switch 2HalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm
Content: ‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call.’Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAOpinionEuropeThe Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and TrumpEditorialIf ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harmTue 27 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTShareFollowing the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, shetoldone interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined theirvisionsof a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally,proposesslashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.View image in fullscreenAlice Weidel.Photograph: AFP/GettySimilar ideas have longcirculatedin far-right thinktanks. But they are now in the programmes of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany – Europe’s historic engines of integration. Ms Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland.Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight. Mario Draghi, the former head of the European Central Bank, haswarnedthat without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. But other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leaderspeakingwith the same sense of urgency.Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defence, the moves towards European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Xi Jinping andVladimir Putin(and any Maga successor to Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit.As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counter-arguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming. But it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms. For the time being, to paraphraseWB Yeats, the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
