title: The Epstein files are a US midterms sledgehammer | Katie Phang | The Guardian
description: Voters have a chance to break America’s two-tiered system of justice and hold powerful people accountable
Author: Katie Phang
Headline: Voters have a chance to break America’s two-tiered system of justice and hold powerful people accountable
Content: ‘The Jeffrey Epstein files are emblematic of a corrupt system. And the fish rots from the head down.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The Jeffrey Epstein files are emblematic of a corrupt system. And the fish rots from the head down.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesHow we winJeffrey EpsteinThe Epstein files are a US midterms sledgehammerKatie PhangVoters have a chance to break America’s two-tiered system of justice and hold powerful people accountableTue 27 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.28 EDTShareWelcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Guardian US columnistRebecca Solnitwrote abouttheGOP’s alignment with the tech overlords. Today’s edition was written byKatie Phang,an independent journalist, trial lawyer and political analyst.Sign up for future editions here.When Americans go to the polls a week from now, accountability will be front and center.TheJeffrey Epsteinfiles are emblematic of a corrupt system. And the fish rots from the head down. Beyond the grifter-in-chief and his spawn are billionaires profiting from pay-to-play relationships and predatory corporations rewarded for choosing profits over people, machines over humanity.As many as 88% of Americans who plan to vote in the midterms prioritize candidates who have promised to hold powerful people to account, including by releasing the full Epstein files, according toa September GBAO poll,which also found that what the files represent – sexual exploitation of children; government corruption; abuse of power and powerful people escaping accountability – was a bigger concern than many of the everyday issues the pollsters tested. The finding echoeda poll from Reuters/Ipsosearlier this summer which found 69% of Americans believe the Epstein files show that “powerful people in the U.S. are rarely held accountable for their actions”.Before he was elected president, Donald Trump sat down with Fox News’s Rachel Campos-Duffy, who, during yet another softball interview typical of that network, posed the following question: “Would you declassify the Epstein files?” Trumpanswered: “Yeah, yeah I would.”Kash Patel, Dan Bongino,JD Vanceand the president’s son,Donald Jr, all sang inthe chorusthat demanded the files be released. But as soon as Trump became president, and Patel took over at the FBI, the tunechanged dramatically. Now that Trump was in a position to actually do something about it, suddenly there was nothing to see. The FBI, under the direction of Patel and joined by Pam Bondi, the then US attorney general, even releaseda memostating there was no client list, no evidence to pursue investigations against third parties and that “no further disclosure would be appropriate or warranted.”Trump went on to declare the Epstein files a“Democrat Hoax”and tried his damnedest to distract the public from demanding justice. As is well known, Congress eventually passed theEpstein Files Transparency Act(EFTA), requiring the attorney general to release the files with very limited grounds for redactions and withholdings.We all saw thebotched rolloutof the 3.5m pages of materials and how egregiously it reviolated Epstein survivors by releasing confidential personal information. The EFTA was supposed to protect those survivors, but Trump’s Department of Justiceblacked out the names of those with money, means and influence but exposed victims and survivors. If you think that was an accident, I’ve got some swampland in Florida to sell you.Then in January of this year, Todd Blanche, then the deputy attorney general,declaredthat Trump’s Department of Justice was done.Just done. In my long career as a trial lawyer and journalist, I’ve been reading documents for what they say and what they leave out, and have personally reviewed tens of thousands of the released Epstein files. I never thought I would see our Department of Justice conceal the crimes of a small, moneyed elite.So,I suedfor the transparency the law required. On 27 April, I filedKatie Phang v Attorney General Todd Blanchein federal court in Washington DC, arguing that Blanche violated the Administrative Procedure Act when he illegally redacted and withheld documents pursuant to the EFTA. Blanche’s illegal conduct was making it impossible for journalists to do their jobs; to bring the truth and transparency that the American people demanded and deserved.On 25 June, the presiding judge in my case, Emmet Sullivan,foundthat Blanche had failed to respond substantively to my arguments and that therefore “the Attorney General has conceded that he is in violation” of EFTA. Judge Sullivan also ordered Trump’s justice department to begin producing specific unredacted documents. Since then, Blanche hasviolated court orders, refused to comply with the law and rules of procedure, blown deadlines and made cheap, insincere excuses. Instead of enforcing the law, the attorney general of the United States has been busy subverting it.double quotation markInstead of enforcing the law, the attorney general of the United States has been busy subverting itHere’s the thing, though: voters have noticed. They’re angry and candidates are seizing the day. More than 160 unique Epstein-relatedcampaign adsworth more than $35m in airtime have aired leading up to the midterms. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown has beenhammeringthe incumbent Republican senator Jon Husted over his acceptance of donations from the billionaire Les Wexner. (Epstein was Wexner’s financial adviser and Wexnerhas deniedknowing about or participating in any of Epstein’s crimes.) In Georgia, Jon Ossoff has positioned himself as someone fighting Washington corruption and the“Epstein class”. In Texas, James Talarico hasstood in solidaritywith Epstein survivors and called on his opponent, Ken Paxton, to do the same. (So far, he hasn’t.) Sky Roberts, the brother ofVirginia Giuffre, an Epstein victim who died by suicide last year, and Giuffre’s sister-in-law, Amanda Roberts, appeared inan adbacking Colorado Democrat Jessica Killin in a House race against Republican Jeff Crank, who refused to meet with Sky and Amanda anddeclined to signthe bipartisan discharge petition to force a vote on the EFTA.Just this week, anew staff reportfrom Democrats on the House judiciary committee alleged that a “growing body of evidence demonstrates that Donald Trump was an active participant in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of young women during the mid-to-late 1990s” and that the DoJ and the FBI “are doing everything they can to keep the American people in the dark about it”. (Trump denies any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.) Although the report mostly cites previously reported allegations against Trump, it reflects the outsized importance of the Epstein files in the election.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor decades, some version of “just the way it is” has protected corrupt actors such as Epstein, his friends and associates. Epstein got a sweetheart plea deal while his elite circle was spared investigations or the ignominy of publicity, allowing them to continue to perpetrate their offenses and live their rarefied lives. And the people who were supposed to protect the survivors and hold the bad actors accountable turned a blind eye in what appears to be an exchange for access and privilege.But survivors refuse to be silenced. A federal judge has told the top cop to stop breaking the law. And voters across party lines are rebelling. “Just the way it is” won’t cut it any more.The Epstein files have become a sledgehammer to break America’s two-tiered standard of justice.That, to me, is the beginning of accountability. That is how we win, and how we build a better future.Want to hear more from our contributors?Follow them on Substack:Stacey Abrams,Robert Reich,Paul Krugman,Naomi Klein,Mehdi Hasan,Bernie Sanders,Rebecca Solnit,Katie Phang,Judd Legum,Margaret Sullivan, andWajahat Ali.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinHow we winDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026US politicsRepublicansDemocratsUS CongresscommentShareReuse this content

title: Not registered to vote yet in the US? There’s a good chance you can still cast a ballot | Laura W Brill | The Guardian
description: Twenty-two states and Washington DC let voters register on election day. Why aren’t politicians doing more to reach young people?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Twenty-two states and Washington DC let voters register on election day. Why aren’t politicians doing more to reach young people?
Content: ‘More than half of US states allow eligible voters to cast provisional ballots either on election day, during some part or all of their early voting period, or both.’Photograph: Seth Wenig/APView image in fullscreen‘More than half of US states allow eligible voters to cast provisional ballots either on election day, during some part or all of their early voting period, or both.’Photograph: Seth Wenig/APOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Not registered to vote yet in the US? There’s a good chance you can still cast a ballotLaura W BrillTwenty-two states and Washington DC let voters register on election day. Why aren’t politicians doing more to reach young people?Tue 27 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTShareWith election day just a week away, candidates are ignoring millions of young Americans who could still cast a decisive ballot but have not yet registered to vote.By contrast, my mailbox has been full of political flyers: the various campaigns gleaned my name from the voter file, recognized that I am a regular voter who hadn’t cast a ballot yet, and assessed through their targeted analysis that it’s worth spending on printing and postage to get their message to me.Honestly, they are wasting their money on me – I have voted now and would have done so anyway, with or without their glossy mailers. What they should be doing is targeting people who are probably way more persuadable than I am, yet are routinely ignored: the millions of Americans who will be old enough to vote for the first time this November.In California alone, for example, there are nearly 300,000 eligible 18-year-olds who can legally show up through election day and cast a provisional ballot. Their votes would count the same as mine. So why are their mailboxes empty?Four million Americans will turn 18 this year. Why aren’t we registering them to vote? | Laura W BrillRead moreIt’s not just the 18-year-olds. We estimate thatmore than 1 million young Californians ages 18-24who have not yet registered and are therefore not in the voter file still have a right to vote on election day or during early voting. And it’s not just California. More than half of US states allow eligible voters to cast provisional ballots either on election day, during some part or all of their early voting period, or both.We estimate that 1.7 million 18-year-olds live in the 22 states (plus Washington DC) that allow voters to register on election day. Voter files show that almost half of them have not yet registered, so are probably not receiving mail from campaigns.Across the country, only 45% of 18-year-old Americans are registered to vote, compared with 82% of the over-45s. It’s not apathy or laziness that stops them – it’s more often that no one bothered to ask them or explained how to do it and why it matters – including the candidates.That’s despite the more than$10bn already spentin this campaign. Imagine if just 0.01% of that were spent building the on-ramp to democracy instead of on throw-away mailers and tune-out ads.Four other states allow provisional voting during all or part of their early voting period for those who aren’t yet registered, but don’t allow it on election day itself: Massachusetts, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina.Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change | Kathryn SikkinkRead moreYou might wonder: does election day registration really matter for first timers? The answer is – absolutely. We looked at the voter files for a sample of four states with same-day registration on election day and they all see far more 18-year-olds making it into the voter file on that final day versus any other day of the year.And this really should not be a surprise, but turnout correlates positively with allowing voting for eligible voters who haven’t signed up in advance.Young people – because they are registered at such low rates and therefore aren’t targeted by candidates – often become aware of elections in the final weeks of campaigns, as more and more money is spent on advertising. In many states though, that is well after early registration deadlines. Plus they are highly mobile compared with other age groups, making early registration more challenging for them. The result is millions of voices left unheard, cycle after cycle.We need to rebuild the systems that bring young voters in and that will take time, money and vision. But in the next few days leading to 3 November, we can all reach out to the people we know in the same-day states and encourage them to register and vote. It’s not too late for them to have their say and it’s never too early to start the habit of voting.Laura W Brill is the founder and CEO ofthe Civics Center, a non-partisan non-profit with a mission to make voter registration a core part of high schoolExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsUS voting rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s Amy Acton ad makes a false – and sickening – argument | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Republican attacks on the candidate for governor are contradictory and hinge on a warped understanding of sexual abuse
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Republican attacks on the candidate for governor are contradictory and hinge on a warped understanding of sexual abuse
Content: ‘Vivek Ramaswamy ran an ad featuring the long-estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, the physician and former public health official Amy Acton.’Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Vivek Ramaswamy ran an ad featuring the long-estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, the physician and former public health official Amy Acton.’Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Vivek Ramaswamy’s Amy Acton ad makes a false – and sickening – argumentMoira DoneganRepublican attacks on the candidate for governor are contradictory and hinge on a warped understanding of sexual abuseTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.49 EDTShareI’ve heard people say that the Ramaswamy team must have been scared.Last week, the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the tech billionaire and onetime Republican presidential candidate who is currently the Republican nominee to be the governor of Ohio,ran an adfeaturing the long-estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, the physician and former public health official Amy Acton.In the clip, Acton’s ageing mother emphasizes that her daughter is dishonest. She refers to what she calls a pattern of lying. She urges Ohioans to not vote for her daughter.The clip was meant to leave a dramatic impression on voters with the drama of its severed family bond: how dramatic must Acton’s dishonesty be, viewers were supposed to wonder, if even her own mother is disturbed by it? Left unsaid in the ad is why Acton and her mother are estranged, or much of what Acton’s mother believes she lies about.According to both of them, Acton and her mother have not spoken in nearly 50 years, since they last saw each other in court. Acton’s mother was there to support her husband on charges of raping and sexually abusing the child Actonfrom the ages of nine to 12. Shortly after their final meeting, the man was released on bond; he and Acton’s motherfled the state; he evaded justice, and remained married to Acton’s mother, until his death in 2004.When the old woman says that her daughter was a liar, this is what she apparently means: she is accusing her of lying about sexual abuse, and siding with her dead husband, the alleged abuser.Analysts say that the Ramaswamy campaign must have reached for this attackout of desperation, afraid of what they were seeing in internal polls. But it is hard to imagine any fear that could justify it. Decent people would rather lose an election if doing such a thing is what it takes to win. What the ad reflects is not a desperate tactic, but a depraved character.In the days since the ad was released, amid widespread condemnation, Ramaswamy has doubled down on the decision to attack his opponent for the sexual abuse that she suffered as a child.“Politics is a tough sport. You point out where you think your opponents are flawed,”he said. Hesaidthat Acton had no vision at all, “other than to complain about what someone else did to her”. That it was Ramaswamy, and not Acton, who made her childhood abuse an issue in the race seemed lost on him.Ramaswamy was soon joined in his defense of the ad by vice-president and 2028 hopeful JD Vance,who said: “The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because, guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”Soon, the president himself joined in. “Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse,” hewrote on Truth Social, his proprietary social media platform.Trumpresponded to callsfor Ramaswamy to take the ad down. “I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate.”There’s enough horror in the brute decision to smear Acton with the shame and condemnation that rightly belongs to a pedophile that it can be difficult to stomach any close reading of such statements.But I think it is illustrative to try. Because in their statements defending and supporting the ad, the likes of Ramaswamy, Vance and Trump have made distinct claims – common, but contradictory – about the episode from Acton’s childhood, and about what sexual abuse means.The litany of smears allege that Acton is “complaining” about child rape, but also that she’s lying about it; they say both that she’s dishonest, but also that she’s “flawed” and “defective”.The claims seem to suggest two accusations that can’t both be true: both that Acton was fabricating her allegations, and was never sexually abused by her stepfather, and also that the abuse was so damaging to her psychologically that it has made her unfit for power.Which is it? Did it not happen, and the little girl lied, or did it in fact happen, and the little girl now can’t be a competent woman?No one is askingVivek Ramaswamythis, and I would like to. But I suspect he does not have an answer.His real allegation is not that Acton wasn’t abused, or that she was too damaged by the abuse to govern. His real allegation is that by being the type of person who rape happens to, Acton – and, by extension, many of the rest of us – are foreclosed from worthiness for authority.His real allegation is that the world should be divided into two types of people: the domineering and the dominated; the kind who wield power, and the kind power is wielded against.Ramaswamy thinks of himself as belonging in the former category. Acton’s stepfather probably thought of himself that way, too.The maximal horror of child sexual abuse – including the kind that Acton suffered, which is classified by experts like the Harvard psychiatrist Judith Herman as a form of incest – can tend to obscure how tragically common it is.We like to imagine that such horrific things don’t happen very often; sadly, that is not the case. There are many adults who, as children, suffered as Acton suffered. You probably know some.Many of them, like Acton, have built lives of meaning, honor and achievement; they are loved by friends, of service to their communities, driven by interests and passions that often have very little to do with what they endured. The abhorrence of the abuse they experienced is not the sum total of their characters.This, too, is common, though it is no less extraordinary: that many women live through the worst kinds of sexual violence, and go on to grasp their own dignity back from among the wreckage that it leaves. Even in the face of adversity and injustice, they persist in their self-respect.It is a profound form of moral effort. And it is something that Vivek Ramaswamy wouldn’t know anything about.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionOhioVivek RamaswamyUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Defund Elon Musk | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine
Content: ‘Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink.’Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreen‘Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink.’Photograph: Matt Rourke/APOpinionElon MuskDefund Elon MuskRobert ReichNo private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in UkraineTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.19 EDTShareHe’s Exhibit A on why billionaire wealth should be taxed, why we must get big money out of politics, why billionaires shouldn’t be allowed to buy up major media, and why our government shouldn’t give them huge military contracts.I’m talking aboutElon Musk, of course.According to theWall Street Journal, Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine”. The decision “sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said”.Musk and Trump, the Journal noted, have both “expressed anger atUkrainefor attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices” – although the high prices are really due to Trump’s war in Iran.This month, Musk slowed “the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network … rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless”.According to the Journal, “Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.”Who gave Musk authority to slow his satellite service in the first place? Musk finally admitted this weekend that he had pulled the plug because, hewrote on Twitter/X: “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”So Musk can decide on hisownwhen a foreign country working alongside the United States against a brutal dictator can have access to vital US intelligence?Every time I list another of Musk’s outrages, someone says: “Yes, but he’s an innovator!”He’s not. As is made clear in Alex Gibney’s smart new documentary,Musk,Elondidn’t invent Tesla. He didn’t invent X. He got plenty of help foundingSpaceX.Musk is to innovation what Trump is to governing.We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro KhannaRead moreBoth are conmen. Both are megalomaniacs. Both love authoritarians and detest democracy. Neither believes in (or harbors an ounce of) empathy toward anyone. Both think nothing of corrupting governments for personal gain.Both spout bigoted filth all hours of the day and night to hundreds of millions of people.OK, let me just say it out loud: both Musk and Trump are loathsome human beings.Someday historians will come up with an explanation of how two such awful people could have become the two most powerful people in the US, if not the world (whatwasit about the US in the early 21st century?).But for now, the goal of all sane people must be to defund both and get them as far away from politics as possible.That will be difficult, to be sure. Musk has so far sunk roughly$445minto the 2026 midterm election cycle – all to help Republicans retain control of Congress. That makes him thelargest single known donorin the entire midterm elections.Will he expect a return on his investment?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHell, hespent a quarter of a billion dollarsin 2024 to help Trump win re-election and ended up with access to vast troves of government data, along withbillions of dollars’ worthof no-bid contracts with the Pentagon.His Starlink satellite system is now key to the military strategy of the United States as well as that of Ukraine. He was also rewarded with a chainsaw inaptly named “department of government efficiency”, which he used todestroy USAIDand slash other government agencies he doesn’t like.Musk has given at least$168mto Texas Super Pacs seeking to elect Republican Ken Paxton to the Senate, despite (or is it because of?) Paxton’slong recordof ethical lapses and legal controversies. Musk’s businesses are headquartered in Texas, so he needs friends there.Musk recentlypushed the false storyto his 242 million followers on X that James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, was absent from the campaign trail because he had suffered a mental breakdown and was receiving counseling at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Ohio.In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane MartinsonRead moreThat story has been thoroughly debunked. Security camera footageshows Talaricoat home, not at an Ohio mental health facility. (Meanwhile, according tothe Wall Street Journal, on New Year’s Eve 2024, Paxtonpartied in Dubai with his extramarital girlfriend and two fugitives from charges of about $300m in healthcare fraud in the US. One of the men donated $190,000 to Paxton, $25,000 of it after he was indicted.)The project of defunding Musk will probably have to wait until after 20 January 2029, when, let’s pray, we have a sane administration in Washington that will end all government contracts with him (his support for rightwing extremists around the world makes him a security risk), bust up his monopolies (a reinvigorated Federal Trade Commission and Federal Communications Commission will see to it), and impose a significant wealth tax on him.No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine.If Musk’s Starlink system has become so central to military strategy that its Pentagon contracts can’t be cancelled, it should be nationalized. (After I suggested this on my podcast last Saturday, Musk posted: “Stealing companies is a serious crime. Prison for Reich.”Butyoudon’t have to wait until Musk is officially defunded. Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink. And support politicians who promise to defund him.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsElon MuskOpinionDonald TrumpUkraineUS politicsEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Are seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz | The Guardian
description: Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid
Author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Headline: Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid
Content: ‘[Seed oils] are high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy’, writes Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘[Seed oils] are high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy’, writes Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAntiviralNutritionAre seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them?Gideon Meyerowitz-KatzRandomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acidRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 18.46 EDTShareIf you’ve been online lately, you’ve probably been bombarded with the discourse about seed oils. Once a completely innocuous food that no one really talked about, they have become the enemy of the moment. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services in the US, hascalled them “toxic”and vowed to act against them. There are countless activewear-clad influencers online saying that nothing harms your health more than these products.Which is odd, because theAustralian dietary guidelinessay seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines andmost experts– why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.”So why the hubbub online?Inflammation claims ‘not supported by evidence’Seed oils are a group of cooking oils that are, unsurprisingly, extracted from seeds. They’re generally quite highly refined – although you can get less refined versions of many of them – and include canola oil, sunflower seed oil, rice bran oil, soya bean oil and corn oil. Most of the time vegetable oil is composed of seed oils – it’s often a mixture of sunflower seed and canola oils.Vitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep? | AntiviralRead moreThe concerns about seed oils boil down to one thing: inflammation. It is asserted that the omega-6 fatty acids contained in most seed oils such as linoleic acid can be harmful in large doses and may cause the body to become more inflamed over time. This isn’t entirely crazy – there issome evidencefrom rodent studies that omega-6s cause inflammation, and that having too many of themcan havelong-term negative outcomes.The problem, of course, is that lab rats and mice aren’t people. Very high levels of omega-6s can cause liver dysfunction and gut issues in rats but that doesn’t mean that a bit of sunflower seed oil is going to destroy your intestines.Data from humans doesn’t really show this connection. People who eat more linoleic acid havesubstantiallylowerrisksof cardiovascular disease than those who eat less. Studies looking at supplementing seed oils in people’s dietshave shownno major impacts – and sometimes even modest benefits – compared with placebos.Human studies also don’t support the inflammation link. Randomised trials of omega-6sdo not showan increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acids. Arandomised crossover studyin which the same people were randomly given either omega-3 or omega-6 fatty acids found that there was no difference in how they affected inflammatory markers. Evidence fromcareful analysesof genetics and causality in humans show little indication that omega-6 fatty acids are inflammatory. As Wu puts it, the pro-inflammatory effects of omega-6 fatty acids are “not supported by evidence”.Scaremongering ignores the scienceOn the other hand, we know that animal fats are probably bad for you. They contain high levels of low-density lipoprotein – bad cholesterol – which goes on to clog arteries and cause heart attacks. Ball notes: “Replacing saturated fats, such as those in butter, with unsaturated fats in oils like canola and sunflower can lower LDL cholesterol, an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease.”In other words, the scientific perspective is simple: seed oils are fine. They’re high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy, and if you’re eating them to replace saturated fat then they’re probably going to improve your health. So why are there crazy-eyed men yelling at canola oil in the supermarket aisle on Instagram?Magnesium is essential for health. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep? | AntiviralRead moreThe story here is mostly about dietary fads. Favourite diets online now are quite high in animal fats. If you’re promoting your new book about keto diets, it’s not great for sales if everyone thinks that eating too many steaks is going to give them heart disease. Yes, there were some scientific concerns but those have been largely disproven in the literature already.There are a lot of people scaremongering about seed oils online, which makes sense. You get a lot more attention for yelling that we’re all being poisoned than by calmly explaining the science. I doubt the furore about seed oils is going away any time soon.But from a health perspective you’re probably better off eating seed oils than any other fats. You should limit consumption, because too many calories is not great, but whether you’re frying, making mayonnaise or whatever, it’s likely that the healthiest choice is a seed oil of some kind.Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of WollongongAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: If the Albanese government wants to cheat the populist death spiral, it needs to go to the barricades with the rest of us | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: This is a difficult time to govern. Chaos reigns. The government needs to recast itself as the champion of change rather than the defenders of a status quo so many are rejecting
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: This is a difficult time to govern. Chaos reigns. The government needs to recast itself as the champion of change rather than the defenders of a status quo so many are rejecting
Content: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese. Peter Lewis writes: ‘The government needs to explain what it is doing to improve the lives of working people.’Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Anthony Albanese. Peter Lewis writes: ‘The government needs to explain what it is doing to improve the lives of working people.’Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOpinionEssential pollIf the Albanese government wants to cheat the populist death spiral, it needs to go to the barricades with the rest of usPeter LewisThis is a difficult time to govern. Chaos reigns. The government needs to recast itself as the champion of change rather than the defenders of a status quo so many are rejectingGuardian Essential poll: One Nation and Labor’s primary vote on par as discontent with Albanese risesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareMidway through its second term, the Albanese government is teetering on the verge of a populist death spiral that is sweeping the globe. To avoid being sucked in will take all its political nerve and skill.One Nation’s rapid rise has focused attention on the risks to the rapidly fracturing Coalition, but Labor is not immune from the chaos torpedoing the binary two-party contest that has underpinned Australian politics since the resolution of“the split”, which kept Labor from power until the mid-1970s.While midterm polls are notoriously skittish, there is no sugarcoating the deteriorating view of the government. Labor’s primary vote isstuck below 30%, disapproval of the prime minister is atan historic highandbroader sentimentabout the direction of the nation is dire.You don’t need a political science degree to read the room. Worsening economic conditions are not just affecting the hip pocket of many Australians. According to this week’s Guardian Essential Report, they are also impacting many people’s physical and emotional wellbeing.Has the cost of living negatively impacted any of the following for you?The primary architect of all this pain is a populist US president in way over his head, strangling the global economy first with counter-productive tariffs and now an ill-advised war in Iran from whichhe appears unable to extricate himself.We can talk about government spending, which the Reserve Bank governor has, but without the accelerant ofthe global oil shock, this would be business-as-usual fiscal friction between a government committed to funding services and a bunch of bankers.Haines tribute speeches to open parliament, but Labor mustn’t overlook broader causes of boiling anger | Josh ButlerRead morePolitically, the Albanese government is hamstrung in explaining its predicament on two levels.First, as this table shows, blaming Trump will be read by the public as failing to take responsibility. But being seen to step up and “fix” a global energy shock means the government inflates its own culpability while attempting an impossible ask.Which of the following do you blame most for the rising cost of living?Second, to call out the elephant in the room the government would need to poke the beast. Having skilfully withdrawn Australia from the president’s line of sight, this carries broader risks.To be fair, the government has been prepared to irk the White House and its tech-bro landlords with the news media bargaining code, the social media ban and now the digital duty of care.But more broadly, the government’s fortunes are deeply embedded with Washington, with the military Keynesian of Aukus and the allure of the US AI hyper-scalers central to its national economic plan.This creates an additional challenge for the Albanese government, with an Australian public far less enthusiastic about a future tethered to the US than what is emerging as the Canberra consensus.In general, do you want Australia to be more or less like the US?This forced silence leaves the government exposed to its own populist backlash as people lose faith in their elected representatives to deal with the impact of the chaos that the self-same populism has unleashed.So, what could the government do to stop itself being dragged into this vortex?First, it needs to provide a coherent analysis of the moment. This is what Paul Keating did so masterfully through the last great global disruption. Yes, it is so much harder in a fragmented info ecosystem to nail home a message, but I’d warrant that “banana republic” would still cut through today.TheCanadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has provided the blueprint to grow his personal popularity in a declining economy even as US’s trade war on his nation hits home. He has removed the Trump straitjacket and positioned himself as the best custodian to meet the challenges of the times.Second, the government needs to explain what it is doing to improve the lives of working people. Not just throwing short-term relief at people that will only add to the inflation pressures but showing how it is meeting the moment in support of the very people who are giving up on it.Three things the Albanese government could do right now to make people feel better offRead moreHere it has some fertile ground to till,rebalancing the tax system’suneven treatment of wages and capital, rebuildingsovereign industrial capacityand taking active steps to putworkplace guardrails around AI adoption. It needs to breathe life into this important work.Finally, the government needs to recast itself as the champion of change rather than the defenders of a status quo that so many are rejecting. While Hanson and the global conga line of Temu Trumps are tapping into the chaos, it would a mistake to think that all this momentum is being driven by rightwing nativism.In street protests across Europe, South America and India, progressive movements are rising up not against immigrants, but the provision of basic services and integrity of their governments.In Francethe conditions of schools drove students to the streets initially. InArgentinait is university funding.In India, the Cockroach movement arose from examination fraud. InSpain,ItalyandPortugalthe target is affordable housing.In is no coincidence many of these movements havebeen led by gen Z– young people facing reduced material prospects thanks to failing housing markets and a looming AI job apocalypse. Their resistance is a counterweight to the surge to the right.The energy emanating from these progressive waves are Labor’s to harness in standing up to the rent-seekers and elites. If it doesn’t, the risk is that the Greens under its new leader steps in to fill the breach.This is a really difficult time to govern. Chaos reigns. The Albanese government’s mandate is its sobriety. But to cheat the populist death spiral it may need to be prepared to go to the barricades with the rest of us.Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of the weekly podcastBurning Platforms. title: A year after the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, this is what our lives look like: no privacy, no peace | Akram Al-Sourani | The Guardian
description: I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves, says Akram Al-Sourani, a writer and poet from Gaza City
Author: Akram Al-Sourani
Headline: I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves, says Akram Al-Sourani, a writer and poet from Gaza City
Content: Two girls walk past collapsed buildings in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip on 25 August 2026.Photograph: Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTwo girls walk past collapsed buildings in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip on 25 August 2026.Photograph: Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionGazaA year after the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, this is what our lives look like: no privacy, no peaceAkram Al-SouraniI look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselvesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.44 EDTShareEvery morning, I look at myself and my neighbours standing in the queue for water, and remember how each of us once had a life of our own, our privacy, our own toothbrush, our own home and our own bathroom. How we used to wash our faces and drink clean water without ever imagining that a day would come when these simple routines would become a battle with ourselves and with every drop of water. Even standing beneath a hot shower has become a dream postponed until further notice.A year has passed since theannouncement of the “ceasefire” in Gaza, yet the spectre of war, bombardment and death has never left our lives.War is not simply the bombing of buildings or the evacuation of a residential neighbourhood. There are small wars inside this one enormous war. The tent is a war. The surveillance drone – thezannana, as we call it, for its incessant buzzing – is a war. Queueing for water is a war. Waiting to use the toilet is a war. The death of privacy is a war. Thirty people crammed into a single room is a war.Every morning, the same question follows me: what will happen today? Will my children return from what remains of their school to what remains of our home, having walked along what remains of a street, when bombardment could take them from me at any moment?They walk long distances because transport is difficult and expensive amid fuel shortages, repeated border crossing closures and the trickle of essential supplies intoGaza. It is as though life itself is being rationed to us, drop by drop.In Gaza, waking up alive is not enough. You must also make sure that the place where you slept is still somewhere you can spend the following night. You must hope that your children can dream of an ordinary day – one in which obtaining a loaf of bread, an education or medical treatment is not an achievement worthy of celebration.As the Israeli bombs fell, my family committed an act of rebellion: we planted a garden in Gaza | Taqwa Ahmed al-WaiRead moreIt is as though the ceasefire never happened. The sounds of bombardment, explosions and surveillance drones have continued to accompany our days and nights. What remains of our homes and tents trembles – and so do our hearts.In Gaza, to be alive is to live on the edge of death. As though we are still trapped in October 2023, when the course of our lives was redrawn into a new geography, and evacuation became a matter of Israeli orders dropped from the sky on leaflets – orders to flee from one place to another, from one tent to another disappointment, from one dangerous patch of land to a corner that seemed slightly less dangerous.On the morning of Friday 13 October 2023, the skies over Gazarained down evacuation leafletsordering us to leave our homes and head south.We left the north, broken, and entered madness.We left, but we have never truly returned to ourselves. We lost the people we were before the war. We are no longer who we used to be. The war has turned us into strangers, unfamiliar even to ourselves.We left everything behind.We left the stairwell, the curtains and the windows. The sofas, the router, the 55in television, the pressure cooker on the stove, the unwashed dishes – and half a lemon that, for some ridiculous reason, we always insisted on keeping in the fridge door.We left behind conversations, arguments, disagreements, embraces and unfinished secrets. Stories told after dinner. A bunch of keys, and a never-ending chain of household troubles.We left our photo albums, our wedding pictures, and the hairstyle that irritated me on my wedding night because of all the hairpins; the clutter in the storeroom, the gas lighter, the bathrobe hanging behind the bathroom door, the dining table, the backgammon table, and the water, electricity and internet bills.And we left behind a precious set of drinking glasses, imprisoned in the display cabinet since 1997 on the charge of being “far too good to bring out for guests”.After the bombing, they ended up out in the street.And it turned out we had been wrong to punish our little boy for breaking a cup.We never imagined that we, too, would be broken.All of us were.Three years have passed, yet we still fear hearing again the announcement that changed our lives: “Leave your homes immediately and head south.”Three years of displacement, tents and fear. Three years in which school years have begun and ended without our children experiencing anything resembling a normal education.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the first time, school years are no longer measured in grades and certificates, but in the number of years children have spent displaced.Third year of tent school.It is as though the words I wrote years ago had been waiting for me in the present. As though I had written an early warning that I myself failed to take seriously.I once wrote, in my 2017 book What’s That:“A tent that lets us down.”And in a Facebook post that same year I wrote:“We are all beggars in the making.”I never imagined that the words I had written in satire would one day become the details of our daily lives.From Gaza to Khan Younis, to Rafah, to al-Mawasi, to al-Zawayda, to Deir al-Balah, from a tent to what remains of our home, we have arrived safely in the unknown.Our dreams have yet to arrive. Our hopes have yet to arrive. I fear they may have evaporated somewhere along the way.And today, a year after the announcement of the “ceasefire”, I am still standing in queues: for aid, for cooking gas, for water – and in the endless queue of those waiting for the unknown.I wait for my children to return from school, and I try to recover something of the life we left behind.The name of this chapter has changed. But fear has not changed its address.There is more to tell – if there is anything left of our minds, or our lives, to tell it.Akram Al-Sourani is a writer and poet from Gaza City, and the author of A Homeland Out of Coverage, Half-Baked Homeland and What’s ThatDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGazaOpinionIsrael-Gaza warPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why won’t MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope | Faiza Shaheen | The Guardian
description: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue, says Faiza Shaheen, executive director of Tax Justice UK
Author: Faiza Shaheen
Headline: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue, says Faiza Shaheen, executive director of Tax Justice UK
Content: March in central London on 7 June 2025.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarch in central London on 7 June 2025.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionBudget 2026Why won’t MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hopeFaiza ShaheenEven most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issueTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTShareIn John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax?Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m?Off the table. Eventhe briefed increasein the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it wasuntil the Conservativescut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.Pollafterpollshows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – includingthree in five Reform-leaningvoters. We know that wealth inequality – with therichest 50 families in the UKpossessing more wealth than half of the UK population – isweakening our economy,eroding our social fabricandundermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source.We interviewed30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully trickingordinary homeownersinto thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actuallyleft a decade ago– and quote “millionaire flight” figures froma seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUltimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UKExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionBudgetTax and spendingThe super-richAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyTaxcommentShareReuse this content

title: Admit it: the English love affair with European food has grown stale – we need a native cuisine we can be proud of | Lewis Bassett | The Guardian
description: It’s boring to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta on menus everywhere. Especially when we have salad cream, custard tarts and stuffed chine, says chef Lewis Bassett
Author: Lewis Bassett
Headline: It’s boring to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta on menus everywhere. Especially when we have salad cream, custard tarts and stuffed chine, says chef Lewis Bassett
Content: Traditional British sticky toffee sponge pudding with custard.Photograph: funkyfood London/Paul Williams/AlamyView image in fullscreenTraditional British sticky toffee sponge pudding with custard.Photograph: funkyfood London/Paul Williams/AlamyOpinionFoodAdmit it: the English love affair with European food has grown stale – we need a native cuisine we can be proud ofLewis BassettIt’s boring to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta on menus everywhere. Especially when we have salad cream, custard tarts and stuffed chineTue 27 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTShareNo discerning dinner party host in England would dream of serving their guests a traditional English ham. You might findjamón ibérico, of which Spain is so proud, but neverstuffed chine, a shoulder cut of salted pork marbled with parsley, once a delicacy in Lincolnshire. It sometimes seems as if the English middle classes are so concerned with other countries’ proud artisanal products that they miss the potential of our own.We’re more likely to find cookery writers and experts in nutrition advocate for Japanese foods than traditional English fare. The Chinese diet, too, has its passionate advocates inEngland. We barely need to mention the English middle classes’ long love affair with France and Italy and Spain.Many well-to-doEnglish eaters project ideals of rustic authenticity on to southern Europe, giving us the “modern European” cooking that has dominated the menus of many smart restaurants in England for decades. Yet perhaps this culinary culture is running out of road? Is it not a little dull to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta almost everywhere? What happened to salad cream and whitebaitand pickled herring and steamed puddings? Where did all the bath buns andsally lunnsgo? Are croissants really all we want from our bakeries? When did England’s middle classes fall out of love with English food?My bookThe Full Englishexplores these topics from the first-person perspective of a chef-cum-sociologist. I describe the history of England’s break with the tastes once shared by elites across medieval Europe, which provided us with our first recognisably national cuisine. For Georgian Britons, food, especially beef, spit-roasted and served with simple garnishes, was everything that France was not. France was said to be popish and tyrannical, and the courtly tradition of French food reflected that. France was viewed by British patriots as weak, because its population supposedly subsisted onweedsand frogs. Beef, by contrast, was hearty, honest and rooted in the self-reliance of the English country gentleman. Many middling and upper sorts in Georgian England, from William Hogarth to William Gladstone,joined clubswhose patriotic motto was “beef and liberty”.But by the late 19th century, among a generation with no direct memory of the Napoleonic wars, elite food preferences changed again, no less because the elite itself had changed. Britain had alreadybecome a majority urban nation in 1851(some 100 years ahead of southern Europe), and in English cities, merchants, financiers, capitalistsand their associated professions – groups whose power came from money, rather than land or title – demanded French cooks and French restaurantsas a modern move away from the country cooking of the older upper classes, one which reflected Britain’s new ease with France.Later, in postwar Britain, an expanding middle class underwent alifestyle revolution. Stiff hats, starched shirts and rigid table manners were out and the supposed informality of Mediterranean food was in, along with bare brick walls, furniture from Habitat, bric-a-bracand olives; all markers of what the cookery writer Elizabeth David deemed a new taste for “the luxury of authenticity”.And why not?Fourteen years of rationinghad undermined a native food culture already hindered by urbanisation and industry, both of which were enabled by our dependence on imported food. Then, on top of these features of Britain’s peculiar modernity, has been the long shadow cast by Georgian patriotism – which deemed French food as effeminate, and so committed us to a view that refinement in food is “posh”. No wonder the middle class in this country projected a greedy gaze upon an idealised, provincial France and Italy.But might it be time to turn our hungry dreamings back to England? The other nations that make up the union have their own culinary traditions and often proud relationship to national identity. But in England,patriotism is often assumed to be a blight. Outside international football tournaments, one senses that flags are flown mostly out of fear and hatred, and almost never out of pride. A positive, prouder version of national identitycould become a powerful way to rebuild connection in our increasingly fragmented society.Nations are inventions, thus so too are national foods. Take the case of British bread. The modern artisanal sourdough loaf – so adored by today’s tote-bag yoga-ing classes – has its roots in France and California and was introduced to England in the mid-1990s. And yet its popularity has seen an explosion of native craft baking across the UK, producing a proud generation of artisans who have brought about a better, and at this point, recognisably British bread.We need such inventions more than ever, since ours is a country with some of the mostunhealthy and unsustainableeating habits in Europe. Roast beef or overfished seafoods cannot be the way to go. Old dishes and familiar ingredients can be adapted, and new traditions can be invented. Yet as the new British artisanal sourdough shows, middle-class trendscan be unaffordablefor many. Such exclusivity can breed resentment, in turn fuelling the popularity of foods and brands, such as Greggs, which reproduce our anti-posh, anti-artisanal culture and our habits of unhealthy, industrial eating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor England to find a popular new culinary heritage, one centred on the dignity of craft production as much as health, will require state policy capable of lifting up our culinary standards across the board.And here, pride can form a common ground for any politics leaning in that direction. As a chef, I know that when I have made a custard tart with a satisfying wobble or perfectly dressed a crop of garden beans with a pouting spike of vinegar, I feel a sense of self-respect. Investing in Britishculinary craft is a way to lend pride to our struggling nation; a decent native cookery culture will be one positive thing worth raising the flag for.Lewis Bassett is a chef and the host ofThe Full English Podcast, and the author ofThe Full EnglishExplore more on these topicsFoodOpinionEnglandRestaurantsBreadcommentShareReuse this content

title: My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: John Healey (right) and Andy Burnham are understood to be planning to raise taxes on banks.Photograph: Ian Vogler/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey (right) and Andy Burnham are understood to be planning to raise taxes on banks.Photograph: Ian Vogler/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionBudget 2026My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hardPolly ToynbeeBankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their matchTue 27 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTShareVibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from cappingbus faresto that small but resonant sum of£45 VAT on average off electricity bills– get people talking, alongside bigger plans for anational care service,electoral reformand a possible journeyback to the EU.Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused,banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.UK profits from the country’s four biggest bankswere reportedly £13bnfor the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Financewrites to the chancellorsaying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries.Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him toscrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, andannounced the tower go-aheadonly after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists hisnet worth as $3.1bn, and hetook home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir,Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islamrecounts that episodeas told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.The bank payroll taxraised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?Officiallythe bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP;others suggest double that amount.Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take.Dimon visited No 10last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, fromthe 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTUC pollingfinds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studiesand Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so isemployment,growth,business investmentand average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest wayto raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyBankingBanking reformFinancial sectorcommentShareReuse this content

title: A leaderless revolution has swept Serbia. The world should be watching | Aleksandar Matković | The Guardian
description: I saw a remarkable experiment take shape in Belgrade. Its lessons should be studied by other European countries struggling with unrest, says Serbian academic Aleksandar Matkovic
Author: Aleksandar Matković
Headline: I saw a remarkable experiment take shape in Belgrade. Its lessons should be studied by other European countries struggling with unrest, says Serbian academic Aleksandar Matkovic
Content: Student List supporters celebrate as Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersView image in fullscreenStudent List supporters celebrate as Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersOpinionSerbiaA leaderless revolution has swept Serbia. The world should be watchingAleksandar MatkovićI saw a remarkable experiment take shape in Belgrade. Its lessons should be studied by other European countries struggling with unrestTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTShareMore than a decade ago, the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange told an interviewer in Belgrade thatSerbiawas “a country where the future happens first”. The phrase circulated widely on Serbian social media in the weeks before Sunday’s election, but in a way that could not have seemed possible 10 years ago. Who would then have imagined that Serbia today could be at the forefront of global democratic change?The images from Belgrade on Sunday night – people dancing and crying in the streets, while inNovi Sad,the city that sparked the student movement, a flag bearing the image of the convicted war criminal Vojislav Šešelj, which had hung from a building since the 1990s, was torn down – reinforced the feeling that the future had truly arrived.Watching my home country from abroad, I found it hard not to share in the excitement and emotion. I became involved with the student movement behind this electoral earthquake and was an election candidate for it, for about six months before moving abroad. My involvement began while lecturing in Belgrade at the university’s blockaded faculties in 2024 and 2025. During these extraordinary blockades, something happened that was not widely discussed in the western media: the emergence of a collective sharing of intelligence and a process of shaping opinion that would become key to Sunday’s outcome.For almost two years, students debated almost every aspect of Serbia’s economy and society – from lithium mining and resource exploitation to the economic power of local oligarchs, as well as issues such as healthcare and education. Sometimes discussions lasted six hours. All of this happened before the students developed any joint programme or formed an organisation capable of outmatching the traditional liberal parties. In a sense, knowledge came first, and organisation followed.Sunday’s election victory for what became theStudent List, therefore, emerged from a novel political culture: a leaderless movement based on collective self-governance and political education, unseen in the Serbian political arena since the collapse of Yugoslavia.Given Serbia’s recent history, how was this remarkable democratic experiment even possible? One answer lies in the movement’s ability to rally a wide range of people who, despite different political convictions, wanted to counter the perceived corruption of Aleksandar Vučić, the authoritarian president. With the economy dependent on foreign direct investment after the destruction of Yugoslavia, the political leadership formed close ties with foreign-owned corporations. Vučić’s name was often intertwined with the activities of multinationals such as Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian mining giant that sought toextract the country’s lithium.In this context I receiveddeath threatsfollowing the publication of a critical scientific paper on thecontested lithium issue; many of my colleagues faced similar intimidation. But the mistreatment of Serbian citizens who challenged large-scale investment projects also began to shape public consciousness in Serbia. Vučić’s party wasaccused of standing by and even participating, while opposition parties offered only lacklustre responses.From the students’ standpoint, party leaders were seen as easy to corrupt when confronted with thefinancial power of international projects. And so, to change the system, you had to start by changing the political structures that enabled it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWill such a movement be able to govern? This is where things get trickyIn this sense, this was not just another election; it was a monumental struggle between the old, which was dying, and the new, which was struggling to be born – to paraphraseAntonio Gramsci.In Serbia, the new movement has arisen out of the old: it began with faculty occupations, blockades and plenary assemblies, before evolving today into the largest political force in the country.By winning the parliamentary election, the Student List has broken the monopoly of political parties. It has become more popular than both the rightwing government and virtually all the opposition parties across the spectrum, most of which did not even win enough votes to meet the electoral threshold. Thus, the “old”, in Serbia’s case, at least, is confirmed as dead.And what the Serbian people chose was not another party but a list of 250 candidates, 134 of whom hold PhDs, 44% of whom are women, and 135–140 of whom are now projected to enter parliament. Behind them stood an organisation unlike anything seen in traditional, leader-based political parties. In this way, “a bunch of students”, asthe Economistdescribed them, has created something that should be studied as it goes beyond the traditional ways of doing politics.Will a leaderless movement be able to govern? This is where things get tricky. In the context of what the historian Adam Tooze calls the world’s “polycrisis”, a collective intelligence based on self-organisation may be a tempting answer. After all, the student protests in France, Italy and Belgium, along with protests in Spain and Albania, have emerged in response to interlocking crises of housing, education and environmental destruction. For these crises elsewhere inEurope, so evidently mismanaged by governments, the lessons of the Serbian experiment may become crucial.On the other hand, one should not idealise the situation. The list comprises ideologically opposed blocs, from rightwing adherents to leftwingers and liberals. Most of those elected have never before held political office, and the parliamentary system will require them to nominate a prime minister and, in future presidential elections, a presidential candidate. Will the Student List bring the same energy to the national assembly without jeopardising the very method that made it so strong? Moreover, for Vučić, losing the election does not necessarily mean losing the system.
