On the contrary, his concession of defeat may also have been a strategic move, allowing him to keep the party apparatus intact for a comeback.Whatever happens, one question has been put on the table: to what extent are self-organisation and decentralised decision-making a basis for government? For the time being, people are celebrating on the streets of Belgrade, Novi Sad and many other cities and towns across Serbia. But the real fight has only just begun. The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics.Aleksandar Matković is a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology in Barcelona and a fellow at the Transnational Institute in Amsterdam. He works on environmental history, political economy and the history of YugoslaviaExplore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionEuropeActivismStudentsProtestUniversitiescommentShareReuse this content

title: G Flip and Chrishell Stause have broken up, and like many in the queer community, I’m in mourning | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: Love may not be dead, but it’s had a difficult morning. As much as I’d like a full investigative report, I will instead be getting on with life, as they will
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: Love may not be dead, but it’s had a difficult morning. As much as I’d like a full investigative report, I will instead be getting on with life, as they will
Content: Chrishell Stause (left) and G Flip at the 2025 Arias in Sydney.Photograph: Brittany Long/Publishd/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChrishell Stause (left) and G Flip at the 2025 Arias in Sydney.Photograph: Brittany Long/Publishd/ShutterstockOpinionRelationshipsG Flip and Chrishell Stause have broken up, and like many in the queer community, I’m in mourningRebecca ShawLove may not be dead, but it’s had a difficult morning. As much as I’d like a full investigative report, I will instead be getting on with life, as they willMon 26 Oct 2026 23.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 01.01 EDTShareIn this current bummer of a world, we often wake up to bad news. This morning, it was devastating. I picked up my phone and saw multiple texts asking me how I felt about the fact that …Chrishell Stause and G Fliphave broken up.If those names seem like some sort of gibberish to you, I won’t expect you to understand the seismic shift. While I was sleeping soundly in Australia in the knowledge that love exists, Strause, from the LA “real estate” show Selling Sunset, posted a vulnerable and deeply sad video where she revealed that she and Australian drummer G Flip have parted ways after being married for several years.Her clear, genuine sadness, her talk of feeling like a failure – it moved me. I posted about it on Instagram and in came the flood of responses: Nooooo. Love is dead. Love isn’t real. Whose fault is this. I’m devastated. I’m in mourning. And so on and so forth. Many queer people in particular have been sliced in the heart by this news. Every group chat I’m in is talking about it (not allinstigated by me).From G-Flip to Tame Impala: why Australian music is soundtracking so much TV right nowRead moreI’ve started seeing comments under posts about the breakup such as “Who?” or worse, “Who cares?” and I have to tell you that I care. We care. To me, and people like me, this relationship was a beautiful queer success story.Chrishell comes from a poor background, and her previous marriage ended in a brutal public dumping by actor Justin Hartley. She joined Selling Sunset as a real estate agent and soon became the main character as she compellingly rebuilt her life. During the process she met and fell in love with a non-binary drummer from Australia.Watching someone from such a hyper heterosexual world like Los Angeles real estate, from a hyper heterosexual show like Selling Sunset, begin to dip her toe into the queer world was amazing. Watching her experiencing a truly fulfilling romantic relationship and falling for someone who loved her back and encouraged her to be her true self was a balm. Bringing that queer dynamic to the world of reality TV was also deeply enjoyable.I think everyone tuned into this public relationship was happy to see Chrishell glowing. She and G Flip travelled together, their love always seeming to become stronger and more joyous. Chrishell seemed to love Australia, and in fact became part of Australia, endearing herself by travelling to all sorts of places G Flip’s music took her, such as Wollongong. When she ordered a flat white in a Selling Sunset scene at a cafe, I felt national pride. When the show introduced wide American audiences to their relationship, and to Chrishell’s hyper femme love for the non-binary G Flip, the couple received homophobic hate. But their love endured.Until now.Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s why | Rebecca ShawRead moreOf course, we don’t know what happened. We know that Chrishell seems heartbroken, posting a video because she felt she owed it to the fans of their relationship, the ones who have been so supportive. We know that she seems confused, saying it won’t be hard for her to be respectful of G Flip “because I am in love with this person”, and adding she doesn’t “have all the information and the reasons” for the breakup.We know that G Flip posted, saying that their head and heart feel very heavy. Ultimately, as much as I would love a full investigative report, a timeline, perhaps a podcast series, we are strangers to these two people and their relationship. Their love seemed genuine and real, and as we all know, that sometimes isn’t enough. Chrishell also said she is “definitely never doing this again”. I hope she doesn’t mean true love, I hope she means that after her public marriage breakup with Justin Hartley and her very visible relationship with G Flip, she won’t be bringing an audience along with her next time.It must be pretty exhausting to have your romantic life turned into a spectator sport, even if the spectators are mostly well-meaning strangers, such as lesbians who love your love.So for now, I and many others will be in a short period of mourning. It’s yet another loss of a nice thing. I will be lighting a candle and accepting condolences. And then, I will be trying to get on with my life, just as Chrishell and G Flip will. Love may not be dead, but it certainly had a difficult morning.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsRelationshipsOpinionSocial mediaAustralian musicCelebritycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the Telephone | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?
Content: ‘It was like being in boot camp’ … from left, Peter Case, Jack Lee and Paul Collins in 1975.View image in fullscreen‘It was like being in boot camp’ … from left, Peter Case, Jack Lee and Paul Collins in 1975.Pop and rockInterview‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the TelephoneAlex DellerThey gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nerves should have had it all. Formed in 1974 and gifted with earworm melodies, good looks and a painstaking work ethic, the trio of Jack Lee (guitar, vocals), Peter Case (bass, vocals) and Paul Collins (drums, vocals) wrote, rehearsed and gigged as if their lives depended on it. Not quite punk and dismissive of the description “power pop”, they aimed to cram epic brilliance into effervescent, two-minute songs.When the music industry ignored them, the Nerves opted to make their own luck, pressing their own EP and booking a gruelling nationwide tour that saw them share stages with Devo and the Ramones. After they split in 1978, a bittersweet coda to their brief career swiftly followed: Parallel Lines, Blondie’s smash-hit third album, opened with a cover version of their song Hanging on the Telephone. Previously a Nerves calling card, theBlondietake seemed to scrub them from history.“I figured it would be two weeks, or a month tops, before we were famous,” smiles Paul Collins from his New York home today. A Juilliard student with a bohemian upbringing and an overriding love of rock’n’roll, Collins dropped out and headed for the west coast. “I was barely 18, I had 80 bucks in my pocket and I was scared to death,” he recalls. Within three days of arriving in San Francisco, he found an ad tacked to the wall of a record store which led him to the enigmatic Jack Lee, a transplant from Sitka, Alaska.double quotation markMy snare drum would be covered with blood because we were playing so fastPeter Case proved harder to woo. Baling on school at 15 and ditching Buffalo for San Francisco, he played blues and country standards on the street to pay for food. “I slept in a beat-up van parked down by the water,” says Case. “It wasn’t even my van.” Lee and Case struck up a friendship when the latter was busking. When Collins came on board, the Nerves were transformed from idea to actuality. “You just couldn’t find people that wanted to do something that was that out of joint,” Case recalls. “There was nobody else like Jack around – someone who had a vision, wanted to go with it and couldwrite.”The band set up shop in a three-storey flophouse, immersing themselves in practice sessions that could last up to 16 hours. “It was like being in boot camp,” says Collins. “My snare drum would be covered with blood because we were playing so fast. It was three people acting as one person, and it was a 24-hour endeavour. There was no on and off.”For all their commitment, it soon became apparent that the Nerves were going nowhere. With no peers beyondthe Flamin’ Grooviesand the aloof, leather-clad Crime, the trio saw no future playing to barflies and fist-swinging off-duty servicemen. After Lee recovered from a near-fatal stabbing, the band left for LA. There they rubbed shoulders with scenesters such asKim FowleyandRodney Bingenheimer, and organised early shows for punk bands the Germs and the Weirdos. “It turned out to be a bitter pill to swallow, because they instantly became much more popular than we did!” says Collins.View image in fullscreenPerennially under the radar … the Nerves in Los Angeles in 1977.Photograph: No creditUnperturbed, the band concocted a national tour in 1977 that spanned 71 days, 39 gigs and 16 cities, during which they connected with the Dead Boys and Cheap Trick, and played a series of dates with the Ramones. “The Ramones’ work ethic was even more stringent than ours,” recalls Collins. “They’d be practising before the show, and afterwards they’d go back to the hotel and work on songs. I remember sitting at this big wooden table with them after a show, and Dee Dee goes, ‘May I be excused? I have to go to the bathroom.’ It was like he was at the dinner table with his parents!”If the Ramones were a picture of politeness, other soon to be stars were less welcoming. “We played Boston, and when we were loading in, there were these four guys completely dressed in leather,” says Collins. “One of them goes, ‘What the fuck do you think you’re doing? You’re touring all over the country. You don’t have a manager. You don’t have an agent. It’s bullshit. We know what we’re fucking doing. We’re going to be huge.’ So we look at them and say, ‘Yeah, well what’s the name of your band? The Cars? What a stupid name…’”Inevitably, travelling thousands of miles in a station wagon and booking gigs on the fly took its toll. “It’s like a plant,” says Collins. “You don’t give it water, you don’t give it sunlight, it’s gonna die. We couldn’t get any industry acceptance, and I think we’d taken all we could.”After a stint in the Breakaways, Collins and Case respectively formed the Beat and the Plimsouls, with both bands enjoying the success that eluded the Nerves. Lee, meanwhile, worked on a solo career, self-funding two albums and encountering more proxy success whenCome Back and Staybecame a hit for Paul Young. While Hanging on the Telephone would be covered by everyone from L7 and Def Leppard to Girls Aloud, the Nerves remained perennially under the radar, never achieving the same cut-through as the bands they’d served with in the trenches.View image in fullscreen‘There’s about three albums’ worth of releasable material’ … Collins, Case and Lee in Denver.Photograph: Patty HeffleyFifty years on, a new anthology may redress the balance. “My dad tasked me with this on his deathbed,” says Lee’s daughter, Cynthia Cook. “His dream was to be on Jack White’s label Third Man Records.” While Cook may have grown up writing songs with her father – their first was titled Rock’n’Roll Rabbit, penned when she was five – the music industry wasn’t her home turf. “My dad was all about the long shot,” she smiles. “You know, I’m a mom who works in real estate … but I should go get a deal with Third Man.”The long shot eventually paid off, however, and Cook seems both overwhelmed and overjoyed by the challenge of sifting through a lifetime’s worth of songs. “I have cassettes from the 70s, 80s, 90s and 2000s,” she says. “There’s about three albums’ worth of releasable material.” Her finds to date include a swiftly junked MySpace cut preserved by a fan, and a live tape recorded by an off-duty Whiskey a Go Go waitress and unearthed in a closet 50 years later.As for the Nerves’ legacy, the surviving members are philosophical. “It makes me realise that we did everything wrong in certain ways, and everything right in others,” says Case. “It didn’t work out well at the time, but the music is here now, 50 years later. Who would have ever thought that?”The Nerves: Best Collection is out now on Third Man RecordsExplore more on these topicsPop and rockPunkBlondiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assault | Cynthia Erivo | The Guardian
description: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success
Content: Cynthia Erivo at the Toronto international film festival in September 2026.Photograph: Josh Telles/Deadline/Contour RAView image in fullscreenCynthia Erivo at the Toronto international film festival in September 2026.Photograph: Josh Telles/Deadline/Contour RACynthia ErivoInterview‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assaultLanre BakareIn Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric successTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCynthia Erivo is contemplating her favourite crisps, the ridged American brand Ruffles, as we sit talking in a quiet corner of a west London restaurant. Dressed all in black and sporting her signature elongated nails, she is known for her healthy lifestyle, but everyone, it seems, has their vices. “Ruffles are just perfect,” she says. “When you get a good batch, and the salt-to-potato ratio is perfect … it’s amazing.”Erivo has just touched down after singing in Phoenix, Arizona, the night before, and has been running me through the health routine that helps her maintain her frantic schedule. Before her concert, there was the Dior front row at Paris fashion week, and she has just been announced as a guest host on SNL UK. Erivo doesn’t drink alcohol (today she orders some peppermint tea); she’s vegan; she doesn’t eat airline food, only her own prepacked meals. She even has an infra-red sauna “to help me heal from the inside”. Earlier this year she ran the London Marathon before jumping on stage to perform Dracula, where she played all 23 parts; she had rehearsed her lines while going on gruelling marathon training runs. All that requires discipline – and snacks – to keep the show on the road.View image in fullscreenErivo in Prima Facie (2026).Photograph: Nicola DoveShe has flown in this morning to promote her new film, the legal drama Prima Facie, an adaptation of the one-woman Suzie Miller play about sexual assault, in which Jodie Comerwowed audiences in 2022. Erivo bristles when I ask if she was hesitant about picking up a role so associated with someone else. “I get asked that question a lot,” she says. The pair actually met at a fashion dinner and spoke about the role – “Not asking any tips or anything” – and Erivo insists she was always going to make Tessa her own. “I’m never worried about what someone else has done,” she says. “I try to be respectful.”Erivo plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual assault. Tessa knows how to dance around the courtroom – and the victim – raising inconsistencies that mean convicting a man “beyond reasonable doubt” becomes almost impossible. When Tessa is raped by a colleague, her world implodes and it’s made clear just how brutal the British justice system can be for women, who,according toRape Crisis, have a one in four chance of being sexually assaulted, while only 2.7% of reported rapes result in charges being brought.double quotation markI think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t beMiller, a former barrister herself,said the inspiration for the storycame from her realisation that: “It’s almost impossible to actually run a sexual assault case and win it.” Tessa, says Erivo, doesn’t see how hard it is for anyone to recall traumatic events in detail, or how lopsided the system is, until it’s swallowing her whole. “I don’t think she realises that until she’s on the other side. I think it’s only then she realises what she’s been asking other people to do – when it comes to recall – is actually impossible.”Is Erivo hopeful the film can have a lasting impact? “We have had judges see it, we’ve had lawyers see it, [but] one of the major issues is the way we view consent,” says Erivo. “I hope that as this film filters out, we start to have a conversation not just among us as people, but within law.”View image in fullscreenWith Daniel Ings in Prima Facie.Photograph: Nicola DoveThe film’s central struggle is twofold: the legal system victims have to navigate, and the bigger question of consent, which is something Erivo thinks is often far simpler than it seems. “I think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t be,” she says, leaning forward. “It’s very clear what consent is: if a person isn’t conscious, or conscious enough to say yes, they’re not saying yes. If a person doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes. If the body language doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes.”Tessa’s rise through the legal ranks as a working-class Black woman mirrors Erivo’s ascent through the West End, Broadway and Hollywood. After arriving at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada), Erivo had to traverse a strange world, deeply rooted in tradition and privilege that she wasn’t exposed to growing up in south London.When I ask Erivo what it was like navigating that space she gives a one-word answer: “Hard.” She held down three jobs, including working every imaginable role at the Stratford East theatre, while classmates with means simply had to turn up. “I was exhausted all the time,” she says. “We’re in the classes, and it’s a Monday; I’ve worked all day on a Sunday, and probably done a gig at night, and I’ve come in. I’m falling asleep in class, so people were like: ‘She doesn’t care.’”View image in fullscreenOn stage as Celie in The Color Purple at Menier Chocolate Factory, London, in 2013.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianErivo tells me the story about how she had to turn down a backing singer gig with Westlife that would have lasted two weeks and paid her £10,000 – enough for a couple of years’ tuition. “When I went to the registrar to say, ‘Hey, can I take these two weeks to go and do this? It will pay for my fees,’ they said, ‘No, you can’t. If you go, you leave. If you stay, you stay.’” Erivo says the incident showed how at Rada there could often be “a deep misunderstanding of what it is like to need money”, which is something she is trying to address in the role she has held since 2024 as vice-president of the institution.“I want it to be different,” she says. “Rada is not an easy place to go to school. It asks a lot of you. If you’re a kid who is just really talented, but you’ve not picked up a Shakespeare before, you now have to learn a new language. If you’ve never read a Greek before, now you have to understand what anything means with the Greeks. That’s a big shift from doing plays at school.”James Norton was in Erivo’s year at Rada and recently recalled how she would occasionally burst into song, something she had been doing since her school days in Clapham, where she’d perform Brandy and Monica’s The Boy Is Mine in the playground. “The room would go completely silent,” said Norton, which is no surprise because despite Erivo being little over 5ft tall, she possesses a gigantic voice. It’s a tool capable of the grandstanding volume needed for musical theatre, but also the subtler demands of R&B. In her forthcoming memoir, Erivo recalls being asked at Rada to sing the parts of a white student who was ill, but rather than being replaced was allowed to mime along. “The powers that be took my voice away and gave it to someone else,” is how she described it. In 2020Rada apologisedfor institutional racism, later publishing an anti-racism action plan andappointing David Harewood presidentalongside Erivo.View image in fullscreenIn Steve McQueen’s film adaptation of Widows (2018).Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyErivo set about reclaiming that voice in her post-Rada career, at first mostly on the stage, including a star-making Broadway turn in 2015 as Celie in The Color Purple. The New Yorker’s Hilton Als went to see the production not expecting much (he’d been disappointed by the film adaptation) but remembers Erivo’s Celie as being a revelation. “It was like listening to Judy Garland when she first started out,” he told me. “She keeps you marvelling at what is surely a God-given talent.” Erivo says that show was pivotal for her. “The Color Purple was one of those moments where I went from a jobbing actress and just pleased to be there to someone who was known for this particular piece. My life looked different after that.”Before Broadway she’d had fleeting TV roles in Michaela Coel’s Chewing Gum and in Mr Selfridge, but things shifted again in 2018 when Erivo starred in Steve McQueen’s take on the Lynda La Plante, all-female heist story Widows. Hollywood took notice and she was cast as two African-American icons: the soul star Aretha Franklin and the abolitionist activistHarriet Tubman. But playing Tubman triggered a backlash. Some argued that because she is British-Nigerian, the casting was “disrespectful to African Americans” and part of a wider trend of Black British actors – including Daniel Kaluuya (who played Fred Hampton in Judas and the Black Messiah) and David Oyelowo (who played Dr Martin Luther King in Selma) – bagging roles that some felt should be reserved for Black Americans.View image in fullscreenWith Ariana Grande at the Screen Actors Guild awards in LA, in 2025.Photograph: Jay L Clendenin/Rex/Shutterstock for SAGThe criticism stung Erivo, and at the time shetold the Guardian: “Before I’m British, I’m a Black woman. The first things people see are the colour of my skin and my sex.” I’m interested in her thoughts now, almost a decade on. “I still think it’s happening,” she says, answering almost before I’m able to get the question out. “And I think it’s a waste of everyone’s time.“I think we could all just sit in a room and be like: ‘OK, so what’s the problem? What’s going on? How do we fix this? How do we stop doing this?’ Because nobody else does this. Nobody else is having this conversation. The Australians and the Americans and the English white folk are not having this conversation. They don’t care.” Does she have sympathy with the argument that African Americans do face – on average – more inbuilt disadvantages than some other Black immigrant groups who move to the US? “I have empathy,” she says. “But I also think that it’s hard for a Black English kid from London to also make it.”In person, Erivo can be measured and precise, her arms and adorned fingernails spreading out wide when she wants to make a point. As we talk, she really comes alive when we discuss her experiences after the release ofWicked: For Goodin 2025, the sequel to the 2024 adaptation of the long-running Wizard of Oz musical Wicked.The film, a heartwarming story of friendship between Ariana Grande’s good witch, Glinda, and Erivo’s bad witch, Elphaba, swiftly became the highest-grossing movie adaptation of a stage musical. For Erivo, it was another new high-water mark, one which shot her into the upper echelons of fame.double quotation markThere was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friendsThe Wicked: For Good press tour became a must-follow, not just for fans of the film but for a meme-hungry internet, which feasted on any interview where Erivo and Grande were paired together. Erivo and Grande sat cheek by jowl; they hugged, cried, and – famously – “held space” for each other while holding each other’s index fingers in micro embrace. Erivo says she has seen most of the gifs and loves many. But there was a point at which it seemed to tip into something else, something darker.Commentators started to ask why the pair were apparently so close. Was it all faked as part of a Hollywood psyop? What was really going on here between Erivo – a queer star – and Grande? “It was interesting that there were many people who had become psychologists from their couches,” says Erivo. “There was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friends. Like, why are they friends? Why are they connected? There must be something wrong with them.”She leans forward and takes off her glasses, before beginning to sound like Tessa, the barrister. “Why are they showing emotion? How dare they cry? And how dare they laugh? And how dare they be emotive and alive?” she asks, sounding both hurt and confused. “It’s a double-edged sword,” she adds. “Because if we were dead behind the eyes and showing no emotion, there would have been something else to say about it. I wish there was someone who could have been like, ‘Right, this is the proper balance of emotion that you should show. Don’t show this. Don’t show that. Just this amount,’” she says, pinching her fingers together.The speculation and online hysteria became even more heightened after an Australian prankster, Johnson Wen, jumped on to the red carpet in Singapore,grabbing Grandein an attempt to get a selfie with her. Erivo, who was by her side, immediately confronted him and put her arm around Grande. The moment was terrifying, says Erivo. “No one else was moving. We were on a carpet. We were exposed. My immediate response was: ‘Get this man away from us now.’”The internet’s response was to give thinly veiled praise to Erivo, who was recast as Grande’s “bodyguard” – something she took exception to,arguing thather “humanity had been bastardised” after the incident. Today, Erivo says the reaction was one cloaked in a mix of misogyny and misogynoir – with people seemingly taking great joy in mocking a queer, muscular, bald, Black woman looking out for her friend. Erivo was asked by a journalist on another red carpet whether she was a “protector”, a question that still rankles. “I was like: ‘Oh, you think because I look like this that you could talk to me this way about something that was a human thing that I would have done for any friend, and hopefully a friend would have done for me,’” she says. “But I must be a bodyguard.‘I felt my humanity was bastardised’: Cynthia Erivo says reaction to Ariana Grande red carpet incident rooted in racismRead more“I think the idea that it’s OK to rip a person to shreds in that way when they’re doing something that’s a naturally human thing to do just felt crazy,” she says. People in the public eye are supposed to just take abuse, she continues. “I think that this particular moment went just too far.”I wonder if that experience made Erivo reconsider her career. She has often talked about wanting to push the limits of what’s possible – does she still feel that way? She reverts to her Tessa barrister mode, firing rhetorical questions like darts. “What else have I not discovered about myself as a person, as an artist, as a friend? Like what can I do? If I’m working towards what could be a possible limit, then it means I’m never doing the same thing over and over again. In order to push a limit, it’s gonna hurt a little bit. It’s gonna feel uncomfortable, which means I’m never staying the same. I’m always having to build.” To this very average human, that sounds exhausting, but for Erivo, perhaps it’s nothing a few Ruffles can’t fix.Prima Facie is in UK cinemas from 13 November and Australian cinemas on 14 January.Explore more on these topicsCynthia ErivoWicked: For GoodWickedMusicalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic | Movies | The Guardian
description: It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t
Content: AI-generated film Episode 1 of the Odyssey series made with Grok ImagineComputer-generated: @ImagineView image in fullscreenAI-generated film Episode 1 of the Odyssey series made with Grok ImagineComputer-generated: @ImagineMoviesReviewElon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epicIt is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’tPeter BradshawTue 27 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThink back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and without having seen the film,condemned the supposed wokeryin Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, for getting Elliot Page to play Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen of Troy? As the plaudits and the box-office receipts forNolan’s Odyssey piled stratospherically up, Musk showed that being a good loser is not among his qualities. He petulantly exclaimed thathe could do his own better and more authentic Odyssey on Grok AI. And now he has released the first online seven-minute “episode” to a world that has long since forgotten about this claim and didn’t care in the first place.In Musk’s version, as the tale begins Odysseus is – off screen – pretending to be mad to avoid fighting in the Trojan war. Grim-faced Palamedes and Agamemnon are shown testing this ruse by taking his baby boy Telemachus and placing him in the harm’s way of a plough in a field; Odysseus instantly rushes to save his child, showing that he isn’t mad, and agrees to fight. We see him join the armada, with Penelope and Telemachus (soon to grow to a little boy) left behind. This, effectively, is a prologue sequence that is not in Nolan. The expeditionary force arrives at Troy, and an intertitle tells us we have cut to a 10-years-later flashforward; the siege is about to escalate into the fake-horse attack.View image in fullscreenNo passion … an image from the AI-generated Odyssey series made with Grok ImagineComputer-generated: @ImagineAs ever, the AI footage is ponderous and inert, demonstrating its familiar uncanny-valley stock-footage quality with classical-age Call of Duty graphics. Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver. The ships are lined up on the sea like a row of high-def space invaders. Perhaps the worst thing about it is the deadly audio and digital-robot voice work. Every character speaks with that even, over-emphatic, declamatory tone.‘Sloppy gruesomeness’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmRead moreWho cares? Certainly not Musk. He has no passion to tell us this story, only to win an argument that he long since lost. Perhaps he will now do hisGrok AIversion of Digger, in which Tom Cruise’s oil baron in fact saves the universe by drilling for more and yet more oil. Or maybe he will release his own Grok AI version of You Can See Everything in which glassy-eyed Elizabeth Holmes will prove her little blood-diagnosis box actually does work before she zooms off with Elon in his flying car.Of course, as we are always being told, AI is continuously improving. With succeeding episodes, this boring and pointless series may look better. But if Elon’s AI-Odyssey is of any value at all, it is to underscore the basic truth: nobody believes AI has any artistic merit, only financial merit. In terms of quality, it is a pitiful fraction of the real thing, but a zillionth of a zillionth of a zillionth of the cost. It is time for Elon to make his own inglorious retreat from this phoney AI Dull-yssey.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyElon MuskGrok AIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’ | David Bowie | The Guardian
description: Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says
Content: ‘The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027’ … David Bowie performing on the 1978 Isolar II tour.Photograph: Masayoshi Sukita/David Bowie ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027’ … David Bowie performing on the 1978 Isolar II tour.Photograph: Masayoshi Sukita/David Bowie ArchiveDavid BowieInterview‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’Dave SimpsonMoonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett MorgenTue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2017, when Brett Morgen began work on his acclaimed 2022 David Bowie documentary,Moonage Daydream, he was given complete access to the late star’s entire, cavernous archive. “My eyes were immediately drawn to a stack of gleaming 35mm cans with the word ‘Stage’ written on them,” he remembers.At first, the director – whose work also includesKurt Cobain: Montage of Heckand the Rolling Stones documentary Crossfire Hurricane – assumed the cans might contain some sort of footage shot around Bowie’s 1978 live album, Stage, recorded in mostly in Philadelphia. However, he soon realised they actually contained the holy grail of Bowie artefacts: footage of the legendary Earl’s Court shows later that year, which had remained unseen for almost 50 years. “Making Moonage Daydream, I had access to every filmed performance in existence of David Bowie,” he says, “but when I saw this one I knew this was without question the greatest filmed performance of his career.”In 1978, Bowie had commissioned Just a Gigolo director David Hemmings to film two of the three sold-out summer shows at the venue – where the star was touring Low and “Heroes” – with a view to showing the film in theatres in lieu of a physical tour (he wouldn’t take the road again until 1983). However, the singer subsequently started making the Lodger album, moved to Switzerland, was reportedly unhappy with the film’s editing and the entire project was subsequently left behind. “He was moving on to other things at the speed of light,” Morgen explains. “So at that point I think the idea of looking backwards was distasteful to him.”The trailer for David Bowie: Stage – videoBefore his death in 2016, though, Bowie had floated the idea of finally putting it out. In the new year it will debut in arenas – not cinemas – almost half a century after it was made. Morgen and team spent nearly 10 years readying it for 2027 as a multimedia experience. “It became something of an obsession,” he admits. “We spent over 1,000 hours colour-grading the footage, which I believe is some sort of record, but we really wanted it to look and feel like something you would experience today.”It helped that the footage had been beautifully shot and perfectly preserved in Bowie’s storage unit, with excellent sound recorded by Bowie’s producer, Tony Visconti. Missing from Morgen’s film will be the extraneous stuff Hemmings added to the concerts. “I found a lot of footage of a young boy playing David that I was a bit confused by,” the director grins. “That’s not in the film.” Instead, it focuses on Bowie – in wonderfully billowing trousers and makeup – at the peak of his performance powers. “He looks amazing,” Morgen smiles. “I’ve looked at close-ups and I think: how on earth is this man not sweating?”By the time the Isolar II tour reached Earl’s Court, Bowie and band were at the pinnacle of their game, signposting the future. “To have an electric violin, a piano and a synth player in a rock show in 1978 was extraordinary,” says Morgen, whose film combines songs from both nights because “It was very improvisational. Different arrangements two nights running. You can feel the danger and excitement that it could have gone off the rails at any moment and David was very charged by that.“The audacity of starting the show with Warszawa, perhaps the lowest-energy first song of any rock concert ever – but that’s Bowie. By the end of the first set he’s reeled them in and by the end of the second set the place is just insane. The performance of Station to Station is incredible.”View image in fullscreenBowie in a still from Brett Morgen’s remastered Stage.Photograph: PRDuring the second show, on 1 July, Bowie quips, “OK, this will be interesting”, and performs Sound and Vision for the first time ever. “And he’s cracking up throughout the song because I think the electric violin was trying to do the horn section, which David thought was kind of amusing. It’s a great moment. Then the camera stays with David when he goes off to the sides, having a glass of beer or smoking a cigarette, and he’s so engaged, dancing and smiling. It’s very joyous. I think this was the first time he’d performed without a mask, or ‘character’, so to speak.”Morgen isn’t giving everything away but promises “surprises” as well as “a new medium of entertainment”.“It’s not a movie that’s being shown in arenas,” he insists. “There’s multiple screens, a fully integrated lighting package, a 7.1 [surround sound] sound mix. The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027. The audience is invited to gaze where they want to gaze: choose your own adventure. Eleven years after his passing, it makes perfect sense that Bowie will be trailblazing again.”Stage premieres at theBerlin film festival, Germany, in February 2027, before touring.Explore more on these topicsDavid BowieDocumentary filmsPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama | Television | The Guardian
description: The Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new light
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new light
Content: Relationship/romance … Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani in the Disney/Hulu series The Dropout.Photograph: Beth Dubber/APView image in fullscreenRelationship/romance … Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani in the Disney/Hulu series The Dropout.Photograph: Beth Dubber/APTelevisionElizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV dramaThe Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything  documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new lightHannah J DaviesTue 27 Oct 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are surprise smash hits, and then there’s You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s documentary-cum-psychodrama about the disgraced US entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes. It arrived in US cinemas with much buzz: this was, after all, an A24 production, helmed by one of TV’s leading performance-art pranksters. But You Can See Everything has surpassed all expectations to become an undeniable hit, and is nowthe highest-grossing US documentary in 15 yearsjust two weeks after its release.Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, it is a surreal and masterly epic; at a press screening in London, the audience appeared to be alternately spellbound by its comedic elements and repulsed by the sheer grossness of some of its characters. That grossness, it should be mentioned, doesn’t pertain only to Holmes, who was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison (this has since beenreduced several times) for defrauding investors, after the collapse of her sham blood-testing startup Theranos). It has also – perhaps unsurprisingly – led audiences towards other media inspired by Holmes’s downfall. Journalist John Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood,has returned to the bestseller lists; the ABC News podcast The Dropout, hosted by Rebecca Jarvis reported a900% surge in listeners; whiletheDisney/Hulu TV seriesof the same name enjoyed a700% bump in viewers, and is now ranked #47 on IMDb’s “Most popular TV shows” list, despite having been released in 2022.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreAs Holmes mania abounds, I decide to fire upthe podcast, a show I listened to when it was released in 2019. Unlike You Can See Everything – which explores whether Holmes can convince us of her innocence, as much as whether she is innocent – The Dropout podcast takes us back to her halcyon days, when she was named America’s youngest self-made billionaire. This was a time when her Steve Jobs-esque black turtlenecks, apparently bogus baritone voice and talent for wooing super-rich investors was a large part of the story (the first episode is titled Myth-Making).But it wasn’t just about Holmes the person – it was about what her company did (or rather, didn’t do) and offered a stark reminder that the claims that she made never matched reality. In one episode, we hear Holmes declare that it is possible to run “any lab test from a drop of blood from a finger”, juxtaposed with a clip from a deposition hearing where she is asked just how many tests her machine was capable of carrying out: “I-I-I don’t know exactly what the number was … I think there were probably tens of tests …” (If this sounds like a straightforward lie, Holmes offers her own explanation of her claims in You Can See Everything.)View image in fullscreenA masterly epic … Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24The TV adaptation of The Dropout recycles the story that the podcast so thoroughly investigated, albeit with a little more artistic licence (Holmes dances like a robot to Lil Wayne, and there’s an entire plot point that’s reverse-engineered to incorporate the Katy Perry song Firework). It’s entertaining, sure: I find myself strangely captivated by the stilted professional relationship/romance between Holmes (Amanda Seyfried) and Sunny Balwani (Naveen Andrews), 19 years her senior, who are obsessed with one another but suggest a cold indifference, too (see also: a real-life text exchange between Holmes and Balwani, where she wrote: “You are the breeze in the desert for me. My water. And ocean. Meant to be only together tiger,” to which Balwani replied: “OK”).But for the first few episodes at least, The Dropout is mostly like watching a campus drama that occasionally morphs into an episode of Law and Order. Seyfried is great – all bulging, marble-like eyes, unsettling jaw placement and off-kilter speech patterns – but there is a sense that this is an almost meme-esque endeavour, gleefully ripped from the headlines (You Can See Everything does, in its own way, ask whether that might have indeed been the case). At the end of episode one, Elizabeth stares at her finger, and – deus ex machina – the idea for Theranos arrives.But The Dropout series, like the podcast before it, was built on inescapable facts and what the Guardian described at the time of release as the“gut-twisting mental gymnastics”of it all – the technological inadequacies of Theranos’s equipment; the surveillance culture that meant employees felt they couldn’t speak out; the third-party machines the company used in place of its own hardware; false positives for HIV, cancer and other serious conditions. It might sound facile, but it’s a reminder of the sheer weight of what Holmes’s company did, and of her ability to fight off the most legitimate of concerns. It touches, too, on the suicide of Ian Gibbons, the company’s former chief scientist, who took his own life before he was due to testify against the company. It would be irresponsible to lay the blame for this death solely on Theranos. But it’s clear, amid the jacked-up comedy, that there was plenty of pain for its writers to mine.Holmes’s story first gripped the world during what was a big moment for scammers, from thephoney heiress Anna DelveytoFyre festival, with its schadenfreude-inducing story of influencers stranded in the Bahamas under disaster relief blankets. In the years since, the conversation around such grifts has become less cut and dried: Delvey has gonefull-on media caricature, while – conversely – many Fyre attenders were revealed to have been normies who got their tickets on Groupon.Aptly, perhaps, for a moment that was so focused on untruths, the narrative of the “golden age of the grift” is now being rewritten again, in real time. Fielder and Oppenheim have done something daring and brilliant with You Can See Everything, incorporating anew era of technofascismand AI in the process, and meeting Holmes not as a Silicon Valley sweetheart but as a mother and soon-to-be-convict. But the facts – be it on TV or on a podcast – remain as unsettling as ever. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” says Holmes in the film. And yet so much of it is hard to ignore.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderAmanda SeyfriedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more | Macklemore | The Guardian
description:
3Arena, Dublin
Several unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: 3Arena, DublinSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon
Content: Macklemore performing on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Zoe RainView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Zoe RainMacklemoreReviewMacklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more3Arena, DublinSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia NixonAlexis PetridisTue 27 Oct 2026 00.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organising this concert,” offers a member of Kneecap, one of several unannounced guests who have turned up for the first European date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour. It’s a characteristically two-fisted approach to the matter in hand from a band who have seldom shied away from controversy, but it has more than a grain of truth in it.The events of the last six weeks are quite something, and perhaps not what Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, had in mind when he led efforts to pressurise Sheeran toremove Macklemore from his summer US tour, after the rapper made a speech about Palestine on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore was duly removed from the tour, but the rapper saw his profile rise dramatically as a result – in fairness, he was hardly unknown, but his biggest hits are a decade old – whileevery other artist on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity. Sheeran’s tour limped on amid much opprobrium, while Macklemore was able to translate the publicity into a tour of his own, in noticeably bigger venues than he played on his last European tour, with proceeds donated to organisations assisting Palestinians. Dublin’s 13,000-capacity 3Arena is sold out, as is every other date on the tour.Accordingly, a certain infectiously giddy excitement attends the event itself: the audience receive everything – speeches from activists; video messages from actors Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon and the Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas, among others; sets of Arabic-themed dance music from Palestinian American DJ Habibeats; and an appearance by longstanding political US hip-hop duo Dead Prez.View image in fullscreenKneecap performing on the Free Palestine tour.Photograph: Zoe RainThey go nuts for Lina Makoul, the first Palestinian to win the Israeli equivalent of The Voice: her brief set opens with a wordless vocal protesting censorship and ends with a song admonishing late-stage capitalism that comes complete with a glancing reference to Guy Debord’s La Société du spectacle, which really isn’t what one would expect from a TV talent show winner. They receive Beoga, the County Kerry folk band who performed on Sheeran’s Galway Girl, but left the singer’s tour alongside Macklemore, like returning heroes. It turns out they’re founding members of an organisation called Irish Artists For Palestine, which does rather beg the question of what Sheeran thought they might do under the circumstances. “You don’t fuck with the Irish, lads,” offers drummer Eamon Murray.There’s something very striking about the fact that the local artists who’ve heeded Macklemore’s call to help out are evidently committed to the cause behind it: you never get a sense of anyone rocking up in order to grab brownie points or reflected glory. Backed by a string section, Hozier’s performance is heavy on audience-pleasing hits – Take Me to Church, Too Sweet – and takes in a rendition of a remarkable 19th-century folk ballad called The Prayer of Shields, which he apparently learned from Ian Lynch of Lankum. Thescreens behind him display a QR code that links to a petition in support of 55 students from Gaza who have not had their visas approved to study inIreland. He goes down a storm, but the real bedlam is caused by Kneecap, who know a thing or two about how controversy can impact an artist’s profile. Their brief set opens with a film that proceeds in a frantic blur of images – The Troubles, Sinéad O’Connor ripping up the pope’s photo on Saturday Night Live – causes an outbreak of moshing and ends with DJ Próvaí struggling to maintain his balance in the midst of the audience: it’s splenetic, chaotic and remarkably powerful.View image in fullscreenFans outside 3Arena in Dublin before Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour gig.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesWhen Macklemore finally appears, it’s hard to miss the effect of recent events upon him, not least because his opening track, Chant – a 2022 single about his struggle with addiction – now sounds remarkably like a defiant comment on them: “This is my moment … you can’t take my voice from me.” He has a point: he’s been writing about Palestine since 2024’s Hind’s Hall, but as he rolls out his old hits – Thrift Shop’s hymning of limiting one’s spending rather than splurging in grandstanding rapper style; Same Love’s backing for same-sex marriage – a fresh sense of energised purpose about his approach is hard to miss. Between songs, he assiduously shifts attention from himself to the cause he’s advocating, but notes that the show itself “makes me feel glorious”. Understandably so: he mentions that he’s “called up a lot of people in the last six weeks” and notes that Kneecap and Hozier were the first to agree to perform alongside him, which makes you wonder how successful his efforts have been elsewhere. But in Dublin at least, the Free Palestine show feels like a worthwhile triumph.Macklemore’sFree Palestine tourgoes to Paris on 29 October and London on 30 OctoberThis article was amended on 28 October 2026 to correct a photo caption.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreRapPop and rockIrelandlive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours | Architecture | The Guardian
description: A low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to star
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: A low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to star
Content: High lights … the glowing polycarbonate ventilation shaftofthe new Yard theatre near the Olympic site.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightView image in fullscreenHigh lights … the glowing polycarbonate ventilation shaftofthe new Yard theatre near the Olympic site.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightArchitectureOur loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighboursA low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to starOliver WainwrightTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but thelegacy of the sporting spectaclerolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of theYard theatre. Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – andIan McKellen set to star in the next show.View image in fullscreenWill the actors’ knees be able to take it? … the concrete stage.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates ofPractice Architectureto conjure anad hoc auditoriumon a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard intoa mixed-use district. That project never materialised, but executive director Ashleigh Wheeler and her team succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (community infrastructure levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.View image in fullscreenSpell it out … the theatre’s name in the multicoloured recycled brickwork.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work ofTakero Shimazaki, a Tokyo-born Londoner who wasshortlisted for the Stirling prize last yearfor an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. It reads like a collage of its context: a shed clad with corrugated fibre-cement sheeting, rising from graffiti-covered warehouse walls on one side and framed by a new brick gable end on the other. The bricks include subtle shades of blue, yellow and magenta, in a nod to the previous printworks, while the name of the theatre is spelt out in the brickwork, recalling the faded factory signs of the area. In keeping with the waste-not ethos, theseK-Briqs, manufactured in Scotland, are unfired and made of 95% construction waste, recycling 16 tonnes of waste that would have otherwise gone to landfill and saving the equivalent of 3.5 tonnes of CO2that regular bricks would have emitted.There is a grandeur to the new theatre’s form. With its central tower and symmetrical pitch roof, Shimazaki says the Yard was inspired by Palladian churches to bring a sense of permanence, as if the building might have been here far longer than it has. “The Yard was interested in the idea of permanence in theatre, and fakery in architecture,” he says. “And how to build something grownup with not much money.” Mirrored panels in some of the windows bring a theatrical touch, while bright pink guttering and yellow coping blend with the local street art vernacular. Miraculously, for now, the new brickwork remains graffiti free.View image in fullscreenOne of the first shows …for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf–Photograph: Philip VileEntering through big double doors – emblazoned with “open me up now” – you find a large open foyer and cafe, with walls and banquettes in rich shades of burgundy, while a glossy blue bar is framed with bands of teal and green, recalling a Josef Albers painting. Gold-painted columns add a touch of theatrical bling, which will be cranked up a notch next year when a vestibule is installed. Designed by artistEd Atkins, it will usher theatregoers through a dramatic ruched silver curtain. The loos add further sparkle, inspired by thebathroom at the Villa Necchi Campiglio in Milan, with glossy black tiles, shiny brass fittings and coloured lino floors – “a little bit of economical opulence”, as Shimazaki puts it.So what of the theatre itself? A central staircase leads up through a dark passage to the new auditorium, where the architects had to strike a tricky balance. “We wanted to retain what people loved about the old space,” says Miller, “and evolve what wasn’t as functional.” It has the same bare bones quality as before, with an exposed back wall built with bricks salvaged from the site, a concrete stage (actors’ knees won’t thank them), and curved, raked seating in the manner of an amphitheatre. The plastic cafe seats were upgraded for upholstered communal benches.“Epic and intimate at the same time” was the brief, and Shimazaki has risen to the challenge, creating a 250-capacity space – more than double the previous theatre – that is at once cosy and grand. Continuing the fakery theme, the cast concrete-looking seating structure is actually cement particle board, while banks of radiators hidden below the seats keep bums warm while aiding the passive stack ventilation system. As before, what you see is what you get: there are no wings, no fly tower, nowhere for the actors to hide. “We wanted to amplify the sense of liveness,” says Miller. “After all, that’s what makes theatre unique.” It still feels raw – although performers now benefit from the luxury of dressing rooms, tucked beneath the seating, saving them from dashing to beat the audience to the loos in the interval.View image in fullscreenInspired by Palladian churches … the corrugated fibre-cement claddingPhotograph: Philip VileAround the other side of the building, the graffitied warehouse offices are being transformed into a youth hub by Jeremy Deller and architect educators Matt+Fiona, alongside local schoolchildren. It’s part of an Arts Council-fundedseriesthat has also seen an Antony Gormley figure appear on the roof – visible from the elevated platform of Hackney Wick station – with further commissions and community collaborations in the works.Fit for a king: Ian McKellen to play Lear at newly rebuilt Yard theatre in east LondonRead moreThe ad hoc ingenuity on show puts what is emerging across the other side of the park into sharp relief. One of the biggest components of the Olympic legacy is the “cultural quarter” ofEast Bankin Stratford, a £1.1bn colossus that houses branches of the V&A, Sadler’s Wells theatre, BBC studios, University of the Arts London and University College London, soon to be garnished with towers of unaffordable flats. The presence of these institutions is welcome – but despite the big budgets, top architects and endless design review panels, the results feel less than world class.It is a cumbersome beast, designed by committee and airlifted in from on high, begat from the loins of mayors hungry for legacies. The Yard, by contrast, shows how a young, agile team with a fraction of the resources can achieve so much, building a project that feels truly grown from its place.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureTheatreYard theatreGreen buildingHackneyLondonOlympic legacyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not my pain. There’s a responsibility in that’: Thea Gilmore on writing songs from anonymous confessional voicemails | Music | The Guardian
description: After tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousands
Author: Shaun Curran
Headline: After tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousands
Content: ‘People know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place’ … Thea Gilmore.Photograph: Carsten WindhorstView image in fullscreen‘People know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place’ … Thea Gilmore.Photograph: Carsten WindhorstMusicInterview‘It’s not my pain. There’s a responsibility in that’: Thea Gilmore on writing songs from anonymous confessional voicemailsShaun CurranAfter tiring of writing about herself, the British singer-songwriter asked the public to share stories to inspire her music – and they responded in their thousandsTue 27 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘This project has changed my whole thinking,” Thea Gilmore says of her new endeavour,The Echo Line. “What am I getting from it? All of humanity.” Disillusioned with the numbers-chasing music industry and wanting a break from her personal songwriting after releasing 22 folk-orientated albums since 1998, the 46-year-old is “putting people back at the centre of it. I’ve said enough about me.”Community building has been key to the Oxford singer-songwriter’s work since debut Burning Dorothy, released when she was just 18, through to her 00s breakthrough albums Avalanche and Harpo’s Ghost all the way to her most recent studio album, 2023’s Thea Gilmore: a body of work that has won Gilmore admiration from Bruce Springsteen, Richard Thompson and collaborator Joan Baez.But The Echo Line goes even further. Akin to a musical iteration of Nick Cave’s interactive fan advice column The Red Hand Files, Gilmore invites people to leave her an anonymous voicemail or written message viaThe Echo Line websiteabout anything they want – hopes and dreams, fears and confessions, triumphs and tribulations – to which people have obliged with bravery and honesty in their thousands. Gilmore then writes a song inspired by one or more messages and uploads it to the website for a limited time only.When it was launched in January, Gilmore was unsure if anyone would call, or even notice – she currently has no management, label or press team – but received 150 messages within two days. The fourth and latest song of the project He Walks Like War was listened to more than 10,000 times before it was taken down. Songs initially remained available for just one week – “music is so disposable and available all the time, I wanted to see what happened if I took it away again” – though demand for He Walks Like War meant Gilmore relented and kept the song up for several weeks.View image in fullscreen‘Listening is a powerful act’ … Thea GilmoreEven as the community grows, Gilmore listens to and reads every message. “Listening has become increasingly undervalued in my lifetime. But it’s a powerful act. People more and more feel very alone. And I think what they’re getting from this is they know they’re actually being listened to, with no judgement.” The anonymity is key. “It’s really important to the integrity of the project that people know it’s genuinely an anonymous safe place.”She admits she wasn’t quite prepared to receive such emotional messages. Certain themes recur: grief, loss and heartbreak; estrangement, especially from parents; messages about children, both pride and worries; the overwhelm of the modern world and distrust of elites. Many tell stories of overcoming adversity; one message detailed surviving an intruder attack at home (“like a Tarantino script”). But there are joyful ones too, including Gilmore’s personal favourite: a message about the interconnectivity of mushrooms as they grow in the ground. “In my bonkers songwriter brain, I’m like: that’s what this whole thing is about! We’re all connected, just like fungus.”The trust placed in her, she says, is a delicate gift. “As a songwriter you feel emboldened in some respects because they obviously think I can do a good job with their story,” she says. “But it is really tough. Because it’s not my pain. You’re making sure you do other people’s lives justice. There’s a weight of responsibility in that.”The Echo Line’s first three songs, beautiful examples of Gilmore’s spectral balladry, are incredibly moving. Blood Bike is an amalgamation of three messages: a blood bike worker delivering neonatal breast milk to hospitals, an overworked NHS nurse and a mother whose daughter was born prematurely. “They’re human stories that show we’re all connected, and this light went on – I was like: this is exactly what I wanted this to be.”‘Shane was rascality personified’: the Pogues on their late frontman, anti-Irish prejudice and the feud over Fairytale of New YorkRead moreThe second song, Silvie, tells the story of a relationship from 30 years ago tragically cut short by a road accident. The contributor was forbidden by their partner’s family to say a proper goodbye and the pain lingers. “That person’s message started ‘I don’t talk much about Silvie anymore’,” Gilmore says. “Those words just sat on top of your heart like a weight.”A long-distance relationship conducted entirely online inspired The Lines (Greg), a non-traditional courtship that ended tragically with Greg’s death by suicide. Even though the messenger is now happily married, “they felt they couldn’t talk about it or explain to people that it had been so important to them. And I really wanted to honour that in a song, that some of the most transformative relationships can be outside the bounds of what society says you can do.”The gnarlier He Walks Like War came after an influx of different types of messages from people across the political spectrum: disillusionment and anger at the billionaire class, tech bros and insidious algorithms dividing society. “You can see the same frustrations in completely different types of people. There are a lot of people out there who feel completely disenfranchised.”With The Echo Line now open 24/7, Gilmore is currently working on the next song, to be released by the end of October. “A very happy song, one of the most beautiful stories framed in the most beautiful way.” She has big ambitions for The Echo Line, including gallery events and live shows. “I would love to see this grow. For me, this is a sort of project that when I die, I’ll be like: that’s what I was meant to do.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockFolk musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies | Neil Young | The Guardian
description: The musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song again
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song again
Content: Neil Young pictured in 2019.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APView image in fullscreenNeil Young pictured in 2019.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APNeil YoungNeil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at ralliesThe musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song againLaura SnapesTue 27 Oct 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeil Young is suing Donald Trump’s political action committee Trump 47 Committee Inc for $10m (£7.47m) over alleged copyright infringement of his song Rockin’ in the Free World after the US president used it as walk-up music in recent midterm election rallies.It is the second time that Young has filed against one of Trump’s organisations over his unlicenced use of the song. He first did so in 2020, against the corporation Donald J Trump for President Inc. Trump settled, promising, according to Young’s suit, that his organisation “would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young”.Filed on Monday in the US district court for the eastern district of Virginia, the suit states that Trump’s ongoing use of the song meant that Young, a very vocal critic of the president, “has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J Trump in any way”.Neil Young: Rockin’ in the Free World – videoTrump’s administration has not yet responded to the suit.Young’s case outlines how diametrically opposed his 1989 song is to Trump’s values, calling it “a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten.“The lyrics pain vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNeil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes goldRead moreLawyers for Young cite the playing of the song at the president’s rally in Ohio on 12 October but state that it has been played “numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections”. Young also seeks an injunction against further public performances.Young’s anti-Trump stance is clear: he has repeatedly damned the president in writings on his website and in 2025released a protest song about his administration, Big Crime. “Don’t need no fascist rules / Don’t want no fascist schools / Don’t want soldiers walking on the streets,” Young sings. “Got to get the fascists out / Got to clean the White House out … no more money to the fascists, the billionaire fascists.”In the past 12 months, the Trump presidency has amped up its strategy oftrolling leftwing musicians– including Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter and SZA – by using their songs to soundtrack ICE propaganda or clips about Trump’s strategy in Iran. In August, Taylor Swift had her song August removed from a video celebrating the Trump presidency.Explore more on these topicsNeil YoungDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgen | David Bowie | The Guardian
description: David Hemmings’ never-released concert film from Bowie’s 1978 world tour will be presented in a multimedia show that aims to ‘create the illusion’ that he is present on stage
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: David Hemmings’ never-released concert film from Bowie’s 1978 world tour will be presented in a multimedia show that aims to ‘create the illusion’ that he is present on stage
Content: ‘A model of agility and physical grace’ … David Bowie performing at Earl's Court, 1978.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘A model of agility and physical grace’ … David Bowie performing at Earl's Court, 1978.Photograph: PRDavid Bowie‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett MorgenDavid Hemmings’ never-released concert film from Bowie’s 1978 world tour will be presented in a multimedia show that aims to ‘create the illusion’ that he is present on stageLaura SnapesTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 50 years after its original run, David Bowie’s 1978 Isolar II tour will return to arenas in 2027, billed as Stage, thanks toMoonage Daydreamdirector Brett Morgen’s painstaking remaster of never-before-seen footage.Bowie originally commissioned David Hemmings, the Blow-Up star turned director, to film two shows centred on the “Heroes” and Low albums at London’s Earls Court arena that summer. Bowie had recently been directed by Hemmings in the critically maligned Just a Gigolo, alongside Marlene Dietrich.Bowie intended for the footage to be released as a concert film that could, according to his associates, play in nontraditional venues such as concert venues in lieu of him touring himself. After the Isolar II tour, Bowie would not tour again until the 1983 Serious Moonlight run.The trailer for David Bowie: Stage – videoBut the always fast-evolving musician soon became busy with other projects: recording and releasing Lodger, working with John Cale on music that was never released and Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps).While an acclaimed live album of the tour, Stage (recorded at US dates that spring), was released in autumn 1978, the footage never saw the light of day. “I simply didn’t like the way it had been shot,” Bowie said in 2000. “Now, of course, it looks pretty good and I would suspect that it would make it out some time in the future.”For fans, it became a holy grail of Bowie footage, alongside his lost lost TV debut on Ready Steady Go! in 1966 (asDavid Bowieand the Buzz) and the original 1972 TV performance of Starman on the regional TV show Lift Off With Ayshea, two weeks before the infamous Top of the Pops performance that changed young viewers’ lives across the UK.View image in fullscreenBowie on the Isolar II tour, in an image from Brett Morgen’s remastered footage.Photograph: PRWhen Morgen got the Moonage Daydream gig, he asked to see Hemmings’ original film.
