Hemmings’ footage of “Heroes” made its way into Morgen’s documentary – which won best music film at the 2024 Grammy awards – and was noted by many fans as a highlight, heightening excitement about the full, mostly unseen tour film.The idea of bringing it to arenas was born in 2018, and Morgen subsequently spent years working on the original 35mm, including meticulous colour grading, relighting and hand painting.View image in fullscreen‘Moved away from the elaborate stage characters of earlier years’ … David Bowie on the Isolar II tour.Photograph: Masayoshi Sukita/David Bowie ArchiveThe Earls Court shows “stand among the most important British concerts” of Bowie’s late-70s career,according to fan site David Bowie World, “a period in which Bowie had moved away from the elaborate stage characters of earlier years and placed an increasing emphasis on musicianship, arrangements, sound and atmosphere”.The Isolar II tour ran from March to December 1978. The concerts were split into two parts, the first focusing on Low and “Heroes”, the second dwelling on his early 70s hits, including plenty of songs from Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars.Guitarists Carlos Alomar and Adrian Belew, bassist George Murray, drummer Dennis Davis, keyboardist Roger Powell, pianist Sean Mayes and violinist Simon House provided backing: “his finest [band] by a mile”, according to a review by NME’s Nick Kent. Brian Eno was set to be part of the touring band but had to pull out owing to health issues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘That shimmering sizzle …’Photograph: PRIn his rave review of the Earls Court show, Kent wrote: “Bowie was constantly onstage, a model of agility, and physical grace, determinedly ‘projecting’ while singing loud and dear in a voice that has seldom sounded better … That shimmering sizzle, that fizzy brilliance that is undeniably attuned to Bowie’s work, was all there … It impressed me, it entertained me and very occasionally had me almost spellbound.”Getting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songsRead moreIn the new Stage incarnation, footage of the concert will play across multiple screens accompanied by a lighting show designed by Patrick Woodroffe and an immersive audio mix by Paul Massey. The use of advanced transparent LED screens will “create the illusion that Bowie and his band are physically present on stage”, according to a press release, “enveloping audiences in the atmosphere of a full-scale rock concert for an unprecedented live experience”.The trailer for Stage shows a young man in a leopard print jacket with his girlfriend. That was Mark Adams, who 21 years later would begin working for Bowie – and still does – and had no idea the footage existed until it was shown to the team recently.Stage will have its premiere as part of the 77th Berlin film festival in February before touring.Morgen also directed the documentariesKurt Cobain: Montage of Heck, andCrossfire Hurricane, about the Rolling Stones. Woodroffe worked on lighting for artists including Abba, the Stones and Michael Jackson, as well as at the London 2012 Olympic Games.Explore more on these topicsDavid BowieDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-Z | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description: Rapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in California
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Rapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in California
Content: Jay-Z, pictured performing in Paris last month. The rapper, who produces the Super Bowl halftime show through his company Roc Nation, is headlining it in 2027.Photograph: ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJay-Z, pictured performing in Paris last month. The rapper, who produces the Super Bowl halftime show through his company Roc Nation, is headlining it in 2027.Photograph: ABACA/ShutterstockJay-ZJay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-ZRapper who has helped produce the Super Bowl show for years is stepping up to perform himself, at SoFi Stadium in CaliforniaSian Cainand agenciesMon 26 Oct 2026 22.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter years of producing theSuper Bowlhalf-time show, Jay-Z has announced that the 2027 headline act will be none other than himself.After days of speculation, the NFL, Apple Music and Jay-Z’s company Roc Nation announced on Monday night that the rapper will be the featured performer for the half-time festivities at the Super Bowl LXI on 14 February at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.“From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” said the 56-year-old rapper in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”Roc Nation has partnered with theNFLsince 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl half-time show, beginning with Shakira and Jennifer Lopez’s performance at Super Bowl LIV in 2020.At the time, Jay-Z said he had told the NFL commissioner, Roger Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.”Goodell said on Monday that the NFL had wanted Jay-Z to perform for years.Jay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzyingRead more“When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him,” he said. “I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”Monday’s announcement came a week after reports first emerged that Jay-Z would perform, with some observers speculating that it was unlikely due to his lack of recent hits. Jay-Z’s last solo album, 4:44, was released in 2017 while his last collaborative album was made with his wife, Beyoncé, in 2018, performing together as the Carters.He just closed his Jay-Z 30 concert tour over the weekend at the SoFi Stadium, after performing several dates in New York and London.Born Shawn Carter, Jay-Z has won 25 Grammy awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife,who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalogue includes the albums Reasonable Doubt, The Blueprint and The Black Album, and hit songs such as Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem), 99 Problems and Empire State of Mind, his collaboration with Alicia Keys.His 1996 debut, Reasonable Doubt, was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.Jay-Z’s career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.Bad Bunny performedat last season’s Super Bowl in February, bringing on special guests including Lady Gaga, Ricky Martin, Jessica Alba, Karol G, Cardi B, Young Miko, and Pedro Pascal.The Puerto Rican superstar’s songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours after the show.Past Super Bowl half-time show headliners includeKendrick Lamar,Rihanna, theWeeknd, Michael Jackson, the Who, Madonna, Coldplay and the Blues Brothers.Associated Press contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsJay-ZSuper BowlUS sportsNFLShareReuse this content

title: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to co-host Junior MasterChef Australia: ‘It was an easy yes’ | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: After Meghan appeared on MasterChef Australia this year, co-host Poh Ling Yeow says being reunited with the Duchess on the children’s version ‘will be a real treat’
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: After Meghan appeared on MasterChef Australia this year, co-host Poh Ling Yeow says being reunited with the Duchess on the children’s version ‘will be a real treat’
Content: The Duchess of Sussex, who will co-host Junior MasterChef Australia in 2027. Meghan’s co-host will be  Poh Ling Yeow.Photograph: 10View image in fullscreenThe Duchess of Sussex, who will co-host Junior MasterChef Australia in 2027. Meghan’s co-host will be  Poh Ling Yeow.Photograph: 10Meghan, the Duchess of SussexMeghan, Duchess of Sussex, to co-host Junior MasterChef Australia: ‘It was an easy yes’After Meghan appeared on MasterChef Australia this year, co-host Poh Ling Yeow says being reunited with the Duchess on the children’s version ‘will be a real treat’Emma JoyceMon 26 Oct 2026 21.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 21.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duchess of Sussex is set to co-host JuniorMasterChef Australia, the children’s version of the popular televised cooking competition, in 2027.Meghan made her debut appearance on the adult version of MasterChef Australia in July this year, which was filmed during afour-day visit to Australiawith Prince Harry in April. Network 10 said the Duchess’s appearance on the show drew its “largest Sunday audience since 2023”.Now the broadcaster has confirmed Meghan will co-host Junior MasterChef Australia, the children’s version of the show with contestants aged between nine and 13.Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine ministerRead moreNo date has been set for production, which will take place at Melbourne Showgrounds.“I had an incredible time with the whole team at MasterChef this past April, so when they approached me to come back and work with this young group of talent, it was an easy yes,” the Duchess of Sussex said in a statement.“I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun. I can’t wait to see what they cook up!”It is unknown whether it means a temporary relocation to Australia for Meghan, Prince Harry and their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. The familyrelocated to the UK in August, after living in California for six years.Meghan will host Junior MasterChef Australia with current MasterChef Australia judge Poh Ling Yeow, who will continue to judge the adult show in 2027 as well.“I had a lovely time filming with Meghan earlier this year, and being reunited will be a real treat,” Yeow said in a statement. “I can’t wait to meet our pint-sized culinary adventurers.”The news of Meghan’s next television appearance comes in the same week the Duchess of Sussex revealed she had been made aware that her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, had been accused of possessing child sexual abuse images.Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities in the Philippines last week alleging that he had discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images at his father’s former home there.Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick” and “a bunch of lies”. He claimed the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025.The allegations against Markle Sr are currently being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu,authorities have confirmed.Met says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forcesRead moreOn Sunday, Meghanrevealed in a statementthrough her spokesperson that the Met had made her aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2019.“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said.The Sussexes are reported to have settled in the Cotswolds after leaving the US. In September, they condemned the“reckless intrusion” of two photographerswho were spotted outside Archie and Lilibet’s school. Their children have since moved schools.The Duchess of Sussex’s lifestyle showWith Love, Meghanran for two seasons on Netflix. It has been widely reported that the show won’t return for a third season despite Netflix reporting it was viewed 5.3m times globally in the first half of 2025.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMasterChef AustraliaChildren's TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: incredible photos of the ‘Black Is Beautiful’ movement | Television | The Guardian
description: This brilliant film follows photographer Kwame Brathwaite and his stunning archive. Plus: unseen Only Fools and Horses gems. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: This brilliant film follows photographer Kwame Brathwaite and his stunning archive. Plus: unseen Only Fools and Horses gems. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The actor Radiah Fyre photographed by Kwame Brathwaite.Photograph: BBC/Kwame S. Brathwaite The Kwame Brathwaite ArchiveView image in fullscreenThe actor Radiah Fyre photographed by Kwame Brathwaite.Photograph: BBC/Kwame S. Brathwaite The Kwame Brathwaite ArchiveTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: incredible photos of the ‘Black Is Beautiful’ movementThis brilliant film follows photographer Kwame Brathwaite and his stunning archive. Plus: unseen Only Fools and Horses gems. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Hannah VerdierandGraeme VirtueTue 27 Oct 2026 02.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 02.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStoryville: Black Is Beautiful – The Kwame Brathwaite Story10pm, BBC Four“Every photo in this film was taken by Kwame Brathwaite or is of Kwame Brathwaite,” starts this brilliant documentary. And what photos! Over seven decades, the Harlem photographer captured shots that helped define the Black Is Beautiful movement – including pictures of big stars and daily African American life. Brathwaite’s family, along with Alicia Keys, Swizz Beatz, Gabrielle Union and Jesse Williams, help tell the story with his stunning archive.Hollie RichardsonThe Handel Scandal: The Making of the Messiah8pm, Sky ArtsBy 1741, Handel needed a hit. As presenter soprano Danielle de Niese relates, he took a gamble on Susannah Cibber, a gifted singer whose career had been damaged by a sex scandal, and cast her in the first performance of Messiah. And, as simply stated here, “she transformed his fortunes – and he gave her back her voice”.Ali CatterallBlue Lights9pm, BBC One“Can you live with it, Helen, all those secrets you’re carrying?” Sandra (Andi Osho) is set on exposing the cover-ups surrounding the collapsed trial for Gerry’s murder. Might Jen be able to help her, even if it involves dobbing in her own mother? Meanwhile, the future of Blackthorn is more precarious than ever.HRStacey Dooley: Death in the Barracks9pm, BBC ThreeDooley’s latest run covers hard-hitting stories and this week she examines the case of Royal Artillery Gunner Jaysley Beck, who was found dead in her army barracks just months after reporting a sexual assault. Beck’s family are still looking for answers, so bravely agree to talk, along with friends and colleagues.Hannah VerdierOnly Fools and Horses: The Lost Archive9pm, U&GoldView image in fullscreenNicholas Lyndhurst (left) and David Jason as Rodney and Derek Trotter in Only Fools and Horses.Photograph: BBCThe second helping of comedy gems that were cut from the classic sitcom, as David Jason, his co-stars and the crew enjoy watching previously unseen outtakes. If you loved Mother Nature’s Son, we get to see inside Grandad’s shed.HRGolden State Killer: Unmasking a Monster9pm, Sky CrimeIn 2020, ex-cop Joseph DeAngelo pleaded guilty to 13 murders and nearly 50 rapes across California in the 1970s and 80s. But could this “serial sexual sadist” be responsible for many more killings and attacks? The opening double bill of this four-parter offers up some fairly convincing, if circumstantial, theories.Graeme VirtueExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightDocumentaryTV comedyClassical musicFactual TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Michael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiver | Biography books | The Guardian
description: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered
Content: Michael Gambon in 2016.Photograph: Roger Askew/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMichael Gambon in 2016.Photograph: Roger Askew/REX/ShutterstockBook of the dayBiography booksReviewMichael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiverFrom the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unansweredKathryn HughesTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the south-east London suburbs embellished his CV with entirely fabricated theatrical experience. It was a gamble, but it worked. In 1962 he made his professional debut as the Second Gentleman in Othello. The following year he was hired by Laurence Olivier for the brand new National Theatre.Gambon carried on telling tall tales long after there was any need. Some were self-aggrandising: he had been a dancer with the Royal Ballet, worked as a nuclear physicist and auditioned for James Bond. To be fair, this last one was half-true – producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli had once called him in for a chat. Others were absurdities for the sake of it: he was thinking of buying a house in Hanoi, his mother had operated cranes in Dublin. Occasionally, the lies were intended to save his skin. Terrified of being sacked for turning up late yet again to rehearsal at the National, he claimed that his mother had died in the night. She went on to live for another 49 years. More often, he lied to make other people laugh, claiming that he had worked with the Russian director Dmitri Shagyerarsoff.Gambon’s compulsion to invent and conceal presents obvious challenges for Jasper Rees, the veteran stage and showbiz journalist who interviewed the actor several times before his death in 2023 and reports always coming away feeling puzzled. Rees’s authorised biography draws on the archive held by Gambon’s wife, Anne, a woman whose existence was unknown to most of his colleagues. For years Gambon had a relationship with the NationalTheatreadministrator Lyn Haill and was later photographed with set designer Philippa Hart, with whom he had two sons. Yet, apart from a brief period in the early 1970s, he remained in the marital home in Kent. That marriage lasted 61 years, and Anne and their son Fergus accompanied Gambon to Buckingham Palace when he was knighted in 1998.Rees largely leaves his subject’s private life tactfully alone, focusing instead on the origins of Gambon’s talent for deflecting scrutiny. He belonged to no obvious cohort or peer group. Unlike Tom Courtenay and Albert Finney, he had not attended drama school. Unlike Ian McKellen and Derek Jacobi, he had not made his way to Cambridge on a scholarship. Instead he emerged from working-class London-Irish amateur dramatics, where his practical skills were useful for building sets. This delight in making and tinkering remained with him throughout his life: in his home workshop he once built an exact replica of an antique pistol that he’d been asked to restore by a West End dealer, “so really I’m a faker”.Rees cross-references Gambon’s tall tales with other actors’ archives and draws on more than 100 new interviews, including conversations with Eileen Atkins, Penelope Wilton, Brian Cox and Simon Russell Beale. He also uses the archive of New York Times critic Mel Gussow, whose collection of interviews with Gambon appeared in 2004. The result is probably as near as anyone will get to a definitive account of Gambon’s life and career, although you would not want to bet on one or two of the actor’s misdirections slipping through undetected.View image in fullscreenMichael Gambon (left) and Brian Cox worked together on a 1968 prodction of Othello.Photograph: PRDespite being chosen by Olivier for the nascent National, Gambon initially failed to progress much beyond spear-carrying. His thuggish good looks – he was over 6ft tall, barrel-built, with a face of fleshy menace – made him useful as background colour. His unfamiliarity with the classical and modern repertory, not to mention the demands of iambic pentameter, left him ill-equipped for more demanding roles. Only after leaving in 1967 in search of better parts did his potential emerge. Most notably he played Tom in the London opening of Alan Ayckbourn’s The Norman Conquests.Gambon’s return to the National in 1978 saw him triumph in Pinter’s new play Betrayal and a revival of Brecht’s The Life of Galileo, which established him as a leading stage actor. In 1986, his performance in the BBC’s The Singing Detective made him a household name. Although he was reportedly not the first choice, the part of Dennis Potter’s Philip Marlow could have been written for him. Confined to a hospital bed by psoriatic arthritis and heavily bandaged, Marlow escapes his anguish by imagining parallel lives. He becomes a private detective and nightclub crooner, inhabiting a world of femmes fatales and Nazi spies, while revisiting a childhood scarred by his parents’ sexual unhappiness. Gambon plays a man who assumes multiple identities but never escapes himself.He liked to give the impression that he never planned anything, simply accepting the next job that came up. Perhaps that was true: there were certainly some poor choices along the way. For the moment, though, Gambon made the most of his newfound stardom. The following year, he played Eddie Carbone in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge. Miller was enchanted: “This guy can really disappear into a role.” The Guardian wrote that it showed “Michael Gambon shaking hands with greatness”.Rees devotes perhaps too much of this nearly 600-page book to Gambon’s mischief on stage and screen. His interviewees recall fart machines, water bombs and ad libs designed to throw fellow actors off their lines. The stories are often funny, but their cumulative effect is less comfortable. Was Gambon merely an antic fool, or was he a bit of a sadist? Rees leaves the verdict to his witnesses. Penelope Wilton recalls that the water pistols “got very tedious”.During RSC rehearsals Eileen Atkins remembers him saying, “I don’t bother with matinees, I just say the words”, which made her furious. He also lost interest once a production had peaked. After the triumphant opening of A View from the Bridge, he began, says co-star Michael Simkins, to “gently destroy it”. His performances deteriorated and the anticipated New York transfer never materialised.Gambon’s gradual decline makes for painful reading. In his late 50s he began to struggle with lines, flubbing them or improvising in ways that were no longer funny. Prompt boards were introduced, followed by “earwigs”, tiny earpieces through which a prompter fed him lines. This worked best on screen, where performances could be patched together from multiple takes, as happened in the Harry Potter films, where Gambon took over as Dumbledore after Richard Harris’s death. On stage, the difficulties became increasingly hard to conceal. Rees reveals that Gambon was diagnosed with dementia, something which he always denied, perhaps because he had watched his mother ravaged by the disease. It is at this late stage that we begin to glimpse the vulnerability and terror of exposure that lay beneath decades of blustery bravado.Rees avoids a conventional cradle-to-grave structure by following each main chapter with an interlude devoted to an aspect of Gambon’s character or career that might otherwise get lost in the narrative. One explores his beautifully elegant hands, evident in his wand work in Harry Potter; another his love of fast cars, memorably displayed on Top Gear’s Star in a Reasonably Priced Car segment, when he almost overturned a family saloon.Rees’s chief challenge is to convey what made Gambon such a great actor. He collates the testimony of colleagues and the verdicts of critics, but neither quite captures the alchemy of a performance. Nor can the actor’s wildly conflicting qualities be assembled into a single coherent character. This unresolved tension is not a failure of the biography so much as its most fitting conclusion: one suspects it is exactly the way that Gambon would have liked it.Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBiography booksBook of the dayActingTheatreMichael GambonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Big Baby review – a screenwriter’s nightmares become reality in a meta-horror misfire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Spider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn characters
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Spider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn characters
Content: ‘There are flashes of something great here’ … Big Baby.Photograph: ShudderView image in fullscreen‘There are flashes of something great here’ … Big Baby.Photograph: ShudderMoviesReviewBig Baby review – a screenwriter’s nightmares become reality in a meta-horror misfireSpider One’s latest shocker has a few good ideas and a strong central performance, but it’s difficult to care about the gory misfortune inflicted upon these unlikable and thinly drawn charactersCatherine BrayTue 27 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn this slasher directed by Michael Cummings, AKA Powerman 5000 singer Spider One, Adam Lewis (Brandon Scott) is a screenwriter who spends too much time fretting about what the film reviewers he claims to despise think about his work, and not enough time writing. It’s a little hard initially to get a handle on exactly where this writing really sits: are we meant to believe he’s a misunderstood genius, or are the reviewers, in fact, correct? When Big Baby opens, Adam’s most recent film is being negatively reviewed by a couple of blowhards on a horror podcast, then he later gets grouchy with his all-too patient and supportive girlfriend (Krsy Fox) when she dares to imply he may never win an Academy Award. It emerges he’s aiming for a career something like Jordan Peele’s, but figures he’s not above trying for something more in the Sean S Cunningham oeuvre.For the first half of Big Baby, a pattern develops: Adam attempts to write, or search for inspiration, only to be haunted by a vision or dream about a slasher villain in a baby mask. Scott, as it happens, is a decent actor and does good work in the dialogue-free scenes, but the words themselves are a problem: it’s would-be smart material that hangs the character out to dry as a self-aggrandising, touchy killjoy and it’s hard to see why most of the people in his life would want to stay in touch. Scott’s charisma helps, but can’t completely counteract an unprepossessingly drawn character.In the horror movie roadmap, Big Baby lives a few degrees south of the likes of meta-slasher Wes Craven’s New Nightmare, and a little west of John Carpenter’s delirious In the Mouth of Madness. This is the kind of horror where in-universe script and reality bleed into each other. Unfortunately, it’s not sharp and tightly delineated enough for the former, while not sufficiently insane for the latter.For its first half, Big Baby is too often bogged down trying for character development: close to 90% of every conversation is about Adam and his anxieties, while the girlfriend character, played with a certain spark by Fox, doesn’t seem to have anything much going on in her own life. It’s a frustrating film, because there are flashes of something great here, but in the final analysis, Big Baby crawls rather than walks.Big Baby is on Shudder and AMC+ from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Arnie & Barney review – dimwit ant double-act from Maya the Bee are on mission to entertain | Movies | The Guardian
description: From the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holiday
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: From the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holiday
Content: Tiresome ant-ics … Arnie & Barney.View image in fullscreenTiresome ant-ics … Arnie & Barney.MoviesReviewArnie & Barney review – dimwit ant double-act from Maya the Bee are on mission to entertainFrom the ugly design to the lacklustre script, this is one parents might want to skip this half-term holidayCatherine BrayTue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1912 in Germany, antisemitic writer Waldemar Bonsels published The Adventures of Maya the Bee, which later became a 1970s anime series in Japan called Maya the Honey Bee, and was later dubbed into English a couple of times, including for kids TV channel Nickelodeon in the 1990s anda bunch of films between 2014 and 2021. Still with us? Recurring characters from the show include Arnie and Barney, a pair of dimwit ants, and now, at long last, they have their own spin-off movie.The film opens very muchin media res, with a young female bee flying through outer space clutching a small pig and droplet of water the size of her head. She’s being pursued aggressively by a handful of wasp-type creatures and a narrator solemnly intones: “Sometimes the most unlikely heroes … become legends.” The bee then stops next to a couple of red ants and asks what they’re doing. They are the narrators, they explain, but this his is all soon revealed as fantasy – the pair of ants are telling a story to a larger platoon of ants. Some exposition follows about the ants’ mission: to find fresh water.This is fine as far as it goes, perhaps, but what a précis can’t convey is quite how staggeringly ugly and uninteresting the whole endeavour is. It starts with the character design: it’s hard to imagine any but the most aesthetically starved children embracing this ant pair. Boy are they a chore to spend time with, both visually and in terms of the lacklustre script. Even if you are struggling for entertainment options you might want to do the kids a favour and skip this one.Arnie & Barney is in UK cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFilm adaptationsFamily filmsTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: We, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop Oil | Movies | The Guardian
description: The levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’
Content: Close to the action … We, The HatedPhotograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenClose to the action … We, The HatedPhotograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewWe, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop OilThe levels of violence aimed at these protesters is depressing, but their aim is to save the planet: ‘If they want to destroy everything, they’ve got to go through us’Cath ClarkeTue 27 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Hated” is not putting it too strongly. The strength of feeling againstJust Stop Oil, as caught by this documentary, is really disturbing. It’s filmed from inside the climate group’s protests, and as activists block roads, furious drivers hurl abuse. “Have a wash you fucking idiots!” “Middle class wankers!” It gets physical, too – punching, kicking and dragging. One man appears to drive his van at protesters. Another walks along a line of them, pouring water over their heads, one by one.Film-maker Rich Felgate could not be closer to the action; his girlfriend, Indigo Rumbelow, is an activist. “Don’t look at the camera. I’m a fly on the wall,” he tells her at their shared house, where books about the suffragettes and Gandhi are on the shelves. On the streets, activists glue themselves to roads and fasten their necks together with bike locks. In October 2022, campaigners notoriously lobbedtomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers. At one road shutdown an angry driver shouts: “You’re children.” But they’re not all young; a vicar in late middle age with Parkinson’s quickly takes his medicine before he’s cuffed.The group’s strategy is to stay disruptive, stay in the news. We watch Just Stop Oil spokespeople appear on TV in increasingly hostile interviews. Their argument is that the planet is in crisis, there is no time to lose. Piers Morgan et al tell them their message is lost in the tactics. And it does look like that: by targeting infrastructure that hits ordinary people after protests aimed directly at the fossil fuel industry don’t work, Just Stop Oil throws away goodwill generated towards protesters acting on their consciences. Still, they claim a victory when Labour wins the election in 2024, pledging no new licences for gas and oilfields. (It seems that last week’sgo-ahead for the Jackdaw North Sea gasfielddoes not break that pledge, since it already holds a licence.)As Just Stop Oil actions escalate, Rumbelow and other activists are arrested and jailed,handed down the longest-ever prison sentencesin England for nonviolent protest. When the credits roll, you have to wonder who the real vandals are..We, the Hated is in UK cinemas from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsJust Stop OilProtestreviewsShareReuse this content

title: City of Masks review – theatreland ghost story with female phantom of the opera out for revenge | Movies | The Guardian
description: In a West End theatre, a young actor hears a disembodied voice coaching his singing. It’s the start of an icky ghost-on-human romance
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: In a West End theatre, a young actor hears a disembodied voice coaching his singing. It’s the start of an icky ghost-on-human romance
Content: Sensual and mysterious … Eve (Amanda Jiang) in City of Masks.Photograph: BUFF StudiosView image in fullscreenSensual and mysterious … Eve (Amanda Jiang) in City of Masks.Photograph: BUFF StudiosMoviesReviewCity of Masks review – theatreland ghost story with female phantom of the opera out for revengeIn a West End theatre, a young actor hears a disembodied voice coaching his singing. It’s the start of an icky ghost-on-human romanceCath ClarkeTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis ghost story set in a West End theatre is creakier than the old wooden floorboards on stage. It’s a gender reversal of Phantom of the Opera with a female phantom: wildly talented composer Eve (Amanda Jiang), who died tragically in a theatre fire. Or did she? That’s the question for earnest young actor Christian (Charlie Goddard) cast as the lead in a revival of Eve’s hit musical, City of Masks. It’s being staged in the very theatre where she died. Then Christian starts hearing a ghostly disembodied voice coaching his singing.Part of the problem with the film is a clash of acting styles. Jiang seems to have stepped out of a David Lynch film to play Eve; sensual and mysterious. Meanwhile, actor Deano Bugatti Mitchison channels Al Pacino in Scarface levels of intensity to play the revival’s director, coked-up theatre impresario Victor – surely the only director in the West End to keep a loaded gun in his desk drawerVictor is suspected of involvement in the fire that killed Eve and the tabloids are sniffing around. Meanwhile, Eve is all out for revenge: lights flicker, bits of rigging fly off the walls. Whether or not she is a ghost, Christian seems to be developing big feelings for her – and as in any film with the prospect of ghost-on-human romance, it gets a bit ick. And as it goes on the film gets more and more baffling, so confusing that I went back and watched it again, convinced I’d missed something vital that would make sense of it. But no.City of Masks is in UK cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsHorror filmsMusicalsTheatreThrillersRomance filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Master Builder review – false swagger and queasy infidelity propel Ibsen’s big-drop drama | Stage | The Guardian
description: David Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignore
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: David Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignore
Content: Hicks is almost antic, and Binder is marvellous … left to right: Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) and Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenHicks is almost antic, and Binder is marvellous … left to right: Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) and Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianStageReviewThe Master Builder review – false swagger and queasy infidelity propel Ibsen’s big-drop dramaArcola theatre, LondonDavid Edgar’s translation grounds Ibsen’s otherworldly play about a middle-aged architect’s fall from power, but its flaws are too loud to ignoreArifa AkbarTue 27 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis outing of Henrik Ibsen’s play, translated by playwright David Edgar, is reassuring afterLila Raicek’s oddly conceived West End version last year starring Ewan McGregor– as well intentioned as its feminist revisionism might have been.Edgar’s is more faithful to the original in form and spirit (although he compresses three acts into two), and its strengths lie in drawing out the psychological aspects of the ageing, anxious master builder at its centre, whose fall from the heights of worldly acclaim is both real and symbolic in a play that blends both those realms together.Halvard Solness (Greg Hicks) is determined to keep his place in the world but also plagued by midlife insecurity – and the protege Ragnar Brovik (Ryan Wichert) whom he perceives to be snapping at his heels – when he is confronted by Hilde Wangel (Louisa Binder), a young woman who has come to claim the “kingdom” he promised her in an encounter when she was 13.Edgar deftly draws out the intimacies and tensions between characters in this curious story, with its enigmatic ending and its growing sense of otherworldliness. Except there is nothing otherworldly to the production: director Mehmet Ergen gives the characters a solidity in his modern-dress production.View image in fullscreenIntimacies and tensions … (from left) Sally George (Aline Solness), Louisa Binder (Hilde Wangel), Peter Guinness (Doctor Herdal) and Greg Hicks (Halvard Solness) in The Master Builder.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThis world is recognisable, with Hilde real and a symbol of his past – or a consequence of it. She brings memories Solness claims to have forgotten and you can read the #MeToo subtext in his amnesia. It is queasy to hear about the kisses he gave her as a girl, and queasier still to feel the flirtation now between them.Hicks is animated, almost antic, as a man at the height of his worldly pomp who is inwardly unravelling. Binder is marvellous as Hilde, almost swaggering as she runs rings around him. Sally George, too, is very believable as Solness’s wife, Aline, forever grieving the death of their twin children and well able to see her husband’s emotional infidelities with the women that float around him, including office assistant Kaja (Jade Williams).Yet the drama still hits against the limits of Ibsen’s strange and static story: you do not quite know if Solness is to be admired or condemned, and what of Hilde’s final triumphalism as she sees him fall from his tower? The puzzle of the ending might be the workings of fate, the personal cost of success, or an Icarus-like comeuppance for a middle-aged man in thrall to a younger woman. This production does not feel like a tragedy. You do not feel for Solness, or his fall. But then, were you ever supposed to?AtArcola theatre, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreHenrik IbsenArcola theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cheer up, Scrooge! The merriest Christmas theatre shows, from musketeers to a penguin party | Christmas shows | The Guardian
description: The festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella
Content: Wrongdoings, reckonings and redemption … Stuart Bowman as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol at the Royal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenWrongdoings, reckonings and redemption … Stuart Bowman as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol at the Royal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicChristmas showsCheer up, Scrooge! The merriest Christmas theatre shows, from musketeers to a penguin partyThe festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s CinderellaArifa AkbarTue 27 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Little Night MusicRoyal Exchange theatre, Manchester, 5 December to 30 JanuarySelina Cartmell is sending in the clowns this Christmas, directing Stephen Sondheim’s fairytale musical about mismatched couples. Originally inspired by an Ingmar Bergman film, it has some of the most exquisite songs of Sondheim’s magnificent oeuvre and is choreographed by former Strictly judge Arlene Phillips.The Three MusketeersRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, 28 November to 9 JanuaryBuckle up for some swashbuckling: the RSC’s version of D’Artagnan’s duelling adventures alongside Athos, Porthos and Aramis is co-produced with Told By an Idiot, a company known for its visual comedy. It is billed as a “wild” new adaptation of Alexandre Dumas’s novel and features an international company of performers.Honk!Barn theatre, Cirencester, 21 November to 3 JanuaryIn George Stiles and Anthony Drewe’s musical drama for all ages, Ugly is a plucky wee duck, teased by siblings and friends alike for his idiosyncratic looks. We find him undertaking a perilous wild goose (duckling?) chase in his quest to discover the beautiful drake within.View image in fullscreenTate Masuku goes walking in the air with Andrew Ashton as the Snowman.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe SnowmanBirmingham Repuntil 1 November, thenPeacock theatre, London, 21 November to 3 January 2027Raymond Briggs’s gorgeous snowman goes walking in the air again ina new version of the Christmas classic, about an unlikely friendship that takes delightful flight. Featuring Howard Blake’s timeless score, it is now directed and choreographed by Will Tuckett and features puppets designed by Tahra Zafar, who recreated Michael Bond’s Paddington Bear for the West End musical.The Merry Adventures of Maid MarianSherman theatre, Cardiff, 27 November to 2 JanuaryThe Robin Hood story is relocated and respun to place a female outlaw at its centre. Now it is Maid Marian of south Wales, whose resistance against the king’s men will be accompanied by familiar faces from the legend. Performed by a band of actor-musicians and directed by Lee Lyford.AntarcticaPolka theatre, London, 27 November to 17 JanuaryHere’s a south pole show filled with icy wildlife, from tripping penguins to cheeky albatrosses. There are clowns, puppets and the promise of some magical surprises in this tale of what lies at the bottom of our planet. A winter wonderland for children, aimed at three- to seven-year-olds.View image in fullscreenHappy anniversary … Hannah Kremer and Rory Macleod in Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella.Photograph: Johan PerssonMatthew Bourne’s CinderellaTouring from 16 NovemberAmid the season’s flurry of fairytale princesses in glass slippers isMatthew Bourne’s 30-year-old ballet, twirling back for an anniversary tour. Set during the second world war, it situates the romance in blitz-torn London. Hannah Kremer and Katrina Lyndon share the role of Cinders, who meets an RAF pilot. The show travels to 17 venues over 24 weeks.Robin Hood and the Merry MandemTheatre Royal Stratford East, 21 November to 2 JanuaryAnother spin on the heroic outlaws of Sherwood folklore. This Robin Hood hails from E15 and hits east London in a hoodie, along with his merry band of “mandem”. Nottinghamshire’s forest is swapped for housing estates, retail jungles and the Central Line commuter rush as Robin’s men take from the undeserving rich to give to the area’s poor.The Reluctant DragonMarlowe theatre, Canterbury, 5 December to 3 JanuaryA child befriends a flamboyant, poetry-reciting dragon and embarks on an intrepid campaign to save it from a slayer who mistakes it for a fire-breathing fiend in Kenneth Grahame’s book. A David and Goliath story in reverse, now told as a musical family show.Santa’s First ChristmasUnicorn theatre, London, 14 November to 3 JanuaryThe elves want old Saint Nicholas to take five from shimmying up and down chimneys and drink in some yuletide spirit himself in this adaptation of Mac Barnett’s book. Directed and choreographed by Olivier award-winner James Cousins, it has songs by Harry Blake.The Jungle BookNational Theatre, London, 13 November to 6 FebruaryThe National Theatre’s Christmas shows have hit the mark in recent years. This one reimagines Rudyard Kipling’s classic tale of Mowgli and friends’ adventures through the mangroves of the Sundarbans. It’s adapted by Anupama Chandrasekhar and staged by the NT’s artistic director, Indhu Rubasingham, with puppetry by Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell.The Further Adventures of Peter Pan: The Return of Captain HookGrand Opera House York, 5 December to 3 JanuaryJust when we thought Neverland was safe! Captain Hook strikes back in this continuation of JM Barrie’s story about the pirate’s feud with the forever young leader of the Lost Boys. Here it comes in the form of a pantomime, complete with songs and aerial stunts.Miss Bennet: Christmas at PemberleyPark theatre, London, 2 December to 10 JanuaryThe hot new takes on Pride and Prejudice keep on coming. This festive permutation by playwrights Lauren Gunderson and Margot Melcon finds the Bennets reuniting at the family estate, and centres on bookish middle sister, Mary, and aChristmasvisit from Lord Arthur de Bourgh.A Christmas CarolRoyal Lyceum theatre, Edinburgh, 28 November to 3 JanuaryWhat’s Christmas without this classic about moral wrongdoings, ghostly reckonings and redemption, featuring the stingy Ebenezer Scrooge? Charles Dickens’ Victorian London is swapped for Edinburgh in the Lyceum’s production, adapted by Deborah McAndrew and directed by James Brining. It might be comfy Christmas fare, but it still contains resonant messages for our times about the duty to be charitable.Explore more on these topicsChristmas showsChristmasTheatreDancePanto seasonMusicalsSherman theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary! | US theater | The Guardian
description: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy
Content: ‘But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.’Photograph: Shaun VadellaView image in fullscreen‘But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.’Photograph: Shaun VadellaUS theaterInterview‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary!Owen MyersThe RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedyTue 27 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlaska may be starring in the most subversive comedy in American theater today, but she carries herself with the poise of a 40s movie star. On a brisk September afternoon, the actor, comedian and RuPaul’s Drag Race alumnus is in a small rehearsal room in New York’s midtown, sipping hot tea from a flask while perched on a hard-shell travel case. She sits bolt upright, as if she has spent her life balancing books on her head.Oh, Mary! review – Cole Escola’s gloriously deranged historical rompRead moreIt has been a madcap time for the actor as she prepares to play Mary Todd Lincoln in a new touring production of Cole Escola’s Tony award-winning comedyOh, Mary!. She is amid a few weeks of rehearsals in the city before the show’s four-month sprint across the US. When I ask how she is handling the upheaval from her Los Angeles home, she smiles indulgently. “I mean, I would go to the planet Remulak for this show,” she says, referencing the home planet of theConeheads. “I didn’t even think about it. I was just like, ‘Let’s make this happen.’”Alaska (AKA Alaska Thunderfuck 5000, born Justin Honard) is on the brink of her biggest career moment yet and is determined to make every moment of it count. Since competing in season five of RuPaul’s Drag Race in 2013, the self-described “extraterrestrial phenomenon from the planet Glamtr0n” has released five electro-pop albums with titles like Anus and Vagina, taken to the high seas for drag-themed cruises and co-written and performed in the off-Broadway hit Drag: The Musical, produced byLiza Minnelli. Her live performances showcase the art of drag at its high-concept creative peak; a recentperformanceof Taylor Swift’s The Fate of Ophelia was a delightfully dizzying hurricane of hairstyles, props, frills and feathers, with three costume changes in as many minutes.View image in fullscreenAlaska and Wesley Taylor in the first national tour of Oh, Mary!Photograph: Evan Zimmerman/MurphyMadeWith Oh, Mary!, Alaska is stepping away from nightlife stages and into the shoes of a character already played by actors including Maya Rudolph, Jane Krakowski and Jinkx Monsoon as well as Escola. A London production opened in 2025, while a live-recorded special of the show will air on HBO next year. The character of Mary Todd Lincoln, in Escola and director Sam Pinkleton’s vision, is stifled by her duties, drinks to escape the unbearable company of her (closeted) husband, and longs to return to the life as a cabaret star that she gave up to be first lady.Director Pinkleton first encountered Alaska over a decade ago when she played Nomi Malone in aShowgirls tributeshow at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre. “It was electric,” he tells me. “I was like, ‘This person is a star; you can’t take your eyes off her.’”Pinkleton cast Alaska in a 2021Los Angelesproduction of Head Over Heels, which reimagined the Broadway musical as a queer rave. “I couldn’t believe how much she cared and how great she was technically,” he says. “I have since worked with a lot of drag queens, and I’ve had exclusively great experiences because they are really hard workers. You know, they make everything happen on their own.”‘Bodies, pornography and disgust’: did 2 Girls 1 Cup change the way a generation thinks about sex?Read moreAfter an initial Zoom workshop with Pinkleton and Escola this March, Alaska was offered the role of Mary this summer. She was particularly struck by the purity of the character’s ambition, even as she resorts to increasingly bizarre tactics to get back on the cabaret stage where she belongs. “This isn’t a comedy show to me,” Alaska says. “This is deathly serious. It’s very real, and I think that’s why so many people can step into the role and make it seem like it’s written for them.“I feel like I can make sense of this role,” she adds. “I can’t name any other role where I feel like I make sense. I mean, being a weird drag queen person, queer-bodied person existing in society … that’s exactly what I felt like when I grew up.”Raised in Erie, Pennsylvania, she was a shy and watchful kid. “I wish that I had the confidence to be like, ‘You know what? I am something and I do deserve more than like being scared to go out of my fucking room,’” she says. “It wasn’t until many years later, when I discovered theater and drag, that I was able to find that in myself. But it is a feeling of like, ‘Fuck, I can’tbe.’”She was introduced to the world of performance while on school trips: she caught a touring production of The Phantom of the Opera while in Canada, and saw a version of Cats at SeaWorld. (“Maybe they should do Oh, Mary! on water skis in Florida,” she muses.) She was especially drawn to the over-the-top femininity of film characters like Jessica Rabbit and Michelle Pfeiffer’s Catwoman. “Not real people”, she notes.As a theater major at the University of Pittsburgh, she starred in a 1922 Czech expressionist drama called The Insect Play (she played a murderous wasp) as well as in Brecht’s Mother Courage and Her Children. Importantly, the program taught every aspect of mounting a production, including directing, playwriting, set design and costume – crucial skills for a drag superstar in the making.After a few years of gigging around LA, Alaska won a slot on RuPaul’s Drag Race season five. For many fans, it’s still the best season, with a cast that also included Jinkx Monsoon (now aBroadwaystar in her own right) as well as much-loved comedy queens Detox and Alyssa Edwards. Alaska was the rare queen that could do it all; she finished as runner-up and after the season aired in 2013, she found herself as one of the most famous drag queens in America. “It was being shot out of a fucking cannon. I was in my late 20s, but still mentally I was still a child.”Alaska and her then-partner Sharon Needles (who had won season four ofDragRace) went from being broke and scraping together money for a 12-pack of beer to being the most famous drag queen couple in America. “Our lives changed a lot really fast, and we made every single mistake that you can make,” she says. “There was no gameplan. There was no roadmap. We suddenly had money and we never had a fucking penny before. It wasdo every drug,drink every thing.”After reading a book by the Buddhist nun Pema Chödrön, who she says “does a really good job of talking about meditation and consciousness in a way that a dumb American can understand”, Alaska became sober for two and a half years. These days, she has a more moderate relationship with alcohol, which has set her up to be in fighting shape for Oh, Mary! “The rehearsal has been really intense,” she says. “It’s like doing cardio every day. Which is great, because I hate cardio.”Despite its financial successes in New York (Oh, Mary! was the first show of the 2024-25 season to recoup its costs), the show is perhaps not the most natural choice to tour a politically divided country, with dates in smaller cities including Hartford, Connecticut, and Saint Paul, as well as Los Angeles and Boston. “I think it’s pretty great,” Alaska says. “It’s going to be interesting because there are going to be people seeing the show who don’t go see Broadway shows all the time. I’m excited to shock people.“I mean, it would even be important even if we didn’t have a piece of shit in the Oval Office,” she says. “But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.”View image in fullscreenJohn-Andrew Morrison and Alaska in Oh, Mary!Photograph: Evan ZimmermanThe pipeline from drag superstar to grande dame of theatre hasn’t always been so well established, and Alaska credits Jinkx Monsoon’s arc from Drag Race to Broadway as an inspiration. “She’s slammed open so many doors for so many people,” Alaska says. “And she continues to do so. I’m glad to walk right through, honey.”Does she face stereotypes because of her background in drag? “It’s definitely better now. I mean, I’ve been doing drag for almost 20 years. On a Hollywood set, a dog would get better treatment than a drag queen. And that’s not even an exaggeration. That’s hard, and that shit still exists and still happens.”I’m curious if Drag Race feels far away to Alaska now. It’s been 10 years since she was crowned the winner of All Stars season two. “Yes and no”, she says. “My job as a podcaster is talking about Drag Race. I still work with all the girls from Drag Race all the time. Yes, it’s in the past, but still it’s very much a part of my life. I wish I was more in that universe, but they won’t fucking invite me. So if they read this, maybe they could call me. I would love to have been inStop! That! Train!” So RuPaul and the film’s producers never got in touch? “No”, she says crisply. That’s a shame. “I agree.”That comedy film seems like small potatoes when compared with the plans Alaska is hatching. After Oh, Mary! wraps, she will embark on her 50-date, 50-stateRevolution Tourthis March, taking in the length and breadth of the country from Fayetteville to Fargo. Even an A-list pop star would balk at such an ambitious schedule. “I know,” she smiles. “This is just something that my fiance and I have wanted to do for a while. There’s a lot of states that we just haven’t been to, let alone gotten to do drag in.“There are gay people everywhere, and they don’t often get to go out to a drag show,” she says, as if casting her mind back to the Catwoman-obsessed kid growing up in rural Pennsylvania. But isn’t it a logistical nightmare? Alaska throws her head back and laughs.“Well”, she says, “nobody has told me no!”Alaska is in the touring production ofOh, Mary!until 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsUS theaterDragPop and rockTheatreRuPaulBroadwayOff-BroadwayinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: LPO/Gardner review – Mark Simpson’s piano concerto leaves its audience panting | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Pianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping up
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Pianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping up
Content: Music with the volume dialled up … Tamara Stefanovich, Mark Simpson and Edward Gardner with the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Julian GuideraView image in fullscreenMusic with the volume dialled up … Tamara Stefanovich, Mark Simpson and Edward Gardner with the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Julian GuideraClassical musicReviewLPO/Gardner review – Mark Simpson’s piano concerto leaves its audience pantingRoyal festival hall, LondonPianist Tamara Stefanovich gave the world premiere of Mark Simpson’s fearless and uncompromising new concerto, with Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic mostly keeping upAlexandra CoghlanTue 27 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Restless and impassioned.” “Very fast.” “Explosive, with abandon!” Before a note of Mark Simpson’s new Piano Concerto has sounded, it’s clear from the movements that this is music with the volume dialled up: louder, faster, bigger, fiercer. And it’s no idle promise. We open in a landslide of sound and barely draw breath for half an hour. This is a concerto that leaves the audience panting – let alone the soloist.Simpson’s music is larger than life. The British composer and clarinettist (who famously won both BBC Young Musician and BBC Young Composer of the Year back in 2006, aged just 17) plays with big forces and sounds at their extremes – whether that’s a barrage of percussion or extremes of register – and is rarely far from the kinetic twitch of nervous energy.His Piano Concerto – premiered here by soloist Tamara Stefanovich with Edward Gardner and theLondon Philharmonic Orchestra– shows no fear of the genre’s historical greats. An opening volley of virtuosity from the soloist could be Rachmaninov or Tchaikovsky, but arrives thickly encrusted with orchestral weight, barely audible through the layers.View image in fullscreenSeizing the fleeting opportunities for lyricism … soloist Tamara Stefanovich.Photograph: Julian GuideraThroughout this first movement we must excavate through sound to find the piano, which finally breaks free in a quicksilver central scherzo that sees it dancing with tuned percussion, rippling briefly above the orchestra in glinting passagework. The finale introduces a new vein of introspection, but once again extremity prevails as the pianist explores the outer reaches of the keyboard, goading the orchestra on to ever more athletic feats. Stefanovich wrestled bodily with Simpson’s demands, assertive and uncompromising, seizing the fleeting opportunities for lyricism, while Gardner and his band mostly kept up.Did the Simpson take all the rehearsal time? The framing works – Dorothy Howell’s pleasant, French-accented tone-poem Lamia and Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird – should have been all drama, all colour. But there was a workaday quality to the Stravinsky, a lack of tension to the pacing, a lack of precision to the woodwind solos and brass ensembles. Everything was there – villain Kashchei’s brooding evil, delicate princesses, the dazzling, darting Firebird itself – but in grayscale, waiting for that spark that turns Kansas into fairytale Oz.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Philharmonic OrchestraEdward GardnerMark SimpsonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween | Games | The Guardian
description: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season
Content: Night moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionView image in fullscreenNight moves … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionGamesEight great new indie horror games for HalloweenWhether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching seasonKeith StuartTue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTis almost All Hallows’ Eve and naturally, the thoughts of all good video game players are turning to horror. 2026 has already been a bloody good year for the genre withResident Evil RequiemandSilent Hill: Townfallleading the rabble. But this autumn sees a festering surge of indie horror releases, featuring everything from cursed card games to Nazi-hunting penguins. Here are eight terrifying titles we think you should sample while jack-o-lanterns burn and spirits walk the moonlit streets.Allogloom (PC)View image in fullscreenShady story … Allogloom.Photograph: Galactic GhostlyMixing dark fairytales with classic point-and-click adventure gameplay, Allogloom follows a young girl who must leave her isolated village alone to hunt for her lost mother. The game’s eerie picture book aesthetic and doll-like characters have the feel of a 1970s Czech animation, making for a surreal and disquieting experience.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival (PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox)View image in fullscreenComing for more … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThis latest extension of Barker’s seminal horror novella The Hellbound Heart received mixed reviews, but then so did the Hellraiser films, and they were largely awesome. You play as Aidan, looking to rescue his girlfriend from the nightmarish realm of the Cenobites and their S&M obsessed followers. Gory, kinky and ridiculous it is quite literally a hell of a ride.Grease Trap 99 (PC)View image in fullscreenFrying to fright … Grease Trap 99.Photograph: James MuirheadYou’re working in a quiet Scottish takeaway, frying and serving fish, chips and pizza, when your boss asks you to start serving a “special” dish. But what is it, and what’s that strange gurgling noise coming from the cellar? Created by lone developer James Muirhead with dialogue in Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig), this is more of a short interactive horror movie than a game, but its glitch-ridden, low-poly visuals and dark humour keep you serving until the gruesome finale.Hunter’s Moon (PS5)View image in fullscreenDark tale … Hunter’s Moon.Photograph: Twin SwansBased on the real-life witch-hunts of the 17th century, this atmospheric immersive adventure has you playing as a young woman accused of devilry and now running for her life through woods, rivers and abandoned mines as her hunters pursue. Poetic and strangely beguiling, fans of the classic folk horror movie Witchfinder General, will feel oddly at home.The Killing Stone (PC, PS5, Xbox)View image in fullscreenFeast of occult delights … The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionFans of deck-building card battlers are spoiled for choice these days, but The Killing Stone is the perfect choice forHalloween. Set in a remote 17th-century mansion, you must play an ancient card game against the devil to win back the soul of your beloved mistress. The set-up is familiar but there are lovely occult touches, and you get to explore the gloomy house in first-person between bouts, leaning its dark lore. An engrossing fireside treat.Penguin Colony (PC)View image in fullscreenShivers … Penguin Colony.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerA Nazi base in the desolate Antarctic is beset by Lovecraftian entities, driving its inhabitants to madness. But in a neat twist, you play as a penguin observing the chaos and exploring the wilderness, discovering weird obelisks and winding labyrinths as the cosmic horrors threaten your colony.Read our review.Silver Pines (PC, PS5, Xbox, Switch 2)View image in fullscreenCurious case … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17On the trail of a missing singer, troubled private investigator Red Walker finds himself in an abandoned town, but quickly discovers he is far from alone. Influenced by Twin Peaks, Silent Hill and Alan Wake, this haunting 2D adventure is rich in atmosphere and crammed with intriguing puzzles.Read our review.Tenebris Somnia(Switch,PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox)View image in fullscreenUnrest room … Tenebris Somnia.Photograph: New Blood InteractiveWhen a young actor visits her estranged boyfriend, she discovers that his apartment has been trashed and he’s nowhere to be seen. Where is he and what are those weird symbols daubed on the wall? Heavily inspired by early 90s point-and-click adventures as well as interactive movie games such as Night Trap, Tenebris Somnia mixes beautiful pixelated visuals and FMV sequences to eerie effect.Explore more on these topicsGamesXboxPCPlayStationPlayStation 5Nintendo Switch 2HalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The view from the Mournes was CS Lewis’s idea of Narnia’: how Northern Ireland inspired a magical kingdom  | Belfast holidays | The Guardian
description: Ahead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imagination
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ahead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imagination
Content: Dunluce Castle, which some scholars believe inspired CS Lewis’s Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Photograph: Shawn Williams/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenDunluce Castle, which some scholars believe inspired CS Lewis’s Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Photograph: Shawn Williams/Getty Images/iStockphotoBelfast holidays‘The view from the Mournes was CS Lewis’s idea of Narnia’: how Northern Ireland inspired a magical kingdomAhead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imaginationGraham LittleTue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the gable walls of the tough, working-class streets of east Belfast, the mystical beasts of Narnia vie for brick space with balaclava-wearing loyalists. The murals of the city have long projected the power of paramilitaries, but in recent years they have also begun to reflect the more positive contributions made by other local people, including the authorCS Lewis.Lewis was born in Dundela in 1898 in an attractive terrace house that has sadly since been demolished to be replaced by rather unattractive flats. But elsewhere in this part of the city, the Lewis connection is being built on and celebrated.CS Lewis Squareis in the Holywood Arches neighbourhood and has a short walking trail featuring metal sculptures of Mr and Mrs Beaver, Mr Tumnus and other beloved characters from The Chronicles of Narnia. The centrepiece is a gigantic Aslan, towering over all from atop a circular mound.View image in fullscreenA CS Lewis mural in east Belfast.Photograph: Stephen Barnes NI/AlamyAbout 15 minutes’ walk away, St Mark’s church on the Holywood Road is the proud custodian of a much smaller lion that may have inspired Lewis’s creation of Aslan. His grandfather,the Rev Thomas Hamilton, ministered here, living in the rectory for 13 years, and his front door was decorated with a beautiful brass lion’s head doorknob. The original has been removed for safekeeping, but an exact replica attracts thousands of Lewis pilgrims each year.Leafy Circular Road, half a mile away, is where the Lewis family moved in 1905 to a large, redbrick house that, back then, was on the outskirts of the city. The road has since been subsumed by the growth of the town, but remains the realm of the prosperous. The house, called Little Lea, is privately owned, but can be seen from the iron gates at the end of the drive.“To a child, it seemed less like a house than a city,” Lewis wrote of the family home in his autobiography, Surprised By Joy. “I am a product of long corridors, empty sunlit rooms, upstairs indoor silences, attics explored in solitude.”View image in fullscreenThe Aslan sculpture in CS Lewis Square, east Belfast.Photograph: Radharc Images/AlamyLittle Lea appears in the opening two Narnia books, first when a boy exploring a large attic in The Magician’s Nephew finds a way into another world, and then in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe when a game of hide and seek leads a group of inquisitive children to that same magical world a generation later.Although it was close to east Belfast’s industrial heartland, it was also just a fence clamber away from the fields, hills and woodland glens that fringed the city like a vast adventure playground. As children, Lewis and his elder brother Warnie seem to have had a freedom to wander that would terrify modern parents. They would trek for hours up into the hills between Belfast and Strangford Lough, and travelling that way today still evokes a sense of romantic escapism.double quotation markIt is easy to imagine, as Lewis wrote in an essay, that a ‘giant might raise his head over the next ridge’ of the Mourne mountainsThe Belmont Road takes you up, climbing dramatically out of the city and into the expansive high ground that towers over Belfast, Bangor and Newtownards. There are many viewpoints up here. Lewis didn’t record the exact spot that inspired the following ethereal description of the views he loved, but for this writer, the crags of theWhitespots country parkon the hill above Newtownards are a pretty good bet, especially as this place also chimes loudly with his descriptions of the stone table on which Aslan was sacrificed in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.View image in fullscreenMussenden Temple on the north coast of Co Derry.Photograph: Ballygally View Images/Getty Images“Looking south with a little east in it, a different world,” he writes in Surprised By Joy. “And having seen it, blame me if you can for being a romantic. For here is the thing itself, utterly irresistible, the way to the world’s end, the land of longing, the breaking and blessing of hearts. You are looking across … the plain of Down, and seeing beyond it the Mourne Mountains.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLewis once told Warnie that the view from the Mournes above Rostrevor looking down over Carlingford Lough was his idea of Narnia. The statement is now stencilled on a bench at a viewpoint in the town’sKilbroney forest park. Sitting there, in the majesty of this area, it is easy to imagine, as Lewis later wrote in an essay, that a “giant might raise his head over the next ridge”.Rostrevor is an hour’s drive south of Belfast, and an hour’s drive in the other direction will take you to the equally spectacular north coast, where Lewis holidayed with his mother as a young child. There’s an ongoing debate among Lewis scholars and his many passionate fans about whether it wasDunluce CastleorDownhill Demesnethat inspired Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.Netflix unveils first trailer for Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s NephewRead moreThe ruins of Dunluce perch precipitously on the coast east of Portrush, while Downhill Demesne, near Castlerock, contains what remains of the old Downhill House but also the iconic Mussenden Temple, which much better fits the description of Cair Paravel looking “like a great star resting on the seashore”.Lewis was writing his autobiography at the same time he was producing the seven Chronicles of Narnia. The experiences and landscapes he was remembering for his memoir very likely bled into the creation of his magical kingdom. And so the heavenly, pastoral landscapes of Narnia on the murals of east Belfast might feel familiar even to those locals who haven’t read the books or watched the screen adaptations. The wholesome images of his imagination being sandwiched between paintings glorifying terrorism is an unusual setting for a tribute to the world’s most famous Christian apologist, but perhaps in Belfast, as in Narnia, good will win in the end.The first ofNetflix’snew The Chronicles Of Narnia adaptations,Narnia:The Magician’s Nephew, will be released in cinemas on12 February 2027and onNetflixon 2 April.
